modules.title: Work out powers

chapter.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2⁵ means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times. The small raised number (the power) counts how many 2s there are; it is not a number to multiply by.

chapter.title: Laws of exponents with one base
text: A power counts how many times the base is multiplied. Multiplying joins the factors (add the powers), dividing cancels them (subtract), and a power of a power repeats them (multiply).
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. A negative power means a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a².
math: Write 9¹⁰ × 9³ as a single power of 9, that is 9 to the power □. What number goes in the box?

chapter.title: The units digit of a large power
text: Only the units digit affects the units digit of a product, and the units digits of powers repeat in a short cycle.
Write the units digits of the first few powers until they repeat. Divide the power by the cycle length; the remainder tells the place in the cycle (remainder 0 means the last place).
math: What is the units digit of 19⁵⁸?
Units digits of the powers of 9 repeat: 9, 1, …
58 ÷ 2 leaves the place 2 in the cycle
The digit in place 2 is 1

chapter.title: Zero and negative powers
text: Each step down in the power divides by the base once: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4.
Combine the powers first (add them, keeping the signs), then a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
math: Find the value of 6⁵ × 6⁻³.
Add the powers: 5 − 3 = 2
6 to the power 2 = 36

chapter.title: Writing a repeated product in exponential form
text: A power is a short way of writing a repeated product: aⁿ means n factors of a multiplied together.
Group equal factors together, count how many there are of each, and write each count as the power of its base.
math: Write 2 × 2 × 3 in exponential form, as 2^□ × 3^□. Give the two powers as (power of 2, power of 3).
2 appears 2 times and 3 appears once: 2² × 3¹

chapter.title: Writing a number as a product of prime powers
text: Every whole number greater than 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way; powers say how many times each prime appears.
Divide by 2 as often as possible, then by 3, 5 and 7, counting the divisions: the counts are the powers.
math: Write 875 as a product of powers of primes: 875 = 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ × 5ᶜ × 7ᵈ. Give (a, b, c, d), writing 0 for a prime that does not divide 875.
Count each prime: 2⁰ × 3⁰ × 5³ × 7¹

chapter.title: The zero exponent
text: aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = aᵐ⁻ᵐ = a⁰, and a number divided by itself is 1, so a⁰ = 1 for any a ≠ 0.
Replace every zero power by 1, then work out the rest.
math: Find the value of 2⁰ + 4⁰.
So 2⁰ + 4⁰ = 2

screens.title: Count them out
text: Write the number as many times as the power says, with × between them. Then multiply two at a time.

strategies.title: Build it up one step at a time

screens.title: Multiply again and again
text: Start with the number and multiply by it again for each extra power. That is one multiplication fewer than the power.

strategies.title: Use the multiplication facts you know

screens.title: Each step is a fact
text: Every step of a power is a multiplication fact: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. If a step is slow, say that times table first.

modules.title: Expand a bracket: a(x + b)

chapter.title: The number outside multiplies everything inside
text: 3(x + 4) means three lots of (x + 4): (x + 4) + (x + 4) + (x + 4). That is three x's and three 4s.
chapter.tip: Multiply every term in the bracket, not only the first one.

chapter.title: Multiplying binomials and monomials with an area model
text: A product of two brackets is the area of a rectangle whose sides are the brackets: split each side into its terms and the rectangle splits into smaller rectangles.
Draw a grid with one bracket's terms across the top and the other's down the side. Multiply to fill each cell, then add the cells, collecting the like terms.
math: Multiply 4x by 6x²y. The area model in the picture may help.
Multiply the numbers: 4 × 6 = 24
Multiply the powers of x by adding: x × x² = x³; y stays: 24x³y

screens.title: Split the rectangle
text: Draw a rectangle a high and x + b long. Split the long side into x and b. The two parts have areas a × x and a × b; together they are the whole rectangle.
math: Expand the bracket: 7(x + 8) = 7x + □. What number goes in the box?

screens.title: Multiply along each arrow
text: Draw an arrow from the number outside the bracket to each term inside it, and multiply along each arrow.
math: Expand the bracket: 10(x + 10) = 10x + □. What number goes in the box?

screens.title: The last term is a fact
text: The number at the end is the number outside times the number inside: 3 × 4 = 12. If that fact is slow, rebuild it from one you know: 3 × 4 is 3 × 2 doubled.

modules.title: Expand (x + a)(x + b)

chapter.title: Four products
text: In (x + 2)(x + 5), each term of the first bracket multiplies each term of the second: x × x, x × 5, 2 × x and 2 × 5.
chapter.tip: The x term is the SUM of the two numbers; the last term is their PRODUCT.

chapter.title: Expanding with (a + b)², (a − b)² and (a + b)(a − b)
text: (a + b)² is the area of a square of side a + b: it splits into a square a², a square b² and two rectangles ab. So (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² because the two ab terms cancel.
Decide what a and b are (a = px, b = q). Work out a², then 2ab (with its sign), then b², and write them in order.
math: Use the identity
a² = (5x)² = 25x²
b² = 2² = 4

chapter.title: Quick calculation with identities
text: A number near a round number is easy to square with an identity: 103 = 100 + 3, so 103² = 100² + 2 × 100 × 3 + 3². Products like 103 × 97 are (100 + 3)(100 − 3) = 100² − 3².
Write the number as a ± b with a a multiple of 10. Work out a², 2ab and b² (all easy) and combine them with the right signs.
math: Use (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² to work out 13 × 7.
Write it as (10 + 3)(10 − 3)

chapter.title: Expanding (x ± a)³, (x + a)(x + b)(x + c) and (x + ay + b)²
text: (a + b)³ = (a + b)(a + b)²: multiplying out gives a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³. (x + a)(x + b)(x + c) collects the sum of the numbers, the sum of their pair products and their product. (a + b + c)² has each square and every pair product twice.
Name the parts (a, b, c), then fill the identity term by term, keeping track of signs: (x − a)³ has alternating signs.
math: Expand

screens.title: Fill the four cells
text: Draw a 2 by 2 grid. Write x and a along the top, x and b down the side. Fill each cell with the product of its row and column, then add the two cells that have an x.
math: Expand (x + 2)(x + 6) = x² + □x + 12. What number goes in the box (it may be negative)?

screens.title: Two of the four products have an x
text: Multiply the first terms, the outer terms, the inner terms and the last terms. The outer and inner products are the two x terms: add them.
math: Expand (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + □x + 6. What number goes in the box (it may be negative)?

screens.title: Keep each sign
text: When a number is negative, keep its sign in each product. The x term is the sum of the two signed products, so a negative product makes it smaller.

modules.title: Differentiate powers of x

chapter.title: The power rule
text: To differentiate k xⁿ, bring the power down as a factor and lower the power by one: the derivative is k n xⁿ⁻¹. Then put in the value of x.
chapter.tip: Lower the power first, then substitute.
math: f(x) = 2x³. What is f′(2)?
Bring the power down: 2 × 3 = 6

chapter.title: Differentiating k xⁿ times sin(ax) or cos(ax)
text: When y = u × v, a small change in x changes both factors: y′ = u′v + uv′. The derivative of sin(ax) is a cos(ax), and of cos(ax) is −a sin(ax).
Name u and v, differentiate each (remember the inner factor a), then write u′v + uv′.
math: Differentiate y = 5x^3 sin(x) with respect to x.
v = sin(x), so v′ = cos(x)
y′ = u′v + uv′ = 15x^2 sin(x) + 5x^3 cos(x)

chapter.title: Differentiating a sum and difference of several terms
text: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor stays in front: d/dx [af + bg] = af′ + bg′. A constant term has derivative 0.
Differentiate each term with d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹ (multiply by the power, then lower the power by 1), keep the signs, and drop the constant.
math: Differentiate f(x) = 2x⁴ + 4x² − 7x + 27 with respect to x.
Differentiate term by term: d/dx(2x⁴) = 8x³, d/dx(4x²) = 8x, d/dx(−7x) = −7, and a constant gives 0

chapter.title: The quotient rule
text: For y = u/v, a small change in x changes the top and the bottom; working it out gives (v u′ − u v′)/v². The minus sign makes the order matter.
Name u (top) and v (bottom), find u′ and v′, put them into (v u′ − u v′)/v², and simplify the top.
math: Differentiate y = (x − 4)/(x + 3) with respect to x, and simplify.
Quotient rule: d/dx (u/v) = (v u′ − u v′)/v²
Here the top simplifies to 7 and v² = (x + 3)²: dy/dx = 7/(x + 3)²

chapter.title: The chain rule for composite functions
text: A composite y = f(g(x)) changes with x through g: if x changes a little, g changes g′(x) times as much, and y changes f′(g) times that. So dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x).
Name the inside u = g(x). Differentiate the outside as if u were the variable, keep u inside, then multiply by du/dx.
math: Differentiate y = sin(4x² + 3) with respect to x.
Chain rule: dy/dx = (derivative of the outer function at the inner one) × (derivative of the inner function)
dy/dx = 8x cos(4x² + 3)

chapter.title: Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions, and one function with respect to another
text: If y = sin⁻¹x then x = sin y, so dx/dy = cos y = √(1 − x²) and dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²); similarly for cos⁻¹ (with a minus sign) and tan⁻¹ (1/(1 + x²)). To differentiate y with respect to u, divide dy/dx by du/dx.
Use d/dx sin⁻¹u = u′/√(1 − u²), d/dx cos⁻¹u = −u′/√(1 − u²), d/dx tan⁻¹u = u′/(1 + u²), then simplify. For 'with respect to', find both derivatives with respect to x and divide.
math: Differentiate y = 4tan⁻¹(x/8) with respect to x.
d/dx tan⁻¹u = u′/(1 + u²)
Simplify: 32/(64 + x²)

chapter.title: Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions
text: eˣ is its own derivative, and log x (the inverse of eˣ) has derivative 1/x. Any aˣ is e^(x log a), so its derivative is aˣ log a.
Use d/dx e^(ax) = a e^(ax), d/dx log x = 1/x, d/dx aˣ = aˣ log a, and the product rule for products.
math: Differentiate y = 4e^(4x) − 6 log x with respect to x (x > 0; log is the natural logarithm).
d/dx e^(ax) = a e^(ax) and d/dx log x = 1/x

strategies.title: A derivative is a rate of change

screens.title: Not the value: how fast it changes
text: f′(3) is how fast f is changing at x = 3, not the value f(3). For f(x) = x², the values at 2.9, 3 and 3.1 are 8.41, 9 and 9.61: they rise by 1.2 over 0.2, which is 6 per unit, and the rule gives 2 × 3 = 6.

screens.title: In this order
text: Multiply the coefficient by the power, then take one off the power. Only then put in the number.
math: f(x) = x². What is f′(2)?
Bring the power down: 1 × 2 = 2

screens.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2² = 2 × 2 = 4 and 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A power is not the number times the power: 2³ is not 6.

modules.title: Integrate powers of x

chapter.title: Reverse the power rule
text: Differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) gives xⁿ. So an antiderivative of k xⁿ is k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1): raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.
math: ∫ k xⁿ dx = k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) + C

chapter.title: Between two limits
text: For a definite integral, work out the antiderivative F at the upper limit and at the lower limit, then subtract: F(upper) − F(lower). The constant C cancels.
math: ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx = ?
Raise the power and divide: F(x) = 3x³ ⁄ 3

chapter.title: Recovering a quantity from its rate of change and a starting value
text: If you know how fast a quantity changes, integrating the rate gives the quantity up to a constant; one known value (where it starts) fixes the constant.
Find an antiderivative of the rate, add C, use the starting value to find C, then substitute the time (or amount) asked about.
math: A cycle moves along a straight road with velocity v(t) = 3t² − 2t + 4 m/s at time t seconds. At t = 0 it is 12 m past a milestone. Find its distance past the milestone, in metres, at t = 1.
Integrate the rate: t³ − t² + 4t + C
Use the starting value at the start: C = 12
Substitute 1: 16

chapter.title: Antiderivatives of the standard functions
text: Integration undoes differentiation, so each standard derivative read backwards is a standard integral: (sin x)′ = cos x gives ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C, (tan x)′ = sec²x gives ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C, (log|x|)′ = 1/x, and so on.

Integrate term by term (constants stay in front): ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), ∫ sin x = −cos x, ∫ cos x = sin x, ∫ sec²x = tan x, ∫ cosec²x = −cot x, ∫ sec x tan x = sec x, ∫ eˣ = eˣ, ∫ 1/x = log|x|; add one constant C.
math: Find ∫ (−5x³ + 5eˣ) dx.
Integrate term by term: ∫ x³ dx = (1/4)x^4 and ∫ eˣ dx = e^x
Multiply by the constants and add C: −(5/4)x^4 + 5e^x + C

chapter.title: Antiderivatives of f(ax + b)
text: By the chain rule, d/dx F(ax + b) = a F′(ax + b). So to integrate f(ax + b), take the usual antiderivative F at ax + b and divide by a.
Integrate as if ax + b were x, then divide by a: ∫ cos(ax + b) dx = sin(ax + b)/a + C, ∫ (ax + b)ⁿ dx = (ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹/(a(n + 1)) + C, ∫ 1/(ax + b) dx = log|ax + b|/a + C.
math: Find ∫ (5x + 5)⁴ dx.
If ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, then ∫ f(ax + b) dx = F(ax + b)/a + C, with a = 5

chapter.title: Finding a function from its derivative and one value
text: All the antiderivatives of f′ differ by a constant: their graphs are the same curve shifted up or down. One known value picks out the one curve that passes through that point.
Integrate f′ term by term, add C, substitute the given x and f(x), and solve for C.
math: f′(x) = 3x² + x + 18 and f(0) = 15. Find f(x).
Integrate: f(x) = x³ + (1/2)x² + 18x + C
Put x = 0: 0 + C = 15, so C = 15

screens.title: Undo, then check
text: Whatever antiderivative you write, differentiate it: you must get back the function you started with. x³ differentiates to 3x², so ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

screens.title: Two moves, then the limits
text: Add one to the power, then divide by that new power. Then put in the upper limit and the lower limit, and subtract.
math: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 12x dx = ?
Raise the power and divide: F(x) = 12x² ⁄ 2

screens.title: What the working needs
text: The working needs powers (2³ = 8) and fractions with the same denominator (16⁄3 − 2⁄3 = 14⁄3). If either is slow, practise it first; the integration itself is two moves.

modules.title: Integrate by substitution

chapter.title: Spot u and du
text: In ∫ 2x(x² + 1)² dx, call the inside of the bracket u = x² + 1. Its derivative, 2x, is already there: du = 2x dx. So the integral is ∫ u² du.
math: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx
∫ 2x(x² + 1)² dx = ∫ u² du = u³ ⁄ 3 + C

chapter.title: Change the limits
text: With limits, change them too: put each x limit into u = x² + 1, and integrate between those u values. You never go back to x.
chapter.tip: Using the x limits for u is the most common slip.
math: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2x(x² + 1)² dx = ?
Let u = x² + 1: x = 0 gives u = 1, x = 1 gives u = 2
2x dx = du, so the integral is ∫ u² du = u³ ⁄ 3
Between u = 1 and u = 2: 7/3

chapter.title: Integration using trigonometric identities and substitution
text: Powers and products of sines and cosines are not standard integrals, but trigonometric identities turn them into sums of single sines and cosines, which are. A substitution u = g(x) works when g′(x) is also present.
Rewrite: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2, tan²θ = sec²θ − 1, 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B). Then integrate term by term. For f′(x)/f(x) the answer is log|f(x)| + C.
math: Find ∫ 4tan²(5x) dx.
Use tan²θ = sec²θ − 1

chapter.title: Integrals of the standard forms 1/(x² − a²), 1/(a² − x²), 1/√(x² ± a²), √(x² ± a²) and (px + q)/(x² + bx + c)
text: Completing the square turns x² + bx + c into (x + h)² ± a², and each such shape has a standard antiderivative; a linear top px + q is split into a multiple of the bottom's derivative plus a constant.

Complete the square; match the form; write the standard result with u = x + h. For (px + q)/(x² + bx + c), write px + q = (p/2)(2x + b) + B: the first part gives (p/2) log|x² + bx + c|, the second a standard form.
math: Find ∫ √(x² + 36) dx.
The form is already standard, with a = 6
∫ √(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)|

chapter.title: Definite integrals of 1/(x² + a²), 1/√(a² − x²) and √(a² − x²)
text: d/dx tan⁻¹(x/a) = a/(a² + x²) and d/dx sin⁻¹(x/a) = 1/√(a² − x²), so these integrands have inverse trigonometric antiderivatives; their values at the limits are standard angles. ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx is a quarter of a circle of radius a.
∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ √(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. Evaluate at the limits in radians.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 3/2 of 4/√(9 − x²) dx. Give the exact value in terms of π.
∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a): sin⁻¹(1/2) − sin⁻¹(0) = π/6

chapter.title: Integrating by partial fractions: repeated factors and improper fractions
text: A repeated factor (x − a)² needs two partial fractions, A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²: the first integrates to a logarithm, the second to a power, −B/(x − a). An improper fraction (top degree ≥ bottom degree) is first divided to give a polynomial plus a proper fraction.
If needed, divide. Split the proper part into partial fractions, find the constants (cover-up or comparing coefficients), integrate each term, add C.
math: Find ∫ (−2x + 7)/(x − 2)² dx.
Write the integrand as A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²: −2/(x − 2) + 3/(x − 2)²

chapter.title: Integration by parts, Bernoulli's formula and ∫ eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx
text: The product rule read backwards gives ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u to be the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated (x, x², log x); repeated parts on x² gives Bernoulli's formula with alternating signs.
Pick u and dv (ILATE order: inverse trig, log, algebraic, trig, exponential for u). Find du and v, write uv − ∫ v du, and integrate the last part. For eˣ[f + f′], the answer is eˣ f + C at once.
math: Find ∫ 3x log(2x) dx (x > 0; log is the natural logarithm).
By parts with u = log(ax) and dv = xⁿ dx

chapter.title: A definite integral by substitution: ∫ c t/√(t² + d²) dt
text: When the integrand contains a function and (a multiple of) its derivative, substitute u for the function: t dt is half of d(t² + d²). The limits change with the variable.
Let u = t² + d², so t dt = du/2. Change the limits (t = 0 gives u = d², t = b gives u = b² + d²), integrate (1/2)u^(−1/2) to √u, and subtract.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 4 of 2t/√(t² + 9) dt, using the substitution u = t² + 9.
u = t² + 9, du = 2t dt; the limits become u = 9 and u = 25

chapter.title: Integrals with inverse trigonometric answers: 1/(x² + a²), 1/√(a² − x²), √(a² − x²) and forms reducible to them
text: d/dx tan⁻¹(x/a) = a/(x² + a²) and d/dx sin⁻¹(x/a) = 1/√(a² − x²), so these integrands have inverse trigonometric antiderivatives. Completing the square brings x² + bx + c to (x + h)² ± a², the same forms with u = x + h.

∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ √(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. For a linear top, split it into a multiple of the bottom's derivative (a logarithm) and a constant (a tan⁻¹).
math: Find ∫ 3/(x² + 2x + 2) dx.
Complete the square: x² + 2x + 2 = (x + 1)² + 1²
∫ dx/(u² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(u/a) + C
3tan⁻¹(x + 1) + C

chapter.title: Integrating by partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
text: A factor x² + a² that does not factorise needs a linear top: (Bx + C)/(x² + a²). Its x part integrates to a logarithm and its constant part to a tan⁻¹.

Write the integrand as A/(x − r) + (Bx + C)/(x² + a²); find A by putting x = r, then B and C by comparing the x² and constant terms. Integrate: A log|x − r| + (B/2) log(x² + a²) + (C/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C.
math: Find ∫
Write the integrand as A/x + (Bx + C)/(x² + 4): A = 2, B = 3, C = 4
A/(x − r) gives A log|x − r|; Bx/(x² + a²) gives (B/2) log(x² + a²); C/(x² + a²) gives (C/a) tan⁻¹(x/a)
2log|x| + (3/2)log(x² + 4) + 2tan⁻¹(x/2) + C

screens.title: Nothing left to divide by
text: du ⁄ dx = 2x, so a small change dx in x changes u by 2x dx. The 2x in the integral is exactly what turns dx into du: there is no extra 2 to divide by.

strategies.title: Make a little table of limits

screens.title: x row, u row
text: Write two rows, x and u. Under x put the two limits; under u put x² + c for each. Then integrate in u between the u values.
math: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2x(x² + 2) dx = ?
Let u = x² + 2: x = 0 gives u = 2, x = 1 gives u = 3
2x dx = du, so the integral is ∫ u¹ du = u² ⁄ 2
Between u = 2 and u = 3: 5/2

screens.title: The last step is arithmetic
text: The last step is powers of whole numbers, like 2³ = 8 and 5³ = 125, then a subtraction and a division. A power is repeated multiplication, not the number times the power.

modules.title: How many solutions? The discriminant

chapter.title: b² − 4ac decides
text: For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac. Positive: two different real solutions. Zero: one (repeated) solution. Negative: no real solutions.
chapter.tip: b² is never negative, even when b is.
math: How many different real solutions does x² + 2x + 5 = 0 have?
b² = 2² = 4
−16 is negative: no real solutions

chapter.title: Finding a parameter for which a quadratic has equal roots
text: ax² + bx + c = 0 has two equal real roots exactly when its discriminant b² − 4ac is 0 (then the parabola just touches the x-axis). If a coefficient contains k, setting the discriminant to 0 gives an equation for k.
Write b² − 4ac with k in it, set it equal to 0 and solve for k. Keep only the values the question allows (positive k, or k ≠ 0).
math: Find the positive value of k for which the quadratic equation 4x² − kx + 16 = 0 has two equal real roots.
Equal roots ⇔ the discriminant b² − 4ac is 0: k² − 256 = 0
Solve: k = 16

chapter.title: Values of a parameter for real or no real roots
text: ax² + bx + c = 0 has real roots when b² − 4ac ≥ 0 (two different roots when > 0, equal roots when = 0) and no real roots when b² − 4ac < 0.

text: Dividing asks how many times a number can be taken away: each take-away is one equal group.

4 groups of 6 make 24
So 24 shared into groups of 4 gives 6: 4 × 6 = 24

text: An equation is the story written in symbols: the unknown is a letter, and each action in the story becomes an operation on it, in the same order.
Name the unknown x. Follow the story: what multiplies x, what is added or taken away, and what the result equals. Check by putting a guessed number for x into both the story and the equation.
math: Anu thinks of a number x. Anu multiplies it by 8 and then adds 16. The result is 120. Which equation describes this situation?
Let x stand for the unknown number in the story
Write the story in order: 8 times x, then add 16, equals 120: 8x + 16 = 120

chapter.title: Forming and solving a linear equation from a word problem
text: Call the number you are asked for x; the story then tells you how to build the total from x, and that is the equation.
Write each quantity in terms of x, add them as the story says, set the result equal to the total, then undo: take away the constant, divide by the coefficient. Check in the story.
math: The length of a rectangle is 7 cm more than its width, and its perimeter is 78 cm. Form an equation and find the width, in cm.
Let x be the number asked for and write the equation: 2(x + x + 7) = 78, so 4x + 14 = 78
Take 14 from both sides: 4x = 64
Divide by 4: x = 16

screens.title: The method
text: Undo the operations in reverse order: first take away the number added, then divide by the number multiplying x.
math: Solve 2x + 4 = 14. What is x?
Take 4 from both sides: 10
Divide by 2: 10 ÷ 2 = 5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve 7x + 5 = 75. What is x?” A common wrong answer is 70.
5 was taken away but the 7 was not divided out: 7x = 70 means x = 70 ÷ 7.
math: Not 70, but 10

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Undo the operations in reverse order: first take away the number added, then divide by the number multiplying x.

modules.title: A direct proportion

chapter.title: A direct proportion
text: In a direct proportion, twice as many costs twice as much: the price of one stays the same.
math: 3 pencils cost ₹21. At the same price each, how much do 6 pencils cost, in rupees?
One pencil: ₹21 ÷ 3 = ₹7
6 pencils: 6 × ₹7 = ₹42
chapter.tip: The difference in pencils was added to the price; in a proportion every pencil costs the same, so the price is multiplied.

chapter.title: Are four numbers in proportion?
text: a, b, c, d are in proportion when a : b = c : d, that is, when the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: a × d = b × c.
Multiply the first and the last numbers, then the middle two. Equal products: in proportion; different: not in proportion.
math: Are 7, 11, 14 and 22 in proportion, in this order?
Product of the extremes: 7 × 22 = 154
Product of the means: 11 × 14 = 154
154 = 154: yes, they are in proportion

chapter.title: The missing term of a proportion
text: In a : b :: c : d the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: a × d = b × c.
Multiply the two known terms that pair up (extremes or means), then divide by the known term of the other pair.
math: Find the missing term: 6 : 13 :: □ : 78
Extremes × means: the known pair multiplies to 468

chapter.title: Do two quantities vary directly?
text: Two quantities vary directly when y = kx: y ÷ x is the same for every pair, so doubling x doubles y.
Work out y ÷ x for each column of the table. All equal: direct variation. Any different: not direct variation.
math: The table in the picture shows four pairs of values of two quantities x and y. Do x and y vary directly?
y ÷ x for each pair: 15/6, 18/9, 21/12, 24/15 — not all equal
No, x and y do not vary directly

screens.title: The method
text: Find the cost of one (divide), then multiply by how many you want.
math: 2 pencils cost ₹4. At the same price each, how much do 8 pencils cost, in rupees?
One pencil: ₹4 ÷ 2 = ₹2
8 pencils: 8 × ₹2 = ₹16

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “8 pencils cost ₹104. At the same price each, how much do 11 pencils cost, in rupees?” A common wrong answer is 107.
The difference in pencils was added to the price; in a proportion every pencil costs the same, so the price is multiplied.
math: Not 107, but 143

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the cost of one (divide), then multiply by how many you want.

modules.title: Factorising x² + px + q

chapter.title: Factorising x² + px + q
text: (x + m)(x + n) = x² + (m + n)x + mn: the two numbers multiply to the constant and add to the x coefficient.
math: Factorise: x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 4)(x + □). What number goes in the box (it may be negative)?
The numbers multiply to 12: 12 ÷ (−4) = −3
Check they add to the x coefficient: −4 + (−3) = −7
chapter.tip: The x coefficient was copied into the bracket; the two numbers in the brackets add up to it.

chapter.title: Factorising a difference of squares or a perfect square
text: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)² and a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)². An expression that matches one of these can be factorised at once.
Take out any common factor first. Then find a and b as the square roots of the first and last terms; for a perfect square, check that the middle term is 2ab.
math: Factorise 100x² − y² using an identity. Write it as (ax + by)(ax − by) with positive whole numbers and type (a, b).
Using the identity: (10x + y)(10x − y)

chapter.title: Factorising with the cube identities
text: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), and a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca).
Write each cube term as (something)³ to find a, b (and c), then fill the second bracket from the identity.
math: Use an identity to factorise: 8x³ + 729 = (2x + 9)(4x² − □x + 81). What number goes in the box?
Match the identity: a = 2x, b = 9
The middle term is 2 × 9 = 18

chapter.title: Factorising by a common factor or by grouping
text: Factorising undoes expanding: a common factor of every term can be taken outside a bracket, and after grouping, a common bracket can be taken out too.
Find the highest common factor of the numbers and the letters. For four terms, take a common factor out of each pair so that the same bracket appears twice, then take that bracket out.
math: Factorise 25x²y − 30xy² completely by taking out the highest common factor. Write it as g·xy(ax − by) and type (g, a, b).
The highest common factor of the two terms is 5xy

chapter.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term
text: If ax² + bx + c = (px + q)(rx + s), then b splits into two parts whose product is a × c: ps and qr.
Find two numbers that multiply to a × c and add to b. Write bx as their sum, group the four terms in pairs, take out the common factor of each pair, then the common bracket.
math: Factorise 30x² + 17x + 2 by splitting the middle term. Write it as (5x + □)(6x + □) and type the two numbers in the boxes in order, for example (3, −2).
Split the middle term into 5x and 12x (their product is a × c and their sum is 17)
Group and take out the common bracket: (5x + 2)(6x + 1)

chapter.title: Splitting the middle term of ax² + bx + c
text: If ax² + bx + c = (mx + p)(nx + q), then a × c = (mn)(pq) = (mq)(np), and b = mq + np. So bx splits into two parts whose product is ac.
Find two numbers with sum b and product a × c. Write bx as the sum of those two terms, group the four terms in pairs, take out the common factor of each pair, and then the common bracket.
math: To factorise 12x² + 17x + 6 by splitting the middle term, 17x is written as rx + sx, where r + s = 17 and rs = 12 × 6 = 72. Find r and s. Enter both, separated by a comma.
Two numbers with sum 17 and product a × c: 8 and 9

screens.title: The method
text: List pairs that multiply to the constant; choose the pair that adds to the x coefficient. Watch the signs.
math: Factorise: x² − 5x + 4 = (x − 4)(x + □). What number goes in the box (it may be negative)?
The numbers multiply to 4: 4 ÷ (−4) = −1
Check they add to the x coefficient: −4 + (−1) = −5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Factorise: x² + 4x − 45 = (x − 5)(x + □). What number goes in the box (it may be negative)?” A common wrong answer is 4.
The x coefficient was copied into the bracket; the two numbers in the brackets add up to it.
math: Not 4, but 9

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract integers. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: List pairs that multiply to the constant; choose the pair that adds to the x coefficient. Watch the signs.

modules.title: The nth term of an arithmetic progression

chapter.title: Adding the same difference
text: 9, 11, 13, … goes up by 2 each time: 2 is the common difference.
To reach term 5 from term 1 you make 4 jumps of 2, not 5.
math: An arithmetic progression starts 9, 11, 13, … What is term number 5?
From term 1 to term 5: 4 jumps
4 jumps of 2: 8
chapter.tip: The first term was multiplied; an arithmetic progression adds the same difference each time.

chapter.title: Deciding whether a list is an AP, with its first term and common difference
text: A list is an arithmetic progression when the same number is added each time: every term minus the one before it gives the same common difference d.
Work out a₂ − a₁, a₃ − a₂, a₄ − a₃, …. If they are all equal, it is an AP with first term a₁ and that difference d; if any one differs, it is not an AP.
math: The first five terms of a list are 16, 13, 10, 7, 4. Which statement is true?
Each term minus the one before: −3, −3, −3, −3
All the differences are −3, so it is an AP with a = 16 and d = −3

chapter.title: Which term, the nth term from the end, and the number of terms of an AP
text: In an AP aₙ = a + (n − 1)d: term n is n − 1 steps of size d after the first term. Read backwards from the last term l, the AP has first term l and difference −d.
Which term is V: solve a + (n − 1)d = V for n. Number of terms: solve a + (n − 1)d = l. The nth term from the end: l − (n − 1)d.
math: Which term of the AP −7, −3, 1, … is 13?

chapter.title: The sum of the first n terms of an AP
text: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: each pair of terms adds to the same total a + l, and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n(a + l).
Find the last term l = a + (n − 1)d, then Sₙ = n(a + l)/2, or in one step Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d].
math: Find the sum of the first 13 terms of the AP 52, 63, 74, ….
The 13th term is l = 52 + 12 × 11 = 184

chapter.title: The condition for three numbers to be in AP
text: Three numbers are in AP exactly when the middle one is halfway between the others: b − a = c − b, or 2b = a + c.
Write 2 × (middle expression) = (first) + (third), collect the k terms on one side and the numbers on the other, and divide.
math: For which value of k are 3k − 6, 2k + 4 and 4k + 11 (in this order) consecutive terms of an AP?
Three numbers a, b, c are in AP when b − a = c − b, that is 2b = a + c: 2(2k + 4) = (3k − 6) + (4k + 11)

chapter.title: Terms of a sequence from a general or a recursive rule
text: A general rule gives any term directly from its position n; a recursive rule gives each term from the one before, starting from a given first term. With aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d the sequence is an AP.
General rule: substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Recursive rule: start from a₁, then apply the rule to get a₂ from a₁, a₃ from a₂, and so on.
math: A sequence is given by aₙ = 3n² + 3n + 2. Write its first four terms as (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄).
Put n = 1, 2, 3, 4 into the rule: 8, 20, 38, 62

chapter.title: An AP as points on a straight line
text: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d) is a linear expression in n, so the points (n, aₙ) of an AP lie on a straight line whose slope is the common difference.
Slope m = d. Intercept c = a − d (the value 'at n = 0'). Going back: d = m and a = m + c.
math: The terms of an AP are plotted as points (n, aₙ) for n = 1, 2, 3, …, and they lie on the line y = 8x + 16. Find the first term a and the common difference d of the AP, as (a, d).
The slope is the common difference: d = 8
The first term is the value at x = 1: 8 + 16 = 24

screens.title: Adding the same difference, step by step
text: To reach term 16 from term 1 you make 15 jumps of 5, not 16.
math: An arithmetic progression starts 12, 17, 22, … What is term number 16?
From term 1 to term 16: 15 jumps
15 jumps of 5: 75

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “An arithmetic progression starts 12, 16, 20, … What is term number 18?” A common wrong answer is 216.
The first term was multiplied; an arithmetic progression adds the same difference each time.
math: Not 216, but 80

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Term n = first term + (n − 1) × d: count the jumps, not the terms.

modules.title: The distance between two points

chapter.title: The distance between two points
text: The distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose sides are the across and up distances.
math: What is the distance between (−5, −2) and (−1, 1)?
Across: from −5 to −1 is 4
Up or down: from −2 to 1 is 3
chapter.tip: The across and up distances were added; the straight distance is the hypotenuse: √(across² + up²).

chapter.title: The section formula: internal division, midpoint and points of trisection
text: The point dividing AB in the ratio m : n is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, in both coordinates: it is a weighted average of A and B, with B weighted by m and A by n.
P = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). The midpoint is m = n = 1; the points of trisection are 1 : 2 and 2 : 1.
math: A is (1, 3) and B is (10, 6). Find the point of trisection of AB nearer to A. Give it as (x, y).
Nearer to A means AP : PB = 1 : 2

chapter.title: The ratio in which a point or an axis divides a segment
text: If P divides AB in the ratio λ : 1, each coordinate of P is (λx₂ + x₁)/(λ + 1). A point on the x-axis has y = 0, which gives one equation for λ.
Write the ratio as λ : 1, put the known coordinate of P (or 0 for an axis) into the section formula, solve for λ, and write λ : 1 as a ratio of whole numbers.
math: The point P(−2, −8) lies on the segment joining A(−2, 0) and B(−2, −14). In what ratio does P divide AB? Give AP : PB in simplest form, as m:n.
Let the ratio be λ : 1 and use the x-coordinate: (λ × (−2) + (−2))/(λ + 1) = −2
λ = 4/3, so the ratio is 4:3

chapter.title: The centroid of a triangle, and a missing vertex from the centroid
text: The centroid, where the three medians meet, is the average of the three vertices: G = ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3). It lies two-thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.
To find G, add the x-coordinates and divide by 3, and the same for y. To find a missing vertex, multiply G by 3 and subtract the two known vertices.
math: Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices A(−3, 2), B(3, −6) and C(−6, −8). Give it as (x, y).
Add the coordinates: (−6, −12)
Divide by 3: G = (−2, −4)

screens.title: The method
text: Find across and up (differences of coordinates), square them, add, and take the square root.
math: What is the distance between (−6, 3) and (6, −6)?
Across: from −6 to 6 is 12
Up or down: from 3 to −6 is 9

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “What is the distance between (−6, 1) and (6, 6)?” A common wrong answer is 17.
The across and up distances were added; the straight distance is the hypotenuse: √(across² + up²).
math: Not 17, but 13

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract integers; Use integer exponent laws; Find squares and square roots. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find across and up (differences of coordinates), square them, add, and take the square root.

modules.title: The highest common factor

chapter.title: Euclid's division algorithm
text: Any number that divides both 33 and 30 also divides the remainder when 33 is divided by 30.
So the HCF does not change when the larger number is replaced by that remainder. Repeat until the remainder is 0: the last divisor is the HCF.
math: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 30 and 33?
30 = 10 × 3 + 0: the remainder is 0, so the HCF is 3
chapter.tip: The lowest common multiple was found; the HCF is the largest number that divides both.

chapter.title: The HCF by repeated division, step by step
text: Any number that divides both a and b also divides the remainder of a ÷ b. So the HCF does not change when (a, b) is replaced by (b, remainder), and the numbers shrink until the remainder is 0: the last divisor is the HCF.
Divide the larger by the smaller; then divide the divisor by the remainder; repeat until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the HCF.
math: Find the HCF of 28 and 19 by repeated division: divide 28 by 19, then divide 19 by the remainder, and keep dividing the last divisor by the last remainder until the remainder is 0. What is the remainder in the second division?
28 ÷ 19 leaves remainder 9
Repeated division of 28 and 19 takes 3 divisions

chapter.title: The steps of Euclid's division algorithm
text: If a = bq + r, every common factor of a and b is also a factor of r, so HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r). Repeating with smaller and smaller numbers must end with remainder 0; the last divisor is the HCF. (Aryabhata's 'mutual division' uses the same chain of divisions.)
Write a = b × q + r. Replace (a, b) by (b, r) and repeat. Stop when the remainder is 0: the divisor at that step is the HCF.
math: Euclid's division algorithm finds the HCF of 928 and 92: divide 928 by 92, then divide 92 by the remainder, and keep dividing the last divisor by the last remainder until a remainder is 0. How many divisions are made altogether (counting the one with remainder 0)?

chapter.title: HCF and LCM from prime factorisations
text: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic every number has exactly one prime factorisation. A common factor can only use primes both numbers have, as often as both allow; a common multiple must contain every prime of each number.
HCF: multiply the common primes, each to the LOWER of its two powers. LCM: multiply every prime that appears, each to the HIGHER power. Check: HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.
math: 20 = 2² × 5 and 225 = 3² × 5². Use these prime factorisations to find the LCM of 20 and 225.
Every prime, higher power: 2² × 3² × 5²

screens.title: Euclid's division algorithm, step by step
text: So the HCF does not change when the larger number is replaced by that remainder. Repeat until the remainder is 0: the last divisor is the HCF.
math: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 54 and 96?
12 = 2 × 6 + 0: the remainder is 0, so the HCF is 6

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 22 and 72?” A common wrong answer is 792.
The lowest common multiple was found; the HCF is the largest number that divides both.
math: Not 792, but 2

modules.title: A 2 × 2 determinant

chapter.title: A 2 × 2 determinant
text: The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc: the product down one diagonal minus the product down the other.
math: Find the determinant of the matrix [[−2, 4], [5, 1]] (first row −2, 4; second row 5, 1).
chapter.tip: The two diagonal products were added; the determinant subtracts them: ad − bc.

chapter.title: Determinants of order 3, and the determinant of a product
text: A 3 × 3 determinant is built from 2 × 2 ones: each entry of a row times its cofactor (its minor with the sign + − + …). The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants: |AB| = |A||B|.
Expand along the first row: a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁). Choose a row or column with zeros to save work.

chapter.title: An unknown vertex of a triangle of given area, by determinants
text: The area of the triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃) is ½ |det[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|. With an unknown vertex the determinant is linear in k, and the absolute value gives two equations.
Expand the determinant to get αk + β. Set αk + β = 2 × area and αk + β = −2 × area, and solve each.
math: The area of the triangle with vertices (0, 3), (1, −1) and (k, −3) is 5 square units. Using determinants, find the possible values of k (fractions are fine).
k = 4 or k = −1

chapter.title: The value that makes a 3 × 3 matrix singular, or a homogeneous system have a non-trivial solution
text: det A = 0 means the rows are dependent: the matrix has no inverse (singular), and the system AX = 0 has solutions besides X = 0. With one unknown entry the determinant is linear in it.
Expand the determinant (along the row or column of the unknown is quickest), set it equal to 0, and solve the linear equation.
math: For which value of k is the matrix [[2, −2, 3], [1, −2, 4], [−1, −2, k]] singular?
A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is 0
Expanding, the determinant is −2k + 12
−2k + 12 = 0 gives k = 6

chapter.title: The inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix
text: A · adj A = |A| I for every square matrix, so when |A| ≠ 0 the inverse is A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|. When |A| = 0 the matrix is singular and has no inverse.
Find |A|. Find all nine cofactors (minors with signs + − + / − + − / + − +), transpose to get adj A, and divide every entry by |A|. Check that A·A⁻¹ = I.
math: A = [[2, −1, −1], [0, 0, 1], [3, −2, −1]]. Find A⁻¹, written as [[a, b, c], [d, e, f], [g, h, i]] (fractions are fine as entries).
|A| = 1 (not 0, so A has an inverse)
adj A (the transpose of the cofactor matrix) = [[2, 1, −1], [3, 1, −2], [0, 1, 0]]

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply top-left by bottom-right, multiply top-right by bottom-left, and subtract the second from the first. Keep the signs.
math: Find the determinant of the matrix [[−3, 3], [1, 5]] (first row −3, 3; second row 1, 5).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the determinant of the matrix [[3, 1], [1, −2]] (first row 3, 1; second row 1, −2).” A common wrong answer is −5.
The two diagonal products were added; the determinant subtracts them: ad − bc.
math: Not −5, but −7

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract integers. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Multiply top-left by bottom-right, multiply top-right by bottom-left, and subtract the second from the first. Keep the signs.

modules.title: A limit that needs factorising

chapter.title: A limit that needs factorising
text: When substituting gives 0 ⁄ 0, the limit still exists: simplify first, then substitute.
math: Find lim (x → 6) of 2(x² − 36) ⁄ (x − 6).
chapter.tip: 0 ⁄ 0 was taken as 0; it means the expression must be simplified first (factorise and cancel).

chapter.title: Estimating a limit from a table, and one-sided limits
text: lim (x → a) f(x) is the value f(x) gets as close as we like to when x is close to a (on both sides), whatever happens at a itself. The left-hand limit uses only x < a, the right-hand limit only x > a; the limit exists when they are equal.
From a table, look at the values for x nearest to a from each side and see what they settle on. For a piecewise rule, use the piece for that side and substitute x = a in it.
math: f(x) = 3x for x < 2, and f(x) = 1 for x ≥ 2. Find the left-hand limit lim (x → 2⁻) f(x).
Left of x = 2 the rule is 3x
As x approaches 2 from that side, f(x) approaches 6

chapter.title: Limits of rational functions: (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(xᵐ − aᵐ) and factorising
text: When substitution gives 0/0, the top and the bottom share the factor x − a. Cancelling it (or using lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ for each part) leaves a function that can be evaluated at a.
Factorise and cancel x − a, then substitute x = a. For (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(xᵐ − aᵐ), divide top and bottom by x − a: the limit is naⁿ⁻¹/(maᵐ⁻¹) = (n/m)aⁿ⁻ᵐ.
math: Evaluate lim (x → 3) of (x² − 8x + 15)/(x² − 9).
Top = (x − 3)(x − 5), bottom = (x − 3)(x + 3); cancel x − 3

chapter.title: lim (t → a) of c(tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a): the limit of an average rate
text: (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) is an average rate of change of tⁿ between a and t; as t → a it approaches the instantaneous rate naⁿ⁻¹.
Use lim (t → a) (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and multiply by the constant in front.
math: Evaluate lim (t → 1) of 3(t⁴ − 1)/(t − 1).
lim (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ = 4 × 1³ = 4
Multiply by 3: 12

chapter.title: Limits from the standard limits of sin x/x, (eˣ − 1)/x and log(1 + x)/x
text: Near 0, sin θ, tan θ, e^θ − 1 and log(1 + θ) all behave like θ itself, so each of them divided by θ tends to 1; 1 − cos θ behaves like θ²/2.
Make the standard form appear: sin ax/(bx) = (sin ax/(ax)) × (a/b), so the limit is a/b. Do the same for tan, eᵃˣ − 1 and log(1 + ax). For 1 − cos ax, use 2 sin²(ax/2).
math: Evaluate lim (x → 0) of (e^(9x) − 1)/(8x).

text: A 0/0 with a square root clears when you multiply by the conjugate: (√A − q)(√A + q) = A − q². At infinity, only the highest powers matter: divide top and bottom by the highest power of x in the denominator.

Divide top and bottom by x²: every term with 1/x or 1/x² tends to 0
What is left is 2/7 = 2/7

modules.title: A conditional probability from a table

chapter.title: A conditional probability from a table
text: P(A given B) counts only the cases where B happened: B becomes the whole.
math: In a class, 2 girls and 4 boys are in the chess club; 6 girls and 2 boys are not. A girl is chosen at random. What is the probability she is in the chess club?
Girls: 2 + 6 = 8
Chess girls out of all girls: 2 ⁄ 8 = 1/4
chapter.tip: The whole class was counted; given that a girl is chosen, only the girls count.

chapter.title: Conditional probability from P(A ∩ B) and P(B)
text: Given that B happened, B becomes the whole sample space: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Conditional probabilities given B obey the usual rules, e.g. P(A′ | B) = 1 − P(A | B).
Divide P(A ∩ B) by P(B). For a joint probability, multiply: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).
math: For events A and B, P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. Find P(A | B).

chapter.title: The multiplication theorem: drawing two without replacement
text: The multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A). Without replacement the second draw depends on the first: there is one ball fewer.
Probability of the first draw times the probability of the second given the first; add the separate ways when more than one outcome counts.
math: A bag has 6 red balls and 8 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other at random, with the first put back before the second is drawn. What is the probability that both are red?
First draw: 6/14
Second draw, given the first: 6/14

screens.title: The method
text: Find the group you are told about (the girls), then the fraction of that group with the property (in the chess club).
math: In a class, 3 girls and 2 boys are in the chess club; 3 girls and 5 boys are not. A girl is chosen at random. What is the probability she is in the chess club?
Girls: 3 + 3 = 6
Chess girls out of all girls: 3 ⁄ 6 = 1/2

text: A question: “In a class, 3 girls and 2 boys are in the chess club; 3 girls and 2 boys are not. A girl is chosen at random. What is the probability she is in the chess club?” A common wrong answer is 3/10.
The whole class was counted; given that a girl is chosen, only the girls count.
math: Not 3/10, but 1/2

chapter.title: Adding two-digit numbers with regrouping
text: Ten ones make one ten. When the ones add up to 10 or more, swap ten of them for a ten.
math: 10 ones = 1 ten and 0 ones: carry the ten

modules.title: Simplifying a square root

chapter.title: Simplifying a square root
text: √(a × b) = √a × √b, so a perfect-square factor can come out of the root as its square root.
math: Write √24 in its simplest form.
24 = 4 × 6, and 4 is a perfect square
chapter.tip: 4 came out of the root as 4; a square comes out as its square root (√4 = 2).

chapter.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing surds
text: Surds behave like letters: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2 (like surds), but √2 + √3 cannot be combined. For multiplying and dividing, √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).
To add or subtract, first simplify each surd (take out square factors) and then combine like surds. To multiply or divide, combine under one root and simplify.
math: Simplify √72 + √50. Which is right?
Simplify each surd in √72 + √50 and combine the like surds

chapter.title: Recognising surds and comparing their sizes
text: A surd is a root of a rational number that is itself irrational, like √2 or √12. √9 = 3 and ∛8 = 2 are not surds. To compare p√m with q√n, compare their squares p²m and q²n.
For 'is it a surd?', check whether the number under the root is a perfect square (or cube). For 'which is greater?', put the outside number inside: 3√2 = √18 and 2√5 = √20, so 2√5 is greater.
math: Which is greater?
Square both: (p√m)² = p² × m; the bigger square belongs to the bigger surd

chapter.title: Rationalising the denominator
text: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number does not change its value. Choosing √b (or the conjugate √b ∓ c) makes the bottom a whole number, because √b × √b = b and (√b + c)(√b − c) = b − c².
For a/√b, multiply by √b/√b. For a/(√b ± c), multiply by (√b ∓ c)/(√b ∓ c). Then simplify, cancelling any common factor.
math: Rationalise the denominator of 6/√3 and simplify. Which is right?
Multiply top and bottom of 6/√3 by the root in the bottom

chapter.title: Fractional exponents and radicals
text: a^(p/q) is the q-th root of a, raised to the power p: (ᵠ√a)ᵖ = ᵠ√(aᵖ). A negative power gives the reciprocal.
Take the root first (the denominator), then the power (the numerator); for a negative power, take the reciprocal at the end.
math: Find the value of 32^(3/5).
The 5th root of 32 is 2

screens.title: The method
text: Find the largest perfect square that divides the number, write the number as square × rest, and take the square root of the square outside.
math: Write √96 in its simplest form.
96 = 16 × 6, and 16 is a perfect square

screens.title: Pair the prime factors
text: Write the number as a product of primes, e.g. 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
Each pair of equal primes comes out as one prime: (2)(3)√2 = 6√2.
math: Write √164 in its simplest form.
164 = 4 × 41, and 4 is a perfect square

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write √99 in its simplest form.” A common wrong answer is 9√11.
9 came out of the root as 9; a square comes out as its square root (√9 = 3).
math: Not 9√11, but 3√11

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Find factors and multiples. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the largest perfect square that divides the number, write the number as square × rest, and take the square root of the square outside.

modules.title: Solving a linear inequality

chapter.title: Solving a linear inequality
text: An inequality stays true when you add, subtract, or multiply and divide by a POSITIVE number; dividing by a negative number flips the order, so the sign reverses.
math: Solve 2x − 1 < 7. Write the answer as an inequality for x (e.g. x > 2).
Add 1 to both sides: the right side becomes 8
Divide both sides by 2: x < 4
chapter.tip: 1 was moved to the other side without changing its sign.

chapter.title: Solving an inequation over whole numbers, natural numbers or integers
text: An inequation has many solutions. When x must be a whole number, natural number or integer, the solution set is the list of those numbers on the right side of the boundary.

Solve it like an equation to find the boundary (reverse the sign if you divide by a negative number). Then list the allowed numbers on the correct side; include the boundary only for ≤ or ≥. Show them as dots on a number line.
math: x is a whole number. Solve 4x − 3 ≤ 10 and list every x in the solution set, separated by commas.
Undo the + or − and divide by 4: the boundary is 13/4
The whole numbers that fit: 0, 1, 2, 3

chapter.title: Solving a system of two linear inequalities
text: A system of inequalities in one variable asks for the numbers that satisfy every inequality at the same time: the overlap (intersection) of their solution sets.
Solve each inequality on its own (reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number). Draw both on one number line and take the part covered by both; use [ ] for ≤ or ≥ and ( ) for < or >.
math: Solve the system of inequalities 2x ≥ 8 and −x ≥ −11, for real x. Write the solution set in interval notation.
Inequality 1 gives x ≥ 4
Inequality 2 gives x ≤ 11
Both must hold: [4, 11]

chapter.title: Modelling a word problem with a linear inequality
text: Words like 'at least', 'at most', 'no more than' and 'between' describe inequalities. Turning them into symbols and solving gives the whole range of answers that work.

Name the unknown, write the condition with ≥, ≤, < or >, solve it like an equation (reversing the sign if you divide by a negative), then check that the answer makes sense in the story (marks up to 100, numbers of people not negative).
math: Imran scored 82 and 53 marks (out of 100) in the first two tests. To get a grade, the average of three tests must be at least 50. Let x be the marks in the third test. Write the possible values of x as an inequality (remember x cannot be more than 100).
Write the condition as an inequality: (82 + 53 + x)/3 ≥ 50
Solve it: 15 <= x <= 100

chapter.title: Neighbourhoods of a point in interval notation
text: |x − a| is the distance from x to a on the number line. The δ-neighbourhood of a is every x less than δ away from a: the open interval (a − δ, a + δ).
Mark a on the number line and go δ to the left and δ to the right. Less than δ: the open interval between; at most δ: include the ends; more than δ: the two outside pieces.
math: Write the set {x ∈ ℝ : |x + 8| ≤ 2} in interval notation.
The points at distance 2 from −8 are −10 and −6
So the set is [−10, −6]

screens.title: The method
text: Get the x term alone as for an equation. When you divide by the coefficient, reverse the sign if it is negative. Check with one number from your answer.
math: Solve −3x + 9 < −12. Write the answer as an inequality for x (e.g. x > 2).
Take 9 from both sides: the right side becomes −21
Divide both sides by −3 and reverse the sign, because dividing by a negative number reverses an inequality: x > 7

strategies.title: Test numbers on a number line

screens.title: Test numbers on a number line
text: Find the boundary by solving the equation ax + b = c.
Try one number on each side in the original inequality: the side where it is true is the answer.
math: Solve −6x + 14 < −16. Write the answer as an inequality for x (e.g. x > 2).
Take 14 from both sides: the right side becomes −30
Divide both sides by −6 and reverse the sign, because dividing by a negative number reverses an inequality: x > 5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve 5x − 6 < 14. Write the answer as an inequality for x (e.g. x > 2).” A common wrong answer is x ≤ 4.
The boundary value was included; with < it is not part of the answer.
math: Not x ≤ 4, but x < 4

text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve linear equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

modules.title: Solving a linear equation with negative numbers

chapter.title: Solving a linear equation with negative numbers
text: An equation is a balance: doing the same to both sides keeps it true. With negative numbers, the inverse of adding −5 is subtracting −5, which is adding 5.
math: Solve 5x − 5 = 40.
Add 5 to both sides (this undoes the −5): 40 + 5 = 45
Divide both sides by 5: 45 ÷ 5 = 9
chapter.tip: −5 was moved to the other side without changing its sign: subtracting −5 from 40 gives 45.

chapter.title: Word problems that lead to a linear equation
text: A word problem becomes an equation when the unknown gets a letter and each sentence is written in symbols. Solving the equation and checking the answer in the story finishes the problem.

Let x be what is asked. Write the other quantities with x (mother's age kx, next multiple x + k, length x + k). Write the fact the story gives as an equation, solve it, and check in the words of the story.
math: The sum of three consecutive multiples of 7 is 147. What is the smallest of them?
Let x be the unknown; the story gives x + (x + 7) + (x + 14) = 147
Solve the equation: x = 42 (the smallest multiple)

chapter.title: An equation with fractions of x
text: Multiplying every term on both sides by the same number keeps an equation true; choosing the least common multiple of the denominators clears all the fractions.
Find the LCM of the denominators, multiply every term by it, collect the x terms, then divide.
math: Solve x/4 + x/5 = 54. What is x?
Multiply every term by 20: the right side becomes 1080
The left side becomes 5x + 4x = 9x

chapter.title: An equation with x on both sides
text: An equation stays balanced when the same thing is added to or taken from both sides, including a number of x's.
Take the smaller x term from both sides so x is on one side only, move the numbers to the other side, then divide by the coefficient of x. Check by substituting.
math: Solve 9x + 15 = −x − 15.
Take −x from both sides: 10x on the left
Take 15 from both sides: −15 − 15 = −30 on the right

screens.title: The method
text: Undo the constant term (subtract it from both sides, with its sign), then divide both sides by the coefficient (watch the sign rules). Check by substituting.
math: Solve −6x + 3 = 51.
Subtract 3 from both sides: 51 − 3 = 48
Divide both sides by −6: 48 ÷ −6 = −8

strategies.title: Check signs on a number line

screens.title: Check signs on a number line
text: Before moving a term, say what it does: “+ (−7)” moves 7 to the left.
Undoing it moves 7 to the right: add 7 to both sides.
math: Solve −4x − 10 = 22.
Add 10 to both sides (this undoes the −10): 22 + 10 = 32
Divide both sides by −4: 32 ÷ −4 = −8

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve −2x + 8 = −2.” A common wrong answer is −3.
8 was moved to the other side without changing its sign: subtracting 8 from −2 gives −10.
math: Not −3, but 5

chapter.title: What comes next in a repeating pattern
text: A repeating pattern has one part that comes again and again, always in the same order.
math: The number cards in the picture make a pattern that repeats: 6, 1, 6, 1, 6, ?. Which number comes next?

The part that repeats is ▲ ▲ ●.

chapter.title: Weaving patterns: over and under as an ordered sequence
text: A weaving pattern is an ordered sequence that repeats: over 2, under 1 is the repeating part 'over, over, under'.

chapter.title: The date of the first, second … Monday on a calendar
text: On a calendar each column is one day of the week, and going down one row moves on 7 days.
math: Look at the calendar for May 2026. What is the date of the second Sunday?
The first Sunday is on date 3.
Each week down the column adds 7: 3 + 7 × 1 = 10.
chapter.tip: The empty box in the first row was counted as a Sunday. Start from the first box in the Sun column that has a date.

chapter.title: How many Mondays (or other days) are in a month
text: Each column of a calendar holds one day of the week; a month of 29 to 31 days has some days 5 times.
Find the column for the day and count the boxes in it that have a date. Skip empty boxes.
math: Look at the calendar for July 2026. How many Wednesdays are there in this month?
The first one is on the 1.
Going down the column there are 5 dates.

chapter.title: Days from one date to another in the same month
text: The number of days from one date to a later one is how many steps you take, one day at a time, from the first date to the second.
Put your finger on today. Count 1 for tomorrow, 2 for the next day … and stop on the day itself. Or take the smaller date from the bigger one.
math: Today is 9 May 2027. Grandma's visit is on 17 May. How many days from today until Grandma's visit? Use the calendar.

chapter.title: Days from a date in one month to a date in the next
text: Months have different numbers of days: April, June, September and November have 30, February has 28 (29 in a leap year), the rest have 31.
Count the days left in this month (its last date minus today), then add the date in the next month.
math: Today is 25 May. Vijay's birthday is on 3 June. How many days from today until the birthday?
From the 25 to the end of the month (31) is 6 days.
Then 3 more days into the next month: 6 + 3 = 9.

chapter.title: The days of the week and the months in order
text: The days of the week always come in the same order, Sunday to Saturday, and then start again; the months go January to December and then start again.
Say the names in order from the one given, one name for each step: forwards for 'after', backwards for 'before'.
math: Which day comes just before Monday?
Say them in order: the answer is Sunday.

chapter.title: Months and seasons
text: A season is a group of months with similar weather. The India Meteorological Department uses four: winter, summer, the monsoon and post-monsoon.
Find the month (count on from the month given if you need to), then find the row of the table that lists it.
math: The table shows the four seasons used by the India Meteorological Department, in order through the year. Which season comes just after Post-monsoon?
The month (or season) to look for is Post-monsoon.
The table says: Winter.

chapter.title: Days in months and years, weeks and days, years and months
text: A week has 7 days and a year 12 months. April, June, September and November have 30 days; February has 28, or 29 in a leap year (a year that divides by 4, like 2028); the rest have 31. A year has 365 days, a leap year 366.
Use the facts: add the days of each month, multiply weeks by 7 and years by 12, then add the extra days or months.
math: How many days are there in February 2032?
That is 29.

chapter.title: Writing and reading dates as DD/MM/YYYY
text: DD/MM/YYYY writes the day in two digits, then the month as a number in two digits (January = 01, December = 12), then the year in four digits.
Write the day (put a 0 in front of 1 to 9), a slash, the month's number, a slash, and the year. To read, take the first part as the day and the middle part as the month.
math: Which shows 19 December 2025 written as DD/MM/YYYY?

chapter.title: Finding a person's age from the date of birth
text: Age in completed years is the number of birthdays that have passed.
Subtract the birth year from this year. If this year's birthday has not come yet, take away 1.
math: Karthik was born on 15/12/2019. How old is Karthik on 10/05/2026, in completed years?
The birthday this year: not yet. Age: 6.

chapter.title: The day of the week for a date
text: On a calendar every date sits under the name of its day of the week.
Find the date in the calendar, then move straight up its column to read the day at the top.
math: Look at the calendar for August 2027. On which day of the week is 6 August?
6 is in the Friday column.

screens.title: The method
text: Find the column for the day. Go down it from the first date in that column, counting first, second, third … The date in the box is the answer.
math: Look at the calendar for December 2026. What is the date of the fifth Wednesday?
The first Wednesday is on date 2.
Each week down the column adds 7: 2 + 7 × 4 = 30.

screens.title: Add 7 for each week
text: Find the date of the first one.
Add 7 for each week after it: the third one is the first one + 7 + 7.
math: Look at the calendar for March 2026. What is the date of the second Tuesday?
The first Tuesday is on date 3.
Each week down the column adds 7: 3 + 7 × 1 = 10.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Look at the calendar for March 2026. What is the date of the third Tuesday?” A common wrong answer is 24.
The Tuesdays were counted one too many. Say first, second, third … as you go down the column.
math: Not 24, but 17

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Combine quantities within 20. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the column for the day. Go down it from the first date in that column, counting first, second, third … The date in the box is the answer.

math: Each parcel was put on a balance with cubes on the other side. The picture shows how many cubes balanced each one. Parcel 4 is the smallest. Which parcel is the lightest? Write its number.

modules.title: Measuring a length with paper clips or matchsticks

chapter.title: Measuring a length with paper clips or matchsticks
text: A length is how many equal units fit along it, end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps.
math: A straw is laid along a line of erasers. It starts at the dot at 5 and ends at the dot at 8. Each jump in the picture is one eraser. How long is the straw, in erasers?
From 5 to 8 there are 3 jumps, so 3 units.
chapter.tip: The number at the end was read, but the straw does not start at 0. Count the erasers it covers.

chapter.title: Which container holds the most cups
text: How much a container holds is how many cups of water fill it. Height alone does not tell: width matters too.
Look at how many cups each one took. The most cups means it holds the most.
math: Each pot was filled using a small cup. The table in the picture shows how many cups each one holds. Pot 1 is the tallest. Which pot holds the most? Write its number.
Number 3 took the number of cups asked for.

chapter.title: Comparing lengths measured in hand spans, clips or sticks
text: With the same unit, the bigger count is the longer thing. When one length is measured with two units, the longer unit fits fewer times.
Same unit: compare the counts. Two units on one length: the unit with the smaller count is the longer one.
math: Ravi measures with hand spans. The mat is 3 spans long and the rope is 10 spans long, as in the picture. Which is longer?
Compare 3 and 10: the rope.

screens.title: The method
text: Count the units (the jumps) from one end to the other. If it does not start at 0, count jumps, or take the start number from the end number.
math: A pencil is laid along a line of paper clips. It starts at the dot at 5 and ends at the dot at 8. Each jump in the picture is one paper clip. How long is the pencil, in paper clips?
From 5 to 8 there are 3 jumps, so 3 units.

screens.title: Hand spans
text: Put your hand flat at one end, then move it so your thumb starts where your little finger ended.
Count each hand you put down: that is the length in spans.
math: A ribbon is laid along a line of matchsticks. It starts at the dot at 4 and ends at the dot at 10. Each jump in the picture is one matchstick. How long is the ribbon, in matchsticks?
From 4 to 10 there are 6 jumps, so 6 units.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A ribbon is laid along a line of matchsticks. It starts at the dot at 5 and ends at the dot at 8. Each jump in the picture is one matchstick. How long is the ribbon, in matchsticks?” A common wrong answer is 8.
The number at the end was read, but the ribbon does not start at 0. Count the matchsticks it covers.
math: Not 8, but 3

chapter.title: How many more to make 10 (or another number up to 20)

modules.title: Which number is more (or less)

chapter.title: Which number is more (or less)
text: A number is more when it comes later when we count; on a number line it is further to the right.
math: Which number is more: 7 or 8?
On the number line, 8 is the one asked for.
chapter.tip: The smaller number was chosen. On the number line, the number further right is more.

chapter.title: The number just before, just after or between
text: Counting goes up by 1 each time: the number after is 1 more, the number before is 1 less.
Say the numbers in order up to the number. The one you said just before it comes before; the next one you say comes after. After 9 ones comes the next ten (39, 40).
math: Which number comes between 56 and 58?
Count: the answer is 57.

chapter.title: Putting numbers up to 99 in order
text: Numbers further along the number line are bigger. For two-digit numbers, the tens tell you most.
Look at the tens digits first and order by them. If two numbers have the same tens, order those two by their ones.
math: Put these numbers in order from the smallest to the biggest: 10, 33, 28. Write them with commas.
In order: 10, 28, 33.

chapter.title: Which group has more or fewer, or are they the same
text: To compare two groups without counting, match them one to one: the group with some left over has more; if none are left over they are the same.
Pair one thing from the first group with one from the second, again and again. Look at what is left.
math: Compare the numbers 1 and 3. Which sentence is true?
Match them one to one: 1 is less than 3.

chapter.title: Which of two things is bigger or smaller
text: Big and small compare how much room things take: an elephant is bigger than a cat, an ant is smaller than a lemon.
Picture the two things side by side. The one that takes up more room is bigger; the other is smaller.
math: Think of a football and a button. Which is bigger?
a football is the one asked for.

chapter.title: Ordering numbers from 9 up to crores, ascending or descending
text: A number with more digits is greater. When two numbers have the same number of digits, the first place from the left where their digits differ decides.
Count the digits of each number. For numbers with the same count, compare the highest place, then the next, until a digit differs. Then write them in the order asked.
math: Put these numbers in descending order (from the greatest to the smallest): 89, 194, 160, 188. Write them in that order, with commas between them.
Compare the numbers: first count the digits, then compare place by place from the left.

chapter.title: Comparing two numbers with <, > or =
text: < means 'is less than' and > means 'is greater than'; the open side faces the greater number. = means the two are the same.
Count the digits; more digits is greater. With the same number of digits, compare from the left until the digits differ.
math: Which sign goes in the box: 1 ☐ 5? Choose <, > or =.

chapter.title: The greatest or smallest number made from given digits
text: The left-most place is worth the most, so the biggest digit there gives the greatest number; for the smallest number the smallest digit goes there, but never 0.
Greatest: write the digits from the biggest to the smallest. Smallest: from the smallest to the biggest, and if the first is 0, swap it with the next digit.
math: Use each of the digits 1, 2, 7, 3, 4 exactly once to make the smallest 5-digit number. Write it without commas.
Arrange the digits: 12347.

screens.title: The method
text: For two-digit numbers, compare the tens first. Only if the tens are the same, compare the ones.
math: Which number is more: 82 or 48?
Compare the tens: 8 tens and 4 tens. So the answer is 82.

screens.title: Build both with blocks
text: Build each number with tens and ones.
The one with more tens is more, whatever the ones.
math: Which number is more: 43 or 61?
Compare the tens: 4 tens and 6 tens. So the answer is 61.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Which number is more: 82 or 75?” A common wrong answer is 75.
The ones digits were compared first. Compare the tens first: the number with more tens is more.
math: Not 75, but 82

chapter.title: Tens and ones: what number do the blocks show
text: Ten ones make one ten. A two-digit number tells how many tens and how many ones: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones.
math: What number do the blocks in the picture show?

3 ones.

chapter.title: The value of a digit in a two-digit number
text: Where a digit stands tells what it is worth: in 47 the 4 is in the tens place, so it means 4 tens, which is 40.
Find the digit. If it is the first of two digits, it counts tens: its value is that digit times 10.
math: In 56, what is the value of the digit 6?
In 56, the last digit is in the ones place.
So the answer is 6.

chapter.title: The greatest and smallest two-digit number from digit cards
text: In a two-digit number the tens digit matters most: 71 is more than 17 because 7 tens is more than 1 ten.
For the greatest, put the biggest digit in the tens place and the next biggest in the ones. For the smallest, put the smallest digit that is not 0 in the tens place.

Tens place: 3.
Ones place: 7.

chapter.title: Writing a number name as a number
text: A number name tells the tens and the ones: sixty-three is 6 tens and 3 ones, written 63. The '-ty' words are tens; the '-teen' words are 1 ten and some ones.

math: Write "ninety" as a number.
9 tens
and 0 ones.

chapter.title: Counting a collection by making groups of ten
text: Counting a big collection is easier in groups of ten: 4 groups of ten and 7 more is 47.

chapter.title: The number name of a two-digit number
text: A two-digit number's name says the tens first (twenty, thirty …) and then the ones; 11 to 19 have their own names (eleven to nineteen).
Name the tens digit as a tens word, add a hyphen and the ones word: 47 is forty-seven. For 11 to 19 use the teen word.
math: Which is the number name of 20?
The tens digit is 2.
20 is written twenty.

screens.title: The method
text: Count the tens in tens (10, 20, 30 …), then count on the ones. If there are 10 or more loose ones, make another ten first.

3 tens are 30.
5 ones.
30 and 5 make 35.

chapter.title: Taking away within 20

chapter.title: How many more: comparing two groups in a picture

chapter.title: How many are left: subtraction story problems
text: When some are taken away from a group, what is left is found by subtracting the part taken away from the whole.

chapter.title: Choosing the subtraction sentence for a take-away story
