modules.title: Sorting a list by comparing neighbours (passes of swaps)

chapter.title: Sorting a list by comparing neighbours (passes of swaps)
text: One pass of comparing neighbours carries the biggest number to the end of the list; each further pass puts the next biggest in its place.
math: A list is sorted by this rule. Compare the 1st and 2nd numbers and swap them if the first is bigger; then compare the 2nd and 3rd, and so on to the end of the list. That is one pass. Start with 54, 99, 95, 83. Write the list after one pass, with commas between the numbers.
chapter.tip: The whole list was sorted. The question asks what the list looks like after only one pass.

chapter.title: Tracing a step-by-step algorithm with a loop
text: An algorithm is a list of exact steps. Tracing it means doing every step in order and writing down each value as it changes, checking the stopping rule each time.
Make a table with columns K and S. Do Step 2 and Step 3, write the new values, then test Step 4 before going round again.
math: Follow the steps in the table exactly. What is the value of S when you stop?
K is now 24, which is more than 21, so stop: S = 81

chapter.title: Where the repeated-subtraction game ends
text: Subtracting the smaller number does not change which numbers divide both cards, so the game ends at the largest number that divides both starting numbers: their HCF.
Write the pair after each move in a table. Keep replacing the larger number by the difference until the two numbers are equal.
math: Two cards show 52 and 11. In each move, the larger number is replaced by (larger − smaller). The game stops when both cards show the same number. What number is on the cards at the end?
52 − 11 = 41: the cards now show 41 and 11
41 − 11 = 30: the cards now show 30 and 11
30 − 11 = 19: the cards now show 19 and 11
19 − 11 = 8: the cards now show 8 and 11
11 − 8 = 3: the cards now show 3 and 8
8 − 3 = 5: the cards now show 5 and 3
5 − 3 = 2: the cards now show 2 and 3
3 − 2 = 1: the cards now show 1 and 2
2 − 1 = 1: the cards now show 1 and 1

chapter.title: Tracing a flowchart with decision boxes
text: A flowchart shows an algorithm as boxes joined by arrows: an oval to start and stop, a parallelogram for input and output, a rectangle for a step, and a diamond for a question with a Yes and a No arrow.
Start at the oval and follow the arrows. At each diamond, answer the question for your number and take that arrow. Keep a note of each value as it changes.
math: The table in the picture describes a flowchart box by box (ovals start and stop, parallelograms are input or output, rectangles are steps, diamonds are decisions). Trace it with the input 102. What number is output?

screens.title: The method
text: Point to the 1st and 2nd numbers; swap them if they are in the wrong order. Move one place right and repeat until the end. Write the new list after each pass.
math: A list is sorted by this rule. Compare the 1st and 2nd numbers and swap them if the first is bigger; then compare the 2nd and 3rd, and so on to the end of the list. That is one pass. Start with 63, 76, 14, 50. Write the list after one pass, with commas between the numbers.

screens.title: The bubble rises
text: Watch the biggest number: once it is reached, it is swapped again and again and moves to the end like a bubble rising.
So after one pass the last number is always the biggest.
math: A list is sorted by this rule. Compare the 1st and 2nd numbers and swap them if the first is bigger; then compare the 2nd and 3rd, and so on to the end of the list. That is one pass. Start with 51, 67, 39, 69. Write the list after one pass, with commas between the numbers.

That is one pass. Start with 42, 28, 84, 55, 40. Write the list after one pass, with commas between the numbers.” A common wrong answer is 28, 40, 42, 55, 84.

modules.title: Patterns on a calendar: moving down, up and along the diagonals

chapter.title: Patterns on a calendar: moving down, up and along the diagonals
text: A calendar has a pattern: going down one row adds 7, going right adds 1, so a step down-right adds 8 and a step down-left adds 6.
math: On the calendar for July 2026, start at 15. Move straight up one row, once. Which date do you reach?
One move changes the date by −7.
15 + 1 moves: 8.
chapter.tip: The move went the wrong way. Up means earlier dates.

chapter.title: What comes next when skip counting
text: In a skip-counting pattern the jump between neighbouring numbers is always the same.
Find the jump from one number to the next. Make that same jump from the last number.
math: What number comes next? 68, 71, 74, 77, ?
From 68 to 71 is a jump of 3.
Make the same jump from 77: the next number is 80.

chapter.title: The missing number in a counting pattern
text: The numbers before and after the gap follow the same rule, so the gap is one jump from the number before it.
Find the jump between two numbers next to each other. Make that jump from the number just before the gap; check it lands one jump before the number after.
math: Which number is missing? 5, ?, 15, 20, 25
Each jump is 5 (going up).
One jump from 5 gives 10.

chapter.title: Casting out nines: the nines check number
text: Adding the digits of a number again and again (with 9 counting as 0) leaves its remainder when divided by 9. A correct sum or product has the check number you get by adding or multiplying the check numbers.
Find each number's check number. Add (or multiply) them and cast out nines again. Then find the check number of the answer: if they differ, the answer is wrong.
math: What is the nines check number of 5793?
The digits of 5793 add up to 24.
Casting out nines leaves 6.

chapter.title: Pascal's triangle: building rows, row sums and diagonals
text: Pascal's triangle starts with 1; each row starts and ends with 1 and each other number is the sum of the two above it. Its rows add up to 1, 2, 4, 8, … and its diagonals are 1s, the counting numbers, the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10 …
To build a new row, write 1, then add each pair of neighbours in the row above, then write 1. Use the patterns to check.
math: The table shows the first rows of Pascal's triangle: each row starts and ends with 1, and every other number is the sum of the two numbers just above it. Two rows below the last row shown, what is the 2nd number from the left?

screens.title: The method
text: Work out how much one move adds or takes away, then add it once for each move.
math: On the calendar for April 2026, start at 17. Move straight down one row, once. Which date do you reach?
One move changes the date by 7.

screens.title: Look at a 2 by 2 square
text: Take any four dates in a square, like 5, 6, 12, 13.
Down adds 7 (5 to 12), right adds 1 (5 to 6), down-right adds 8 (5 to 13), down-left adds 6 (6 to 12).
math: On the calendar for October 2027, start at 10. Move straight down one row, 3 times. Which date do you reach?
One move changes the date by 7.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “On the calendar for July 2027, start at 5. Move one row down and one column to the right, once. Which date do you reach?” A common wrong answer is 16.
Each row was taken to add 10, as on a hundred chart. A calendar row has 7 days, so one row down adds 7.
math: Not 16, but 13

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Combine quantities within 20. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Work out how much one move adds or takes away, then add it once for each move.

chapter.title: Letters made of straight or curved lines

modules.title: The shortest path along a grid

chapter.title: The shortest path along a grid
text: On a grid you can only move across or up and down, so the shortest way is the number of moves across plus the number of moves up or down.
math: On the grid, S is the start and E is the end. You may move only along the grid lines: left, right, up or down. How many squares long is the shortest way from S to E?
Across: 2 squares.
Up or down: 1 square.
2 + 1 = 3 squares.
chapter.tip: The path cut across a square diagonally. Moves must follow the grid lines.

chapter.title: Where you end after moves on a grid
text: A point on the grid is named by how far across it is and how far up it is. Moving right or up adds; moving left or down takes away.
Change the across number for the left or right move, then change the up number for the up or down move.
math: Anu starts at the point A, which is at (3, 1) on the grid. She moves 1 square to the left, then 2 squares up. Where does she end? Write it as (across, up), for example (2, 3).
Across: 3 − 1 = 2.

chapter.title: The four directions: North, South, East and West
text: The four main directions are North, East, South and West. Facing North, East is on your right, West on your left and South behind you. On maps North is at the top.
Picture yourself facing the direction given. A quarter turn right goes North → East → South → West; a quarter turn left goes the other way; a half turn faces the opposite way.
math: Divya stands facing South. Which direction is behind Divya?
The answer is North.

chapter.title: Distances on a map: using a scale and choosing the shortest route
text: A map scale tells how much real distance one unit on the map stands for. A route's length is the sum of its parts; the shortest route is the one with the smallest total.
Count the squares along the path and multiply by the scale. For routes, add the roads along each one, then compare the totals.
math: On the map, each side of a square stands for 5 km. Ravi starts at S, walks 3 squares East and then 3 squares North to E. How far does Ravi walk, in kilometres?
3 + 3 = 6 squares.

chapter.title: Seats in rows and columns
text: A seat in a hall is found by two numbers: the row (counted from the front) and the seat in that row (counted from the left).
Find the row first, counting from row 1 at the front; then go along the row from the left to the seat. Write (row, seat).
math: The table is the seating plan of a classroom: row 1 is at the front and seat 1 is on the left. In which row and seat does Lakshmi sit? Answer as (row, seat).
Row 1.
Seat 5.

screens.title: The method
text: Count how many squares across S is from E, then how many up or down. Add the two numbers.
math: On the grid, S is the start and E is the end. You may move only along the grid lines: left, right, up or down. How many squares long is the shortest way from S to E?
Across: 4 squares.
Up or down: 1 square.
4 + 1 = 5 squares.

screens.title: Walk it with a finger
text: Put your finger on S. Move across one square at a time until you are in E's column, counting each move.
Then move up or down to E, still counting. The last number is the length of the path.
math: On the grid, S is the start and E is the end. You may move only along the grid lines: left, right, up or down. How many squares long is the shortest way from S to E?
Across: 1 square.
Up or down: 1 square.
1 + 1 = 2 squares.

modules.title: Counting sides and corners of flat shapes

chapter.title: Counting sides and corners of flat shapes
text: A side is a straight edge of a flat shape; a corner is where two sides meet. A shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides; a circle has none.
math: There are 3 hexagons, as in the table. How many corners do they have in all?
A hexagon has 6 corners.

chapter.title: Faces, edges and corners of solids
text: A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a corner is where edges meet. A cube and a cuboid have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners; a square pyramid has 5, 8 and 5.
Hold the solid (or picture it) and count the top, the bottom and all round, marking each one as you go. For several solids, add the counts for each one.
math: Kavya has 1 cube and 1 square pyramid. How many flat faces do they have in all?
A cube has 6 flat faces.
A square pyramid has 5 flat faces.
Add for every solid: 11 in all.

chapter.title: Shapes with straight sides, curved sides or both
text: A side can be straight, like the side of a triangle, or curved, like the edge of a circle. A half circle has one straight side and one curved side.
Run a finger along the edge of each shape. If it never bends, the side is straight; if it bends, it is curved. Sort the shapes, then count.
math: How many shapes in the picture have only straight sides?
There are 3.

chapter.title: Sides, corners and diagonals of flat shapes, and sorting by them
text: A shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides. A diagonal joins two corners that are not next to each other: a triangle has none, a square or rectangle 2, a pentagon 5, a hexagon 9.
For each shape, count its sides (or corners, or diagonals), then add for every shape. To sort, check each shape against the rule and count the ones that fit.
math: There are 2 pentagons and 1 triangle. How many corners do they have in all?
A pentagon has 5 corners.
A triangle has 3 corners.
That makes 13.

chapter.title: Faces, curved surfaces, edges and corners of cylinders, cones and spheres
text: A cylinder has 2 flat faces, 1 curved surface, 2 curved edges and no corners; a cone has 1 flat face, 1 curved surface, 1 edge and 1 corner (its tip); a sphere has only a curved surface.
Picture each solid: count its flat faces, its curved surfaces, the edges where surfaces meet and the corners. Then add for every solid.
math: Priya has 3 cones and 2 cuboids. How many solids with both a flat face and a curved surface are there?
A cone: 1.
A cuboid: 0.
In all: 3.

screens.title: The method

math: There are 2 squares and 3 pentagons, as in the table. How many sides do they have in all?
A square has 4 sides.
A pentagon has 5 sides.
2 × 4 and 3 × 5: 23 in all.

screens.title: Skip count for many shapes

Add the counts for each kind of shape.
math: There are 3 squares and 1 triangle, as in the table. How many corners do they have in all?
A square has 4 corners.
A triangle has 3 corners.

chapter.title: Hours and minutes into minutes

180 + 25 = 205 minutes

chapter.title: Minutes into hours and minutes
text: Every 60 minutes make 1 hour. The minutes left over, fewer than 60, stay as minutes.

3 minutes = 3 × 60 = 180 seconds
180 + 10 = 190 seconds

modules.title: Adding and subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
text: Ten ones make a ten and ten tens make a hundred, so a column that gets too big passes a ten (or a hundred) on, and a column that is too small can break one from the next column.
math: Ones: 6 + 3 = 9
Tens: 7 + 5 = 12: write 2, carry 1 hundred
Hundreds: 3 + 4 + 1 carried = 8
chapter.tip: A ten (or a hundred) made in one column was not carried to the next column.

chapter.title: Column addition and subtraction from three to five digits, with and without regrouping
text: Write the numbers with ones under ones, tens under tens and so on; each column is added or subtracted on its own, passing a 1 to the next column (or taking one from it) when needed.
Start with the ones and work left. Adding: if a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry 1. Subtracting: if the top digit is smaller, regroup 1 from the next column as 10.
math: Ones: 0 + 8: write 8
Tens: 7 + 2: write 9
Hundreds: 5 + 0: write 5

chapter.title: Mental shortcuts: making 100 and 10,000, and taking away or adding 9 or 99
text: Round numbers are easy: 9 is 10 − 1 and 99 is 100 − 1. To make 100 or 10,000, every digit pairs to 9 except the ones, which pair to 10.
To take away 9, take away 10 and add 1 back; to add 99, add 100 and take 1 away. To make 10,000, find what makes each digit 9 and the ones digit 10.
math: Use a shortcut (take away 10, then add 1 back): 1,581 − 9 = ?

chapter.title: Adding three-digit numbers without regrouping
text: In column addition each column counts one place: ones, tens, hundreds. When no column adds up to 10 or more, each column's sum is simply written below it.
Line up the ones digits. Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds, writing each sum under its column.
math: Ones: 3 + 0 = 3
Tens: 0 + 6 = 6
Hundreds: 1 + 2 = 3

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting four- and five-digit numbers with regrouping
text: Large numbers are added and subtracted column by column, exactly as with small ones. Ten in any place makes one of the next place (and one of a place can be broken into ten of the place to its right).
Write the numbers with the ones lined up. Start at the ones: carry (when adding) or regroup (when subtracting) as needed, then move one column left at a time.
math: 9,291 + 29,532: column by column from the ones, carrying 2 times: 38,823

screens.title: The method
text: Write the numbers one under the other, ones under ones. Work from the ones to the hundreds, regrouping as you go: carry a ten when adding, exchange a ten for 10 ones when subtracting. Check with an estimate.
math: Ones: take 1 ten to make 12 ones; 12 − 3 = 9
Tens: take 1 hundred to make 9 tens; 9 − 0 = 9
Hundreds: 4 − 3 = 1

chapter.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding to tens

38 is nearest to 40
87 is nearest to 90

chapter.title: Estimating and checking weights and capacities

Round: 550 and 100
Estimate: 550 − 100 = 450

11 is nearest to 10
39 is nearest to 40

chapter.title: Using a pattern rule to find a later number
text: A rule like "add 5 each time" tells you how to get from one number to the next. The 1st number is the start, so the n-th number is n − 1 jumps after it.

From the 1st number to the 9th there are 8 jumps
8 jumps of 6 make 48
Start at 11 and add 48: 59

chapter.title: Moving on a 1–100 number grid
text: Each row of the grid holds 10 numbers, so the number just below is always 10 more, and the number just to the right is 1 more.
Add 10 for every row you move down, then add 1 for every square you move right.

Work out a few cases, look for what repeats, then use the rule: even and odd sums alternate along a row, and ab + ba = 11 × (a + b).

The sums go even, odd, even … in turn: 5 of the 11 are even

text: A right angle (90°) is a square corner. Smaller than a right angle is acute, between a right angle and a straight line is obtuse, and a straight line is a straight angle (180°).

text: An angle is an amount of turn. A full turn is 360°, a half turn 180°, and a quarter turn is a right angle, 90°. On a clock, each number is one twelfth of a full turn: 30°.
Count how many numbers the hand moves past clockwise, then multiply by 30°.
math: On a clock face, a hand points at 5. It turns clockwise until it points at 9. Through how many degrees has it turned?
A full turn of 360° is shared by 12 numbers: 30° from one number to the next
4 steps of 30° make 120°

chapter.title: Spotting right angles in pictures and objects
text: A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a page: a quarter of a full turn. Folding a paper twice makes a right-angle tester.

Hold the folded corner in the angle with one edge along one arm. If the other arm lies along the other edge, it is a right angle; if the angle fits inside the corner it is smaller; if the corner fits inside the angle it is bigger.
math: Which of these makes a right angle (a square corner)?
Only the square corner fits a folded-paper right angle exactly

chapter.title: Classifying angles, including reflex angles
text: Angles are named by comparing them with a right angle (90°) and a straight angle (180°): acute < 90° < obtuse < 180° < reflex < 360°.
Look at how far the arc turns. Less than a square corner: acute; a square corner: right; less than a straight line: obtuse; a straight line: straight; more than a straight line: reflex.
math: What kind of angle is the shaded angle at the centre of the circle in the picture?
25° is less than 90°: acute

chapter.title: The vertex and arms of an angle, and comparing angles by turning
text: An angle is made by two rays (its arms) starting from one point (its vertex). Its size is the amount of turn from one arm to the other.
In ∠ABC the middle letter B is the vertex and the arms are BA and BC. To compare two angles, put one on the other with vertices and one arm together: the one whose second arm turns further is bigger.
math: ∠X is the turn made by the minute hand of a clock moving from 12 to 1. ∠Y is drawn with arms twice as long, and is the turn of the hand moving from 12 to 2. If ∠X is placed on top of ∠Y with the vertices and one arm together, which is true?
Compare the amounts of turn: 30° for each number the hand passes

screens.title: The method
text: Compare each angle with 90°: less is acute, equal is right; more than 90° but less than 180° is obtuse; exactly 180° is straight.
math: The table gives the sizes of four angles: P = 90°, Q = 105°, R = 180°, S = 60°. Which one is an obtuse angle? Write its size in degrees.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°: 105°

screens.title: Check with a folded-paper corner
text: Fold a paper twice to make a square corner: that is a right angle.
Hold the corner in the angle: if the angle fits inside the corner it is acute; if the corner fits inside the angle (and the arms are not one straight line) it is obtuse.
math: The table gives the sizes of four angles: P = 30°, Q = 90°, R = 145°, S = 180°. Which one is a straight angle? Write its size in degrees.
A straight angle is exactly 180°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The table gives the sizes of four angles: P = 90°, Q = 105°, R = 180°, S = 50°. Which one is an obtuse angle? Write its size in degrees.” A common wrong answer is 180.
A straight angle (180°) is not obtuse; an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°.
math: Not 180, but 105

modules.title: Radius and diameter of a circle

chapter.title: Radius and diameter of a circle
text: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii.
math: A circle has a diameter of 2 cm. How long is its radius, in cm?
Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 cm

widget.note: edge, centre, edge: two radii make the diameter

chapter.tip: The diameter and the radius were taken as the same length; the radius goes only from the centre to the edge, half of the diameter.

chapter.title: Naming the parts of a circle
text: Every point of a circle is the same distance from the centre. A radius joins the centre to the circle; a chord joins two points of the circle, and the chord through the centre is a diameter. An arc is a piece of the circle itself.

Ask: is it a point, a straight segment, a curved piece or a region? For a segment, where do its ends lie and does it pass through the centre? For a region, is it cut off by two radii (sector) or by a chord (segment)?
math: A circle has centre P. What is the name for the curved part of the circle from G to H?
That is an arc

screens.title: The method
text: To find the diameter, double the radius. To find the radius, halve the diameter.
math: A circle has a radius of 14 cm. How long is its diameter, in cm?
Diameter = 2 × radius = 2 × 14 = 28 cm

widget.note: edge, centre, edge: two radii make the diameter

screens.title: Fold a paper circle
text: Cut out a circle and fold it in half: the fold is a diameter, and it passes through the centre.
Fold again: the two folds cross at the centre, and each half of the first fold is a radius.
math: A circle has a radius of 16 cm. How long is its diameter, in cm?
Diameter = 2 × radius = 2 × 16 = 32 cm

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A circle has a radius of 9 cm. How long is its diameter, in cm?” A common wrong answer is 9.
The radius and the diameter were taken as the same length; the diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
math: Not 9, but 18

modules.title: Letters with a vertical or horizontal line of symmetry

chapter.title: Letters with a vertical or horizontal line of symmetry
text: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves of a shape match exactly, like a mirror image.
math: Look at these capital letters: M  V  G  F  A. How many of them have a vertical line of symmetry (a fold going straight up and down, so that the two halves match exactly)?
M, V, A have a vertical line of symmetry: 3
chapter.tip: The letters were folded the other way (across); a vertical line goes up and down, so the left half must match the right half.

chapter.title: Counting the lines of symmetry of a design or a shape
text: A line of symmetry is a fold line where one half lands exactly on the other. A shape can have none, one, or several.
Try each possible fold: up and down, across, and along the diagonals (and, for regular shapes, through every corner and every side's middle). Count only the folds where every part matches.
math: The picture shows a square design made of shaded and white squares. How many lines of symmetry does the design have?
Fold along each of the four lines: 0 folds make the halves match

chapter.title: Lines of symmetry in digits and numbers
text: On a digital clock each digit is made of straight bars. Some digits, like 8 and 0, match when folded either way; 3 matches only when folded across.

For a fold across, check each digit's top and bottom halves. For a fold down the middle of a whole number, the left end must match the right end: read the mirrored digits in reverse order and see if you get the same number.
math: These are written the way a digital clock shows them, with straight bars: 2, 1, 90, 8, 12. How many of them have a horizontal line of symmetry (a fold straight across the middle of the whole number, top half onto bottom half)?
1, 8 have a horizontal line of symmetry: 2

chapter.title: Which word looks the same in a mirror
text: A mirror standing beside a word flips it left to right: the letters come in the reverse order and each letter is flipped. Water below flips it top to bottom: the order stays, but each letter is turned upside down.
For a mirror beside the word: every letter must have an up-and-down line of symmetry AND the word must read the same backwards. For water below: every letter must have an across line of symmetry.
math: A word is written in plain capital letters on a card, and the card is held next to a mirror standing straight up beside it. Which of these words looks exactly the same in the mirror as on the card?
In a mirror beside it, AHA is reversed and every letter is flipped left to right, and it comes back the same

screens.title: The method
text: Imagine folding each letter along the line (or stand a mirror on it): if the half you see in the mirror finishes the letter exactly, the letter has that line of symmetry.
math: Look at these capital letters: E  A  D  T  M. How many of them have a horizontal line of symmetry (a fold going straight across, left to right, so that the two halves match exactly)?
E, D have a horizontal line of symmetry: 2

screens.title: Use a mirror
text: Write the letter big and stand a small mirror on the line down its middle (or across its middle).
If the letter you see, half on paper and half in the mirror, looks just like the real letter, that line is a line of symmetry.
math: Look at these capital letters: R  O  S  D  J. How many of them have a vertical line of symmetry (a fold going straight up and down, so that the two halves match exactly)?
O has a vertical line of symmetry: 1

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Look at these capital letters: W  J  I  N  L. How many of them have a horizontal line of symmetry (a fold going straight across, left to right, so that the two halves match exactly)?” A common wrong answer is 2.
The letters were folded the other way (up and down); a horizontal line goes across, so the top half must match the bottom half.
math: Not 2, but 1

modules.title: Reflecting a point in a mirror line on a grid

chapter.title: Reflecting a point in a mirror line on a grid
text: A mirror image is as far behind the mirror line as the object is in front of it, straight across, at right angles to the line.
math: In the picture, the point P is at (0, 5) and the mirror line is x = 5. Reflect P in the mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image? Write them as (x, y).
P is 5 units from the mirror line
Go the same distance to the other side of the line: the image is (10, 5)
chapter.tip: The point was moved only as far as the mirror line; the image is as far beyond the line as P is in front of it.

chapter.title: Translating a point on a grid
text: A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it: every point moves the same distance across and the same distance up or down.
Add the move to the right to x (take away a move to the left), and add the move up to y (take away a move down).
math: The point P is at (4, 1). Slide it 3 units to the right and 4 units up. Where is it now? Write (x, y).
Across: 4 + 3 = 7
Up or down: 1 + 4 = 5

screens.title: The method
text: Count how far P is from the mirror line, then count the same distance on the other side. Only the coordinate that crosses the line changes.
math: In the picture, the point P is at (6, 2) and the mirror line is y = 5. Reflect P in the mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image? Write them as (x, y).
P is 3 units from the mirror line
Go the same distance to the other side of the line: the image is (6, 8)

screens.title: Fold the grid paper
text: Draw the point on squared paper and fold the paper along the mirror line.
Press hard on the point: the mark it makes on the other side is the image.
math: In the picture, the point P is at (0, 4) and the mirror line is x = 5. Reflect P in the mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image? Write them as (x, y).
P is 5 units from the mirror line
Go the same distance to the other side of the line: the image is (10, 4)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “In the picture, the point P is at (7, 8) and the mirror line is y = 6. Reflect P in the mirror line. What are the coordinates of its image? Write them as (x, y).” A common wrong answer is (5, 8).
The wrong coordinate was changed: a mirror line y = 6 goes across, so the point moves up or down and only y changes.

modules.title: Writing a 12-hour time in 24-hour form

chapter.title: Writing a 12-hour time in 24-hour form
text: The 24-hour clock counts the hours of the whole day from 00 at midnight to 23. Morning (a.m.) hours stay the same; afternoon and evening (p.m.) hours go on past 12: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14, and so on.
math: Write 6:20 p.m. in 24-hour time. Give the hours and the minutes as (hours, minutes); for example, 13:05 is written (13, 5).
p.m.: add 12 to the hours: 6 + 12 = 18
chapter.tip: 12 was not added for a p.m. time; after noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14 …

chapter.title: Reading a 24-hour time on a 12-hour clock
text: After 12 noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting (13, 14, … 23), but a 12-hour clock starts again at 1. 00 hours is midnight, shown as 12.
If the hours are more than 12, take away 12 (it is p.m.). 12 stays 12 (noon). 00 becomes 12 (midnight, a.m.). Keep the minutes.
math: A railway timetable shows 15:10. What time does an ordinary 12-hour clock show then? Write it as (hours, minutes); for example, 4:05 is written (4, 5).
After noon, take away 12: 15 − 12 = 3

chapter.title: Time between two 24-hour times
text: Time is counted in sixties: 60 minutes make 1 hour. So when you take away times and need to regroup, 1 hour is exchanged for 60 minutes, not 100.
Count on from the start to the next full hour, then the full hours, then the minutes to the end time, and add them up.
math: How much time passes from 07:10 to 10:20 on the same day? Write it as (hours, minutes); for example, 2 hours 5 minutes is (2, 5).
Minutes: 20 − 10 = 10
Hours: 10 − 7 = 3

chapter.title: Writing a 24-hour time with a.m. or p.m.
text: a.m. means before noon (from midnight to 12 noon); p.m. means after noon (from 12 noon to midnight). 12 a.m. is midnight and 12 p.m. is noon.
If the 24-hour hour is 0 to 11 it is a.m. (00 becomes 12). If it is 12 to 23 it is p.m.: take away 12 from 13 to 23 (12 stays 12).
math: A railway clock shows 11:50 (24-hour time). How is this time written on a 12-hour clock with a.m. or p.m.?
Before noon: a.m.; the hours after 12 start again at 1

screens.title: The method
text: For a.m., keep the hour (but 12 a.m. becomes 00). For p.m., add 12 to the hour (but 12 noon stays 12). The minutes do not change.
math: Write 6:25 p.m. in 24-hour time. Give the hours and the minutes as (hours, minutes); for example, 13:05 is written (13, 5).
p.m.: add 12 to the hours: 6 + 12 = 18

strategies.title: A line for the whole day

screens.title: A line for the whole day
text: Draw a line from 0 (midnight) to 24 (the next midnight), with 12 (noon) in the middle.
Morning times are on the first half; for an afternoon time, count on past 12: 3 p.m. is 3 more than 12, which is 15.
math: Write 4:40 a.m. in 24-hour time. Give the hours and the minutes as (hours, minutes); for example, 13:05 is written (13, 5).
a.m.: the hours stay 4

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write 6:20 a.m. in 24-hour time. Give the hours and the minutes as (hours, minutes); for example, 13:05 is written (13, 5).” A common wrong answer is (18, 20).
12 was added to a morning time; a.m. times keep the same hour in 24-hour time.

modules.title: Area of a rectangle by counting unit squares

chapter.title: Area of a rectangle by counting unit squares
text: Area is how much flat space a shape covers. We measure it by counting how many unit squares cover it with no gaps and no overlaps.
math: Each small square in the picture is 1 square unit. The rectangle has 2 rows with 10 squares in each row. What is its area, in square units?
2 rows of 10 squares: 2 × 10 = 20 square units
chapter.tip: The edges round the outside were counted; that is the perimeter. Area counts the squares that cover the inside.

chapter.title: Choosing area or perimeter in a problem
text: Area is the space inside a shape (how many unit squares cover it). Perimeter is the distance all the way round its edge.
Ask: am I covering the inside (area: multiply length × width) or going round the edge (perimeter: add all four sides)?
math: A rectangular card is 10 cm long and 9 cm wide. How many centimetres of lace are needed to go once round the edge of the card?
Going round needs the perimeter: 10 + 9 + 10 + 9 = 38

chapter.title: Estimating the area of an irregular shape and comparing two areas
text: Area is the number of unit squares a shape covers. For a curved shape the squares on the edge are only partly covered, so we estimate: more than half counts as a whole square, exactly half as ½, less than half as nothing.
Count the full squares, then the more-than-half squares, then the half squares (each ½). Add them. To compare two shapes, count each and subtract.
math: The picture shows a leaf traced on squared paper. ■ is a square fully covered, ◕ more than half covered, ◑ exactly half covered, ◔ less than half covered, □ not covered. Estimate the area of the leaf in square units: count a full square as 1, a square more than half covered as 1, a half-covered square as ½, and leave out squares less than half covered.
Full squares and squares more than half covered: 9 + 6 = 15
2 half squares make 1
About 15 + 1 = 16 square units

screens.title: The method
text: Count the squares in one row, then count the rows. Equal rows can be counted by multiplying: rows × squares in each row.
math: Each small square in the picture is 1 square unit. The rectangle has 2 rows with 2 squares in each row. What is its area, in square units?
2 rows of 2 squares: 2 × 2 = 4 square units

strategies.title: See the rows as an array

screens.title: See the rows as an array
text: The squares sit in equal rows, like chairs in a hall.
Skip-count one row at a time: 6, 12, 18, … until every row is counted.
math: Each small square in the picture is 1 square unit. The rectangle has 9 rows with 11 squares in each row. What is its area, in square units?
9 rows of 11 squares: 9 × 11 = 99 square units

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Each small square in the picture is 1 square unit. The rectangle has 2 rows with 11 squares in each row. What is its area, in square units?” A common wrong answer is 26.
The edges round the outside were counted; that is the perimeter. Area counts the squares that cover the inside.
math: Not 26, but 22

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Count the squares in one row, then count the rows. Equal rows can be counted by multiplying: rows × squares in each row.

modules.title: Adding and subtracting measures in two units

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting measures in two units
text: Measures in two units work like tens and ones, but the change-over is 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 g = 1 kg and 1000 mL = 1 L.
math: Add: 2 kg 800 g + 1 kg 400 g. Write the answer as (kg, g); for example, 3 kg 45 g is (3, 45).
Small units: 800 + 400 = 1200
1200 = 1000 + 200: change 1000 of the small units into 1 large unit
Large units: 2 + 1 + 1 carried = 4
chapter.tip: 1200 g was left as it is; 1000 g make 1 kg, so change 1000 of them into 1 kg.

chapter.title: Multiplying a measure in two units
text: Multiplying a measure is repeated adding: multiply the small units and the large units, then change extra small units into large ones.
Multiply the small units; take out every full 100 cm (or 1000 g, 1000 mL) as a large unit. Multiply the large units and add the ones you took out.
math: Work out 4 × 1 m 60 cm. Write the answer as (m, cm); for example, 3 m 45 cm is (3, 45).
Small units: 60 × 4 = 240
240 small units make 2 large units and some left over
Large units: 1 × 4 + 2 = 6

chapter.title: Dividing a measure in two units
text: Dividing a measure shares the large units first; whatever large units are left over are changed into small units and shared with the small units.
Divide the large units. Change the ones left over into small units (× 100 or × 1000), add the small units, and divide those. Check: multiply the answer back.
math: Divide 24 L 250 mL into 5 equal parts. How much is each part? Write the answer as (L, mL); for example, 3 L 45 mL is (3, 45).
Large units: 24 ÷ 5 = 4, with 4 left over
Change the 4 left over into small units and add the 250: 4250
Small units: 4250 ÷ 5 = 850

screens.title: The method
text: Add or subtract the small units first. If the small units reach the change-over number, change them into 1 large unit; if there are too few to subtract, change 1 large unit into small units. Then do the large units.
math: Add: 2 m 80 cm + 6 m 30 cm. Write the answer as (m, cm); for example, 3 m 45 cm is (3, 45).
Small units: 80 + 30 = 110
110 = 100 + 10: change 100 of the small units into 1 large unit
Large units: 2 + 6 + 1 carried = 9

strategies.title: Change everything into the small unit

screens.title: Change everything into the small unit
text: Write both measures in the small unit only (for example 2 m 45 cm = 245 cm).
Add or subtract these numbers, then change the answer back (310 cm = 3 m 10 cm).
math: Add: 2 L 850 mL + 5 L 250 mL. Write the answer as (L, mL); for example, 3 L 45 mL is (3, 45).
Small units: 850 + 250 = 1100
1100 = 1000 + 100: change 1000 of the small units into 1 large unit
Large units: 2 + 5 + 1 carried = 8

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Subtract: 7 kg 350 g − 3 kg 850 g. Write the answer as (kg, g); for example, 3 kg 45 g is (3, 45).” A common wrong answer is (4, 500).
350 − 850 cannot be done, so 350 was taken from 850; instead, change 1 kg into 1000 g first.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract multi-digit numbers with regrouping; Convert common metric units. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Add or subtract the small units first. If the small units reach the change-over number, change them into 1 large unit; if there are too few to subtract, change 1 large unit into small units. Then do the large units.

modules.title: Changing a measure into the smaller unit

chapter.title: Changing a measure into the smaller unit
text: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 L = 1000 mL and 1 km = 1000 m. A measure in two units is the large part changed into small units, plus the small part.
math: 4 L 605 mL = how many mL?
chapter.tip: The two numbers were simply added; first change the large units into small units.

chapter.title: How many parts make a kilogram or a litre
text: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL. Two 500 g packets make 1 kg, four 250 g packets make 1 kg, and so on.
Find how many parts make 1 kg (or 1 L): 1000 ÷ the part. Then multiply by the number of kilograms (or litres).
math: How many bottles of 500 mL together make 5 L?
5 units are 5000 small units

chapter.title: Changing a measure into the larger unit and what is left
text: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 L = 1000 mL, 1 km = 1000 m. To change into the larger unit, see how many whole large units fit, and what is left.
Divide by 100, 10 or 1000: the whole number of times is the large unit; the remainder is the small unit (3450 g = 3 kg 450 g).
math: 7560 mg = how many g and mg? Write the answer as (g, mg); for example, 3 g 5 mg is (3, 5).
7560 ÷ 1000: 7 whole large units
7560 − 7000 = 560 small units left

chapter.title: Writing a measure as a decimal of the larger unit
text: A small unit is a fraction of the large unit: 1 g is one thousandth of a kg, so 3450 g = 3450 thousandths of a kg = 3.450 kg = 3.45 kg.
Divide by 1000 (or 100, or 10): move the decimal point 3 (or 2, or 1) places to the left, filling empty places with zeros (3045 g = 3.045 kg).
math: Write 1710 g in kilograms (as a decimal).

chapter.title: Comparing weights in different units with <, = or >
text: Weights can be compared only in the same unit: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 g = 1000 mg.
Change the weight in two units into the small unit (2 kg 50 g = 2050 g), then compare the numbers.
math: Which sign goes in the box: 8 g 250 mg ☐ 8340 mg? Choose <, = or >.
8 large units 250 small units = 8250 small units
Compare 8250 and 8340

chapter.title: Feet, inches and centimetres, and estimating with a known length
text: Feet and inches are older units still used for heights: 12 inches make 1 foot, 1 inch is about 2.5 cm and 1 foot about 30 cm. A known length (a door, a step, a bus) can be used as a ruler to estimate bigger lengths.
Change feet to cm (× 30) and inches to cm (× 2.5) and add. To estimate with a known length, count how many of it fit and multiply.
math: A railway coach is about 25 m long. A train has 7 coaches. About how many metres is that?

chapter.title: Converting units with a conversion factor
text: A conversion factor says how many of one unit make one of the other: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s. Converting is multiplying by the factor, because the amount is proportional.
Write the factor as 'new units per old unit' and multiply. Check the direction: going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.
math: 1 inch = 2.54 cm. A tablet screen is 11 inches across. How many centimetres is that?

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the large units by 100 or 1000, then add the small units. Check the small part fills its places: 3 kg 25 g = 3000 g + 25 g = 3025 g.
math: 4 L 955 mL = how many mL?

screens.title: Use a place-value chart
text: Write the large units in the thousands place (for g, mL, m) or hundreds place (for cm).
Write the small units ending in the ones place, and fill any empty places with 0.
math: 6 L 745 mL = how many mL?

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “6 kg 470 g = how many g?” A common wrong answer is 476.
The two numbers were simply added; first change the large units into small units.
math: Not 476, but 6470

modules.title: Writing ones, tenths and hundredths as a decimal

chapter.title: Writing ones, tenths and hundredths as a decimal
text: Splitting 1 whole into 10 equal parts gives tenths; splitting each tenth into 10 gives hundredths. After the decimal point, the first place is tenths and the second is hundredths.
math: In the picture, a big square (flat) is 1 whole, a rod is one tenth and a small cube is one hundredth. The picture shows 3 flats, 8 rods and 7 small cubes. Write the number they show as a decimal.
8 tenths = 0.8
7 hundredths = 0.07
chapter.tip: The tenths and hundredths were put in each other's places: the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths.

chapter.title: Comparing a tenths decimal with a hundredths decimal
text: Decimals are compared place by place from the left, like whole numbers: first the wholes, then the tenths, then the hundredths. More digits does not mean bigger.
Write both with the same number of places (0.7 = 0.70) and compare them as hundredths: 70 hundredths is more than 65 hundredths.
math: Which number is greater: 3.1 or 3.42? Write the greater number.
Compare the tenths: 1 and 4. The greater number is 3.42

chapter.title: Place value, expanded form and place-value form of decimals with thousandths
text: Each place is ten times the place to its right: tens, ones, then after the point tenths (1/10), hundredths (1/100), thousandths (1/1000). A digit's place value is the digit times its place.
Write the number in a place-value chart (T, O . t, h, th). Read each digit with its place; for the expanded form, add the place values of the non-zero digits.
math: What is the place value of the digit 7 in 19.753?
In 19.753, that digit is in the tenths place

chapter.title: Ordering decimals
text: Decimals are compared place by place from the left: wholes, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Writing them all with the same number of places (0.5 = 0.500) makes this easy.
Fill each number with zeros to three decimal places, then compare them like whole numbers of thousandths: 0.500, 0.450, 0.505, 0.550.
math: Write these decimals in ascending order (smallest first): 0.5; 0.41; 0.501; 0.51. Write them in brackets, separated by commas, for example (0.1, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4).
Give every number three decimal places (0.500, 0.410, 0.501, 0.510) and compare: (0.41, 0.5, 0.501, 0.51)

chapter.title: Decimals as fractions and fractions as decimals
text: A decimal is a fraction with a bottom number of 10, 100 or 1000: 0.07 = 7/100, 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. A fraction is a division, so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
Decimal to fraction: write the digits over 10, 100 or 1000 (by the last place) and simplify. Fraction to decimal: make the bottom 10, 100 or 1000 by multiplying, or divide the top by the bottom.
math: Write 1.2 as a fraction in its simplest form.
Write 1.2 over 10, 100 or 1000 and cancel common factors

9 hundredths = 0.09

modules.title: Picking out the even numbers

chapter.title: Picking out the even numbers
text: An even number of things can be put into pairs with none left over; an odd number always leaves one. Tens and hundreds always pair up, so only the ones digit decides.
math: Which of these numbers are even? 30, 196, 468, 90, 21, 875. Write all the even ones, separated by commas.
Look at the ones digit: numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 are even: 30, 196, 468, 90

chapter.title: Even or odd by putting things in pairs
text: An even number of things can be put into pairs with none left over. An odd number always leaves exactly one without a partner.
Join the things two by two (a full ten frame is 5 pairs: each counter in the top row with the one below it). If every one has a partner, the number is even; if one is left over, it is odd.
math: The ten frames in the picture are filled row by row. A full ten frame makes 5 pairs; put the counters in the last frame into pairs too (two side by side or one above the other). Is the number of counters even or odd?
8 make 4 pairs
None is left over: even

text: Look at the last digit: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd.

Look at the ones digit: numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 are even: 932, 852, 580, 926

If every dot has a partner the number is even; if one dot is left alone it is odd.
math: Which of these numbers are even? 38, 50, 655, 758, 53, 91. Write all the even ones, separated by commas.

modules.title: Writing a number in lakhs and thousands in figures

chapter.title: Writing a number in lakhs and thousands in figures
text: In the Indian system the places are grouped as ones–tens–hundreds, then thousands–ten thousands, then lakhs–ten lakhs. Every place gets a digit, so empty places get 0.
math: Write in figures: seven lakh fifty-nine thousand four hundred three.
59 thousand = 59,000
4 hundred and 3 = 403; put the periods together
chapter.tip: The numbers heard were written one after another, without zeros for the empty places; each period has a fixed number of places (lakhs, then 2 for thousands, then 3 for hundreds, tens and ones).

chapter.title: Putting large numbers in ascending order
text: A number with more digits is bigger. When two numbers have the same number of digits, the first place where their digits differ decides.
First sort by how many digits each number has. Then, for numbers with the same number of digits, compare ten thousands, then thousands, then hundreds … until the digits differ.
math: Write these numbers in ascending order (smallest first): 10,726; 17,206; 3,276; 17,026. Write the list in brackets without commas inside the numbers, for example (1234, 5678, …).

chapter.title: Number names, commas and expanded forms of large numbers

Starting from the right, mark off three digits, then twos (Indian) or threes (International). Read each period with its name; a zero keeps its place even when it is not said.
math: Which shows 50207990 with commas placed correctly in the Indian system?
Group the digits from the right: 5,02,07,990

99 thousand = 99,000
4 hundred and 5 = 405; put the periods together

Fill each period from its right, and put 0 in any empty box.
math: Write in figures: seven lakh eighty-six thousand three hundred three.
86 thousand = 86,000
3 hundred and 3 = 303; put the periods together

modules.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000

chapter.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
text: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much, so each digit moves one place to the left and a 0 fills the ones place. Dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
math: × 10: each digit moves 1 place left: 974 → 9740
chapter.tip: 10 was added instead of multiplied.

chapter.title: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 or 100
text: Multiplying by 40 is multiplying by 4 and then by 10, because 40 = 4 × 10.
Multiply by the non-zero digit first, then put the zeros of the multiplier on the end of the answer.
math: × 10: put 1 zero on the end: 5760

chapter.title: Dividing a multiple of 10, 100 or 1000 by a one-digit number
text: 2400 is 24 hundreds, so 2400 ÷ 6 is 24 hundreds ÷ 6 = 4 hundreds = 400.
Cover the zeros, divide using the table fact, then put the zeros back on the answer.
math: So 4 hundreds: 400

screens.title: The method
text: × 10, × 100, × 1000: write 1, 2 or 3 zeros on the end. ÷ 10, ÷ 100, ÷ 1000 (of a number ending in enough zeros): take 1, 2 or 3 zeros off the end.
math: × 10: each digit moves 1 place left: 679 → 6790

strategies.title: Swap each block for a bigger one

screens.title: Swap each block for a bigger one
text: × 10 changes every one into a ten, every ten into a hundred, every hundred into a thousand.
So 34 (3 tens, 4 ones) × 10 is 3 hundreds and 4 tens: 340.
math: × 100: each digit moves 2 places left: 692 → 69200

1000 was added instead of multiplied.

modules.title: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand

chapter.title: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
text: Rounding finds the nearest 'round' number: on a number line, which ten (hundred, thousand) is the number closer to? A number exactly halfway is rounded up.
math: Round 2,854 to the nearest thousand.
Look at the digit after the place you round to: it is 8
2854 is nearer to 3000
chapter.tip: The digits after the thousands were just changed to zeros; when the next digit is 5 or more, round up.

chapter.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding
text: An estimate is a quick, close answer. Rounding each number to a ten or hundred first makes the sum or difference easy to do in your head, and it tells you if an exact answer is sensible.
Round each number to the place asked for, then add or subtract the rounded numbers.
math: Estimate 475 + 857 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred first.
475 rounds to 500
857 rounds to 900

chapter.title: Rounding large numbers in real situations
text: Large numbers in news and plans are usually rounded: 4,37,862 people is 'about 4,40,000' to the nearest ten thousand. Rounding finds the nearer of the two round numbers on either side.
Find the place you round to, look at the digit just to its right: 0–4 keep the place and write zeros after it; 5–9 add 1 to the place and write zeros after it.
math: The number of votes cast in a district election is 86,05,763. Round this number to the nearest lakh.
Look at the digit just after the place you round to: it is 0

chapter.title: Estimating a product by rounding
text: Rounding both numbers turns a hard product into an easy one (48 × 32 ≈ 50 × 30). The estimate shows roughly how big the exact answer must be.
Round each number as asked, multiply the non-zero digits, then put back all the zeros of both rounded numbers.
math: Estimate 78 × 53 by rounding each number to the nearest ten first.
78 rounds to 80
53 rounds to 50

chapter.title: Judging answers with an estimate
text: An estimate is a quick, nearly-right answer. It tells you how big an exact answer should be, so a worked answer far from it must have a mistake. Some situations (giving change, a medicine dose) need exact answers; others (a crowd, a distance for planning) need only an estimate.
Round each number (to the nearest ten or hundred), work out the estimate in your head, and compare. Close: reasonable. Many times bigger or smaller: check the working.
math: Which of these needs an EXACT answer (an estimate is not good enough)?
Ask whether only the rough size matters, or every unit counts

chapter.title: Rounding a decimal to a whole number, tenths or hundredths
text: Rounding a decimal works like rounding whole numbers: find which of the two numbers on either side, at the place asked for, it is nearer to.
Find the place you round to. Look at the digit just to its right: 0–4 keep the place and drop the digits after it; 5–9 add 1 to the place and drop the digits after it.
math: Round 40.922 to the nearest whole number.
Look at the digit after the ones place: it is 9
40.922 rounds to 41

chapter.title: Estimating a large product by rounding
text: Rounding each factor to its greatest place gives an easy product that is close to the real one: a quick check of size.
Round each number, multiply the first digits, then write all the zeros of both rounded numbers: 5,000 × 40 = 20 × 10,000 = 2,00,000.
math: Estimate 6,205 × 71 by rounding each number to its greatest place (for example 4,870 to 5,000 and 36 to 40) and then multiplying.
6,205 rounds to 6,000
71 rounds to 70
Put back the zeros: 6,000 × 70 = 4,20,000

screens.title: The method
text: Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 0–4, round down (keep the place, zeros after). If it is 5–9, round up (add 1 to the place, zeros after).
math: Round 7,274 to the nearest hundred.
Look at the digit after the place you round to: it is 7
7274 is nearer to 7300

screens.title: The rounding hill
text: Picture the numbers from one ten to the next as a hill, with the halfway number at the top.
A number before the top rolls back down to the lower ten; at the top or after it, it rolls on to the higher ten.
math: Round 9,431 to the nearest thousand.
Look at the digit after the place you round to: it is 4
9431 is nearer to 9000

text: A question: “Round 1,820 to the nearest thousand.” A common wrong answer is 1000.
The digits after the thousands were just changed to zeros; when the next digit is 5 or more, round up.
math: Not 1000, but 2000

modules.title: Shopping: total cost and change

chapter.title: Shopping: total cost and change
text: A multi-step problem is a chain of small questions: what does each kind of item cost, what is the whole bill, and what is left from the note.
math: In a shop, story books cost ₹24 each and colour pens cost ₹80 each. Anu buys 5 story books and 3 colour pens, and pays with a ₹500 note. How much change, in rupees, should Anu get back?
chapter.tip: The price of one of each item was used; the prices must be multiplied by how many were bought.

chapter.title: Water lost from a dripping tap
text: When something happens at the same rate every minute, the total is the amount each minute times the number of minutes. Hours must be changed into minutes first.
Change the hours into minutes (× 60), then multiply by the millilitres lost each minute.
math: A tap drips 25 mL of water every minute. How many millilitres of water drip out in 3 hours?
3 hours = 180 minutes
25 mL × 180 minutes = 4500 mL

chapter.title: A table of quantities and costs with missing values
text: In each row, cost = how many × price of one. Knowing any two of the three gives the third: multiply for the cost, divide the cost to find the number or the price.
Fill each missing value first (multiply or divide in its row), then answer the question, adding the costs for a total.
math: The table in the picture shows a school's order from a stationery shop; some values are missing (?). What is the price of one notebook, in rupees?

chapter.title: Problems that combine time, distance and money
text: Speed links distance and time: distance = speed × time, and time = distance ÷ speed. A charge per km or per hour then turns the distance or the time into money.
Decide what the money depends on (km or hours). Find that quantity first from the speed, then multiply by the charge.
math: A taxi travels at 60 km per hour for 2 hours. The fare is ₹13 for every kilometre. What is the fare, in rupees?
Distance = 60 km/h × 2 h = 120 km

chapter.title: Multi-step problems with large numbers
text: Large numbers in real life (people, rupees, kilometres) follow the same rules as small ones: decide what joins (add), what leaves (subtract) and what repeats (multiply).
Write the steps in order in words first, then calculate each one, keeping the places lined up. Use Indian commas to read the answer.
math: A town had 3,77,458 people. In one year 5,938 babies were born and 8,231 people moved away. How many people lived in the town at the end of the year?

chapter.title: An attribute-matching puzzle
text: In a matching puzzle every person goes with exactly one thing and every thing with exactly one person. Each clue rules out (or fixes) some pairs; when only one choice is left in a row or column, it must be the answer.
Draw a 4 × 4 grid (people down, things across). Mark ✗ for each 'does not' clue and ✓ for each 'does' clue (with ✗ for the rest of that row and column). Keep filling until every row has one ✓.
math: Arjun, Divya, Priya and Meena each play a different sport: kabaddi, cricket, chess, football. Clues: Arjun plays kabaddi. Divya does not play chess. Divya does not play football. Priya does not play chess. Who plays cricket?
Make a grid of people and things, put ✗ for every clue that rules a pair out and ✓ for every clue that fixes one; a row or column with three ✗ has its ✓ in the last place

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply to find the cost of each kind of item, add the costs to get the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.
math: In a shop, notebooks cost ₹40 each and pencil boxes cost ₹12 each. Anu buys 5 notebooks and 2 pencil boxes, and pays with a ₹500 note. How much change, in rupees, should Anu get back?

screens.title: Count up like a shopkeeper
text: After finding the bill, count up from the bill to the note: ₹265 → ₹270 → ₹300 → ₹500.
Add the jumps: 5 + 30 + 200 = ₹235 change.
math: In a shop, notebooks cost ₹150 each and pencil boxes cost ₹50 each. Anu buys 2 notebooks and 3 pencil boxes, and pays with a ₹500 note. How much change, in rupees, should Anu get back?

text: A question: “In a shop, bars of soap cost ₹48 each and packets of biscuits cost ₹150 each. Priya buys 5 bars of soap and 1 packet of biscuits, and pays with a ₹500 note. How much change, in rupees, should Priya get back?” A common wrong answer is 302.
The price of one of each item was used; the prices must be multiplied by how many were bought.

modules.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference

chapter.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference
text: A sum or difference is a true sentence, so each column must work out, including any regrouping with the column on its right (a ten carried in, or 1 exchanged for 10 ones).
math: Find the missing digit: 390 − 232 = 1□8. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right is regrouped: 1 from this column is exchanged for 10 there, so this column has 1 less
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 5
chapter.tip: In that column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, regroup first: exchange 1 from the next column on the left for 10 in this column.

chapter.title: Winning move in a take-away game
text: Work backwards from the end. Some numbers of counters are "safe" to leave for the other player: from them, whatever they take, you can get back to the next safe number.
If each turn takes 1 to k, the safe numbers go up in steps of k + 1 (0, k + 1, 2(k + 1) … when the last counter wins; 1 more than these when it loses). Take enough to leave a safe number.
math: There are 26 counters in the picture. Two players take turns. On each turn a player removes 1, 2 or 3 counters. The player who takes the last counter wins. It is your turn. How many counters should you take now so that you can always win?
Whatever the other player takes, you can make the pair of turns add up to 4. So leave a number that is a multiple of 4
26 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 2: take 2

chapter.title: River-crossing puzzles: the fewest crossings
text: Act the puzzle out one trip at a time and look for the pattern that repeats. A round trip (across and back) is what moves people, and the boat's rower has to come back each time.
Work out what one full round achieves (how many more people end up across), count how many rounds are needed before the last trip, then add the last trip.
math: 16 scouts must cross a river in one small boat. The boat holds at most 2 people, and someone must be in it to row it, so after each trip across someone rows it back. What is the smallest number of crossings needed to get all 16 scouts across?
Each round trip (across and back) leaves 1 more person on the far bank, because one rows the boat back
Before the last trip, 14 people must be moved by round trips: 14 ÷ 1 rounded up = 14 round trips
28 crossings for the round trips + 1 last trip with a full boat = 29

screens.title: The method
text: Start from the ones column and move left. In each column, note whether the column regroups: a ten carried (addition) or 1 exchanged for 10 in the column on the right (subtraction), then find the digit that makes the hidden column right. Check by doing the whole calculation.
math: Find the missing digit: 387 − 169 = □18. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right needs no regrouping (nothing is carried or exchanged)
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 2

screens.title: Try the digits and check
text: Put a digit in the box and work out the whole sum.
If it is not right, see whether the answer came out too big or too small and try a better digit. Only one digit works.
math: Find the missing digit: 5□4 + 281 = 835. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right needs no regrouping (nothing is carried or exchanged)
Work the hidden column, using the carry: the missing digit is 5

screens.title: Undo the operation
text: A missing part of an addition is total − other part.
A missing first number of a subtraction is answer + number taken away. Work out that calculation and read off the digit.
math: Find the missing digit: 8□1 − 363 = 508. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right is regrouped: 1 from this column is exchanged for 10 there, so this column has 1 less
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 7

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the missing digit: 427 + 405 = 8□2. Which digit goes in the box □?” A common wrong answer is 2.
The ten carried from the column on the right was forgotten. When a column adds up to 10 or more, 1 goes to the next column.
math: Not 2, but 3

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Subtract with regrouping. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Start from the ones column and move left. In each column, note whether the column regroups: a ten carried (addition) or 1 exchanged for 10 in the column on the right (subtraction), then find the digit that makes the hidden column right. Check by doing the whole calculation.

modules.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)

chapter.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)
text: Every choice from one group can be matched with every choice from the next, so the number of combinations is the product of the numbers of choices.
math: The table shows Imran's 2 shirts and 3 pairs of shorts. An outfit is one shirt with one pair of shorts. How many different outfits are possible?
Each of the 2 first choices goes with each of the 3 second choices: 2 × 3 = 6
chapter.tip: The numbers of choices were added. Each choice from the first group goes with every choice from the next, so multiply.

chapter.title: How many numbers can be made from given digits
text: Fill the places one at a time from the left. The number of ways is the product of the choices for each place.
Count the choices for the first place (0 is not allowed there), then for the next place (one fewer if digits cannot repeat), and so on; multiply.
math: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make from the digits 3, 5, 7, 0, if a digit may be used more than once?
Choices for each place, from the left: 3 × 4
Multiply the choices: 3 × 4 = 12

chapter.title: Counting the rectangles, squares or triangles hidden in a figure
text: Counting hidden figures goes wrong when we just look and count. Instead, describe each figure by the lines that make it, and count the choices of lines systematically.

Rectangles in a grid: choose 2 of the upright lines and 2 of the lines across, and multiply the numbers of ways. Squares: count each size separately and add. Triangles from one corner: choose 2 of the lines from the corner, times the number of lines across.
math: The picture shows a rectangle divided into a grid of 3 rows and 6 columns of small squares. How many rectangles of any size can you find in it?
A rectangle needs 2 of the 7 upright lines: 21 ways
and 2 of the 4 lines across: 6 ways
Altogether 126

screens.title: The method
text: Fix the first choice and count how many ways the rest can go; that number is the same for every first choice, so multiply. With a third group, multiply again.
math: The table shows a canteen's 6 main dishes, 2 side dishes and 3 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 6 first choices goes with each of the 2 second choices: 6 × 2 = 12
Each of those 12 goes with each of the 3 last choices: 12 × 3 = 36

screens.title: Make an organised list
text: Take the first shirt and list it with every skirt, then the second shirt with every skirt, and so on.
Each row of the list has the same length, so the total is rows × length of a row.
math: The table shows a canteen's 6 main dishes, 2 side dishes and 4 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 6 first choices goes with each of the 2 second choices: 6 × 2 = 12
Each of those 12 goes with each of the 4 last choices: 12 × 4 = 48

screens.title: Draw a tree
text: Draw one branch for each first choice; from the end of each, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches.
math: The table shows a canteen's 3 main dishes, 3 side dishes and 2 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 3 first choices goes with each of the 3 second choices: 3 × 3 = 9
Each of those 9 goes with each of the 2 last choices: 9 × 2 = 18

text: A question: “The table shows a canteen's 2 main dishes, 2 side dishes and 2 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?” A common wrong answer is 6.
The numbers of choices were added. Each choice from the first group goes with every choice from the next, so multiply.

modules.title: Reading a pie chart

chapter.title: Reading a pie chart
text: A pie chart shows the whole group as a full circle; each part's size is a fraction of the whole group.
math: The pie chart shows how the 24 children of a school travel to school. How many children come by bus?
chapter.tip: The number for all the other parts was found instead of this part.

chapter.title: Sector angles in a pie chart
text: The whole group is the whole circle, 360°. Each part gets the same fraction of 360° as it is of the group.
Angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. Going back: part = (angle ÷ 360°) × total.
math: In a class of 20 students, 11 chose cricket as their favourite game. In a pie chart of the whole class, what angle (in degrees) does the cricket sector make at the centre?
Fraction of the whole: 11 out of 20 = 11/20

screens.title: The method
text: Find the fraction for the part (the whole circle is 1, so a missing part is 1 minus the others). Then find that fraction of the total: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top.
math: The pie chart shows how the 48 children of a school travel to school. One part's fraction is not written. How many children come by cycle?
The whole circle is 1, so the missing part is 1 − 3/4 = 1/4

screens.title: Cut into equal pieces
text: Imagine the circle cut into equal pieces (for example 8 eighths). Share the total equally among the pieces.
Count how many pieces the part covers, and add up their shares.
math: The pie chart shows how the 40 people in a survey chose their favourite fruit. How many people chose apple?

chapter.title: Reading a bar chart with a scale

screens.title: Skip-count up the scale
text: Put a finger at the bottom of the bar and count up the lines in steps of the scale: 5, 10, 15 …
Stop at the top of the bar: that number is its value.
math: The bar chart shows mangoes sold at a shop. Read the scale carefully. How many mangoes were sold on Friday?
The bar reaches 8 lines; each line is 50, so it shows 400

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The bar chart shows saplings planted by each class. Read the scale carefully. How many saplings were planted by Class 2?” A common wrong answer is 9.
The lines were counted as 1 each. On this chart each line on the scale stands for 50.
math: Not 9, but 450

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Read simple bar charts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find how much one line stands for (the difference between two numbers on the scale). Read each bar against the scale, then add or subtract as the question asks.

modules.title: Writing a number rule with a letter

chapter.title: Writing a number rule with a letter
text: A letter stands for any number. A rule written with the letter works for every number at once.
math: A number machine adds 11 to any number put in. The number put in is x. Write the number that comes out, using x.
Start with x and do what the machine does: x + 11
chapter.tip: 11x means 11 × x. Adding 11 is written x + 11.

chapter.title: Writing the rule of a growing pattern with a letter
text: If a pattern grows by the same amount each time, that amount is the number multiplied by n; a fixed extra makes the first shape right.
Find how much the pattern grows each time (say 3): the rule starts 3n. Compare 3 × 1 with shape 1 to find what to add. Check with shape 4.
math: The table shows the number of matchsticks in the first four shapes of a growing pattern. Write a rule for the number of matchsticks in shape n.
Each shape has 2 more than the one before (9 − 7)
2 × 1 = 2, and shape 1 has 7, so add 5
Rule: 2n + 5

screens.title: The method
text: Do to the letter exactly what you would do to a number: 'add 5' gives n + 5; 'multiply by 4' gives 4n (4 × n). Test your rule with a small number.
math: A number machine multiplies any number put in by 2, then adds 3. The number put in is m. Write the number that comes out, using m.
Start with m and do what the machine does: 2m + 3

screens.title: Try numbers first
text: Make a small table: put in 1, 2, 3 and write what comes out.
Look at what you did to each number every time, and write the same thing with the letter.
math: A number machine multiplies any number put in by 2, then adds 8. The number put in is m. Write the number that comes out, using m.
Start with m and do what the machine does: 2m + 8

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A number machine multiplies any number put in by 2, then adds 1. The number put in is m. Write the number that comes out, using m.” A common wrong answer is m + 3.
Multiplying by 2 was written as adding 2.
math: Not m + 3, but 2m + 1

modules.title: Continuing square, triangular and other number patterns

chapter.title: Odd numbers
text: The odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 go up by the same amount each time: the gap is always 2.
A pattern with a constant gap of 2 that starts at 1 has the rule 2 × n − 1.
math: The table shows the first four odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. What is the 13th number in this pattern?
The rule for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd … number: 2 × n − 1
For n = 13: 25
chapter.tip: The 13th odd number is 2 × 13 − 1; 2 × 13 + 1 is the next one.

chapter.title: Links between square, odd and triangular numbers
text: Dot pictures show the links: odd numbers wrap round a square to make the next square; two neighbouring triangles fit together into a square.
Draw (or imagine) the dot picture. Going from n × n to (n + 1) × (n + 1) adds n + n + 1 dots, an odd number; so adding the odd numbers from 1 gives the square numbers.
math: How much bigger is the 9th square number (9 × 9) than the 8th square number (8 × 8)?
From 8 × 8 to the next square add a row, a column and a corner: 8 + 8 + 1 = 17

chapter.title: Which rule makes the sequence?
text: A rule must explain EVERY number of the sequence, not just the first step. Look at the steps between numbers: equal steps mean 'add the same each time'; steps that grow by 1 give triangular numbers, by 2 square numbers; numbers that double are powers of 2.
Write the steps (differences) between neighbouring numbers. If they are equal, the rule adds that number. If not, test the special sequences (squares, triangular, cubes, doubling) on all the numbers.
math: Look at the sequence 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, … Which rule makes it?
The steps from one number to the next are 32, 64, 128, 256
The rule that fits every number: Each number is double the one before (powers of 2)

screens.title: Triangular numbers, step by step
text: The n-th triangular number is 1 + 2 + … + n, which is half of n × (n + 1).
math: The table shows the first four triangular numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10. What is the 8th number in this pattern?
The rule for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd … number: n × (n + 1) ÷ 2
For n = 8: 36

screens.title: Look at the gaps
text: For the rectangular numbers 2, 6, 12, 20 the gaps are +4, +6, +8: each gap is 2 more than the one before.
Keep adding the next gap until you reach the term you need, or use the rule to jump straight there.
math: The table shows the first four rectangular numbers (each picture has one more column than rows): 2, 6, 12, 20. What is the 5th number in this pattern?
The rule for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd … number: n × (n + 1)
For n = 5: 30

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The table shows the first four square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16. What is the 15th number in this pattern?” A common wrong answer is 93.
The last gap (7) was added again and again. In this pattern the gap changes each time.
math: Not 93, but 225

modules.title: Reading an angle from a protractor

chapter.title: Reading an angle from a protractor
text: A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions. Both arms must be read on the same scale; the angle is how far apart the readings are.
math: A protractor is placed with its centre on the corner of an angle. One arm passes through the mark that reads 145 on the inner scale and 35 on the outer scale. The other arm passes through the mark that reads 75 on the inner scale and 105 on the outer scale. What is the size of the angle, in degrees?
Use one scale for both arms (here the inner one): the readings are 145 and 75
The angle is the difference: 145 − 75 = 70°
chapter.tip: One reading came from the inner scale and the other from the outer scale. Use the same scale for both arms.

screens.title: The method
text: Put the centre on the corner. Find the scale that reads 0 on one arm (or use either scale for both arms). Read the other arm on that same scale; if neither arm is on 0, subtract the smaller reading from the larger.
math: A protractor is placed with its centre on the corner of an angle. One arm passes through the mark that reads 40 on the inner scale and 140 on the outer scale. The other arm passes through the mark that reads 145 on the inner scale and 35 on the outer scale. What is the size of the angle, in degrees?
Use one scale for both arms (here the inner one): the readings are 40 and 145
The angle is the difference: 145 − 40 = 105°

screens.title: Estimate first
text: Look at the angle: is it smaller than a right angle (less than 90°) or bigger?
If your reading says acute but the angle looks obtuse (or the other way round), you read the wrong scale.
math: A protractor is placed with its centre on the corner of an angle. One arm passes through the mark that reads 145 on the inner scale and 35 on the outer scale. The other arm passes through the mark that reads 70 on the inner scale and 110 on the outer scale. What is the size of the angle, in degrees?
Use one scale for both arms (here the inner one): the readings are 145 and 70
The angle is the difference: 145 − 70 = 75°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A protractor is placed with its centre on the corner of an angle. One arm passes through the mark that reads 5 on the inner scale and 175 on the outer scale. The other arm passes through the mark that reads 135 on the inner scale and 45 on the outer scale. What is the size of the angle, in degrees?” A common wrong answer is 40.
One reading came from the inner scale and the other from the outer scale. Use the same scale for both arms.
math: Not 40, but 130
