modules.title: Missing angle in a complementary or supplementary pair

chapter.title: Missing angle in a complementary or supplementary pair
text: Complementary angles together make a right angle (90°); supplementary angles together make a straight angle (180°).
math: Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 130°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
Supplementary angles add up to 180°
chapter.tip: 360° is a full turn. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.

chapter.title: Angles where two straight lines cross
text: Where two straight lines cross, angles next to each other make a straight line (180°), so opposite angles are equal; all four make a full turn (360°).
Opposite angle: the same. Angle next to it: 180° minus it. All the others together: 360° minus it.
math: Two straight lines cross each other, making four angles. One of the angles is 149°. What is an angle next to it (they form a straight line together), in degrees?
Angles on a straight line add to 180°: 180° − 149° = 31°

screens.title: The method
text: Take the given angle away from 90° (complementary) or 180° (supplementary). Check: the two angles should add up to the total.
math: Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 133°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
Supplementary angles add up to 180°

screens.title: Count on to the total
text: Start at the angle you know and count on to 90 (or 180), in tens and then ones.
math: Two angles are supplementary. One of them is 135°. What is the other angle, in degrees?
Supplementary angles add up to 180°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Two angles are complementary. One of them is 36°. What is the other angle, in degrees?” A common wrong answer is 144.
Complementary angles make a right angle, 90°. 180° is for supplementary angles.
math: Not 144, but 54

modules.title: Turns between compass directions as fractions of a full turn

chapter.title: Turns between compass directions as fractions of a full turn
text: A full turn brings you back to where you started. The four main directions split it into quarters; with the in-between directions (North-East and so on) it is split into eighths.
math: Anu is facing North-West. Anu turns clockwise until facing South-East. What fraction of a full turn is that?
Count the steps clockwise from North-West to South-East: 4 eighths
4 out of 8 steps = 1/2 of a full turn
chapter.tip: Each step between neighbouring directions was counted as a quarter turn. With the in-between directions (North-East …) there are 8 steps in a full turn, so each is one eighth.

chapter.title: Degrees turned by the minute hand
text: The minute hand makes a full turn (360°) in an hour, passing 12 numbers, so it turns 30° from one number to the next.
Count how many numbers the hand moves past (clockwise), then multiply by 30°. A quarter turn (3 numbers) is 90°; a half turn (6 numbers) is 180°.
math: The minute hand of the clock in the picture points to 10. It turns clockwise until it points to 7. Through how many degrees has it turned?
12 numbers share a full turn: 360° ÷ 12 = 30° from one number to the next
9 numbers × 30° = 270°

chapter.title: The compass direction faced after a turn
text: The eight compass directions split a full turn into eight equal steps; a quarter turn is two steps and a half turn is four. Clockwise goes North → East → South → West.
Change the turn into eighths (a quarter = 2, a half = 4, three quarters = 6), then count that many steps round the compass, the way of the turn.
math: Kavya is facing North and makes a half turn anticlockwise. Which direction is Kavya facing now?
The turn is 4 eighths of a full turn: 4 steps round the 8 directions
Count 4 steps anticlockwise from North: South

screens.title: The method
text: Count the steps from the starting direction to the final one, going the way of the turn (clockwise is the way clock hands move). Each step is 1/8 of a turn; two steps make a quarter.
math: Anu is facing North-West. Anu turns anticlockwise until facing South-East. What fraction of a full turn is that?
Count the steps anticlockwise from North-West to South-East: 4 eighths
4 out of 8 steps = 1/2 of a full turn

screens.title: Use a clock face
text: Imagine North at 12, East at 3, South at 6, West at 9.
North to East clockwise is like the minute hand going from 12 to 3: a quarter turn.
math: Arjun is facing East. Arjun turns clockwise until facing North-East. What fraction of a full turn is that?
Count the steps clockwise from East to North-East: 7 eighths
7 out of 8 steps = 7/8 of a full turn

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Imran is facing North. Imran turns clockwise until facing South-West. What fraction of a full turn is that?” A common wrong answer is 3/8.
The turn was counted the other way round. Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move: North → East → South → West.
math: Not 3/8, but 5/8

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Represent fractions of a whole. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Count the steps from the starting direction to the final one, going the way of the turn (clockwise is the way clock hands move). Each step is 1/8 of a turn; two steps make a quarter.

modules.title: Counting the pieces at a stage of a repeating pattern

chapter.title: Counting the pieces at a stage of a repeating pattern
text: In a fractal pattern the same rule is used again and again on every piece, so the number of pieces is multiplied by the same number at every stage.
math: A pattern starts (stage 0) with 2 shaded squares. At each stage, every shaded square is replaced by 2 smaller shaded squares. The table shows stages 0 and 1. How many shaded squares are there at stage 2?
Stage 1: 2 pieces, each replaced by 2: 2 × 2 = 4
Stage 2: 4 pieces, each replaced by 2: 4 × 2 = 8
chapter.tip: The pattern was taken to grow by the same number each stage (2). Every piece is replaced, so the number is multiplied by 2 each stage.

screens.title: The method
text: Start with the pieces at stage 0 and multiply by the number of new pieces each piece becomes, once for every stage. A table of stages helps you keep count.
math: A pattern starts (stage 0) with 2 shaded squares. At each stage, every shaded square is replaced by 4 smaller shaded squares. The table shows stages 0 and 1. How many shaded squares are there at stage 2?
Stage 1: 2 pieces, each replaced by 4: 2 × 4 = 8
Stage 2: 8 pieces, each replaced by 4: 8 × 4 = 32

screens.title: A table of stages
text: Write the stages 0, 1, 2, … in a row.
Under each stage write the number of pieces: each is the one before times the number of new pieces per piece.
math: A pattern starts (stage 0) with 3 shaded squares. At each stage, every shaded square is replaced by 3 smaller shaded squares. The table shows stages 0 and 1. How many shaded squares are there at stage 5?
Stage 1: 3 pieces, each replaced by 3: 3 × 3 = 9
Stage 2: 9 pieces, each replaced by 3: 9 × 3 = 27
Stage 3: 27 pieces, each replaced by 3: 27 × 3 = 81
Stage 4: 81 pieces, each replaced by 3: 81 × 3 = 243
Stage 5: 243 pieces, each replaced by 3: 243 × 3 = 729

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A fractal tree starts (stage 0) with 2 branches. At each stage, every branch tip grows 2 new branches, and each new branch has one tip. The table shows stages 0 and 1. How many branch tips are there at stage 2?” A common wrong answer is 6.
The pattern was taken to grow by the same number each stage (2). Every piece is replaced, so the number is multiplied by 2 each stage.
math: Not 6, but 8

modules.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids

chapter.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids
text: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base joined to a top point by triangles. Counting part by part makes the counts easy.
math: How many edges does a nonagonal pyramid have?
Count base, top and sides: 18
chapter.tip: Only the 9 edges of the base were counted. There are also 9 edges going up to the top point.

chapter.title: Painted faces in a block of small cubes
text: Where a small cube sits decides its paint: corners get three faces, the rest of each edge two, the middle of each face one, and the hidden inside none.
Take 2 off each length (the two outer layers). Edges: 4 × (sum of the shortened lengths). Faces: 2 × (sum of the products of pairs). Inside: the product of all three.
math: A 2 × 3 × 4 block is built from small cubes, as in the picture. The whole outside of the block is painted. How many small cubes have paint on exactly two faces?
Leave out the outside layer on both sides: the inside lengths are 0, 1, 2
Each of the 12 edges has its middle cubes: 4 × (0 + 1 + 2) = 12

chapter.title: Cube nets: opposite faces, and which shapes fold into a cube
text: A net is a solid unfolded flat. For a cube the six squares must fold into six different faces; a square's neighbours in the net become its neighbours on the cube, and the face opposite it is one that never touches it.

Pick a square as the bottom and fold up the squares round it one at a time, saying which face each becomes (front, back, left, right, top). Opposite pairs are bottom–top, front–back, left–right; in a straight row of squares, the squares one apart are opposite.
math: The picture shows a net of a cube with its six squares lettered. When it is folded into a cube, which face is opposite face F?
Folding square by square, face B ends up opposite face F

chapter.title: Matching solids with their nets and views
text: A net is the solid's faces unfolded flat; a view is what you see from one side. Both come from the solid's parts: a prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles, a pyramid a base joined by triangles to a point; a cylinder has two circles and a curved side, a cone one circle and a curved side.

For a net, count the pieces and look at their shapes: the ends or base name the solid. For a view, picture yourself looking from that side: from above you see the base's outline; from the front, straight upright sides look like a rectangle and sides meeting at a point look like a triangle.
math: A cone stands on a table on its base. What do you see when you look at it from the front, at eye level?
The front view of a cone: a triangle

chapter.title: Top, front and side views of a building of cubes
text: A view shows only what faces you: from above, the top of each stack; from the front, the tallest stack in each column (cubes behind are hidden); from the side, the tallest stack in each row.
Top view: count the squares that have cubes. Front view: for each column find the biggest number and add these. Side view: for each row find the biggest number and add these.
math: The table is a plan of a building made of cubes standing on a mat: each number tells how many cubes are stacked on that square. The front of the building is the bottom row of the table. When you look at the building from the front, how many squares do you see?
The tallest stack in each column: 3, 2, 3
Add them: 8 squares

screens.title: The method
text: Prism on an n-sided base: faces n + 2, edges 3n, vertices 2n. Pyramid: faces n + 1, edges 2n, vertices n + 1. Check with Euler's rule: faces + vertices − edges = 2.
math: How many vertices (corners) does a heptagonal prism have?
Count base, top and sides: 14

screens.title: Count part by part
text: Count the base, then the top (or the top point), then what joins them.
For edges: round the bottom, round the top, then the ones going up.
math: A solid with flat faces has 12 vertices and 18 edges. Using Euler's rule (faces + vertices − edges = 2), how many faces does it have?
Rearrange faces + vertices − edges = 2 for the missing count: 8

screens.title: Unfold it into a net
text: Imagine cutting the solid open and laying it flat: each face becomes one shape of the net.
Count the shapes in the net to get the faces.
math: How many vertices (corners) does a hexagonal pyramid have?
Count base, top and sides: 7

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A solid with flat faces has 10 faces and 10 vertices. Using Euler's rule (faces + vertices − edges = 2), how many edges does it have?” A common wrong answer is 22.
Faces + vertices − edges = 2, so edges = faces + vertices − 2 (take 2 away, not add it).
math: Not 22, but 18

modules.title: Classifying quadrilaterals from their sides and angles

chapter.title: Classifying quadrilaterals from their sides and angles
text: Shape names describe properties, so one shape can have several names: a square is a rectangle (four right angles), a rhombus (four equal sides) and a parallelogram (opposite sides equal and parallel).
math: The table describes five quadrilaterals, A to E. The sides and the angles are listed in order going round each shape. How many of the five are rhombuses?
Name each shape by its sides and angles: parallelogram, parallelogram, parallelogram, rectangle, square
Count every shape that fits (including the special ones): 1
chapter.tip: The squares were left out. A rhombus has four equal sides, so every square is also a rhombus.

chapter.title: Unknown angles in a parallelogram or rhombus
text: In a parallelogram (and so in a rhombus) opposite angles are equal, and angles next to each other add up to 180°. In a rhombus each diagonal also cuts its angles in half.
Opposite angle: the same. Neighbouring angle: 180° minus it. Rhombus diagonal: half the angle it starts from.
math: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A is 130°. What is angle C (opposite A), in degrees?
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: 130°

chapter.title: Naming a quadrilateral from its properties (kites and trapeziums included)
text: Each name is a list of properties. A square has every property; a kite has two pairs of equal sides NEXT to each other; a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides. The best name is the most special one whose properties all hold.

Check, in order: both pairs of opposite sides parallel? (parallelogram family: then all sides equal → rhombus, right angles → rectangle, both → square). Exactly one pair parallel? → trapezium. No parallel sides but two pairs of equal neighbouring sides? → kite.
math: The table describes quadrilateral ABCD (the sides are listed in order round the shape). Which name describes it best, the most special name that fits?
The sides in order are 7, 6, 7, 6 (cm)
Parallel sides: AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC
So the most special name is parallelogram

chapter.title: Unknown sides of a parallelogram or rhombus
text: In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is twice (one side + the next side). In a rhombus all four sides are equal.

Parallelogram: halve the perimeter and take away the side you know. Rhombus: divide the perimeter by 4. When sides are given as expressions, set the two equal sides equal, solve for x, then substitute.
math: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = (2x + 4) cm and CD = (4x − 2) cm. What is the length of AB, in cm?
The two sides are equal: 2x + 4 = 4x − 2, so x = 3
The side is 2 × 3 + 4 = 10 cm

screens.title: The method
text: For each shape, check the property the name needs. Rectangle: all angles 90°. Rhombus: all sides equal. Parallelogram: opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal. Count every shape that has it.
math: The table describes five quadrilaterals, A to E. The sides and the angles are listed in order going round each shape. How many of the five are parallelograms?
Name each shape by its sides and angles: parallelogram, rectangle, parallelogram, square, rhombus
Count every shape that fits (including the special ones): 5

screens.title: A family tree of shapes
text: Parallelograms are a big family. Rectangles and rhombuses are inside it, and squares are inside both rectangles and rhombuses.
When you count a family, count everyone inside it too.
math: The table describes five quadrilaterals, A to E. The sides and the angles are listed in order going round each shape. How many of the five are rhombuses?
Name each shape by its sides and angles: rectangle, rectangle, square, parallelogram, rectangle
Count every shape that fits (including the special ones): 1

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The table describes five quadrilaterals, A to E. The sides and the angles are listed in order going round each shape. How many of the five are parallelograms?” A common wrong answer is 1.
Only the slanted shapes with unequal sides were counted. Squares, rectangles and rhombuses also have opposite sides equal and parallel, so they are parallelograms too.
math: Not 1, but 5

modules.title: Order and angle of rotational symmetry

chapter.title: Order and angle of rotational symmetry
text: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than a full turn. The order is how many times it fits onto itself in one full turn.
math: A parallelogram with no right angles and unequal sides is turned about its centre. What is the smallest angle, in degrees, after which it looks exactly the same?
It looks the same 2 times in a full turn
360° ÷ 2 = 180° each time
chapter.tip: 180° was shared out instead of a full turn, 360°.

screens.title: The method
text: Count the identical parts that go round the centre (sides of a regular shape, blades, petals): that is usually the order. The smallest turn is 360° ÷ order, which is 1/order of a full turn.
math: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a regular pentagon
It looks the same 5 times in a full turn

screens.title: Trace and turn
text: Trace the shape on thin paper, put a pin through the centre and turn the tracing slowly.
Count each time the tracing sits exactly on the shape before you get back to the start.
math: A paper windmill with 4 identical blades is turned about its centre. What is the smallest angle, in degrees, after which it looks exactly the same?
It looks the same 4 times in a full turn
360° ÷ 4 = 90° each time

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A regular dodecagon (a shape with 12 equal sides) (as in the picture) is turned about its centre. It looks exactly the same several times during a full turn. At what angle, in degrees, does it look the same for the 10th time?” A common wrong answer is 330.
The starting position was counted as the first time. The first time it looks the same is after the smallest turn.
math: Not 330, but 300

modules.title: Classifying triangles by their angles

chapter.title: Classifying triangles by their angles
text: Every triangle has at least two acute angles, so the type is decided by its largest angle: less than 90° acute-angled, exactly 90° right-angled, more than 90° obtuse-angled.
math: The table gives the three angles of five triangles, A to E. How many of them are obtuse-angled?
The largest angle decides: acute-angled, right-angled, acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled
Count them: 1
chapter.tip: A 90° angle was counted as obtuse. Obtuse means more than 90°.

chapter.title: Classifying triangles by their sides
text: Triangles are named by how many sides are equal: all three equal is equilateral, exactly two equal is isosceles (with two equal sides), none equal is scalene.
For each triangle compare the three lengths in pairs (first and second, second and third, first and third). Count the equal pairs, name the triangle, then count the ones asked for.
math: The table gives the side lengths of five triangles, A to E. How many of them are scalene (no two sides equal)?
Compare the three sides of each: equilateral, scalene, equilateral, isosceles, isosceles
Count them: 1

screens.title: The method
text: For each triangle find the largest angle and compare it with 90°. Then count the ones asked for.
math: The table gives the three angles of five triangles, A to E. How many of them are obtuse-angled?
The largest angle decides: right-angled, obtuse-angled, acute-angled, right-angled, right-angled
Count them: 1

screens.title: The square-corner test
text: Hold the corner of a sheet of paper (a right angle) against each angle.
If one angle fits exactly it is right-angled; if one is wider it is obtuse-angled; if all are narrower it is acute-angled.
math: The table gives the three angles of five triangles, A to E. How many of them are obtuse-angled?
The largest angle decides: right-angled, acute-angled, obtuse-angled, obtuse-angled, acute-angled
Count them: 2

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The table gives the three angles of five triangles, A to E. How many of them are obtuse-angled?” A common wrong answer is 3.
A 90° angle was counted as obtuse. Obtuse means more than 90°.
math: Not 3, but 1

modules.title: Rectangles with the same area or the same perimeter

chapter.title: Rectangles with the same area or the same perimeter
text: Area counts the squares inside; perimeter is the distance round the edge. Rearranging the same squares can change the perimeter, and the same length of fence can enclose different areas.
math: The rectangle in the picture is 10 cm long and 2 cm wide (each square is 1 cm by 1 cm). Another rectangle has the same area, and one of its sides is 1 cm. What is the perimeter of the other rectangle, in cm?
Area of the first rectangle: 10 × 2 = 20 square cm
The other side: 20 ÷ 1 = 20 cm
Perimeter: 2 × (1 + 20) = 42 cm
chapter.tip: Rectangles with the same area do not always have the same perimeter. Find the other side first, then go round the new rectangle.

screens.title: The method
text: Same area: find the other side by dividing the area by the side you know, then add all four sides. Same perimeter: half the perimeter is one long side plus one short side, so take away the side you know, then multiply.
math: The rectangle in the picture is 9 cm long and 3 cm wide (each square is 1 cm by 1 cm). Another rectangle has the same perimeter, and one of its sides is 1 cm. What is the area of the other rectangle, in square cm?
Perimeter: 2 × (9 + 3) = 24 cm
The other side: 12 − 1 = 11 cm
Area of the first rectangle: 1 × 11 = 11 square cm

screens.title: Rearrange the squares
text: Imagine cutting the rectangle into its unit squares and laying them out in rows of the new length.
Count the rows to get the other side, then walk round the edge to get the perimeter.
math: The rectangle in the picture is 11 cm long and 8 cm wide (each square is 1 cm by 1 cm). Another rectangle has the same area, and one of its sides is 22 cm. What is the perimeter of the other rectangle, in cm?
Area of the first rectangle: 11 × 8 = 88 square cm
The other side: 88 ÷ 22 = 4 cm
Perimeter: 2 × (22 + 4) = 52 cm

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The rectangle in the picture is 12 cm long and 9 cm wide (each square is 1 cm by 1 cm). Another rectangle has the same area, and one of its sides is 4 cm. What is the perimeter of the other rectangle, in cm?” A common wrong answer is 42.
Rectangles with the same area do not always have the same perimeter. Find the other side first, then go round the new rectangle.
math: Not 42, but 62

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Calculate rectangle area; Calculate rectangle perimeter. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Same area: find the other side by dividing the area by the side you know, then add all four sides. Same perimeter: half the perimeter is one long side plus one short side, so take away the side you know, then multiply.

modules.title: Distance covered in one hour or one minute

chapter.title: Distance covered in one hour or one minute
text: Speed tells how far something goes in ONE hour (or one minute). If the speed is steady, every hour covers the same part of the journey.
math: A girl walks 126 metres in 2 minutes, walking the same distance every minute. How many metres does she walk in 1 minute?
126 metres are covered in 2 equal minutes
Share it equally: 126 ÷ 2 = 63 in each one
chapter.tip: The distance was multiplied by the time. In 1 minute the distance is less than the whole journey, so share it out: divide by 2.

chapter.title: Comparing two speeds from distance and time
text: To compare speeds fairly, compare the distance each covers in the SAME time: one minute (or one hour).
For each one, divide distance by time to get the distance in 1 minute. The bigger result is the faster one.
math: The table shows how far Priya and Meena cycled and how long each took, each at a steady speed. How many metres in 1 minute does the faster child cycle?
Priya: 195 m ÷ 5 minutes = 39 m in each minute
Meena: 240 m ÷ 3 minutes = 80 m in each minute
39 and 80 metres a minute: the faster speed is 80 metres a minute

screens.title: The method
text: Share the whole distance equally among the hours: distance ÷ time. Check by multiplying back.
math: A van travels 138 km in 2 hours, going the same distance every hour. How many km does it travel in 1 hour?
138 km are covered in 2 equal hours
Share it equally: 138 ÷ 2 = 69 in each one

screens.title: Build an hour-by-hour table
text: Make a table: after 1 hour, after 2 hours, and so on.
Guess the distance for 1 hour, keep adding it, and adjust the guess until the last row gives the whole distance.
math: A van travels 70 km in 2 hours, going the same distance every hour. How many km does it travel in 1 hour?
70 km are covered in 2 equal hours
Share it equally: 70 ÷ 2 = 35 in each one

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A girl walks 248 metres in 4 minutes, walking the same distance every minute. How many metres does she walk in 1 minute?” A common wrong answer is 992.
The distance was multiplied by the time. In 1 minute the distance is less than the whole journey, so share it out: divide by 4.
math: Not 992, but 62

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Divide multi-digit numbers. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Share the whole distance equally among the hours: distance ÷ time. Check by multiplying back.

modules.title: Adding and subtracting decimals with different places

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting decimals with different places
text: Each place has a value: ones, tenths, hundredths. Only digits of the same place can be added or taken away, so the decimal points must line up.
math: Work out 15.2 + 2.38.
Line up the decimal points: 15.2 = 15.20
15.20 + 2.38 = 17.58, column by column from the hundredths
chapter.tip: The digits were lined up from the right, as for whole numbers, so tenths were added to hundredths. Line up the decimal points: write 15.2 as 15.20.

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting money in rupees and paise
text: 100 paise make ₹1. Paise go with paise and rupees with rupees, and 100 paise can be swapped for ₹1 (or ₹1 for 100 paise).
Line up the decimal points. Work on the paise first, exchanging ₹1 and 100 paise when needed, then the rupees.
math: ₹61.95 + ₹22.55 = ? Give the answer in rupees (for example, write 12.50 for ₹12.50).
Paise: 95 + 55 = 150 paise
150 paise = ₹1 and 50 paise: carry ₹1
Rupees: 61 + 22 + 1 carried = ₹84

chapter.title: Measurement problems with two units (m and cm, kg and g, km and m, L and mL)
text: Only amounts in the same unit can be added or taken away. 1 m = 100 cm, and 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 L = 1000 mL, so the smaller unit becomes a decimal of the larger one.
Change the amount in the smaller unit into the larger unit (divide by 100 or 1000), line up the decimal points, then add or subtract.
math: Divya buys 5.7 kg of tomatoes and 450 g of beans. What is the total mass, in kg?
5.7 + 0.45 = 6.15, with the decimal points lined up

screens.title: The method
text: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a line. Fill empty places with 0, then add or subtract from the right as with whole numbers, and keep the point in the answer.
math: Work out 1.6 + 5.93.
Line up the decimal points: 1.6 = 1.60
1.60 + 5.93 = 7.53, column by column from the hundredths

screens.title: Think of rupees and paise
text: Read 4.5 as ₹4.50 and 2.37 as ₹2.37: 50 paise and 37 paise are both paise, so they go together.
Add the paise, then the rupees, exchanging 100 paise for ₹1 when needed.
math: Work out 16.2 + 4.37.
Line up the decimal points: 16.2 = 16.20
16.20 + 4.37 = 20.57, column by column from the hundredths

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Work out 4.4 + 7.24.” A common wrong answer is 7.68.
The digits were lined up from the right, as for whole numbers, so tenths were added to hundredths. Line up the decimal points: write 4.4 as 4.40.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Represent tenths and hundredths. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a line. Fill empty places with 0, then add or subtract from the right as with whole numbers, and keep the point in the answer.

modules.title: The lowest common multiple of two numbers

chapter.title: The lowest common multiple of two numbers
text: A common multiple is in both times tables. The lowest one is the first time they meet.
math: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 13 and 18?
13 and 18 have no common factor other than 1
LCM = 13 × 18 = 234 (check: both 18 and the other number divide it)
chapter.tip: The highest common factor was found. The LCM is the smallest number that BOTH divide into: it is never smaller than the larger number.

chapter.title: The highest common factor of three numbers
text: The HCF is the biggest number that divides every one of the numbers exactly.
Find the HCF of the first two numbers, then find the HCF of that result and the third number.
math: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 28, 64 and 68?
HCF of 28 and 64 is 4
Now with 68: the HCF of 4 and 68 is 4

chapter.title: Which pair of numbers is co-prime?
text: Co-prime numbers have no common factor except 1, so their HCF is 1. Neither number needs to be prime: 8 and 15 are co-prime, but 9 and 15 are not.
For each pair, test the small primes 2, 3, 5, 7, … : if one of them divides both numbers, the pair is not co-prime. If none does, it is.
math: Two numbers are co-prime when their only common factor is 1. Which pair of numbers is co-prime?
HCF of 13 and 39 is 13
HCF of 20 and 34 is 2
HCF of 39 and 65 is 13
HCF of 26 and 35 is 1: co-prime

chapter.title: The lowest common multiple of three numbers
text: The LCM of three numbers is the smallest number in all three times tables.
Find the LCM of two of the numbers, then the LCM of that and the third. Or go up the times table of the largest number until the other two both divide it.
math: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 4, 6 and 14?
LCM of 4 and 6 is 12
LCM of 12 and 14 is 84

chapter.title: Sharing, grouping and timing problems: HCF or LCM?
text: Sharing or cutting into the biggest equal parts with nothing left over uses the HCF (it divides both). Waiting for two repeating events to happen together, or buying equal amounts in packets, uses the LCM (both divide it).
Ask: is the answer smaller than the numbers (a part of them)? Then it is the HCF. Is it bigger (a time or amount both reach)? Then it is the LCM. Then work it out.
math: A school has 32 girls and 80 boys going on a trip. They must be put into groups of the same size, each group all girls or all boys. What is the largest possible group size?
The parts must divide both amounts exactly and be as large as possible: use the HCF
HCF of 32 and 80 = 16

chapter.title: Using HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
text: For two numbers, HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers: the common prime factors are counted once in the HCF and the rest in the LCM, so together they use every prime factor of both numbers exactly once.
Write HCF × LCM = first number × second number, put in the three values you know, and divide to find the fourth.
math: The HCF of 22 and 99 is 11. Use HCF × LCM = product of the numbers to find their LCM.

screens.title: The method
text: Go up the times table of the larger number and stop at the first one the smaller number divides exactly.
math: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 13 and 19?
13 and 19 have no common factor other than 1
LCM = 13 × 19 = 247 (check: both 19 and the other number divide it)

screens.title: Use prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 14 = 2 × 7.
Take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either: 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 84.
math: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 12 and 14?
The highest common factor of 12 and 14 is 2
LCM = 6 × 14 = 84 (check: both 14 and the other number divide it)

screens.title: Divide both together
text: Divide both numbers by a common factor and write the quotients below; repeat until no common factor is left.
Multiply the divisors on the left by the numbers left at the bottom.
math: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 11 and 22?
The highest common factor of 11 and 22 is 11
LCM = 1 × 22 = 22 (check: both 22 and the other number divide it)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 12 and 16?” A common wrong answer is 192.
12 × 16 is a common multiple, but 12 and 16 share the factor 4, so a smaller one comes first.
math: Not 192, but 48

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Go up the times table of the larger number and stop at the first one the smaller number divides exactly.

modules.title: Writing a mixed number as an improper fraction

chapter.title: Writing a mixed number as an improper fraction
text: A whole cut into d equal pieces is d/d. So w wholes are w × d pieces, and the fraction part adds a few more pieces of the same size.
math: Write the mixed number 4 5/7 as an improper fraction (for example 7/3).
4 wholes = 4 × 7 = 28 pieces
28 + 5 = 33 pieces in all
chapter.tip: 4 was added to the numerator. Each whole is 7/7, so 4 wholes are 28 pieces of size 1/7.

chapter.title: Writing an improper fraction as a mixed number
text: A whole is made of d pieces of size 1/d. Dividing the numerator by the denominator tells how many wholes there are; the remainder is the pieces left.
Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays the same.
math: Write 33/5 as a mixed number (for example 2 1/3).
33 ÷ 5 = 6 whole ones
33 − 30 = 3 pieces left over

chapter.title: Fractions greater than 1 on a number line
text: On a number line every whole is cut into equal parts. A fraction greater than 1 lies beyond 1: its whole-number part says how many wholes are passed, and the fraction part how far into the next whole.
Count the jumps: that many parts is (jumps)/(parts in a whole). Take out the whole ones (each is one full set of parts) and write the rest as the fraction part; simplify it.
math: Meena starts at 0 and makes 30 equal jumps of 1/7 along the number line in the picture. At which number does she land? Write it as a mixed number in its simplest form (for example 2 1/3).
30 jumps of 1/7 take her to 30/7
30/7 = 4 2/7: count the whole ones (each is 7 jumps) and the jumps left over

chapter.title: Proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers
text: A proper fraction is less than 1 (top smaller than bottom). An improper fraction has the top equal to or bigger than the bottom, so it is 1 or more. A mixed number writes a value over 1 as a whole number and a proper fraction.
Is there a whole number in front? Then it is a mixed number. If not, compare the top and the bottom: top smaller → proper; top equal or bigger → improper.
math: What kind of number is 31/12?
31/12 is an improper fraction

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and write the total over the same denominator.
math: Write the mixed number 9 5/7 as an improper fraction (for example 7/3).
9 wholes = 9 × 7 = 63 pieces
63 + 5 = 68 pieces in all

screens.title: Cut every whole into pieces
text: Draw each whole as a bar cut into the same number of pieces as the denominator.
Count all the pieces, including the extra ones: that count goes on top.
math: Write the mixed number 9 5/6 as an improper fraction (for example 7/3).
9 wholes = 9 × 6 = 54 pieces
54 + 5 = 59 pieces in all

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write the mixed number 6 3/10 as an improper fraction (for example 7/3).” A common wrong answer is 9/10.
6 was added to the numerator. Each whole is 10/10, so 6 wholes are 60 pieces of size 1/10.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and write the total over the same denominator.

modules.title: Order of operations with brackets

chapter.title: Order of operations with brackets
text: Everyone agrees on one order so an expression has only one value: brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −; equal ranks go from left to right.
math: Work out 4 × (12 − 4).
Brackets first: 12 − 4 = 8
Then 4 × 8 = 32
chapter.tip: The brackets were ignored. Work out what is inside the brackets first.

chapter.title: Writing an expression for a situation
text: An expression is the story written in numbers and signs. Brackets show what must be worked out first; without brackets, × and ÷ are done before + and −.
Say the story in steps: what is there at the start, what is added or taken away, what is repeated. Write each step, and put brackets round anything that must happen before a multiplication.
math: Farhan has ₹33 and buys 4 pens costing ₹4 each. How many rupees are left? Which expression gives the answer?
The story is 33 − 4 × 4

chapter.title: The terms of an expression
text: The terms of an expression are the parts joined by + and − (outside brackets). Each term carries the sign in front of it: 20 − 3 × 4 + 6 is 20 + (−12) + 6, with terms 20, −3 × 4 and 6.
Read along the expression and cut it at every + and − that is not inside brackets. Each piece, with the sign before it, is a term; work out each term on its own.
math: How many terms does the expression 8 × 9 + (7 + 1) × 7 + 31 + 63 ÷ 9 have?
Cut at each + and − outside brackets: 8 × 9 | +(7 + 1) × 7 | +31 | +63 ÷ 9
4 terms

screens.title: The method
text: Look for brackets and work them out. Next do every × and ÷, left to right. Last do + and −, left to right.
math: Work out 10 − 9 + 10.
Left to right: 10 − 9 = 1

screens.title: Draw it as a tree
text: Put the last operation at the top of a tree, with its two parts as branches: 6 + 4 × 3 has + at the top, with 6 on one branch and 4 × 3 on the other.
Work from the bottom of the tree upwards: 4 × 3 = 12, then 6 + 12 = 18.
math: Work out 12 + 6 × 5.
Multiply first: 6 × 5 = 30

screens.title: Split into terms
text: Cut the expression at every + and − that is not inside brackets: each piece is a term.
Work out each term on its own, then add and take away the terms from left to right.
math: Work out 11 + 8 × 8.
Multiply first: 8 × 8 = 64

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Work out (15 + 6) × 2.” A common wrong answer is 27.
The brackets were ignored. Work out what is inside the brackets first.
math: Not 27, but 42

modules.title: Writing a fraction or decimal as a percentage

chapter.title: Writing a fraction or decimal as a percentage
text: Per cent means 'out of 100'. A percentage is a number of hundredths: 37% = 37/100 = 0.37.
math: Write 0.17 as a percentage.
0.17 is 17 hundredths, so it is 17%

chapter.title: Writing a percentage as a decimal
text: Per cent means hundredths, so x% is x/100. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right of where it was.
Write the percentage over 100, then write it as a decimal: the last two digits of the number become the tenths and hundredths.

0.15 is 15 hundredths, so it is 15%

screens.title: Shade a hundred square

0.34 is 34 hundredths, so it is 34%

modules.title: Listing the prime numbers in a range

chapter.title: Listing the prime numbers in a range
text: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.
math: List all the prime numbers from 34 to 52.
Test each number from 34 to 52 for factors other than 1 and itself: the primes are 37, 41, 43, 47

chapter.title: Testing for primes by dividing up to the square root
text: Factors come in pairs: if n = a × b, one of a and b is at most √n. So if no prime up to √n divides n, n has no factor other than 1 and itself: it is prime.
Find the whole number just below √n (the largest k with k² ≤ n). Divide n by each prime up to k. The first one that divides exactly is the smallest prime factor; if none does, n is prime.
math: To decide whether 541 is prime, Ravi divides it by the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, … in order. If none of them divides 541 exactly, what is the largest prime Ravi needs to have tried before saying 541 is prime?
√541 is a little more than 23 (23² = 529)
The largest prime not more than 23 is 23

screens.title: The method
text: For each number, try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7 (enough up to 100, unless the number is that prime). If none divides it exactly, it is prime.
math: List all the prime numbers from 47 to 61.
Test each number from 47 to 61 for factors other than 1 and itself: the primes are 47, 53, 59, 61

screens.title: Use a sieve
text: Write the numbers in a grid. Cross out 1.
Keep 2 and cross out every other multiple of 2; keep 3 and cross out its multiples; do the same for 5 and 7. The numbers left are prime.
math: List all the prime numbers from 34 to 53.
Test each number from 34 to 53 for factors other than 1 and itself: the primes are 37, 41, 43, 47, 53

screens.title: Only one rectangle
text: Try to arrange the number as dots in a rectangle with more than one row.
If the only rectangle is a single row, the number is prime.
math: List all the prime numbers from 67 to 87.
Test each number from 67 to 87 for factors other than 1 and itself: the primes are 67, 71, 73, 79, 83

modules.title: Finding a counterexample to a claim

chapter.title: Finding a counterexample to a claim
text: A claim that says 'every' must work for ALL numbers. One number where it fails, a counterexample, is enough to show it is not always true; numbers where it works never prove it.
math: Selvi says: "Every number that ends in 6 is a multiple of 4." Selvi tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 106 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample
chapter.tip: 16 agrees with the claim, so it does not show the claim is wrong. To show a claim is not always true, find ONE number where it fails.

screens.title: The method
text: Test each number: does it fit the first part of the claim? If yes, does the rest of the claim hold? The number that fits the first part but not the rest is the counterexample.
math: Farhan says: "Every multiple of 3 is an odd number." Farhan tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 48 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample

screens.title: Two ticks
text: Make two columns: 'is it one the claim talks about?' and 'does the claim hold?'.
The counterexample has a tick in the first column and a cross in the second.
math: Farhan says: "Every multiple of 3 is an odd number." Farhan tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 90 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample

text: A question: “Selvi says: "Every number that ends in 6 is a multiple of 4." Selvi tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?” A common wrong answer is 76.
76 agrees with the claim, so it does not show the claim is wrong. To show a claim is not always true, find ONE number where it fails.
math: Not 76, but 46

modules.title: Solving a one-step equation

chapter.title: Solving a one-step equation
text: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone.
math: Find x: x − 4 = 11.
Add 4 to both sides: x = 11 + 4 = 15
chapter.tip: 4 was taken away from 11; x − 4 = 11 is undone by adding 4 back.

screens.title: The method
text: Look at what is done to x (+, −, ×, ÷). Do the opposite to both sides. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.
math: Find x: x − 4 = 8.
Add 4 to both sides: x = 8 + 4 = 12

screens.title: Guess, check and improve
text: Ask: which number makes the equation true? Try one, work out the left side, and compare.
If the left side is too big, try a smaller number; too small, try a bigger one.
math: Find x: x − 4 = 9.
Add 4 to both sides: x = 9 + 4 = 13

screens.title: Keep the balance level
text: Picture the two sides on a balance.
Whatever you take off or add on one side, do the same on the other, until x is alone.
math: Find x: 3x = 42.
Divide both sides by 3: x = 42 ÷ 3 = 14

text: A question: “Find x: 3x = 33.” A common wrong answer is 30.

modules.title: Collecting like terms

chapter.title: Collecting like terms
text: Like terms have the same letter part: 3x and −5x are like terms, 3x and 2y are not. Like terms can be added because they count the same thing.
math: Simplify 6x + 2y + 4x + 3y.
x terms: 6 + 4 = 10, so 10x
y terms: 2 + 3 = 5, so 5y
Together: 10x + 5y
chapter.tip: x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.

chapter.title: Subtracting one expression from another
text: Taking away a bracket takes away every term inside it, so each sign in the bracket changes: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4.
Remove the brackets, changing every sign in the second one. Then collect the x terms and the number terms.
math: Simplify (7x + 8) − (10x + 12).
−(10x + 12) = −10x − 12: every sign in the bracket changes
x terms: 7x − 10x = −3x
Numbers: 8 − 12 = −4

chapter.title: Coefficients and the constant term
text: An expression is a sum of terms. Each term is a number (the coefficient, with its sign) times letters; a term with no letter is the constant term.
Split the expression at each + or −, keeping the sign with the term after it. The coefficient is the signed number in front of the letters; no number means 1.
math: In the expression 7x² − 8xy − 4y − 4, what is the constant term?
The constant term is the term with no letter: −4

chapter.title: The top of a number pyramid
text: In a four-row pyramid the corner blocks of the bottom row reach the top once and the two middle blocks reach it 3 times each, so the top is 1, 3, 3, 1 times the bottom blocks.
Write the second row as sums, then the third row, then the top, collecting like terms at each step.
math: In a number pyramid each block is the sum of the two blocks just below it. The bottom row is x, 4, 9, 10. Write a simplified expression for the block at the top.
Keep adding pairs to the top and collect like terms: x + 49

screens.title: The method
text: Group the x terms and the y terms, keeping each sign with the term after it. Add the numbers in front of each group and write one term for each letter.
math: Simplify 6x − 4y + 7x − y.
x terms: 6 + 7 = 13, so 13x
y terms: −4 − 1 = −5, so −5y
Together: 13x − 5y

strategies.title: Count things of the same kind

screens.title: Count things of the same kind
text: Read x as 'apples' and y as 'bananas': 3 apples + 2 bananas + 4 apples is 7 apples + 2 bananas.
You cannot add apples to bananas to get 'applebananas', just as 3x + 2y is not 5xy.
math: Simplify 9x + 2y + 5x − 3y.
x terms: 9 + 5 = 14, so 14x
y terms: 2 − 3 = −1, so −y
Together: 14x − y

screens.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 2 and y = 1 into the question and into your answer.
If the two values are different, a term has been combined wrongly.
math: Simplify 7x − 7y − 2x − 7y.
x terms: 7 − 2 = 5, so 5x
y terms: −7 − 7 = −14, so −14y
Together: 5x − 14y

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Simplify 9x − 9y − 5x − 3y.” A common wrong answer is −8xy.
x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.
math: Not −8xy, but 4x − 12y

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract integers. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Group the x terms and the y terms, keeping each sign with the term after it. Add the numbers in front of each group and write one term for each letter.

modules.title: An expression for a growing pattern

chapter.title: An expression for a growing pattern
text: If a pattern grows by the same amount d each time, Figure n is d × n plus a fixed part. The fixed part is what makes Figure 1 come out right.
math: A pattern of figures uses 11, 14, 17 and 20 square tiles for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of square tiles. Write an expression for the number of square tiles in Figure n.
Each figure adds 14 − 11 = 3, so the expression has 3n
Figure 1 has 11; 3 × 1 = 3, so add 8
chapter.tip: The rule 'add 3 each time' was written as n + 3. Figure n has 3 added n times, which is 3n, plus a fixed part.

chapter.title: Why a 'think of a number' trick works
text: Using a letter for the number lets you follow the trick for every number at once. When the added numbers cancel, the answer depends only on n, which is why the trick always works.
Write each step as an expression, using brackets when a whole result is multiplied. Expand the brackets and collect like terms.
math: Think of a number n. Multiply it by 3. Add 3. Multiply the result by 5. Then take away 15. Write a simplified expression for the final result.
Following the steps: 5(3n + 3) − 15
Open the bracket: 15n + 15 − 15
The numbers cancel, leaving 15n: the result is always 15 times the starting number

chapter.title: Patterns in calendar and number-grid squares
text: In a grid with w numbers in each row, the number to the right of n is n + 1 and the number below it is n + w. So every square of numbers can be written in terms of n, and its sum is an expression in n.
Write the numbers of the square in terms of n (as in the picture) and add them: a 2 × 2 square gives 4n + 2w + 2, a 3 × 3 square gives 9n + 9(w + 1). Substitute n, or solve the equation for n.
math: A 2 × 2 square of four numbers is marked on a 1 to 100 number grid (10 numbers in each row). Its smallest number is 86. Without adding them one by one, use an expression in n to find the sum of the numbers in the square.
With n the smallest, the square's numbers add up to 4n + 22

screens.title: The method
text: Find how many are added each time: that number multiplies n. Then compare d × 1 with Figure 1 to find what to add or take away. Check with Figure 2.
math: A pattern of figures uses 12, 17, 22 and 27 matchsticks for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of matchsticks. Write an expression for the number of matchsticks in Figure n.
Each figure adds 17 − 12 = 5, so the expression has 5n
Figure 1 has 12; 5 × 1 = 5, so add 7

screens.title: Go back to Figure 0
text: Step back once from Figure 1: Figure 0 would have (Figure 1) − d.
That is the fixed part; then add d for each figure: d n + (Figure 0).
math: A pattern of figures uses 8, 12, 16 and 20 square tiles for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of square tiles. Write an expression for the number of square tiles in Figure n.
Each figure adds 12 − 8 = 4, so the expression has 4n
Figure 1 has 8; 4 × 1 = 4, so add 4

strategies.title: See the groups in the picture

screens.title: See the groups in the picture
text: In a row of squares made of matchsticks, each new square needs 3 more sticks and the first square needs one extra.
So n squares need 3n + 1 sticks: 3 for each square, plus the first stick.
math: A pattern of figures uses 13, 21, 29 and 37 matchsticks for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of matchsticks. Write an expression for the number of matchsticks in Figure n.
Each figure adds 21 − 13 = 8, so the expression has 8n
Figure 1 has 13; 8 × 1 = 8, so add 5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A pattern of figures uses 12, 17, 22 and 27 square tiles for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of square tiles. Write an expression for the number of square tiles in Figure n.” A common wrong answer is n + 5.
The rule 'add 5 each time' was written as n + 5. Figure n has 5 added n times, which is 5n, plus a fixed part.
math: Not n + 5, but 5n + 7

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use arithmetic progressions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find how many are added each time: that number multiplies n. Then compare d × 1 with Figure 1 to find what to add or take away. Check with Figure 2.

modules.title: Terms from a recursive rule

chapter.title: Terms from a recursive rule
text: A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the one before it; the first term starts the chain.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 2 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 2. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).
chapter.tip: 2 was added before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then adds.

chapter.title: From a recursive rule to a formula for tₙ
text: Adding d each time means tₙ is the first term plus (n − 1) steps of d: tₙ = t₁ + (n − 1)d.
Write t₁ + (n − 1)d with the numbers, open the bracket and collect the numbers. Check that n = 1 gives t₁ and n = 2 gives t₂.
math: A sequence has t₁ = −9 and tₙ₊₁ = tₙ + 3. Write a formula for tₙ in terms of n.
From t₁ to tₙ there are n − 1 steps of 3: 3n − 3
Add t₁ = −9: tₙ = 3n − 12

chapter.title: A Virahanka-Fibonacci style sequence
text: Each new term is made from the two terms before it, so you must keep the last two terms in view as you go.
Write the terms in a numbered row: add the last two to get the next, until you reach the term you need.
math: A sequence begins 8, 9, and every term after that is the sum of the two terms just before it. What is term number 5?

chapter.title: Counting rhythms, climbs and tilings: Virahanka numbers
text: Every arrangement of length n ends with a short part (after an arrangement of length n − 1) or a long part (after one of length n − 2). So the counts follow Virahanka's rule: each is the sum of the two before (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …).

Start with length 1: 1 way, length 2: 2 ways. Add the last two counts to get the next, up to the length asked. For arrangements that must start with a given part, count the arrangements of what is left.
math: Meena lays ₹1 and ₹2 coins in a row so that they add up to ₹8. How many different rows can she make (the order of the coins matters)?
Length 2: 1 (ending with a short part) + 1 (ending with a long part) = 2
Length 3: 2 (ending with a short part) + 1 (ending with a long part) = 3
Length 4: 3 (ending with a short part) + 2 (ending with a long part) = 5
Length 5: 5 (ending with a short part) + 3 (ending with a long part) = 8
Length 6: 8 (ending with a short part) + 5 (ending with a long part) = 13
Length 7: 13 (ending with a short part) + 8 (ending with a long part) = 21
Length 8: 21 (ending with a short part) + 13 (ending with a long part) = 34

chapter.title: From an explicit rule to its terms and its recursive rule
text: An explicit rule gives any term straight from its position n; a recursive rule gives the first term and how each term comes from the one before. For tₙ = an + b each term is a more than the last; for tₙ = b × aⁿ⁻¹ each term is a times the last.
Put n = 1, 2, 3 into the explicit rule to get the terms. The first term is t₁; the step d = t₂ − t₁ (or the ratio r = t₂ ÷ t₁).
math: A sequence has the explicit rule tₙ = 9n + 2. Write its first three terms (t₁, t₂, t₃).
Put n = 1: t₁ = 11

screens.title: The method
text: Write t₁. Put it into the rule to get t₂, put t₂ in to get t₃, and so on. Do the operations in the order the rule gives.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 2 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

strategies.title: A table of n and tₙ

screens.title: A table of n and tₙ
text: Make two columns: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and tₙ.
Fill each row from the row above using the rule, showing the working.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 8 and tₙ₊₁ = tₙ + 1. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

screens.title: A number machine
text: Think of the rule as a machine: a term goes in, the next term comes out.
Feed each output back in as the next input.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 5 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A sequence has t₁ = 9 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ − 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).” A common wrong answer is (9, 12, 18, 30, 54).
3 was taken away before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then takes away.

modules.title: An inverse proportion

chapter.title: An inverse proportion
text: In an inverse proportion, when one quantity is multiplied by some number the other is divided by it, so their product never changes (workers × days = the total work).
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 4, y = 3. What is y when x = 3?
x × y stays the same: 4 × 3 = 12
chapter.tip: The product 4 × 3 = 12 is right, but it must then be shared by 3.

chapter.title: Time taken working together
text: Think of the work done in one day: a person who takes p days does 1/p of the job each day. Working together, the parts done per day add up.
Add 1/p and 1/q to get the part of the job done in one day together; the number of days is 1 divided by that fraction.
math: Arjun can finish a job alone in 3 days, and Meena can finish it alone in 9 days. Working together at the same rates, how many days will they take?
Part of the job done in one day together: 1/3 + 1/9 = 4/9
Days for the whole job: 1 ÷ 4/9 = 9/4

chapter.title: Direct proportion, inverse proportion or neither?
text: Two quantities are in inverse proportion when their product stays the same (double one, the other halves). They are in direct proportion when their ratio stays the same. One going up while the other goes down is not enough for inverse proportion.
Multiply x × y in every row: all equal means inverse proportion. Divide y ÷ x in every row: all equal means direct proportion. Otherwise neither.
math: The table shows pairs of values of two quantities x and y. Are x and y in direct proportion, in inverse proportion, or neither?
x × y in each row: 32, 72, 128, 200
y ÷ x in each row: 2, 2, 2, 2
So: direct proportion

chapter.title: Inverse proportion: workers and time, speed and time
text: When one quantity goes up and the job stays the same, the other goes down in the same ratio: workers × days (or speed × time) is constant.
Multiply the first pair to get the whole job (worker-days, or distance). Divide by the new number of workers (or the new speed).
math: 4 workers can build a wall in 27 days. How many days would 18 workers take, working at the same rate?
The whole job is 4 × 27 = 108 (it stays the same)

chapter.title: Compound variation: workers, hours and days
text: With two changes, look at each separately: more workers or more hours a day mean fewer days (inverse); more work to do means more days (direct). The total work (worker-hours, or worker-days per item) stays the same.

Write the total work for the first situation (workers × hours a day × days). The second situation needs the same total, so divide it by workers × hours a day. For items, scale by the new number of items first.
math: 16 workers, working 5 hours a day, finish a job in 14 days. How many days will 7 workers take for the same job, working 10 hours a day?
The work stays in proportion: 16 × 5 × 14 = 1120

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the two given values to get the fixed product, then divide it by the new value.
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 3, y = 24. What is y when x = 12?
x × y stays the same: 3 × 24 = 72

screens.title: Go through one worker
text: If a workers take d days, 1 worker takes a × d days (one person does all the work).
Then b workers share it: (a × d) ÷ b days.
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 3, y = 16. What is y when x = 2?
x × y stays the same: 3 × 16 = 48

screens.title: Invert the ratio
text: If x becomes twice as big, y becomes half as big.
So y(new) = y(old) × x(old) ÷ x(new).
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 4, y = 3. What is y when x = 6?
x × y stays the same: 4 × 3 = 12

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 8, y = 10. What is y when x = 10?” A common wrong answer is 80.
The product 8 × 10 = 80 is right, but it must then be shared by 10.
math: Not 80, but 8

modules.title: The third angle of a triangle

chapter.title: The third angle of a triangle
text: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°: tear off the corners and they fit together on a straight line.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 35° and 90°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?
The two angles together: 35° + 90° = 125°
Third angle: 180° − 125° = 55°
chapter.tip: The angles were taken from 360°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°; 360° is the sum around a point or in a quadrilateral.

chapter.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
text: An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it make a straight line (180°), and the three interior angles also make 180°, so the exterior angle equals the two far interior angles together.
To find the exterior angle, add the two interior opposite angles. To find one of those, subtract the other from the exterior angle.
math: One side of a triangle is extended. The two interior angles opposite the exterior angle are 31° and 118°. What is the exterior angle, in degrees?
Exterior angle = sum of the interior opposite angles: 31° + 118° = 149°

chapter.title: Angles of an isosceles triangle
text: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the two equal sides are equal; with the angle sum of 180°, one angle tells you the other two.
Vertex angle known: take it from 180° and halve. Base angle known: double it and take that from 180°.
math: In an isosceles triangle each of the two equal angles (opposite the equal sides) is 62°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
The two equal angles: 2 × 62° = 124°

chapter.title: How long can the third side be?
text: In a triangle, any two sides together are longer than the third. So the third side is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference.
Longest: one less than the sum of the two sides. Shortest: one more than their difference (for whole numbers).
math: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 14 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the longest it can be, in cm?
The third side must be less than 4 + 14 = 18 cm
The longest whole number below 18 is 17

screens.title: The method
text: Add the two angles you know, then take the sum from 180°.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 56° and 85°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?
The two angles together: 56° + 85° = 141°
Third angle: 180° − 141° = 39°

screens.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a paper triangle, tear off its three corners and place them side by side.
They make a straight line, which is 180°.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 36° and 127°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?
The two angles together: 36° + 127° = 163°
Third angle: 180° − 163° = 17°

screens.title: Count on to 180
text: Start from the sum of the two angles and count up to 180 in easy jumps (to the next ten, then tens).
The total of the jumps is the third angle.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 85° and 49°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?
The two angles together: 85° + 49° = 134°
Third angle: 180° − 134° = 46°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Two angles of a triangle are 66° and 43°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?” A common wrong answer is 251.
The angles were taken from 360°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°; 360° is the sum around a point or in a quadrilateral.
math: Not 251, but 71

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Measure and draw angles. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Add the two angles you know, then take the sum from 180°.

modules.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles

chapter.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles
text: When ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the letters are written in matching order: A goes with X, B with Y, C with Z. Matching parts are equal.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 7 cm, BC = 9 cm and CA = 4 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle QRP. What is the length of RP, in cm?
In the statement, RP sits in the same places as BC, so RP = BC = 9 cm
chapter.tip: P, Q, R were matched with A, B, C in alphabetical order. The order of the letters in the congruence statement shows the matching: the first letters match, the second letters match, and the third letters match.

chapter.title: Which figure is congruent to the given one?
text: Two figures are congruent when one can be placed exactly on the other (perhaps after turning or flipping it): the same shape and the same size, so all matching sides and angles are equal.

Compare the measurements, not their order: list each figure's sides from smallest to largest (or its radius) and check they match exactly. The same shape at a different size, or the same area or perimeter, is not enough.
math: A rectangle is 15 cm long and 8 cm wide. Which of these rectangles is congruent to it?
Match the measurements in any order (8, 15): a rectangle 15 cm wide and 8 cm long fits exactly

screens.title: The method
text: Write the two names one above the other. Find the asked letters in the second name, read the letters above them in the first name, and use that side or angle.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 9 cm, BC = 10 cm and CA = 8 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle RQP. What is the length of QR, in cm?
In the statement, QR sits in the same places as BA, so QR = BA = 9 cm

screens.title: Stack the names
text: Write A B C on one line and the second triangle's name under it.
Each column is a matching pair of vertices; a side is two columns.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 4 cm, BC = 7 cm and CA = 6 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle RQP. What is the length of PQ, in cm?
In the statement, PQ sits in the same places as CB, so PQ = CB = 7 cm

screens.title: Trace and place
text: Imagine tracing triangle ABC and placing the tracing exactly on the other triangle.
Each vertex lands on its matching vertex, so matching sides lie on top of each other.
math: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 75° and ∠C = 55°. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle QPR. What is ∠P, in degrees?
In the statement, P sits in the same places as B, so P = B = 75°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “In triangle ABC, AB = 8 cm, BC = 4 cm and CA = 7 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle PRQ. What is the length of RP, in cm?” A common wrong answer is 7.

P, Q, R were matched with A, B, C in alphabetical order. The order of the letters in the congruence statement shows the matching: the first letters match, the second letters match, and the third letters match.
math: Not 7, but 8

modules.title: Angles made by a transversal with parallel lines

chapter.title: Angles made by a transversal with parallel lines
text: A transversal crosses parallel lines at the same slant, so the angles at the two crossings repeat: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°.
math: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles between the parallel lines is 145°. What is the size of its angle that makes a linear pair with it, in degrees?
linear pair angles add to 180°: 180° − 145° = 35°
chapter.tip: The linear pair angle was taken to be equal. Angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.

chapter.title: Finding x from angles at parallel lines
text: The angle facts become equations: alternate angles give 'angle = angle', co-interior angles give 'angle + angle = 180'.
Write the equation from the angle fact, collect the x terms and the numbers, and divide. Then check both angles with your x.
math: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A pair of alternate interior angles measure (4x + 20)° and (2x + 32)°. What is x?
Alternate angles are equal: 4x + 20 = 2x + 32, so 2x = 12

chapter.title: Naming corresponding, alternate, co-interior and vertically opposite angles
text: Where a transversal crosses two lines it makes the same four angles at each line. Corresponding angles are in matching places; alternate interior angles are between the lines on opposite sides of t; co-interior angles are between the lines on the same side; vertically opposite angles face each other at one crossing.

Find the given angle: which line, above or below it, which side of t. Corresponding: same place at the other line. Alternate interior: other line, other side of t, still between the lines. Co-interior: other line, same side of t, between the lines. Vertically opposite: same line, both other side and other position.
math: Line t crosses two parallel lines l and m, making eight angles. The table shows where each angle lies (above or below each line, and on which side of t). Which angle is the vertically opposite angle to angle e?
Find angle e in the table and move to the matching place: h

screens.title: The method
text: Decide whether the two angles are the same 'shape' (equal: corresponding, alternate, vertically opposite) or together make a straight line (add to 180°: co-interior, linear pair).
math: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles between the parallel lines is 37°. What is the size of its vertically opposite angle, in degrees?
vertically opposite angles are equal: 37°

screens.title: F, Z and C shapes
text: Corresponding angles sit in an F shape, alternate angles in a Z shape: they are equal.
Co-interior angles sit inside a C (or U) shape: they add up to 180°.
math: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles between the parallel lines is 66°. What is the size of its co-interior angle (on the same side of the transversal, between the lines), in degrees?
co interior angles add to 180°: 180° − 66° = 114°

strategies.title: Slide one crossing onto the other

screens.title: Slide one crossing onto the other
text: Slide the upper crossing along the transversal until it lies on the lower one.
Because the lines are parallel the angles match exactly: that is why corresponding angles are equal.
math: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles between the parallel lines is 144°. What is the size of its vertically opposite angle, in degrees?
vertically opposite angles are equal: 144°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles between the parallel lines is 37°. What is the size of its angle that makes a linear pair with it, in degrees?” A common wrong answer is 37.
The linear pair angle was taken to be equal. Angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.
math: Not 37, but 143

modules.title: A missing side of a right triangle

chapter.title: Finding the hypotenuse
text: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, and the longest side. Here the two shorter sides are 24 cm and 70 cm.
The square on the hypotenuse is the sum of the squares on the other two sides: c² = a² + b².
math: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 24 cm and 70 cm, as in the picture. How long is the hypotenuse, in cm?
chapter.tip: The two sides were added. The theorem adds the squares of the sides, then takes the square root.

chapter.title: Is the triangle right-angled? The converse of Pythagoras
text: The converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle. If not, there is no right angle.
Find the longest side. Square it, and add the squares of the other two. Equal: right-angled. Not equal, even by a little: not right-angled.

From the even member 2m, halve it to get m, then work out m² − 1 and m² + 1. With m and n given, substitute into the three expressions.

modules.title: The missing angle at a point of a tiling

chapter.title: The missing angle at a point of a tiling
text: Tiles fit around a point with no gaps or overlaps only when their corner angles add up to exactly 360°.
math: At one point of a floor tiling, one regular pentagon and one regular nonagon meet, together with one more tile, with no gaps and no overlaps. What angle must the corner of the last tile be, in degrees?
Each corner of a regular 5-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 5 = 108°
Each corner of a regular 9-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 9 = 140°
Corners already there: 1 × 108° + 1 × 140° = 248°
The gap left: 360° − 248° = 112°
chapter.tip: The angle of each polygon was taken as 360° ÷ (number of sides), which is its exterior angle. A tile's corner is the interior angle, 180° − 360° ÷ n.

screens.title: The method
text: Find each regular polygon's interior angle (180° − 360° ÷ number of sides), add the angles already at the point, and take the total from 360°; share the gap if more than one tile fills it.
math: At one point of a floor tiling, 3 equilateral triangles and one regular dodecagon (12 sides) meet, together with one more tile, with no gaps and no overlaps. What angle must the corner of the last tile be, in degrees?
Each corner of a regular 3-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 3 = 60°
Each corner of a regular 12-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 12 = 150°
Corners already there: 3 × 60° + 1 × 150° = 330°
The gap left: 360° − 330° = 30°

screens.title: Know the polygon angles
text: Triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, octagon 135°, decagon 144°, dodecagon 150°.
Squares (4 × 90°), triangles (6 × 60°) and hexagons (3 × 120°) tile on their own; pentagons do not, since 360 ÷ 108 is not whole.
math: At one point of a floor tiling, 3 equilateral triangles and one regular decagon meet, together with one more tile, with no gaps and no overlaps. What angle must the corner of the last tile be, in degrees?
Each corner of a regular 3-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 3 = 60°
Each corner of a regular 10-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 10 = 144°
Corners already there: 3 × 60° + 1 × 144° = 324°
The gap left: 360° − 324° = 36°

screens.title: Split into triangles
text: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°.
In a regular polygon all n corners are equal: divide by n.
math: At one point of a floor tiling, one regular octagon and one regular decagon meet, together with one more tile, with no gaps and no overlaps. What angle must the corner of the last tile be, in degrees?
Each corner of a regular 8-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 8 = 135°
Each corner of a regular 10-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 10 = 144°
Corners already there: 1 × 135° + 1 × 144° = 279°
The gap left: 360° − 279° = 81°

screens.title: A common wrong answer
