modules.title: Finding an unknown coefficient from a condition on the zeros

chapter.title: Finding an unknown coefficient from a condition on the zeros
text: For ax² + bx + c the zeros α, β satisfy α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. A condition on the zeros therefore becomes an equation for the unknown coefficient.
math: The sum of the zeros of p(x) = x² + kx − 2 is −3. Find k.
Sum of the zeros = −k/1 = −3, so k = 3
chapter.tip: The sum of the zeros is −b/a: the minus sign was left out.

chapter.title: The zeros of a quadratic polynomial by factorising
text: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so the zeros of (px + q)(rx + s) are −q/p and −s/r.
Factorise by splitting the middle term, set each bracket equal to 0 and solve. Check: the zeros add to −b/a and multiply to c/a.
math: Find the zeros of p(x) = 6x² + 47x − 63 by factorising. Type both zeros separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Each bracket is 0: x = −9 or x = 7/6

chapter.title: Checking zeros against the coefficients
text: For p(x) = ax² + bx + c with zeros α and β, α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. A pair that fails either check cannot be the zeros.
Add the claimed zeros and compare with −b/a; multiply them and compare with c/a. Both must agree.
math: Arjun factorised p(x) = 6x² + 43x − 40 and found the zeros −8 and 5. Check them using α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. Which statement is true?

chapter.title: A symmetric expression in the zeros of a quadratic
text: For ax² + bx + c, the zeros satisfy α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. Any expression that stays the same when α and β swap can be written using only these two.
Write the expression in terms of α + β and αβ (for example α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ), then substitute.
math: α and β are the zeros of p(x) = 3x² − 9x + 5. Without finding α and β, find the value of α² + β².
α + β = −b/a = 3
αβ = c/a = 5/3
α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 17/3

chapter.title: A quadratic polynomial from its zeros
text: A quadratic with zeros α and β is (x − α)(x − β) = x² − (α + β)x + αβ.
Find the sum and the product of the zeros (for m + √n and m − √n: sum 2m, product m² − n), then write x² − (sum)x + (product).
math: Write the quadratic polynomial of the form x² + bx + c whose zeros have sum 6 and product −2.
Sum of the zeros: 6
Product of the zeros: −2
x² − (sum)x + (product) = x² − 6x − 2

chapter.title: The value of k for equal roots
text: A quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 has two equal real roots exactly when its discriminant b² − 4ac is 0 (two different real roots when it is positive, none when negative).
Write b² − 4ac with k in its place, set it equal to 0 and solve for k (take the positive square root if a positive k is asked).
math: For which value of k does the equation kx² + 4x − 4 = 0 have two equal
Equal roots when the discriminant b² − 4ac = 0: 16 − 4 × k × (−4) = 0
So k = −1

chapter.title: The number of zeros of a polynomial from its graph
text: A zero of p(x) is an x with p(x) = 0, that is, where the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis (crossing it or just touching it). A quadratic has at most 2 zeros and a cubic at most 3.
Follow the curve from left to right and count each point where it meets the x-axis; count a point where it touches the axis without crossing as well.
math: The picture shows the graph of y = p(x) for a polynomial p(x). How many zeros does p(x) have?
The curve meets the x-axis at 0 points, so p(x) has 0 zeros

screens.title: The method
text: Write the condition with the relations: sum = −b/a, product = c/a, or substitute a known zero into p(x) = 0. Solve the equation for k.
math: The sum of the zeros of p(x) = 4x² + kx + 8 is −6. Find k.
Sum of the zeros = −k/4 = −6, so k = 24

screens.title: Substitute a zero
text: If r is a zero, then p(r) = 0.
Put x = r into the polynomial and solve the resulting equation for k.
math: The sum of the zeros of p(x) = 5x² + kx + 8 is −6. Find k.
Sum of the zeros = −k/5 = −6, so k = 30

screens.title: Use the factor form
text: p(x) = a(x − α)(x − β) = a x² − a(α + β)x + aαβ.
Compare coefficients with the given polynomial.
math: The sum of the zeros of p(x) = 4x² + kx + 9 is −6. Find k.
Sum of the zeros = −k/4 = −6, so k = 24

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The sum of the zeros of p(x) = x² + kx + 3 is −4. Find k.” A common wrong answer is −4.
The sum of the zeros is −b/a: the minus sign was left out.
math: Not −4, but 4

modules.title: The missing angle of a polygon

chapter.title: The missing angle of a polygon
text: From one corner, the diagonals cut a polygon with n sides into n − 2 triangles, and each triangle's angles add to 180°. So the angles of the polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°.
math: A pentagon has 5 angles. 4 of them are 95°, 115°, 80° and 90°. What is the size of the last angle, in degrees?
Triangles from one corner: 5 − 2 = 3
Angle sum: 3 × 180 = 540
Last angle: 540 − 380 = 160
chapter.tip: The angle sum was taken as 5 × 180°. A pentagon splits into 3 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to 540°.

chapter.title: Angle sums and regular polygons
text: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon all the angles are equal, and the turns at the corners (exterior angles) add to 360°.
For the sum, work out (n − 2) × 180°. For one angle of a regular polygon, divide the sum by n (or take 360° ÷ n from 180°). For the number of sides, divide 360° by the exterior angle.
math: What is the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with 11 sides, in degrees?
Triangles: 11 − 2 = 9
Angle sum: 9 × 180 = 1620

screens.title: The method
text: Find the angle sum (n − 2) × 180°, add the angles you know, and take that total from the angle sum.
math: A pentagon has 5 angles. 4 of them are 135°, 105°, 115° and 90°. What is the size of the last angle, in degrees?
Triangles from one corner: 5 − 2 = 3
Angle sum: 3 × 180 = 540
Last angle: 540 − 445 = 95

screens.title: Walk around the edge
text: Walk around the polygon: at each corner you turn through 180° minus the angle there.
One full walk turns you once round, 360°. Add the turns you know; the last turn is what is left of 360°, and the last angle is 180° minus that turn.
math: An octagon has 8 angles. 7 of them are 140°, 130°, 120°, 155°, 155°, 135° and 155°. What is the size of the last angle, in degrees?
Triangles from one corner: 8 − 2 = 6
Angle sum: 6 × 180 = 1080
Last angle: 1080 − 990 = 90

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A pentagon has 5 angles. 4 of them are 115°, 135°, 105° and 85°. What is the size of the last angle, in degrees?” A common wrong answer is 460.
The angle sum was taken as 5 × 180°. A pentagon splits into 3 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to 540°.
math: Not 460, but 100

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Combine quantities within 20. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the angle sum (n − 2) × 180°, add the angles you know, and take that total from the angle sum.

text: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base and triangles meeting at a top point. The shape of the end or base tells you all the counts.

chapter.tip: Only two of the three given angles were taken from 360°; all three (115°, 100° and 75°) must be taken away.

chapter.title: Angles of a parallelogram or rhombus
text: In a parallelogram (a rhombus is one), opposite sides are parallel, so neighbouring angles add to 180° and opposite angles are equal.
Decide whether the angle you want is opposite ∠A (then it equals ∠A) or next to ∠A (then it is 180° − ∠A).
math: ABCD is a rhombus with ∠A = 170°. Find ∠D, in degrees.
∠A and this angle are neighbours on parallel sides, so they add to 180°: 180° − 170° = 10°

chapter.title: Diagonals of rectangles and parallelograms
text: The diagonals of every parallelogram cut each other in half. In a rectangle they are also equal in length.
Mark O as the midpoint of each diagonal. For a rectangle, BD = AC, so OB = AC ÷ 2. For a parallelogram, AC = 2 × OA.
math: In rectangle ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD cross at O. AC = 32 cm and AB = 26 cm. How long is OB, in cm?
The diagonals of a rectangle are equal: BD = AC = 32 cm
They cut each other in half: OB = 32 ÷ 2 = 16 cm

chapter.title: Convex, non-convex, or not a quadrilateral?
text: A quadrilateral (4-gon) is a closed figure of four line segments meeting only at their ends, with no three corners in a line. It is convex when every inside angle is less than 180° (no dents); if one angle is more than 180°, it is non-convex.
Check for a straight angle (180°) or three corners in a line: then it is not a quadrilateral. Otherwise look for an angle bigger than 180° (a corner pointing inwards): non-convex. If none, convex.

Look at the angles: it is a convex quadrilateral

chapter.title: Area of a circle
text: Cut a circle into many thin slices and lay them head to tail: they make a shape close to a rectangle, half the circumference (πr) long and r high. So the area is πr × r = πr².
Find the radius (half the diameter), square it, and multiply by π.
math: A circle has a radius of 2 cm. Taking π = 3.14, find its area, in cm².

chapter.title: Distance travelled by a wheel
text: In one full turn, a wheel rolls a distance equal to its circumference, π × diameter.
Distance = circumference × number of turns; turns = distance ÷ circumference. Keep the units the same (change m to cm or cm to m).
math: A wheel has a diameter of 84 cm. How far does it roll in 58 full turns, in metres?
One turn rolls the circumference: 22/7 × 84 = 264 cm

chapter.title: Arc length, area and perimeter of a sector
text: A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the whole circle, so its arc is θ/360 of the circumference and its area is θ/360 of the circle's area.
Arc = θ/360 × 2πr; area = θ/360 × πr²; perimeter = arc + 2r.
math: A sector of a circle has a radius of 21 cm and an angle of 60°. Taking π = 22/7, find its area, in cm².
Whole circle: 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 1386 cm²
Sector: 60/360 of 1386 = 231 cm²

chapter.title: Area of a circular path (a ring)
text: A ring is a big circle with a small circle taken out of the middle.
Outer radius R = inner radius + width. Area of the path = πR² − πr² = π(R² − r²).
math: A circular garden has a radius of 7 m. A path 3 m wide runs all the way round its outside. Taking π = 3.14, find the area of the path, in m².
Outer radius: 7 + 3 = 10

chapter.title: Circumference ÷ diameter, and values of π through history
text: For every circle, big or small, the circumference is a little more than 3 times the diameter: C ÷ d is always the same number, π ≈ 3.1416. Mathematicians in India and elsewhere found better and better fractions for it (Aryabhata: 62832/20000).
Divide the circumference by the diameter (both in the same unit) and round to the places asked. For a fraction, divide the top by the bottom.
math: Anu measures a bicycle wheel with a tape: its circumference is 1916 mm and its diameter is 610 mm. Work out circumference ÷ diameter, correct to two decimal places.
The same ratio comes out for every circle, whatever its size: this constant is π

chapter.title: Finding the radius or diameter from the circumference
text: C = πd = 2πr. Working backwards: d = C ÷ π and r = C ÷ 2π. A wheel rolls its circumference in one turn.
Divide the circumference by 22/7 (multiply by 7/22) to get the diameter; halve it for the radius. For a wheel, first divide the distance by the number of turns (in the same unit).
math: The circumference of a circle is 308 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its diameter, in cm.

screens.title: The method
text: C = π × diameter = 2 × π × radius. Double the radius first if you are given the radius.
math: A circle has a radius of 33 cm. Taking π = 3.14, find its circumference, in cm.
Diameter = 2 × radius = 66 cm

screens.title: Measure with a string
text: Wrap a string around a bangle or a lid and lay it flat against a ruler.
It is a little more than 3 diameters long: that number is π.
math: A circle has a radius of 49 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its circumference, in cm.
Diameter = 2 × radius = 98 cm

text: A question: “A circle has a radius of 17 cm. Taking π = 3.14, find its circumference, in cm.” A common wrong answer is 907.46.
πr² is the area (the space inside); the circumference is the distance around, 2πr.

modules.title: Area and perimeter of a parallelogram

chapter.title: Area and perimeter of a parallelogram
text: Cut a triangle off one end of a parallelogram and slide it to the other end: it becomes a rectangle with the same base and height.
math: A parallelogram has a base of 19 cm, slanting sides of 10 cm and a height of 5 cm. Find its area, in cm².
Area = base × height = 19 × 5 = 95 cm²
chapter.tip: The slanting side was used; the height is the straight-up distance between the parallel sides.

chapter.title: Area of a rhombus from its diagonals
text: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and cut it into four equal right triangles; together they fill half of the rectangle d₁ by d₂.
Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂. To find a missing diagonal, double the area and divide by the diagonal you know.

modules.title: Total surface area of a cuboid or cube

chapter.title: Total surface area of a cuboid or cube
text: A cuboid has six rectangular faces in three matching pairs: top and bottom, front and back, two ends.
math: A cuboid is 7 cm long, 6 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its total surface area, in cm².
Top (and bottom): 7 × 6 = 42
One end (and the other): 6 × 4 = 24
Front (and back): 4 × 7 = 28
Three different faces: 42 + 24 + 28 = 94
Total surface area: 2 × 94 = 188
chapter.tip: The volume was found; surface area is the total area of the six faces.

chapter.title: Area of the four walls of a room (lateral surface area)
text: Unrolled, the four walls of a room make one long rectangle: as long as the distance round the floor and as tall as the room.
Lateral surface area = 2(l + w) × h.

Distance round the floor: 2 × 15 = 30
Four walls: 30 × 6 = 180

Top (and bottom): 10 × 10 = 100
One end (and the other): 10 × 4 = 40
Front (and back): 4 × 10 = 40
Three different faces: 100 + 40 + 40 = 180
Total surface area: 2 × 180 = 360

screens.title: Unfold into a net
text: Unfold the box flat: it makes six rectangles.
Find each rectangle's area and add all six.
math: A cuboid is 10 cm long, 10 cm wide and 2 cm high. Find its total surface area, in cm².
Top (and bottom): 10 × 10 = 100
One end (and the other): 10 × 2 = 20
Front (and back): 2 × 10 = 20
Three different faces: 100 + 20 + 20 = 140
Total surface area: 2 × 140 = 280

modules.title: Volume of a cylinder

chapter.title: Volume of a cylinder
text: A cylinder is a stack of equal circles, like a pile of coins: the volume is the area of one circle times the height.
math: A cylinder has a diameter of 28 cm and a height of 17 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its volume, in cm³.
Base area πr² = 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616 cm²
Volume = base area × height = 616 × 17 = 10472 cm³
chapter.tip: 2πrh is the curved surface area; the volume is base area × height, πr²h.

chapter.title: Curved and total surface area of a cylinder
text: Cut the curved surface of a cylinder straight down and unroll it: it is a rectangle, as long as the circumference (2πr) and as tall as the cylinder.
Curved surface area = 2πrh. Total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r).
math: A closed cylinder has a radius of 21 cm and a height of 28 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its curved surface area, in cm².
Curved surface 2πrh = 2 × 22/7 × 21 × 28 = 3696 cm²

chapter.title: Surface area and volume of a hollow cylinder (a pipe)
text: A hollow cylinder is a big cylinder with a smaller one taken out. Its curved surface has an outside part 2πRh and an inside part 2πrh; each end is a ring of area πR² − πr²; its volume is π(R² − r²)h.
Work out the outer and inner curved surfaces and add them. For the total surface, add two rings. For the volume, find the ring's area and multiply by the length.
math: A hollow metal pipe is 70 cm long. Its outer radius is 35 cm and its inner radius is 21 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find the volume of metal in it, in cm³.
Area of the ring: πR² − πr² = 2464
Volume of metal: 2464 × 70 = 172480

screens.title: The method
text: Volume = πr²h. Halve the diameter first if you are given it.
math: A cylinder has a diameter of 7 cm and a height of 18 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its volume, in cm³.
Base area πr² = 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 = 38.5 cm²
Volume = base area × height = 38.5 × 18 = 693 cm³

screens.title: Like a prism
text: For a cuboid, volume = base area × height.
A cylinder works the same way; only the base is a circle (πr²).
math: A cylinder has a radius of 3.5 cm and a height of 18 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its volume, in cm³.
Base area πr² = 22/7 × 3.5 × 3.5 = 38.5 cm²
Volume = base area × height = 38.5 × 18 = 693 cm³

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A cylinder has a diameter of 21 cm and a height of 8 cm. Taking π = 22/7, find its volume, in cm³.” A common wrong answer is 528.
2πrh is the curved surface area; the volume is base area × height, πr²h.
math: Not 528, but 2772

screens.title: What it uses

modules.title: Area of a trapezium

chapter.title: Area of a trapezium
text: Two copies of a trapezium, one turned upside down, fit together into a parallelogram with base (a + b) and the same height. The trapezium is half of it.
math: A trapezium has parallel sides of 21 cm and 11 cm, and the distance between them is 15 cm. Find its area, in cm².
Parallel sides added: 21 + 11 = 32
Area: half of 480 = 240
chapter.tip: The sum of the parallel sides × height was not halved; two copies of the trapezium make that parallelogram.

chapter.title: Area and perimeter of an L-shape
text: An L-shape is a big rectangle with a small rectangle taken away. Its area is less than the big rectangle's, but its perimeter is the same: the two new edges replace the two that were cut off.
Area = big rectangle − cut-out. Perimeter: add all six sides (here it equals 2 × (width + height) of the big rectangle).
math: The shape in the picture is a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a 3 cm by 1 cm rectangle cut out of one corner. Going round, its sides are 4 cm, 1 cm, 3 cm, 3 cm, 7 cm and 4 cm. Find its area, in cm².
Whole rectangle: 7 × 4 = 28
Cut-out corner: 3 × 1 = 3

chapter.title: Area of a rectangular path
text: A path around (or inside) a rectangle is the space between two rectangles: the bigger one minus the smaller one.
Outside path: (L + 2x)(W + 2x) − LW. Inside path: LW − (L − 2x)(W − 2x). The width is added (or taken off) on both sides.
math: A rectangular garden is 9 m long and 8 m wide. A path 2 m wide runs all round its outside. Find the area of the path, in m².
Garden with path: 13 × 12 = 156
Garden: 9 × 8 = 72

chapter.title: Areas of fields and polygons split into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums
text: Any polygon can be cut into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums whose areas you know; the pieces' areas add up to the whole. A trapezium's area is ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × the distance between them.
Split the shape along a diagonal or a line you know, find each piece's area, and add. For a cost, multiply the area by the rate; to find a missing distance, put the area into the formula and solve.
math: A field ABCD is split by the diagonal AC into two triangles. AC = 31 m, and the perpendicular distances from B and from D to AC are 9 m and 10 m (so AC is the base of both triangles ABC and ACD, and these distances are their heights). Find the area of the field, in m².
Triangle ABC: half of 279 = 139.5
Triangle ACD: half of 310 = 155

chapter.title: Area and perimeter of composite shapes with semicircles, quadrants, triangles and trapeziums
text: A composite shape is cut into pieces whose areas are known (rectangle, triangle, trapezium, semicircle πr²/2, quadrant πr²/4); the area is the sum of the pieces, or a whole minus the piece cut away. A perimeter goes round the outside only.

Split the shape along straight lines, find each piece's area and add (or subtract a cut-out). For a perimeter, add only the outer edges: a semicircle's curved edge is πd/2 and it replaces the side it stands on.
math: A garden is a rectangle 6 m long and 28 m wide, with a semicircle on one of its 28 m sides. Find its area, in m². Take π = 22/7.
Rectangle: 168
Semicircle πr²/2: 308

screens.title: The method
text: Area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height.
math: A trapezium has parallel sides of 5 cm and 2 cm, and the distance between them is 10 cm. Find its area, in cm².
Parallel sides added: 5 + 2 = 7
× height: 7 × 10 = 70
Area: half of 70 = 35

screens.title: Split into pieces
text: Draw a diagonal: the trapezium becomes two triangles with the same height, bases a and b.
Add their areas: ½ × a × h + ½ × b × h.
math: A trapezium has parallel sides of 28 cm and 13 cm, and the distance between them is 7 cm. Find its area, in cm².
Parallel sides added: 28 + 13 = 41
Area: half of 287 = 143.5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A trapezium has parallel sides of 19 cm and 17 cm, and the distance between them is 12 cm. Find its area, in cm².” A common wrong answer is 432.

math: Not 432, but 216

modules.title: Multiplying decimals

chapter.title: Multiplying decimals
text: Tenths times tenths make hundredths (0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01), so the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers together.
math: Multiply as whole numbers: 94 × 88 = 8272
Decimal places: 0 + 2 = 2
Put 2 decimal places in 8272: 82.72
chapter.tip: The digits were multiplied but the decimal point was left out.

chapter.title: Dividing decimals
text: Multiplying both numbers in a division by the same amount does not change the answer (12 ÷ 4 = 120 ÷ 40), so you can make the divisor a whole number first.
Move the decimal point in the divisor to make it whole, move the dividend's point the same number of places, then divide as usual, keeping the point in line.
math: Multiply both numbers by 1 so the divisor is whole: the dividend becomes 16.8

chapter.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals by 10, 100 and 1000
text: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth ten times as much, so every digit moves one place to the left; dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
Count the zeros in 10, 100 or 1000 and move the decimal point that many places: right for ×, left for ÷. Fill empty places with zeros.
math: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit 2 places to the left (the number gets bigger): 45.5 → 4550

chapter.title: Estimating decimal products and quotients
text: An estimate tells roughly how big an answer should be, so a misplaced decimal point shows up at once. Rounding the numbers first makes the calculation easy to do in your head.
Round each number to the nearest whole number (look at the tenths: 5 or more, round up). Multiply or divide the rounded numbers. Compare with the exact answer: they should be close.
math: Estimate 5.6 × 8.2 by first rounding each number to the nearest whole number.
Round the first number: 5.6 → 6
Round the second number: 8.2 → 8
The estimate: 6 × 8 = 48

chapter.title: Word problems with dividing decimals
text: Dividing by a decimal asks how many of it fit (or how much each gets). Multiplying both numbers by the same power of 10 does not change the answer, and makes the divisor a whole number.
Move the decimal point in both numbers the same number of places until the divisor is whole. Then divide as usual, placing the point in the answer above the point in the dividend. Estimate to check.
math: ₹103.18 is shared equally among 7 friends. How much does each friend get, in rupees?
Make the divisor a whole number: 103.18 ÷ 7

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the numbers as if there were no decimal points, count the decimal places in both, and give the answer that many decimal places. Estimate to check (e.g. 1.9 × 3.1 is about 2 × 3 = 6).
math: Multiply as whole numbers: 83 × 59 = 4897
Decimal places: 2 + 1 = 3
Put 3 decimal places in 4897: 4.897

screens.title: Use fractions
text: Write each decimal as a fraction: 0.7 × 1.3 = 7/10 × 13/10.
math: Multiply as whole numbers: 49 × 27 = 1323
Decimal places: 0 + 2 = 2
Put 2 decimal places in 1323: 13.23

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “8.5 × 5.7 = ?” A common wrong answer is 484.5.
The decimal point was placed as in addition (lined up); in a product, the decimal places of both numbers are added.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Multiply the numbers as if there were no decimal points, count the decimal places in both, and give the answer that many decimal places. Estimate to check (e.g. 1.9 × 3.1 is about 2 × 3 = 6).

modules.title: Multiplying fractions and mixed numbers

chapter.title: Multiplying fractions and mixed numbers
text: a/b × c/d means c/d of a/b: cutting each of the b pieces into d smaller ones makes pieces of size 1/(b × d), and you take a × c of them.
math: Tops: 2 × 3 = 6
Bottoms: 11 × 4 = 44
Simplify 6/44 (divide top and bottom by 2): 3/22
chapter.tip: The fractions were added; 'of' and '×' mean multiply.

chapter.title: Dividing fractions using reciprocals
text: Dividing asks 'how many lots of the divisor fit?'. Dividing by c/d is the same as multiplying by d/c, its reciprocal, because c/d × d/c = 1.
Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, turn the second fraction upside down, then multiply and simplify.
math: Dividing by 1/10 is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal 10/1

chapter.title: Dividing a whole number by a fraction
text: w ÷ (c/d) asks how many c/d's fit into w. Each whole holds d/c of them, so w wholes hold w × d/c: dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal.
Turn the divisor upside down (its reciprocal) and multiply the whole number by it; simplify.
math: The reciprocal of the divisor: 4/9 → 9/4
Multiply by it: 4 × 9/4 = 9

chapter.title: Word problems with multiplying or dividing fractions
text: 'How many parts of size … fit into …' is a division; 'a fraction of an amount' is a multiplication. Deciding which comes first, then the calculation.

Ask what the question wants: a number of equal parts (divide the amount by the size of a part) or a part of an amount (multiply the fraction by the amount). Then multiply by the reciprocal to divide, or multiply tops and bottoms.
math: A tailor has 12 m of cloth. Each school bag needs 2/7 m. How many bags can be made from the cloth?
Decide the operation: how many fit: divide

chapter.title: A fraction product in an area model
text: a/b × c/d is the part of a whole that is both a/b one way and c/d the other way: an overlap of a × c small rectangles out of b × d.

How many small rectangles are shaded in both colours?
1 blue columns × 3 yellow rows: 3 rectangles shaded twice

Bottoms: 7 × 8 = 56

screens.title: Area model
text: Draw a square. Shade a/b of it across and c/d of it down.
The part shaded both ways is the product: a × c small rectangles out of b × d.
math: Tops: 1 × 8 = 8
Bottoms: 7 × 11 = 77
Simplify 8/77 (divide top and bottom by 1): 8/77

The fractions were added; 'of' and '×' mean multiply.

modules.title: Adding and subtracting integers

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting integers
text: On a number line, adding a positive number moves right and adding a negative number moves left. Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite.
chapter.tip: Two negatives were taken to make a positive; that rule is for multiplying. Adding two debts makes a bigger debt.

chapter.title: Integer differences in temperature and height
text: The change from one value to another is end − start. On a number line it is the distance between the two points, counting through zero.
Subtract the start from the end; subtracting a negative start means adding its size.
math: A diver is at −2 m (below sea level). A seagull is at 13 m (above sea level). How many metres higher is the seagull than the diver?
Rise = end − start = 13 − (−2) = 15

chapter.title: Several integer changes in a row: temperatures, lifts and divers
text: Rises and trips up are positive changes, falls and trips down are negative changes. Apply them one after another, in order.
Start at the first value. Add each rise, subtract each fall, one at a time; when you cross zero, count down to 0 and carry on into the negatives.

Second change: 4 − 8 = −4
Third change: (−4) + 6 = 2

chapter.title: Areas of wipers, tile designs and lighthouse beams
text: A sector of angle θ is θ/360 of a circle, so its area is (θ/360) × πr². Shapes from wipers and designs are built from sectors, squares and triangles by adding and taking away.

chapter.title: Area of a segment of a circle
text: A chord cuts a circle into two segments. The minor segment is the sector OAB with the triangle OAB taken away; the major segment is the rest of the circle.
Sector = θ/360 × πr². Triangle OAB = ½r² for 90°, or (√3/4)r² for 60° and 120°. Minor segment = sector − triangle; major = πr² − minor.
math: In a circle of radius 36 cm, the chord AB makes an angle of 60° at the centre O. Taking π = 3.14 and √3 = 1.73, find the area of the minor segment cut off by AB, in cm².
Triangle OAB: 1.73/4 × 36² = 560.52

chapter.title: Area swept and distance travelled by a clock hand
text: A clock hand sweeps out a sector. The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes (6° a minute); the hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours (30° an hour).
Find the angle turned, then take that fraction of 360° of the whole circle: area θ/360 × πr², or distance θ/360 × 2πr.
math: The minute hand of a clock is 9 cm long. Taking π = 3.14, find the area it sweeps in 30 minutes, in cm².
Angle turned: 30 × 6° = 180°
Whole circle: 3.14 × 9² = 254.34

chapter.title: Finding the angle or radius of a sector
text: A sector is θ/360 of its circle, so the arc is θ/360 of the circumference and the area is θ/360 of the circle's area. Knowing the part and the whole gives θ.
Angle = (arc ÷ 2πr) × 360°, or (area ÷ πr²) × 360°. For the radius, r² = area × 360 ÷ (θπ), then take the square root.
math: A sector of a circle of radius 42 cm has an area of 462 cm². Taking π = 22/7, find the angle of the sector, in degrees.
Whole circle's area: 22/7 × 42² = 5544
Angle = fraction of the circle × 360°: 462 ÷ 5544 × 360 = 30

screens.title: The method
text: Split the shape: a wiper's path is a big sector minus a small one; corner quarter circles together make a whole circle; a leaf is two segments, each a quarter circle minus a right triangle. Work out each part, then combine.
math: A lighthouse lights up the sea in a sector of angle 135° out to a distance of 35 km. Taking π = 22/7, what area of sea does it light, in km²?

strategies.title: Think in fractions of a circle

screens.title: Think in fractions of a circle
text: 72° is 72/360 = 1/5 of a full turn of 360°.
So the sector is 1/5 of the whole circle of radius 7 km: its area is 1/5 × π × 7².
math: A lighthouse lights up the sea in a sector of angle 72° out to a distance of 7 km. Taking π = 22/7, what area of sea does it light, in km²?

screens.title: Add and take away
text: Write the shaded area as (big shape) − (pieces cut out) or (piece) + (piece).
Work out each piece separately and combine them at the end.
math: A car's wiper blade cleans the part of the windscreen between 7 cm and 56 cm from its pivot as it sweeps through 90°. Taking π = 22/7, what area does it clean in one sweep, in cm²?
Sector out to the blade's tip: 90/360 × 22/7 × 3136 = 2464
Sector the blade does not reach: 90/360 × 22/7 × 49 = 38.5
Area cleaned: outer sector − inner sector = 2425.5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “In a square of side 7 cm, two quarter circles of radius 7 cm are drawn with their centres at two opposite corners. They overlap in a leaf shape. Taking π = 22/7, find the area of the leaf, in cm².” A common wrong answer is 77/2.
The area of a whole quarter circle was given. The leaf is the part where the two quarter circles overlap: quarter circle − triangle, twice.
math: Not 77/2, but 28

modules.title: Ordering positive and negative integers

chapter.title: Ordering positive and negative integers
text: On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move to the right. Every negative number is left of 0, and the further a negative number is from 0, the smaller it is.
math: Arrange these integers in increasing order (smallest first): 4, −6, −5, 2. Write them separated by commas.
On the number line, numbers increase from left to right: (−6, −5, 2, 4)

chapter.title: Integers on the number line and in real situations
text: On a number line, positive integers are to the right of 0 and negative integers to the left. Every integer has an opposite, the same distance from 0 on the other side.
Decide the direction first (above or below, gain or loss, left or right), then count the units from 0 or from the starting point.
math: The opposite of a rise is a fall, and the opposite of a gain is a loss. Write the opposite of "a deposit of ₹30 into a bank account" as an integer (positive for above or a gain, negative for below or a loss).
The opposite is the same distance from 0 on the other side: −30

modules.title: Multiplying by a number near 100 using the distributive property

chapter.title: Multiplying by a number near 100 using the distributive property
text: Multiplication spreads over addition and subtraction: k × (100 − 2) = k × 100 − k × 2.
math: Work out 20 × 101 without long multiplication.
chapter.tip: 101 is 100 plus 1, so 20 × 1 must be added to 20 × 100.

chapter.title: Removing brackets after a minus sign
text: Taking away a bracket takes away everything inside it: taking away (b − c) takes away b but gives c back.
Remove the brackets and change the sign of every term inside, then group numbers that are easy to combine.
math: Remove the brackets first, then work out: 96 − (56 − 26) = ?
Without brackets: 96 − 56 + 26 (the minus sign changes every sign inside)

chapter.title: Comparing two expressions without working them out
text: Two expressions can be compared by rewriting one to look like the other: removing a bracket after a minus sign changes the signs inside, and a multiplier spreads over every term of a bracket.
Rewrite the side with brackets without them, then see what is left over: if the two sides now differ only by an extra + c or − c, you know which is bigger without working anything out.
math: Without working out either side, decide which sign goes in the box: 7 × (48 − 3) □ 7 × 48 − 3
a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c, which is less than a × b − c

chapter.title: Naming the property: closure, commutative, associative, distributive, identity and inverse
text: Closure: the result stays in the set. Commutative: the order can change. Associative: the grouping can change. Distributive: multiplication spreads over addition. Identity: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication. Inverse: what brings a number back to the identity.

Compare the two sides: same numbers in a different order (commutative), same order with brackets moved (associative), a product spread over a sum (distributive), a 0 or 1 that changes nothing (identity), or a result of 0 or 1 (inverse).
math: Which property does this statement show? 82 ×
The statement shows the distributive property.

screens.title: The method
text: Write the number near 100 as 100 plus or minus a little, multiply k by each part, then add or take away.
math: Work out 20 × 102 without long multiplication.

screens.title: Split a rectangle
text: Think of k × 98 as the area of a rectangle k by 98.
It is a k by 100 rectangle with a k by 2 strip cut off: k × 100 − k × 2.
math: Work out 57 × 99 without long multiplication.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Work out 88 × 98 without long multiplication.” A common wrong answer is 8976.
98 is 100 minus 2, so 88 × 2 must be taken away from 88 × 100.
math: Not 8976, but 8624

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use multiplication facts. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write the number near 100 as 100 plus or minus a little, multiply k by each part, then add or take away.

modules.title: Writing a number as a product of primes

chapter.title: Writing a number as a product of primes
text: Every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or can be split into primes in exactly one way (apart from order).
math: Write 256 as a product of prime numbers. List the primes from smallest to largest, repeating a prime as often as it occurs (for example, 12 is written 2, 2, 3).
chapter.tip: 1 was written as a factor. 1 is not a prime number, so it is not part of the list.

chapter.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect square
text: In a perfect square every prime factor comes in pairs, because the number is something times itself.
Write the number as a product of primes and pair equal primes. Multiply together the primes that have no partner: that is the smallest multiplier.
math: What is the smallest whole number that 396 must be multiplied by so that the product is a perfect square?
Primes without a partner: 11 = 11

chapter.title: Divisibility and co-primeness from prime factorisations
text: B divides A exactly when every prime of B appears in A at least as many times. Two numbers are co-prime when they share no prime factor, so their only common factor is 1.
Compare the powers prime by prime: if each power in B is at most the power in A, A is divisible by B. If no prime appears in both, they are co-prime.
math: A = 3 × 5 and B = 2² × 3² × 5 × 7. Using only these prime factorisations (no long division), decide which statement is true.
Every prime power in A also appears in B (at least as high), so B is divisible by A

screens.title: The method
text: Divide by the smallest prime that goes exactly (2, then 3, then 5 …) again and again until 1 is left. The divisors are the prime factors.
math: Write 255 as a product of prime numbers. List the primes from smallest to largest, repeating a prime as often as it occurs (for example, 12 is written 2, 2, 3).

screens.title: A factor tree
text: Split 96 into two factors: 96 = 8 × 12.
Keep splitting every factor that is not prime: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2; 12 = 2 × 2 × 3.
The primes at the ends of the branches are the answer: 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3.
math: Write 96 as a product of prime numbers. List the primes from smallest to largest, repeating a prime as often as it occurs (for example, 12 is written 2, 2, 3).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write 280 as a product of prime numbers. List the primes from smallest to largest, repeating a prime as often as it occurs (for example, 12 is written 2, 2, 3).” A common wrong answer is (1, 2, 2, 2, 5, 7).
1 was written as a factor. 1 is not a prime number, so it is not part of the list.

modules.title: A ratio in its simplest form

chapter.title: A ratio in its simplest form
text: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind. Dividing both by the same number gives an equal ratio, like an equivalent fraction.
math: Write the ratio 117 : 65 in its simplest form.
The highest common factor of 117 and 65 is 13
chapter.tip: The ratio was written the other way round; the first quantity named comes first.

chapter.title: The missing term of an equivalent ratio
text: Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number, just like equivalent fractions.
Find what the known term was multiplied by, then multiply the other term by the same number.
math: Fill in the box: 12 : 11 = □ : 33. What number goes in the box?
33 ÷ 11 = 3: the terms were multiplied by 3

chapter.title: Comparing two ratios, or deciding whether they are equivalent
text: Ratios compare by multiplication. a : b and c : d are equivalent when a/b = c/d; the one with the larger fraction is the greater ratio.
Cross-multiply: compare a × d with b × c. Equal products mean equivalent ratios; otherwise the larger product shows the greater ratio. Or write both with the same second term.
math: Compare the ratios 1 : 9 and 4 : 36. Which statement is true?
Cross-multiply: 36 and 36. They are equal, so the ratios are equivalent.

screens.title: The method
text: Make the units the same, then divide both numbers by their highest common factor.
math: Write the ratio 132 : 48 in its simplest form.
The highest common factor of 132 and 48 is 12

screens.title: Equal groups
text: 18 : 24 means 18 of one thing for every 24 of another.
Make groups of 6: 3 groups and 4 groups. So for every 3 of the first there are 4 of the second: 3 : 4.
math: Write the ratio 16 : 6 in its simplest form.
The highest common factor of 16 and 6 is 2

text: A question: “Write the ratio 60 : 18 in its simplest form.” A common wrong answer is 3:10.
The ratio was written the other way round; the first quantity named comes first.
math: Not 3:10, but 10:3

modules.title: Finding a unit rate

chapter.title: Finding a unit rate
text: A unit rate is the amount for one unit: one kilogram, one hour, one kilometre or one day.
math: 7 kg of rice cost ₹623. What is the cost of 1 kg, in rupees?
chapter.tip: The total was multiplied by 7. To find the amount for one, share the total equally: divide by 7.

chapter.title: The better buy by unit price
text: To compare packs of different sizes, compare the same amount from each: the price of one item is the fairest comparison.
Divide each pack's price by the number of items, then choose the lower price per item.
math: Pack A has 7 soaps for ₹343. Pack B has 8 soaps for ₹288. Find the price of one soap in the pack that is better value, in rupees.
Pack A: ₹343 ÷ 7 = ₹49 per soap
Pack B: ₹288 ÷ 8 = ₹36 per soap
₹36 is the lower price per soap

chapter.title: Time taken working together
text: Rates add: if Arun does 1/6 of the job each day and Bala 1/12, together they do 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 each day.
Add the work done per day, then divide 1 whole job by that rate.
math: Arun can finish a job in 8 days. Bala can finish the same job in 24 days. Working together at these rates, how many days do they take?
In one day together they do 1/8 + 1/24 = 1/6 of the job
Days = 1 ÷ (work per day) = 192/32 = 6

chapter.title: Total cost from a fixed rate per kilometre or metre
text: At a fixed rate, every kilometre (or metre) costs the same, so the total is the rate times the number of units.
Multiply the rate by the distance. Check by estimating: about ₹10 a km for about 10 km is about ₹100.
math: A shop sells ribbon at ₹6 per metre. How much do 24 metres of ribbon cost, in rupees?

screens.title: The method
text: Divide the total by the number of units. Check by multiplying back.
math: 7 kg of rice cost ₹273. What is the cost of 1 kg, in rupees?

screens.title: Share it out
text: Imagine the total being shared equally among the units, one by one.
Each unit gets the same amount: that amount is the rate.
math: A bus travels 450 km in 6 hours at a steady speed. How many km does it travel in 1 hour?

chapter.title: Crores and lakhs in figures; millions and billions in lakhs and crores
text: In the Indian system the places after thousands are lakhs and crores: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 and 1 crore = 1,00,00,000. 10 lakh = 1 million and 100 crore = 1 billion.

modules.title: Selling price or cost price from a profit or loss per cent

chapter.title: Selling price or cost price from a profit or loss per cent
text: Profit or loss per cent compares the profit or loss with the cost price: 20% profit means the selling price is 120% of the cost price.
math: A shopkeeper buys a fan for ₹180 and sells it at a 5% profit. What is the selling price, in rupees?
chapter.tip: The profit was taken away. A profit means selling for more than the cost; a loss means selling for less.

chapter.title: Simple interest, amount, rate or time
text: Simple interest is the same every year: R% of the principal, so T years give T times as much. SI = P × R × T ÷ 100.
Write SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, put in the three numbers you know, and work out the fourth.
math: ₹500 is lent for 1 year at 7% simple interest per year. What is the amount (principal + interest) at the end, in rupees?
One year's interest: 7% of ₹500 = ₹35
For 1 years: ₹35 × 1 = ₹35

chapter.title: Discount and GST
text: A discount is a per cent of the marked price taken off; GST is a per cent of the price added on.
Find the per cent of the price, then subtract it (discount) or add it (GST).
math: A shirt is marked ₹1,550. The shop gives a 30% discount. What is the selling price, in rupees?

chapter.title: Profit or loss in rupees, and a missing price
text: Profit = selling price − cost price when the selling price is more; loss = cost price − selling price when it is less.
To find a price: SP = CP + profit (or CP − loss), and CP = SP − profit (or SP + loss).
math: A shopkeeper bought a wall clock for ₹980 and made a loss of ₹140. What was the selling price, in rupees?

chapter.title: Overhead expenses and the marked price
text: Overheads (repairs, transport) are part of what was spent, so they belong in the cost price; a discount is a percentage of the marked price.
CP = price paid + overheads; profit % = profit ÷ CP × 100. If the discount is d%, the selling price is (100 − d)% of the marked price, so MP = SP × 100 ÷ (100 − d).
math: A trader buys an old bicycle for ₹280, spends ₹120 on repairs, and sells it for ₹540. What is the profit per cent?
Cost price = price paid + overheads: 280 + 120 = ₹400

screens.title: The method
text: To find the selling price, find p% of the cost price and add it (profit) or take it away (loss). To find the cost price, divide the selling price by (100 ± p) and multiply by 100.
math: A shopkeeper sells a fan for ₹546 and makes a 30% loss on it. What did the fan cost him (the cost price), in rupees?
The selling price is 70% of the cost price

screens.title: Think of 100 parts
text: Split the cost price into 100 equal parts.
With a 15% profit the selling price is 115 of those parts; with a 15% loss it is 85 parts.
math: A shopkeeper buys a fan for ₹380 and sells it at a 5% profit. What is the selling price, in rupees?

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A shopkeeper sells a fan for ₹399 and makes a 5% profit on it. What did the fan cost him (the cost price), in rupees?” A common wrong answer is 379.
5% of the selling price was taken away from it. Profit and loss per cent are of the COST price, so the selling price is 105% of the cost price: divide by 105 and multiply by 100.
math: Not 379, but 380

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Calculate percentages. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: To find the selling price, find p% of the cost price and add it (profit) or take it away (loss). To find the cost price, divide the selling price by (100 ± p) and multiply by 100.

modules.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers

chapter.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers
text: Rational numbers follow the same rules as fractions, together with the sign rules for integers.

chapter.tip: The sign is wrong: same signs give a positive answer, different signs a negative one.

chapter.title: Inverses of rational numbers and the distributive property
text: The additive inverse of x is −x, because x + (−x) = 0. The multiplicative inverse of a/b is b/a, because a/b × b/a = 1. The distributive property x × y + x × z = x × (y + z) can make a calculation easy.
Additive inverse: change the sign. Multiplicative inverse: turn the fraction upside down and keep the sign. For x × y + x × z, add y and z first and multiply once.
math: What is the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of −2/5?

chapter.title: A rational number in standard form
text: A rational number is in standard form when its denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.
If the denominator is negative, multiply top and bottom by −1. Then divide both by their highest common factor.

chapter.title: Comparing two rational numbers

modules.title: Compound interest and depreciation

chapter.title: Compound interest and depreciation
text: With compound interest, each period's interest joins the principal, so the next period's interest is bigger. Depreciation works the same way, downwards.
math: Find the compound interest on ₹20,000 for 2 years at 13% per year, compounded annually, in rupees.
Each year multiplies the value by (1 + 13/100)^2
chapter.tip: Simple interest was found. With compound interest, each year's interest is added on and earns interest too.

chapter.title: Compound interest half-yearly or quarterly, and compared with simple interest
text: Compounding more often means more periods at a smaller rate: half-yearly uses R/2 per half-year, quarterly R/4 per quarter. Compound interest is more than simple interest because interest earns interest.
Amount = P × (1 + r/100)ⁿ with r the rate per period and n the number of periods; CI = amount − P. For the difference, also find SI = P × R × T ÷ 100 and subtract.
math: Find the difference between the compound interest (compounded yearly) and the simple interest on ₹20,000 for 2 years at 8% per year, in rupees.

text: Amount = P × (1 + R/100)ⁿ (depreciation: 1 − R/100). Half-yearly: use R/2 for each half-year and 2n half-years. Interest = amount − principal.

Year 2: interest on the new amount, add it on. Repeat for each year, then subtract the starting principal.

modules.title: Cubes and cube roots

chapter.title: Cubes and cube roots
text: A cube is a number times itself three times; a cube root undoes it. Three negative factors make a negative, so negative numbers have negative cube roots.
chapter.tip: 8³ was worked out as 8 × 3; a cube multiplies 8 by itself three times.

chapter.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect cube
text: In a perfect cube every prime factor comes in groups of three, because the number is something times itself three times.
Write the number as a product of primes and group equal primes in threes. Multiply by whatever primes are needed to complete every group.
math: What is the smallest whole number that 100 must be multiplied by so that the product is a perfect cube?
Complete each group of three equal primes: multiply by 10

chapter.title: Numbers that are sums of two cubes in two ways
text: Some numbers are the sum of two cubes in two different ways, like 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³ (Ramanujan's taxicab number).
Subtract the known cube from the number, then find the cube root of what is left (by prime factorisation, or by trying numbers whose cube ends in the right digit).
math: Find the number that equals both 20³ + 54³ and 38³ + 48³.

screens.title: The method
text: For a cube root, use the units digit to guess the last digit of the root and the size to guess the tens, then check by cubing. Or use prime factors in groups of three.
math: The cube root of a negative number is negative: −19

screens.title: Group prime factors in threes
text: Write the number as a product of primes, e.g. 1728 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Take one prime from each group of three equal primes: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “∛(−5832) = ?” A common wrong answer is −1944.
The number was divided by 3; a cube root is the number that, multiplied by itself three times, gives it.
math: Not −1944, but −18

modules.title: When doubling overtakes adding

chapter.title: When doubling overtakes adding
text: Adding grows by the same amount each step (linear); doubling grows by more and more each step (exponential), so doubling always overtakes in the end.
math: Plan A: ₹42 on day 0, then ₹9 more each day. Plan B: ₹9 on day 0, then doubled each day. On which day is Plan B first worth more than Plan A?
Day 2: Plan A ₹60, Plan B ₹36
Day 3: Plan A ₹69, Plan B ₹72
chapter.tip: After n days of doubling the amount is ₹9 × 2ⁿ, not ₹9 × 2 × n: each day multiplies by 2 again.

screens.title: The method
text: Make a table of the two plans day by day: add for one, double for the other, and look for the first day the doubling plan is bigger.
math: Plan A: ₹41 on day 0, then ₹25 more each day. Plan B: ₹2 on day 0, then doubled each day. On which day is Plan B first worth more than Plan A?
Day 6: Plan A ₹191, Plan B ₹128
Day 7: Plan A ₹216, Plan B ₹256

screens.title: Folding paper
text: Fold a sheet in half again and again: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 … layers.
Adding one sheet each time gives only 2, 3, 4, 5 …: doubling soon leaves adding far behind.
math: Plan A: ₹41 on day 0, then ₹41 more each day. Plan B: ₹3 on day 0, then doubled each day. On which day is Plan B first worth more than Plan A?
Day 6: Plan A ₹287, Plan B ₹192
Day 7: Plan A ₹328, Plan B ₹384

text: A question: “Plan A: ₹41 on day 0, then ₹9 more each day. Plan B: ₹2 on day 0, then doubled each day. On which day is Plan B first worth more than Plan A?” A common wrong answer is 5.

modules.title: A numeral in another base, in base ten

chapter.title: A numeral in another base, in base ten
text: In base b, each place is worth b times the place to its right: 1, b, b², b³, … just as base ten has 1, 10, 100.
math: The numeral 406 is written in base 8. What is its value in base ten?
chapter.tip: The digits were read as a base-ten number. In base 8 the places are worth 1, 8, 64, …, not 1, 10, 100.

chapter.title: A base-ten number in another base
text: Writing a number in base b means making groups of 1, b, b², … : the remainders after dividing by b are the digits, ones first.
Divide by b again and again, writing each remainder. Stop at 0, then read the remainders from the last to the first.
math: Write the base-ten number 106 in base 5. Type the digits of the base-5 numeral.
106 ÷ 5 = 21 remainder 1
21 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 1
4 ÷ 5 = 0 remainder 4

math: The numeral 2121 is written in base 3. What is its value in base ten?

modules.title: Writing a number in scientific notation

chapter.title: Writing a number in scientific notation
text: Each place the decimal point moves left divides by 10, so to keep the value the same we multiply by 10 that many times: 45,200 = 4.52 × 10⁴. Moving the point right multiplies by 10, so it is balanced by a negative power: 0.0045 = 4.5 × 10⁻³.
math: Write 0.777 in scientific notation, a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Give your answer as (a, n): for example, 3.5 × 10⁴ is written (3.5, 4).
Move the decimal point 1 places to the right to get 7.77, so n = −1
chapter.tip: The power was written as positive. A number less than 1 has a negative power of 10: 7.77 is divided by 10 again and again, not multiplied.

chapter.title: Writing a number in scientific notation as an ordinary number
text: × 10ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the right; × 10⁻ⁿ moves it n places to the left. Empty places are filled with zeros.
Look at the sign of the power. Move the point that many places (right for positive, left for negative), writing zeros in any empty places.
math: Write 5.84 × 10⁵ as an ordinary number.
Multiply 5.84 by 10 5 times: move the point 5 places to the right to get 584000

chapter.title: The largest of four numbers in scientific notation
text: In scientific notation the power of 10 tells the size: a number with a higher power is bigger, whatever number stands in front (that number is always between 1 and 10).
Compare the powers of 10 first (for negative powers, −3 is higher than −7). Only when the powers are equal compare the numbers in front.
math: Which of these is the largest? 3.6 × 10¹²;  8.6 × 10¹¹;  6.9 × 10¹⁰;  3.2 × 10¹¹
Compare the powers of 10 first, then the numbers in front

chapter.title: Orders of magnitude of real quantities, and judging a claim
text: The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 nearest below it: it tells the size at a glance (thousands, lakhs, crores, billions) and lets you spot a claim that is wildly wrong.
Multiply the facts (round them if you like), write the result as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, and read n. To judge a claim, compare its power of 10 with yours.
math: A town of 33 thousand people uses about 135 litres of water per person each day. About how many litres does the town use in a year of 365 days? Write the answer as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. What is n (the order of magnitude)?
1,62,60,75,000 has 10 digits, so it is about 10⁹

chapter.title: Multiplying and dividing numbers in scientific notation
text: (a × 10ᵐ) × (b × 10ⁿ) = (a × b) × 10ᵐ⁺ⁿ and (a × 10ᵐ) ÷ (b × 10ⁿ) = (a ÷ b) × 10ᵐ⁻ⁿ. Then the front number may need adjusting to lie between 1 and 10.
Work out the front numbers, add (or subtract) the powers, then if the front number is 10 or more divide it by 10 and add 1 to the power (if it is less than 1, multiply by 10 and subtract 1).
math: Work out (9.9 × 10¹²) ÷ (1.5 × 10⁻⁸). Give the answer in scientific notation as (a, n) for a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10: for example 3.5 × 10⁴ is (3.5, 4).
First divide the numbers in front: 6.6
Then subtract the powers: 20
In scientific notation: 6.6 × 10²⁰

screens.title: The method
text: Put the point just after the first non-zero digit to get a. Count how many places the point moved: to the left gives a positive n, to the right gives a negative n.
math: Write 0.00000468 in scientific notation, a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Give your answer as (a, n): for example, 3.5 × 10⁴ is written (3.5, 4).
Move the decimal point 6 places to the right to get 4.68, so n = −6

strategies.title: Use the place value of the first digit

screens.title: Use the place value of the first digit
text: Find the place of the first non-zero digit. In 4,52,000 the 4 is in the lakhs place, and 1,00,000 = 10⁵, so n = 5.
In 0.00045 the 4 is in the ten-thousandths place, and 1/10000 = 10⁻⁴, so n = −4.
math: Write 0.00885 in scientific notation, a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Give your answer as (a, n): for example, 3.5 × 10⁴ is written (3.5, 4).
Move the decimal point 3 places to the right to get 8.85, so n = −3

text: A question: “Write 0.000581 in scientific notation, a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Give your answer as (a, n): for example, 3.5 × 10⁴ is written (3.5, 4).” A common wrong answer is (5.81, 4).

modules.title: Probability from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain)

chapter.title: Probability from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain)
text: Probability measures chance on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When every marble is equally likely to be picked, P(event) = favourable marbles ÷ all the marbles. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
math: A bag has 7 red and 5 blue marbles, as in the table. Anu picks one marble without looking. What is the probability that it is yellow?
There are 7 + 5 = 12 marbles in all
0 of them fit: yellow
Probability = 0 ÷ 12 = 0
chapter.tip: An impossible event was given a small chance. There are no yellow marbles at all, so it cannot happen: its probability is 0.

chapter.title: Placing an event on the probability scale
text: The probability scale runs from 0 (impossible) through 1/2 (even chance) to 1 (certain). Fewer than half the outcomes: unlikely; more than half: likely.
Count the outcomes in the event and all the outcomes. None: impossible; all: certain; exactly half: even chance; otherwise compare with half.
math: A bag has 6 red and 8 blue marbles. One marble is picked without looking. Where on the probability scale is the event "the marble is green"?
0 of the 14 equally likely outcomes are in the event, so the probability is 0: impossible (0).

chapter.title: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (no common outcome). Exhaustive events between them cover every outcome. Events that are both are complementary: B is 'not A', and P(A) + P(B) = 1.
List the outcomes of each event. Any outcome in both? Then not mutually exclusive. Any outcome in neither? Then not exhaustive.
math: A card is picked from cards numbered 1 to 10. Event A: an even number. Event B: an odd number. Which statement is true?
A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}; B = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}; A and B are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (complementary)

screens.title: The method
text: Count all the marbles. Count the ones that fit the event. Write favourable over total. Nothing fits: 0. Everything fits: 1.
math: A bag has 3 red, 8 blue and 4 green marbles, as in the table. Arjun picks one marble without looking. What is the probability that it is not blue?
There are 3 + 8 + 4 = 15 marbles in all
7 of them fit: not blue
Probability = 7 ÷ 15 = 7/15

screens.title: Words on the scale
text: Draw a line from 0 to 1. Mark 0 'impossible', 1/2 'even chance' and 1 'certain'.
Place the event: no matching marbles at 0, all of them at 1, some of them in between — more matching marbles means nearer 1.
math: A bag has 6 red and 8 blue marbles, as in the table. Meena picks one marble without looking. What is the probability that it is not blue?
There are 6 + 8 = 14 marbles in all
6 of them fit: not blue
Probability = 6 ÷ 14 = 3/7

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A bag has 2 red, 8 blue and 5 green marbles, as in the table. Arjun picks one marble without looking. What is the probability that it is red?” A common wrong answer is 2/13.
Red marbles were compared with the other marbles. A probability compares the red marbles with ALL the marbles.
math: Not 2/13, but 2/15

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Combine quantities within 20. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Count all the marbles. Count the ones that fit the event. Write favourable over total. Nothing fits: 0. Everything fits: 1.

modules.title: Experimental probability from a frequency table

chapter.title: Experimental probability from a frequency table
text: Experimental probability is the fraction of the trials in which the event really happened: (number of times it happened) ÷ (number of trials).
math: Imran tossed a coin 50 times and recorded the results in the table. Based on these results, what is the experimental probability of getting a tail?
Tail happened 19 times
Experimental probability = 19 ÷ 50 = 19/50
chapter.tip: The theoretical probability (1/2) was given. The question asks what happened in this experiment: use the counts in the table.

screens.title: The method
text: Read the count for the event from the table, add all the counts to get the number of trials, and divide.
math: Kavya rolled a die 50 times and recorded the results in the table. Based on these results, what is the experimental probability of rolling a 1?
1 happened 6 times
Experimental probability = 6 ÷ 50 = 3/25

screens.title: Experiment and theory
text: Theory says a fair coin gives a head half of the time, but in 20 tosses you might get 12 heads: an experimental probability of 12/20.
The experiment uses what actually happened. With many more trials, the two usually get closer.
math: Farhan rolled a die 100 times and recorded the results in the table. Based on these results, what is the experimental probability of rolling a 6?
6 happened 13 times
Experimental probability = 13 ÷ 100 = 13/100

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Kavya rolled a die 50 times and recorded the results in the table. Based on these results, what is the experimental probability of rolling a 2?” A common wrong answer is 1/6.
The theoretical probability (1/6) was given. The question asks what happened in this experiment: use the counts in the table.
math: Not 1/6, but 9/50

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Build frequency tables. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Read the count for the event from the table, add all the counts to get the number of trials, and divide.

modules.title: Counting the outcomes of choices made in stages

chapter.title: Counting the outcomes of choices made in stages
text: If the first stage can happen in a ways and, for each of them, the next stage in b ways, there are a × b outcomes altogether (the multiplication principle).
math: There are 3 roads from village P to village Q and 2 roads from Q to R. How many different ways are there to travel from P to R, passing through Q?
chapter.tip: The numbers of choices were added. Each choice at the first stage can go with every choice at the next, so multiply.

chapter.title: Probability from the sample space of two dice or spinners
text: For two stages, the sample space is every pair (first, second). With equally likely numbers, all m × n pairs are equally likely, so P(event) = pairs that fit ÷ all pairs.
Draw a table: first numbers down the side, second numbers along the top, the total in each cell. Count the cells that fit the event and divide by the number of cells.
math: Anu uses a spinner numbered 1 to 4 and a spinner numbered 1 to 5. The first gives a number from 1 to 4 and the second a number from 1 to 5, every number equally likely. What is the probability that the total of the two numbers is 3?
There are 4 × 5 = 20 equally likely pairs
2 pairs fit: the total of the two numbers is 3
Probability = 2 ÷ 20 = 1/10

chapter.title: Listing a sample space, and an event as a subset of it
text: The sample space is the list of every possible outcome of an experiment. An event is a part (subset) of the sample space: the outcomes that make it happen.

Build the outcomes systematically (for two coins: first coin H with each of H, T, then first coin T with each). For an event, go through the sample space one outcome at a time and keep those that fit.
math: A card is picked at random from cards numbered 1 to 15. Which set is the event "the number is an odd number"?
Go through 1 to 15 and keep each number that is an odd number: {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15}

chapter.title: Counting arrangements that meet a condition
text: Listing in an organised way (fix the first place, then the next …) makes sure no arrangement is missed or counted twice. A condition fixes or removes some places first.
Deal with the condition first (put the fixed person at the end, glue the pair together, or choose the last digit), then count the ways to fill the remaining places one at a time and multiply.
math: In how many different ways can Ravi, Meena and Imran stand in a row if Ravi must stand at the left end?
Fix the first place; the other 2 can be arranged in 2! ways: 2

screens.title: The method
text: Count the choices at each stage and multiply them. A tree diagram or table shows why: every branch splits into the same number of branches.
math: A school canteen offers 2 kinds of rice, 5 curries and 4 sweets. A meal is one rice, one curry and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?

screens.title: Draw a tree diagram
text: Draw one branch for each first choice. From the end of each branch, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches: that is every possible outcome.
math: A school canteen offers 4 kinds of rice and 3 curries. A meal is one rice and one curry. How many different meals are possible?

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “There are 3 roads from village P to village Q and 2 roads from Q to R, and 5 roads from R to S. How many different ways are there to travel from P to S, passing through Q and R?” A common wrong answer is 10.
The numbers of choices were added. Each choice at the first stage can go with every choice at the next, so multiply.
math: Not 10, but 30

modules.title: One step of Kaprekar's routine

chapter.title: One step of Kaprekar's routine
text: Kaprekar noticed that repeating this routine on four-digit numbers always seems to reach 6174 — a conjecture you can test with your own numbers. Each step must be done exactly.
math: Kaprekar's routine: arrange the four digits of 6999 to make the largest possible number and the smallest possible number (the smallest may start with 0, like 0379 = 379), then subtract the smaller from the larger. What do you get?
Digits from largest to smallest: 9996
Digits from smallest to largest: 6999
chapter.tip: The two numbers were added. The routine subtracts the smaller from the larger.

chapter.title: Terms of a Collatz sequence
text: Each number comes from the one before by a fixed rule. The Collatz conjecture says every starting number eventually reaches 1 — it has been checked for huge numbers, but nobody has proved it.
Write the numbers in a row and number them 1st, 2nd, 3rd …. For each one, check even or odd before using the rule.
math: Start with 23. If a number is even, the next number is half of it; if it is odd, the next number is 3 times it plus 1. 23 is the 1st number. What is the 3rd number?

chapter.title: Using the odd-number pattern for squares
text: Each odd number is an L-shaped layer that turns a square into the next square: 1, then 1 + 3 = 2 × 2, then + 5 = 3 × 3. So the first n odd numbers add to n².
Count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to the last one ((last + 1) ÷ 2) and square it. If the sum starts later, subtract the square for the odd numbers that are missing.
math: Use the pattern 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 2², 1 + 3 + 5 = 3², … to find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 55.
From 1 to 55 there are 28 odd numbers

chapter.title: Testing digit conjectures: Kaprekar's 6174, repeated digit sums, reverse-and-add palindromes
text: A conjecture is a guess from patterns: every four-digit number (not all digits equal) reaches 6174 by Kaprekar's routine in at most 7 steps; repeated digit sums give the remainder on dividing by 9 (or 9); reversing and adding usually reaches a palindrome. Testing many numbers builds confidence, but only a proof makes it certain.

Carry out the process carefully, writing every number, and count the steps. Check against the conjecture: the answer for Kaprekar is never more than 7; the digit-sum answer is the remainder on dividing by 9.
math: Add the digits of 8030. If the result has more than one digit, add its digits, and keep going until a single digit is left. What digit is left?
Digit sum of 8030: 11
Digit sum of 11: 2

chapter.title: How a Collatz sequence behaves: steps to reach 1, and its highest number
text: Every starting number tried so far reaches 1 and then loops 4, 2, 1 — the Collatz conjecture — but no one has proved it. The sequences can climb high before they fall.
Write each number with an arrow to the next. Count the arrows for the number of steps, and look along the row for the largest number.
math: Collatz rule: if a number is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Start with 40 and keep applying the rule until you reach 1. How many steps does it take to reach 1?

screens.title: The method
text: Sort the four digits from largest to smallest for the big number and from smallest to largest for the small one (keep any 0 at the front), then subtract.
math: Kaprekar's routine: arrange the four digits of 4189 to make the largest possible number and the smallest possible number (the smallest may start with 0, like 0379 = 379), then subtract the smaller from the larger. What do you get?
Digits from largest to smallest: 9841
Digits from smallest to largest: 1489

screens.title: Test the conjecture
text: Use your answer as the new number and do the routine again (write it with four digits, adding a 0 in front if needed).
Within at most seven steps you should reach 6174, which gives 7641 − 1467 = 6174 again.
math: Kaprekar's routine: arrange the four digits of 1021 to make the largest possible number and the smallest possible number (the smallest may start with 0, like 0379 = 379), then subtract the smaller from the larger. What do you get?
Digits from largest to smallest: 2110
Digits from smallest to largest: 0112

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Kaprekar's routine: arrange the four digits of 3503 to make the largest possible number and the smallest possible number (the smallest may start with 0, like 0379 = 379), then subtract the smaller from the larger. What do you get?” A common wrong answer is 2295.
The smallest number was written without a 0 in front. In this routine the 0 may go first, which makes the smallest number smaller.
math: Not 2295, but 4995

text: Each step builds on another skill: Add and subtract multi-digit numbers with regrouping. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Sort the four digits from largest to smallest for the big number and from smallest to largest for the small one (keep any 0 at the front), then subtract.

modules.title: The smallest missing digit that makes a number divisible

chapter.title: The smallest missing digit that makes a number divisible
text: A number is divisible by 3 (or 9) exactly when its digit sum is; by 11 when the sums of alternate digits differ by a multiple of 11 (0, 11, 22 …); by 6 when it passes the tests for both 2 and 3. These come from place value: 10 = 9 + 1, 100 = 99 + 1, 10 = 11 − 1.
math: What is the smallest digit that can go in the box so that 28683□ is divisible by 3?
The known digits add to 2 + 8 + 6 + 8 + 3 = 27
The smallest digit that works is 0
chapter.tip: A digit that works was chosen, but not the smallest one. Try 0, 1, 2 … in order.

chapter.title: Which number is divisible: tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10
text: Because 10 is divisible by 2 and 5, only the ones digit decides divisibility by 2, 5 and 10. Because 100 is divisible by 4 and 1000 by 8, only the last two (for 4) or last three (for 8) digits matter.
By 2: ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. By 5: ones digit 0 or 5. By 10: ones digit 0. By 4: the number made by the last two digits is divisible by 4. By 8: the last three digits are divisible by 8.
math: Which of these numbers is divisible by 10? 20794;  83084;  75880;  92455
By 10: the ones digit is 0

chapter.title: Reasoning about remainders
text: Only the remainders matter: a number is a multiple of d plus its remainder, so the remainder of a sum (or product) is the remainder of the sum (or product) of the remainders.
Combine the remainders, then divide by d again if the result is d or more. Numbers leaving remainder r are r, r + d, r + 2d, …
math: How many numbers from 1 to 140 leave remainder 4 when divided by 5?
The first such number is 4; then every 5th number
136 ÷ 5, rounded down, plus 1: 28

screens.title: The method
text: Use the test with the digits you know, work out what the missing digit must be to pass, and choose the smallest digit from 0 to 9 that does.
math: What is the smallest digit that can go in the box so that 82□16 is divisible by 6?
The known digits add to 8 + 2 + 1 + 6 = 17
The smallest digit that works is 1

screens.title: Try the digits in order
text: Put 0 in the box and apply the test, then 1, then 2, and so on.
The first digit that passes is the smallest one.

math: In this addition, the letters P and Q stand for two different digits: 3P + Q2 = 116. What digit is P?
Ones column: P + 2 ends in 6, so P = 4

chapter.title: Deciding whether sums and products are even or odd
text: An even number is made of pairs; an odd number is pairs with one left over. In a sum, the left-overs pair up, so the sum is odd only when there is an odd number of odd numbers. A product is odd only when every number multiplied is odd.

15 × 92 gives an even answer
45 × 55 gives an odd answer
617 + 386 gives an odd answer
646 − 483 gives an odd answer
955 − 308 gives an odd answer
4 of the five give an odd answer

582 + 691 + 929 gives an even answer
22 × 68 gives an even answer
83 × 41 × 37 gives an odd answer

Put two odd numbers together: the two extra dots make a new pair, so nothing is left over and the total is even.

521 + 517 + 371 gives an odd answer
44 × 88 gives an even answer
521 − 405 gives an even answer

modules.title: Scaling in proportion, not by adding

chapter.title: Scaling in proportion, not by adding
text: Keeping the shape (or the amount per person) means keeping the ratio the same, so both numbers are multiplied by the same factor. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio.
math: A recipe for 4 people uses 12 cups of rice. How many cups are needed for 12 people, so that everyone gets the same amount?
The scale factor is 12 ÷ 4 = 3
Multiply: 12 × 3 = 36
chapter.tip: The same amount was added (8). Keeping the amount per person means multiplying both numbers by the same factor, 12 ÷ 4.

chapter.title: Direct proportion, inverse proportion or neither?
text: Direct proportion: y ÷ x is the same for every pair (doubling x doubles y). Inverse proportion: x × y is the same for every pair (doubling x halves y).
Work out y ÷ x for each column; if they are all equal, it is direct. Otherwise work out x × y; if they are all equal, it is inverse. If neither stays the same, it is neither.
math: Look at the table of x and y in the picture. Is y in direct proportion to x, in inverse proportion, or neither?
y ÷ x: 6/1, 6/1, 6/1, 6/1; x × y: 24, 96, 216, 384. y ÷ x is the same each time: direct proportion.

screens.title: The method
text: Find the scale factor: new ÷ old for the pair you know. Multiply the other number by the same factor (or find the amount for 1 first, then multiply).
math: A photo is 12 cm wide and 14 cm tall. Meena prints a smaller copy that is 6 cm wide, without stretching or squashing the picture. How tall is the copy, in cm?
The scale factor is 6 ÷ 12 = 6/12
Multiply: 14 × the factor = 7

screens.title: Why adding goes wrong
text: A photo 2 cm wide and 4 cm tall, made 10 cm wide by adding 8 cm to both sides, would be 10 by 12: it now looks squashed.
Multiplying both by 5 gives 10 by 20: the height is still twice the width, so the shape is kept.
math: A recipe for 5 people uses 8 cups of rice. How many cups are needed for 15 people, so that everyone gets the same amount?
The scale factor is 15 ÷ 5 = 3
Multiply: 8 × 3 = 24

screens.title: Unitary method
text: Find the amount for one unit first: cups for 1 person = cups ÷ people.
Multiply by the new number of people.
math: A recipe for 12 people uses 11 cups of rice. How many cups are needed for 24 people, so that everyone gets the same amount?
The scale factor is 24 ÷ 12 = 2
Multiply: 11 × 2 = 22

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A recipe for 12 people uses 11 cups of rice. How many cups are needed for 30 people, so that everyone gets the same amount?” A common wrong answer is 29.
The same amount was added (18). Keeping the amount per person means multiplying both numbers by the same factor, 30 ÷ 12.
math: Not 29, but 27.5

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve direct proportions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the scale factor: new ÷ old for the pair you know. Multiply the other number by the same factor (or find the amount for 1 first, then multiply).
