modules.title: Mean of grouped data

chapter.title: Mean of grouped data
text: In grouped data the exact values are lost, so each class is represented by its class mark (its midpoint); then the mean is Σfx ÷ Σf as for a frequency table.
math: Find the mean of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2, e.g. (0 + 10) ÷ 2 = 5
Σfx = 980
Σf = 50
chapter.tip: The class marks were averaged without their frequencies; each class mark counts as many times as its frequency.

chapter.title: Median of grouped data
text: The median is the value with half the observations below it. In grouped data we find the class where the cumulative frequency passes n/2, and assume the values are spread evenly across that class.

Make a cumulative frequency column, find n/2 and the median class, then use median = l + ((n/2 − cf) ÷ f) × h with l its lower limit, cf the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency and h the width.
math: Find the median of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
The cumulative frequency first reaches n/2 in the class 10–20

chapter.title: Mode of grouped data
text: The modal class has the highest frequency. Inside it, the mode is pulled towards whichever neighbouring class is bigger.
Pick the modal class; with l its lower limit, f₁ its frequency, f₀ and f₂ the frequencies before and after, and h the width: mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h.
math: Find the mode of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
The highest frequency is 17, so the modal class is 70–80

chapter.title: The assumed-mean and step-deviation methods for a grouped mean
text: Mean = a + Σfd/Σf (assumed mean) = a + h × Σfu/Σf (step deviation): shifting every value by a and scaling by h makes the numbers small, and the mean shifts and scales back the same way.
Choose a (a middle class mark) and h (the class width). Work out d = x − a (or u = d/h) for each class, multiply by f, add, then mean = a + Σfd/Σf (or a + h·Σfu/Σf).
math: To find the mean of the grouped data in the table by the assumed-mean method, take the assumed mean a = 25 (the class mark of 20–30) and d = x − a for each class mark x. Find Σfd.
The values of d for the five classes are −20, −10, 0, 10, 20
Multiply each by its frequency and add: −230

chapter.title: The median of a frequency table
text: The median has half the observations at or below it. In a frequency table the cumulative frequency (cf) says how many observations are at or below each value.

Find N = Σf. If N is odd the median is the ((N + 1)/2)th observation; if even, the mean of the (N/2)th and (N/2 + 1)th. Find them by reading down the cf column to the first cf that reaches the position.
math: The table shows the values x and their frequencies f. Find the median of the data.
N = Σf = 24
The cumulative frequencies are 5, 8, 16, 18, 24; the median is the 12th and 13th observation
So the median is 24

chapter.title: The mode of a frequency table and the empirical relation
text: The mode is the value that occurs most often (the largest frequency). For moderately skewed data, mean − mode ≈ 3(mean − median), that is mode ≈ 3 median − 2 mean (Karl Pearson's empirical relation).
For a table, find the largest frequency and read its value. For the relation, write mode = 3 median − 2 mean, put in the two known numbers and solve for the third.
math: For a moderately skewed distribution the mean is 20 and the median is 16. Use the empirical relation between the mean, median and mode to estimate the mode.
Empirical relation: mode = 3 median − 2 mean
So the answer is 8

screens.title: The method
text: Find each class mark x, multiply by the frequency f, add the products (Σfx) and the frequencies (Σf), and divide.
math: Find the mean of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2, e.g. (0 + 5) ÷ 2 = 2.5
Σfx = 755
Σf = 50

screens.title: Step-deviation method
text: Choose an assumed mean a (a middle class mark) and the class width h. For each class, u = (x − a) ÷ h is a small whole number.
Mean = a + h × Σfu ÷ Σf — the numbers stay small.
math: Find the mean of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2, e.g. (20 + 40) ÷ 2 = 30
Σf = 67

screens.title: Assumed-mean method
text: Take d = x − a for an assumed mean a.
Mean = a + Σfd ÷ Σf.
math: Find the mean of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.
Class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2, e.g. (0 + 10) ÷ 2 = 5
Σf = 48

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the mean of the grouped frequency distribution in the table.” A common wrong answer is 70.
The class marks were averaged without their frequencies; each class mark counts as many times as its frequency.
math: Not 70, but 72

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Combine quantities within 20; Find and interpret a mean. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find each class mark x, multiply by the frequency f, add the products (Σfx) and the frequencies (Σf), and divide.

modules.title: Heights and distances with one right triangle

chapter.title: Heights and distances with one right triangle
text: The height, the distance along the ground and the line of sight form a right triangle; the angle of elevation (or depression, which is equal to it by alternate angles) links two of its sides.
math: A kite is flying at a height of 10 m above the ground. Its string, pulled tight, makes an angle of 45° with the ground. Find the length of the string in metres (exact value).
The sides involved need sin 45° = √2/2
So the answer is 10√2 m
chapter.tip: The height was multiplied by sin θ; since sin θ = height ÷ length, the length is height ÷ sin θ.

chapter.title: Heights and distances with two observation points
text: Each observation point gives a right triangle; the two triangles share the height h, and their bases differ by the distance walked.
Let x be the distance from the nearer point. Write h = x tan β and h = (x + d) tan α, set them equal, solve for x, then find h.
math: From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30°. After walking 6 m straight towards the tower, the angle of elevation becomes 60°. Find the distance from the second point to the foot of the tower in metres. Give the exact value with a rational denominator (rationalise the denominator if a surd is left in it).
h = x tan 60°, with tan = √3
h = (x + 6) tan 30°, with tan = √3/3
Equate the two expressions for h and solve: x = 3

screens.title: The method
text: Draw the triangle, mark the known side and the side you want, choose the ratio that uses exactly those two (tan for height and distance, sin or cos with the hypotenuse), and solve.
math: A tower stands vertically on level ground. From a point 15 m from its foot, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 60°. Find the height of the tower in metres (exact value, e.g. 10√3).
The sides involved need tan 60° = √3
So the answer is 15√3 m

screens.title: Use the special triangles
text: A 30°–60°–90° triangle has sides in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2; a 45°–45°–90° triangle has sides 1 : 1 : √2.
Match the known side to its place in the ratio and scale.
math: A tower stands vertically on level ground. From a point 100 m from its foot, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 30°. Find the height of the tower in metres (exact value, e.g. 10√3).
The sides involved need tan 30° = √3/3
So the answer is 100√3/3 m

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The angle of elevation of the top of a 15 m high tower, seen from a point on the level ground, is 60°. How far is the point from the foot of the tower, in metres (exact value)?” A common wrong answer is 15√3.
The height was multiplied by tan θ; since tan θ = height ÷ distance, the distance is height ÷ tan θ.
math: Not 15√3, but 5√3

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use trigonometric ratios. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

Then the method is: Draw the triangle, mark the known side and the side you want, choose the ratio that uses exactly those two (tan for height and distance, sin or cos with the hypotenuse), and solve.

modules.title: Using sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 when sec θ + tan θ is known

chapter.title: Using sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 when sec θ + tan θ is known
text: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 factorises: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1. So knowing the sum gives the difference as its reciprocal, and the sum and difference together give each ratio.
math: If sec θ + tan θ = 7/3 for an acute angle θ, find tan θ.
(sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1 ÷ 7/3 = 3/7
Subtract the two equations and halve: (7/3 − 3/7) ÷ 2 = 20/21
chapter.tip: The two equations were subtracted but the result was not halved: that gives 2tan θ.

chapter.title: Simplifying with the trigonometric identities
text: Three facts do almost everything: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (and, dividing by cos²θ or sin²θ, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ), the reciprocals (sec = 1/cos, cosec = 1/sin, cot = 1/tan), and tan = sin/cos.
Write everything in sin θ and cos θ, use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to replace 1 − sin²θ or 1 − cos²θ, cancel, and name the result.
math: Simplify 3 tan θ ÷ sec θ. Which of these is it equal to?
Using the identities, tan θ ÷ sec θ = sin θ
Multiply by 3: 3 sin θ

screens.title: The method
text: sec θ − tan θ = 1 ÷ (sec θ + tan θ). Add the two equations and halve for sec θ; subtract and halve for tan θ. Then sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ. (The same works for cosec θ and cot θ.)
math: If sec θ + tan θ = 7/3 for an acute angle θ, find sec θ.
(sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1 ÷ 7/3 = 3/7
Add the two equations and halve: (7/3 + 3/7) ÷ 2 = 29/21

screens.title: Build the triangle
text: Once sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent are known, draw the right triangle with those sides.
Every other ratio can be read off it; check with Pythagoras.
math: If cosec θ + cot θ = 5/3 for an acute angle θ, find cosec θ − cot θ.
(cosec θ + cot θ)(cosec θ − cot θ) = 1, so cosec θ − cot θ = 1 ÷ 5/3 = 3/5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “If sec θ + tan θ = 7/3 for an acute angle θ, find sin θ.” A common wrong answer is 29/20.
The ratio was turned upside down: sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ.

modules.title: Evaluating expressions with standard angles

chapter.title: Evaluating expressions with standard angles
text: The ratios of 30°, 45° and 60° come from two triangles: half an equilateral triangle of side 2 (sides 1, √3, 2) and half a square of side 1 (sides 1, 1, √2).
math: Find the exact value of sin 45° sin 30°.
Combine the values: √2/4
chapter.tip: The values of sin and cos were swapped (and tan taken as cot): for example sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √3/2.

chapter.title: Finding the other trigonometric ratios from one
text: A ratio fixes the shape of the right triangle: sin θ = 3/5 means opposite : hypotenuse = 3 : 5, whatever the size (similar triangles). Pythagoras gives the third side, and then every ratio can be read off.
Draw a right triangle with the two given sides, find the third by Pythagoras, then write the asked ratio (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) and rationalise any surd in the denominator.
math: If cos θ = 4/9, where θ is an acute angle, find cot θ. Give the exact value.
cos θ = 4/9: take those two sides of a right triangle
By Pythagoras the third side is √65

chapter.title: Complementary angles: sin(…) = cos(…)
text: In a right triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other. So sin x = cos(90° − x): the sine of an angle is the cosine of its complement.
If sin(first angle) = cos(second angle) with both acute, the angles add to 90°. Write that equation in A and solve it.
math: If sin(2A − 18°) = cos(A + 24°), where both angles are acute, find A in degrees.
cos y = sin(90° − y), so the angles are complementary: 2A − 18° + A + 24° = 90°

chapter.title: Simplifying with complementary angles
text: For complementary angles θ and 90° − θ: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, cot(90° − θ) = tan θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ, cosec(90° − θ) = sec θ.

Spot the pairs of angles that add up to 90°, rewrite one function of each pair as the co-function of the other angle, and simplify (a ratio of equal values is 1; tan θ × cot θ = 1; sin²θ + cos²θ = 1).
math: Without using tables, find the value of 2 sin 50° ÷ cos 40° + tan 65° ÷ cot 25°.
Use cos(90° − θ) = sin θ and cot(90° − θ) = tan θ
So the value is 3

chapter.title: Reading trigonometric tables (degrees, minutes, mean differences)
text: A table gives each ratio to four decimal places for every 6′; for the minutes in between, the mean-difference columns give the small change to add (for sine and tangent, which increase) or to subtract (for cosine, which decreases).

Find the row of the degrees and the column of the largest multiple of 6′ not above the minutes; read the value. Then read the mean difference for the extra minutes in the same row and add it (subtract for cosines) in the last decimal place.
math: Using the table of natural sines in the picture (with its mean differences), find sin 46°32′.
In the 46° row, under 30′: 0.7254
Add the mean difference for 2′ (4 in the last place): 0.7258

screens.title: The method
text: Write down each value (sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, cos the reverse order, tan = sin ÷ cos), then do the arithmetic with surds exactly.
math: Find the exact value of sin²45° + sin²30°.
Combine the values: 3/4

screens.title: The square-root pattern
text: cos θ is the same list backwards, and tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.
math: Find the exact value of tan 45° − sin 60°.
Combine the values: (2 − √3)/2

screens.title: Draw the two triangles
text: Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: the half has sides 1, √3 and 2 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°.
Cut a unit square along its diagonal: sides 1, 1, √2 and angles 45°, 45°, 90°. Read any ratio off these.
math: Find the exact value of tan²45° + sin²60°.
Combine the values: 7/4

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the exact value of cos 45° − tan 60°.” A common wrong answer is (3√2 − 2√3)/6.
The values of sin and cos were swapped (and tan taken as cot): for example sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √3/2.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Simplify radicals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write down each value (sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, cos the reverse order, tan = sin ÷ cos), then do the arithmetic with surds exactly.

modules.title: Union, intersection, difference and complement of finite sets

chapter.title: Union, intersection, difference and complement of finite sets
text: A ∪ B collects every element in A or in B, A ∩ B keeps only the elements in both, A − B keeps what is in A but not in B, and the complement A′ is everything in U outside A.
math: Let U = {1, 2, 3, …, 12}, A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4} and B = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 5}. List the elements of A ∪ B, separated by commas.

chapter.title: Counting subsets and proper subsets of a finite set
text: Building a subset means deciding, for each element, in or out: two choices per element, so a set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, including ∅ and the set itself.
Count all subsets as 2ⁿ, then remove what the question excludes: A itself for proper subsets, ∅ as well for non-empty proper subsets. Subsets of a fixed size r are ⁿCᵣ.
math: A = {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k}. How many non-empty proper subsets does A have?
Each of the 11 elements is either in a subset or not: 2¹¹ = 2048 subsets
So the number asked for is 2046

chapter.title: Counting with n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
text: When n(A) and n(B) are added, the elements in both sets are counted twice, so n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Write the formula, put in the three numbers you know and solve for the fourth. For 'A only', take n(A ∩ B) away from n(A).
math: For finite sets A and B, n(A) = 44, n(B) = 15 and n(A ∩ B) = 8. Find n(A ∪ B).

chapter.title: Converting between roster, set-builder and descriptive forms
text: One set can be written three ways: roster form lists the elements in braces, set-builder form gives the rule {x : condition}, and descriptive form says it in words. All three must give exactly the same elements.
To check a set-builder form, put n = 1, 2, 3, … (or test numbers) into the rule and list what it gives; compare with the roster, including the first and the last element.
math: Which set-builder form describes the set {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}?
So the answer is {x : x = n + 1, n ∈ ℕ and n ≤ 6}

chapter.title: Empty, singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent and disjoint sets, subsets and power sets
text: A set is empty (∅) if it has no elements, a singleton if it has one, finite if its elements can be counted to an end, and infinite otherwise. A = B when they have the same elements; A and B are equivalent when n(A) = n(B); disjoint when A ∩ B = ∅. A ⊂ B when every element of A is in B and B has more.
First write each set in roster form (each element once), paying attention to the universe (ℕ, ℤ or ℝ). Then count, compare the elements one by one, and decide.
math: A is the set of letters of the word SALEM and B is the set of letters of the word TAMIL. Which statement is true?
Listing the elements shows: Neither set is a subset of the other
So the answer is: Neither set is a subset of the other

chapter.title: Verifying the associative property of union and intersection
text: Union and intersection are associative: (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C) and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C). They are also commutative: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
Work out the bracket first, then combine the result with the third set. Do the other grouping too; the two answers are the same set.
math: A = {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}, B = {1, 2, 4, 5, 7} and C = {3, 4, 6, 8, 10}. Find (A ∪ B) ∪ C, working out the bracket first. (By the associative property it equals A ∪ (B ∪ C).) List its elements, separated by commas.
Check: A ∪ (B ∪ C) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10} too, as the associative property says

chapter.title: Counting with three overlapping sets in a survey
text: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(C ∩ A) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C): adding the three totals counts the overlaps too often, subtracting the pairs removes the middle three times, so it is added back once.
Draw three overlapping circles. Write n(A ∩ B ∩ C) in the middle, then each 'two only' region (pair minus middle), then each 'one only' region. Add the regions the question asks for.
math: In a survey of students of a class in a Coimbatore school, 13 play cricket, 4 play football and 13 play kabaddi; 1 plays both cricket and football, 1 plays both football and kabaddi, 5 play both kabaddi and cricket, and 1 plays all three. How many students play at least one of the three games?

chapter.title: Sample spaces and events in set notation
text: The sample space S of a random experiment is the set of all its possible outcomes; an event is a subset of S — the outcomes for which it happens.
List the outcomes stage by stage (a tree diagram: every choice at the first stage, then every choice at the second). Then go through S and keep the outcomes that fit the event.
math: Three coins are tossed together (H for head, T for tail, the coins listed in order: first, second, third). Which set is the event "no tail"?
Listing the outcomes systematically gives {HHH}
So the answer is {HHH}

chapter.title: Reading an interval from its number-line picture
text: On a number line, the shaded part is the set; a filled dot at an end means the end belongs to it ([ ] or ≤), a hollow dot that it does not (( ) or <), and an arrow that it goes on to ∞ or −∞ (always a round bracket).
Read the left end and its dot, then the right end and its dot (or the arrow), and write the smaller end first. Two shaded pieces are joined with ∪.
math: The shaded part of the number line in the picture is a set of real numbers (a filled dot means the end belongs to the set, a hollow dot that it does not, an arrow that it goes on for ever). Write the set in interval notation (or as an inequality in x).
Read the ends and their dots: (−2, ∞)
In interval notation: (−2, ∞)

screens.title: The method
text: First write A and B in roster form. Then go through U one element at a time and decide, from the definition, whether it belongs to the set asked for.
math: Let U = {1, 2, 3, …, 17}, A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 3} and B = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 2}. List the elements of (A ∪ B)′, separated by commas.

strategies.title: Place the elements in a Venn diagram

screens.title: Place the elements in a Venn diagram
text: Draw two overlapping circles A and B inside a rectangle U and write each element of U in its region: A only, both, B only, or outside both.
Then read off the regions the operation asks for: the union is all three circle regions, the intersection the middle, the complement of the union the outside.
math: Let U = {1, 2, 3, …, 16}, A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 3} and B = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4}. List the elements of A ∪ B, separated by commas.

screens.title: A membership table
text: Make a row for each element with two columns, 'in A?' and 'in B?', filled with yes or no.

modules.title: Counting elements of A × B and relations from A to B

chapter.title: Counting elements of A × B and relations from A to B
text: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B, so n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B). A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B.
math: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} and n(A × B) = 48. How many elements does B have?
chapter.tip: n(A) was subtracted from n(A × B); n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B), so divide by 8.

chapter.title: Is a relation given by a rule reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
text: Reflexive: every element is related to itself. Symmetric: whenever (a, b) is in R, so is (b, a). Transitive: whenever (a, b) and (b, c) are in R, so is (a, c) — including chains with a = c.
Test the rule itself: put b = a for reflexive; swap a and b for symmetric; for transitive, take a chain (a, b), (b, c) and check (a, c). A single counter-example from A is enough to say 'not'.
math: On the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, the relation R = {(a, b) : a, b ∈ A, a < b}. Which statement is true?
Reflexive (every (a, a) in R): no
Symmetric (each (a, b) has its (b, a)): no
Transitive (each chain (a, b), (b, c) has its (a, c)): yes

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the sizes for the product. For the number of relations, raise 2 to the power n(A) × n(B).
math: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and n(A × B) = 16. How many elements does B have?

strategies.title: Draw the pairs as a grid

screens.title: Draw the pairs as a grid
text: Write A down the side and B along the top: each cell is one ordered pair.
The grid has n(A) rows and n(B) columns; a relation is a choice of cells to tick.
math: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} and B = {p}. How many ordered pairs are in A × B?

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} and B = {p}. How many relations are there from A to B?” A common wrong answer is 7.
The number of ordered pairs was given; a relation is any subset of A × B, and a set of mn pairs has 2^(mn) subsets.
math: Not 7, but 128

modules.title: The domain of a real function

chapter.title: The domain of a real function
text: The domain of a real function is every real x for which the formula gives a real number: what is under a square root must be ≥ 0, and a denominator must not be 0.
math: Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(3x − 3). Write it in interval notation.
The quantity under the root must be non-negative: 3x − 3 ≥ 0
Solve the condition: x ∈ [1, ∞)
chapter.tip: x = 1 was left out; √0 = 0 is a real number, so the end point belongs to the domain.

chapter.title: The range of a quadratic function
text: Writing f(x) = a(x − h)² + k shows the range: (x − h)² takes every value ≥ 0, so f takes every value from k upwards when a > 0, and from k downwards when a < 0.
Complete the square (or find the vertex at x = −b/(2a)), work out k = f(h), and write [k, ∞) or (−∞, k].
math: Find the range of f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3x² − 12x + 13. Write it in interval notation.
Complete the square: f(x) = 3(x − 2)² + 1
The square is never negative, so the least value is f(2) = 1

chapter.title: Is a quadratic on a restricted domain one-one, onto, both or neither?
text: One-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) only when x₁ = x₂. Onto: every element of the codomain is f(x) for some x in the domain. For a quadratic both depend on where the domain starts compared with the vertex.

Complete the square to find the vertex (h, c). If the domain [d, ∞) starts at or to the right of h, f only increases (one-one) and its range is [f(d), ∞); otherwise f(d) = f(2h − d) and the range is [c, ∞). Compare the range with the codomain.
math: Let f : [3, ∞) → [6, ∞) be given by f(x) = x² − 6x + 15. Which statement is true?
Complete the square: f(x) = (x − 3)² + 6, so the vertex is at x = 3
One-one (the domain starts at 3, not left of the vertex): yes
Onto (the range is [6, ∞); is every element of the codomain reached?): yes

chapter.title: Deciding whether a relation is a function
text: A relation R from A to B is a function when every element of A has exactly one image in B. Two elements may share an image (many-one), but one element may not have two images, and none may be left without an image.

Go through A one element at a time and count its pairs in R. If every count is exactly 1, R is a function. On a graph this is the vertical line test: no vertical line through an element of A meets the graph twice.
math: A = {−2, −1, 0, 1} and B = {1, 3, 5}. The picture shows the pairs (x, y) of a relation R from A to B as points; use the vertical line test. Is R a function from A to B?
Count the images of each element of A: No: an element of A has two or more images in B
So: No: an element of A has two or more images in B

chapter.title: Naming a function: one-one or many-one, onto or into, identity or constant
text: f : A → B is one-one if different elements have different images, and many-one otherwise; it is onto if every element of B is an image, and into otherwise. On A → A, the identity sends each x to x, and a constant function sends every x to one value.
List the images f(a). Repeated images → many-one. Compare the set of images (the range) with B: equal → onto, smaller → into.
math: A = {2, 3, 4, 5}, B = {2, 5, 8, 11} and f : A → B is the function f = {(2, 2), (3, 5), (4, 8), (5, 11)}. Which statement is true?
Checking images: f is one-one and onto (a bijection)
So: f is one-one and onto (a bijection)

screens.title: The method
text: Write the condition (≥ 0, > 0 or ≠ 0), factorise any quadratic, decide the sign of each region between the roots, and write the answer in interval notation.
math: Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(3x − 1). Write it in interval notation.
The quantity under the root must be non-negative: 3x − 1 ≥ 0
Solve the condition: x ∈ [1/3, ∞)

screens.title: A sign chart
text: Mark the roots on a number line; they cut it into regions.
Pick one number in each region and find the sign of the quadratic there; keep the regions that meet the condition, and decide each end point separately.
math: Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(−x² − 8x − 12). Write it in interval notation.
Factorise: (x + 6)(x + 2)
Condition on (x − a)(x − b): ≤ 0
Solve the condition: x ∈ [−6, −2]

screens.title: Test numbers in f
text: Try a few values of x in the formula: if you need the square root of a negative number, or divide by zero, x is not in the domain.
The boundary values are where the quantity is exactly 0: test them separately.
math: Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(−x² − 7x − 6). Write it in interval notation.
Factorise: (x + 6)(x + 1)
Condition on (x − a)(x − b): ≤ 0
Solve the condition: x ∈ [−6, −1]

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the domain of the real function f(x) = √(3x − 2). Write it in interval notation.” A common wrong answer is (2/3, ∞).
x = 2/3 was left out; √0 = 0 is a real number, so the end point belongs to the domain.

text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve linear inequalities. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write the condition (≥ 0, > 0 or ≠ 0), factorise any quadratic, decide the sign of each region between the roots, and write the answer in interval notation.

modules.title: A point on a transformed graph

chapter.title: A point on a transformed graph
text: In y = a·f(x − h) + v, the graph moves h to the right, is stretched by a (reflected if a < 0) and moves v up. A point (p, q) goes to (p + h, aq + v); f(h − x) also reflects it in the line x = h.
math: The point (4, −2) lies on the graph of y = f(x). Which point must lie on the graph of y = f(x + 2) − 5? Write it as (x, y).
The input to f must be 4: x = 2
chapter.tip: The graph was moved the wrong way; f(x + 2) takes the value f(4) when x = 2.

text: Find the x that makes the input of f equal to p, then work out the output: multiply q by a, then add v.
math: The point (4, 4) lies on the graph of y = f(x). Which point must lie on the graph of y = 2f(1 − x) − 5? Write it as (x, y).
The input to f must be 4: x = −3

modules.title: Evaluating the greatest integer function

chapter.title: Evaluating the greatest integer function
text: [x] is the greatest integer that is not more than x: on the number line it is the integer at x or the first one to its left. So [2.7] = 2 but [−2.7] = −3.
math: [x] denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Find [−2.9] − [5.3].
[−2.9] = −3: the integer at or just below it
[5.3] = 5: the integer at or just below it
chapter.tip: The decimal part was simply removed; for a negative number that moves up, but [x] is the integer at or below x: [−2.3] = −3.

chapter.title: Recognising the graph of a standard function
text: Each standard function has a recognisable graph: y = x a line through the origin, x² a parabola, x³ an S-shaped curve, |x| a V, 1/x two branches, sgn x three levels −1, 0, 1, [x] steps, 2ˣ an always-positive rising curve and log₂ x its mirror image for x > 0.
Look at where the graph is defined, where it crosses the axes, whether it has corners or jumps and how it behaves far out; then check one or two points, e.g. x = 1 and x = 2, in each option.
math: Which function has the graph shown in the picture?
Its shape, where it is defined and where it crosses the axes match y = |x| − 1
So the answer is y = |x| − 1

screens.title: The method
text: Place each number on the number line and step left to the nearest integer (stay if it is already an integer), then add or subtract.
math: [x] denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Find [−0.3] − [2.5].
[−0.3] = −1: the integer at or just below it
[2.5] = 2: the integer at or just below it

strategies.title: Step left on the number line

screens.title: Step left on the number line
text: Mark the number between two integers.
The greatest integer function always takes the left-hand one, even for negative numbers.
math: [x] denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Find [−0.5] − [6.2].
[−0.5] = −1: the integer at or just below it
[6.2] = 6: the integer at or just below it

text: A question: “[x] denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Find [−5.7] − [9.6].” A common wrong answer is −14.
The decimal part was simply removed; for a negative number that moves up, but [x] is the integer at or below x: [−2.3] = −3.
math: Not −14, but −15

modules.title: The corner point of a feasible region off the axes

chapter.title: The corner point of a feasible region off the axes
text: Each constraint ≤ is a half-plane bounded by a line; the corner points of the feasible region are where two boundary lines meet inside the region.
math: The feasible region of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, 5x + y ≤ 44 and 3x + 4y ≤ 40 has exactly one corner point that is on neither axis. Find it, as (x, y).
The corner is where the boundary lines meet: 5x + 1y = 44, 3x + 4y = 40
Solve them together: (x, y) = (8, 4)
chapter.tip: The smaller x-intercept and the smaller y-intercept were put together; the corner off the axes is where the two lines cross, found by solving them together.

screens.title: The method
text: Replace ≤ by = in the two constraints and solve the pair of equations (by elimination); check the point satisfies x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
math: The feasible region of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, 3x + 5y ≤ 54 and 5x + 2y ≤ 52 has exactly one corner point that is on neither axis. Find it, as (x, y).
The corner is where the boundary lines meet: 3x + 5y = 54, 5x + 2y = 52
Solve them together: (x, y) = (8, 6)

screens.title: Eliminate one variable
text: Multiply the equations so that the y terms have the same coefficient, and subtract to find x.
Put x back into either equation to find y.
math: The feasible region of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, 3x + 4y ≤ 53 and x + y ≤ 15 has exactly one corner point that is on neither axis. Find it, as (x, y).
The corner is where the boundary lines meet: 3x + 4y = 53, 1x + 1y = 15
Solve them together: (x, y) = (7, 8)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “The feasible region of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, 4x + y ≤ 25 and 2x + y ≤ 13 has exactly one corner point that is on neither axis. Find it, as (x, y).” A common wrong answer is (25/4, 13).
The smaller x-intercept and the smaller y-intercept were put together; the corner off the axes is where the two lines cross, found by solving them together.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve pairs of linear equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Replace ≤ by = in the two constraints and solve the pair of equations (by elimination); check the point satisfies x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

modules.title: Solving |ax + b| = c

chapter.title: Solving |ax + b| = c
text: |A| is the distance of A from 0, so |A| = c (with c > 0) means A = c or A = −c: two equations.
math: Solve |x + 6| = 10. Give every solution, separated by commas.
Divide by 1: x = −16 or x = 4

chapter.title: Solving |ax + b| < c, ≤ c, > c, ≥ c
text: |A| < c means A is within c of 0: −c < A < c. |A| > c means A is further than c from 0: A < −c or A > c.
Rewrite without the modulus (one double inequality, or two inequalities joined by 'or'), solve for x, and write the answer in interval notation with the right brackets.
math: Solve |6x + 1| ≤ 8. Write the answer in interval notation.
Remove the modulus: −8 ≤ 6x + 1 ≤ 8
Solve for x: [−3/2, 7/6]

screens.title: The method
text: Write the two cases ax + b = c and ax + b = −c, and solve each.
math: Solve |5x − 6| = 7. Give every solution, separated by commas.
|A| = 7 means A = 7 or A = −7: 5x − 6 = 7 or 5x − 6 = −7
Divide by 5: x = −1/5 or x = 13/5

screens.title: Distance on the number line
text: |ax + b| = c says ax is at distance c from −b.
Step c units left and right of −b to find the two values of ax, then divide by a.
math: Solve |2x − 5| = 6. Give every solution, separated by commas.
|A| = 6 means A = 6 or A = −6: 2x − 5 = 6 or 2x − 5 = −6
Divide by 2: x = −1/2 or x = 11/2

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve linear equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

modules.title: Solving a quadratic inequality

chapter.title: Solving a quadratic inequality
text: A quadratic with roots a < b keeps one sign between the roots and the other sign outside them; the sign outside is the sign of the x² coefficient.
math: Solve 2x² − 18x + 16 ≤ 0. Write the answer in interval notation.
Factorise: 2(x − 1)(x − 8)
Roots 1 and 8; with the sign of each region: [1, 8]
chapter.tip: The wrong region was chosen; (x − 1)(x − 8) is negative between 1 and 8 and positive outside.

chapter.title: Solving a rational inequality (x − a)/(x − b) compared with 0
text: A fraction is positive when top and bottom have the same sign and negative when they differ; it is 0 where the top is 0 and undefined where the bottom is 0.
Mark the zeros of the top and of the bottom, find the sign of the fraction in each region, and keep the regions asked for. The zero of the bottom is always left out.
math: Solve (x − 5)/(x − 1) > 0. Write the answer in interval notation.
The top is 0 at x = 5; the bottom is 0 at x = 1, which is never allowed
Signs in each region give (−∞, 1) ∪ (5, ∞)

text: Factorise, mark the roots on a number line, find the sign in each region, keep the regions the inequality asks for, and include the roots only for ≤ or ≥.

Factorise: −2(x − 3)(x − 6)
Roots 3 and 6; with the sign of each region: (−∞, 3) ∪ (6, ∞)

screens.title: Picture the parabola
text: With a positive x² coefficient the parabola opens upwards: it is below the x-axis only between the roots.
With a negative coefficient it opens downwards: it is above the x-axis only between the roots.
math: Solve x² − 14x + 48 ≥ 0. Write the answer in interval notation.
Factorise: (x − 6)(x − 8)
Roots 6 and 8; with the sign of each region: (−∞, 6] ∪ [8, ∞)

screens.title: A sign chart
text: Write the sign of each factor in each region.
Multiply the signs (and the sign of the leading number) to get the sign of the product.
math: Solve x² − 9x + 8 ≤ 0. Write the answer in interval notation.
Factorise: (x − 1)(x − 8)
Roots 1 and 8; with the sign of each region: [1, 8]

modules.title: Partial fractions with two distinct linear factors

chapter.title: Partial fractions with two distinct linear factors
text: (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) means px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a) for every x, so choosing x = a and x = b each removes one unknown.
math: Resolve (x − 12)/(x² − 3x − 10) into partial fractions of the form A/(x + 2) + B/(x − 5). Write the pair (A, B).
Factorise the denominator: (x + 2)(x − 5)
chapter.tip: In the cover-up step the other factor was worked out the wrong way round: at x = −2 the factor x − 5 is −7, not 7.

chapter.title: Partial fractions with a linear and an irreducible quadratic factor
text: A quadratic factor x² + k with no real roots needs a linear numerator Bx + C. Multiplying out, N(x) = A(x² + k) + (Bx + C)(x − a) holds for every x.
Put x = a to find A. Then compare the x² coefficients to find B and the x (or constant) terms to find C.
math: Resolve (5x² − 2x + 3)/((x − 1)(x² + 1)) into partial fractions of the form A/(x − 1) + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1). Write the triple (A, B, C).
x² terms: A + B = 5, so B = 2
x terms: C − (1)B = −2, so C = 0

chapter.title: Integrating by partial fractions or by decomposition
text: A fraction whose denominator factorises splits into simple fractions A/(x − a), each of which integrates to A log|x − a|. If the top has the same degree as the bottom, divide first.
Factorise the denominator, find A and B (put x = a, then x = b), then integrate each part: ∫ A/(x − a) dx = A log|x − a|. For (x + k)/(x − a), write it as 1 + (a + k)/(x − a).
math: Find ∫
Write the integrand as 1 + −3/x
Integrate term by term (∫ 1/(x − a) dx = log|x − a|): x − 3 log|x| + C

screens.title: The method
text: Factorise the denominator, multiply through, then put x = a to find A and x = b to find B. Check at one more value of x.
math: Resolve (−4x + 4)/(x² + 6x + 5) into partial fractions of the form A/(x + 5) + B/(x + 1). Write the pair (A, B).
Factorise the denominator: (x + 5)(x + 1)

screens.title: Compare coefficients
text: Expand A(x − b) + B(x − a) = (A + B)x − (Ab + Ba).
Match the x coefficient and the constant with px + q and solve the two equations for A and B.
math: Resolve (−6x + 33)/(x² − 9x + 18) into partial fractions of the form A/(x − 3) + B/(x − 6). Write the pair (A, B).
Factorise the denominator: (x − 3)(x − 6)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Resolve (−7x + 36)/(x² − 11x + 30) into partial fractions of the form A/(x − 5) + B/(x − 6). Write the pair (A, B).” A common wrong answer is (1, 6).
In the cover-up step the other factor was worked out the wrong way round: at x = 5 the factor x − 6 is −1, not 1.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Factor algebraic expressions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Factorise the denominator, multiply through, then put x = a to find A and x = b to find B. Check at one more value of x.

modules.title: Permutations of r out of n distinct objects

chapter.title: Permutations of r out of n distinct objects
text: Filling r places in order from n distinct objects: n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on, so ⁿPᵣ = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1) = n!/(n − r)!.
math: Find ¹⁶P₂, the number of ways of arranging 2 of 16 distinct objects in a row.
2 places, filled one after another: 16 × 15 = 240
chapter.tip: The objects were chosen without order (¹⁶C₂); in an arrangement the order matters.

chapter.title: Combinations: choosing r out of n
text: Choosing without order: each group of r objects appears r! times among the ordered arrangements, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ / r! = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
Use the smaller of r and n − r (ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ), multiply that many numbers down from n, and divide by its factorial.
math: Find ⁹C₆, the number of ways of choosing 6 of 9 distinct objects.
⁹C₆ = ⁹C₃ (choosing 6 to take is choosing 3 to leave)
In order: ⁹P₃ = 504
Each choice was counted 6 times (its arrangements): 504 ÷ 6 = 84

chapter.title: Selections with a condition: exactly k from one group
text: A condition splits the selection into independent parts: choose the women, choose the men, and multiply (every choice of one goes with every choice of the other).
Work out ʷCₖ for the women and ᵐCᵣ₋ₖ for the men, then multiply.
math: A committee of 6 is to be chosen from 7 men and 4 women. In how many ways can this be done if the committee must have exactly 3 women?
Women: ⁴C₃ = 4
Men: ⁷C₃ = 35
Each choice of women goes with each choice of men: 4 × 35 = 140

chapter.title: Arrangements when some objects are identical
text: If all n objects were different there would be n! arrangements; each arrangement of identical objects is counted p! × q! × … times, once for every shuffle of equal objects.
Work out n! and divide by the factorial of the size of each group of identical objects.
math: Find the number of distinct arrangements in a row of the 9 letters A, A, A, A, A, B, B, B, B, where equal letters are identical.
If all letters were different: 9! = 362880
Divide by the shuffles of equal letters: 362880 ÷ (120 × 24 × 1) = 126

chapter.title: The multiplication and addition principles of counting
text: Multiplication principle: if one thing can be done in m ways and then another in n ways, both can be done in m × n ways. Addition principle: if a choice is either one of m things or one of n other things (not both), there are m + n ways.
Ask: is it 'this AND then that' (multiply) or 'this OR that' (add)? For codes, count the choices for each place in turn; with no repetition, each place has one fewer choice.
math: A canteen menu has 2 South Indian dishes, 4 North Indian dishes and 2 Chinese dishes. In how many ways can a student choose exactly one dish?
Separate cases (one or the other), so add: 2 + 4 + 2 = 8

chapter.title: Evaluating and simplifying expressions with factorials
text: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1, and n! = n × (n − 1)!. So a bigger factorial contains every smaller one: 8! = 8 × 7 × 6!.
To simplify a quotient, write the bigger factorial down to the smaller one and cancel. To add fractions with factorials, rewrite each over the biggest factorial.
math: Evaluate 6!/5!.
Cancel the common factorial: 6 → 6

chapter.title: Using ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, ⁿPᵣ = r!·ⁿCᵣ and Pascal's rule
text: Choosing r to take is choosing n − r to leave, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ. Each selection of r can be arranged in r! ways, so ⁿPᵣ = r!·ⁿCᵣ. A selection of r from n + 1 either includes one particular object or not: ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ = ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁.
For ⁿCₐ = ⁿC_b (a ≠ b), use a + b = n. Divide ⁿPᵣ by ⁿCᵣ to get r!. For a sum ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁, write ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ and evaluate.
math: Find ¹⁰C₄ + ¹⁰C₃.
By Pascal's rule the sum is ¹¹C₄
¹¹C₄ = 330

chapter.title: Counting diagonals, triangles and lines with combinations
text: A segment needs 2 points and a triangle 3 non-collinear points, with no order, so they are counted with ⁿC₂ and ⁿC₃. Then remove what does not count: the sides (for diagonals), or the choices from collinear points.
Diagonals: ⁿC₂ − n = n(n − 3)/2. Triangles: ⁿC₃ − ᵐC₃. Lines: ⁿC₂ − ᵐC₂ + 1 (the collinear points give one line).
math: How many diagonals does a polygon with 7 sides have?
Pairs of points: ⁷C₂ = 21
Remove the 7 sides: 14

chapter.title: Deciding whether order matters, and combining selection with arrangement
text: Order matters when swapping two chosen things gives a different result (different posts, places, positions, a word); then count arrangements (ⁿPᵣ). If swapping gives the same result (a group, a team, a committee), count selections (ⁿCᵣ). Many problems first select, then arrange.
Ask: if I swap two of the chosen, is it a different outcome? Select with combinations, then multiply by the number of arrangements (or of ways to fill the special posts).
math: A teacher must send 3 of her 7 students to represent the class at a science exhibition. In how many ways can she pick them?
The wording means no order: use a combination
⁷C₃ = 35

chapter.title: Arrangements with repetition, restrictions, around a circle, and the rank of a word
text: With repetition each place has all n choices (nʳ). For 'together', glue the two into a block; for 'not together', subtract. Around a circle only relative positions count: (n − 1)!, and a necklace can also be flipped: (n − 1)!/2. A word's rank is 1 + the number of arrangements that come before it in dictionary order.

Name the restriction, count with the matching rule, and check the answer with a very small case. For a rank, go letter by letter: (number of unused smaller letters) × (factorial of the places left), add them up and add 1.
math: How many 2-letter codes can be made from 6 different letters if a letter may be used more than once?
2 places with 6 choices each: 6² = 36

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply r numbers, starting at n and going down by one each time.
math: Find ¹⁶P₄, the number of ways of arranging 4 of 16 distinct objects in a row.
4 places, filled one after another: 16 × 15 × 14 × 13 = 43680

screens.title: Draw the places as boxes
text: Draw r boxes in a row and write in each how many objects are still free to go there.
By the multiplication principle, multiply the numbers in the boxes.
math: Find ²⁷P₂, the number of ways of arranging 2 of 27 distinct objects in a row.
2 places, filled one after another: 27 × 26 = 702

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find ¹⁶P₃, the number of ways of arranging 3 of 16 distinct objects in a row.” A common wrong answer is 560.
The objects were chosen without order (¹⁶C₃); in an arrangement the order matters.
math: Not 560, but 3360

modules.title: A coefficient in the expansion of (ax + b)ⁿ

chapter.title: A coefficient in the expansion of (ax + b)ⁿ
text: The general term of (u + v)ⁿ is ⁿCᵣ uʳ vⁿ⁻ʳ. With u = ax and v = b, the term with xʳ is ⁿCᵣ aʳ bⁿ⁻ʳ xʳ.
math: Find the coefficient of x in the expansion of (2x + 1)³.
The term with x is ³C₁ (2x)¹ (1)²
³C₁ = 3
Coefficient: 3 × 2 = 6
chapter.tip: Only ³C₁ was given; the term also carries (2x)¹ and (1)², so their powers are part of the coefficient.

chapter.title: Expanding (ax + b)ⁿ
text: (u + v)ⁿ = ⁿC₀uⁿ + ⁿC₁uⁿ⁻¹v + … + ⁿCₙvⁿ: the power of u goes down while the power of v goes up, and the coefficients are a row of Pascal's triangle.
Write the row of Pascal's triangle for n, then each term ⁿCᵣ (ax)ⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, and simplify each coefficient with its sign.
math: Expand (2x − 4)² using the binomial theorem.
Row 2 of Pascal's triangle: 1, 2, 1
Multiply each by the powers of 2x and −4: 4x² − 16x + 16

chapter.title: The term independent of x in (xᵖ ± k/x^q)ⁿ
text: In (xᵖ + k/x^q)ⁿ the general term is ⁿCᵣ (xᵖ)ⁿ⁻ʳ (k/x^q)ʳ = ⁿCᵣ kʳ x^(p(n − r) − qr). The term independent of x is the one whose power of x is 0.
Write the power of x in the general term, set it equal to 0 to find r, then work out ⁿCᵣ kʳ.
math: Find the term independent of x in the expansion of (x³ + 2/x³)⁸.
General term: ⁸Cᵣ x^(24 − 6r) 2ʳ
The power of x is 0 when 6r = 24: r = 4

chapter.title: Building Pascal's triangle and reading binomial coefficients from it
text: Pascal's triangle starts with 1; each row starts and ends with 1, and every other entry is the sum of the two entries above it. Row n gives the coefficients ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ of (a + b)ⁿ.
To build the next row, add each pair of neighbours and put a 1 at each end. The coefficient of aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ is the entry in position r (the first 1 is position 0).
math: Row 7 of Pascal's triangle is 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1. Use it to find the coefficient of a⁶b in the expansion of (a + b)⁷.
The coefficient is in position 1 of row 7: 7

chapter.title: Exact values and approximations by the binomial theorem
text: Writing a number close to a power of 10 as 10ᵏ ± a makes the binomial expansion easy to work out exactly. For (1 + x)ⁿ with x small, the terms x², x³, … shrink fast, so 1 + nx + ⁿC₂x² is already a good approximation.
Exact: expand (10ᵏ + a)ⁿ term by term (keeping signs) and add. Approximation: write the base as 1 + x, work out nx and ⁿC₂x², and add them to 1.
math: Use the binomial theorem to evaluate 11³ exactly, writing 11 = 10 + 1.
The terms ⁿCᵣ (10ᵏ)ⁿ⁻ʳ aʳ are 1000, 300, 30, 1; they add up to 1331

chapter.title: The middle term or terms of (ax + b)ⁿ
text: (u + v)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, T₍ᵣ₊₁₎ = ⁿCᵣ uⁿ⁻ʳ vʳ. If n is even there is one middle term, T₍ₙ/₂₊₁₎; if n is odd there are two, T₍₍ₙ₊₁₎/₂₎ and T₍₍ₙ₊₃₎/₂₎.
Count the terms, find which one is in the middle and its r, then work out ⁿCᵣ (ax)ⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ with signs.
math: Find the middle term in the expansion of (3x + 1)⁶.
There are 7 terms; the one asked for is T₄, so r = 3
T₄ = ⁶C₃ (3x)³ (1)³
20 × 27 × 1 gives 540x³

screens.title: The method
text: Pick the term whose power of x is r, then multiply ⁿCᵣ by aʳ and by bⁿ⁻ʳ, keeping the signs.
math: Find the coefficient of x in the expansion of (−2x + 3)⁶.
The term with x is ⁶C₁ (−2x)¹ (3)⁵
⁶C₁ = 6
Coefficient: 6 × (−486) = −2916

strategies.title: Read the row of Pascal's triangle

screens.title: Read the row of Pascal's triangle
text: Row n of Pascal's triangle gives ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, … ⁿCₙ.
Each one multiplies a power of ax and a power of b whose powers add up to n.
math: Find the coefficient of x in the expansion of (3x + 2)⁷.
The term with x is ⁷C₁ (3x)¹ (2)⁶
⁷C₁ = 7
Coefficient: 7 × 192 = 1344

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (−2x + 1)⁸.” A common wrong answer is 56.
Only ⁸C₃ was given; the term also carries (−2x)³ and (1)⁵, so their powers are part of the coefficient.
math: Not 56, but −448

text: Each step builds on another skill: Count permutations and combinations; Use integer exponent laws. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Pick the term whose power of x is r, then multiply ⁿCᵣ by aʳ and by bⁿ⁻ʳ, keeping the signs.

modules.title: The nth term of a geometric progression

chapter.title: The nth term of a geometric progression
text: In a GP each term is the one before times r, so going from the 1st to the nth term multiplies by r exactly n − 1 times: aₙ = a r^(n − 1).
math: Find the 9th term of the geometric progression 3, 6, 12, …
chapter.tip: The common difference was used as in an AP; each term here is 2 times the one before.

chapter.title: The sum of the first n terms of a GP
text: Sₙ = a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹. Multiplying by r shifts every term along one place, so rSₙ − Sₙ = arⁿ − a and Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
Find a and r, then put them in Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), working out rⁿ with its sign first.
math: Find the sum of the first 9 terms of the geometric progression 8 + 24 + 72 + ⋯

chapter.title: The sum to infinity of a geometric series
text: When |r| < 1 the terms shrink towards 0 and the partial sums a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) approach a/(1 − r), because rⁿ → 0.
Find r = second term ÷ first term, check |r| < 1, and work out a/(1 − r).
math: Find the sum to infinity of the geometric series 8 + 8/5 + 8/25 + ⋯
r = 8/5 ÷ 8 = 1/5; |r| < 1, so the series converges

chapter.title: Identifying a geometric progression
text: A sequence is a geometric progression when each term (after the first) is the previous term multiplied by the same non-zero number r, the common ratio: a, ar, ar², ar³, …
Divide every term by the term before it. If all the ratios are equal, it is a GP; if any ratio is different, it is not. Checking only the first two terms is never enough.
math: All four sequences below start with the same two terms. Which one is a geometric progression?
Second term ÷ first term = 3
Only 7, 21, 63, 189, 567, … keeps that same ratio between every pair of neighbouring terms

chapter.title: Growth, depreciation and compound interest with geometric progressions
text: Growing by r% a year multiplies the amount by 1 + r/100 every year; losing r% multiplies it by 1 − r/100. So the amounts at the start, after 1 year, after 2 years, … form a GP: P, PR, PR², …, and after n years the amount is PRⁿ.
Write the common ratio R (1.1 for 10% growth, 0.9 for 10% decrease), then work out P × Rⁿ. Note it is the (n + 1)th term, because the first term is the starting amount.
math: A culture has 1,000 bacteria. The number of bacteria doubles every hour. How many bacteria will there be after 8 hours?
Each hour the amount is multiplied by the same number, r = 2: a geometric progression
After 8 steps: 1000 × 2⁸ = 256000

chapter.title: Using the sum to infinity: recurring decimals, a bouncing ball, nested shapes
text: Many situations hide an infinite geometric series with |r| < 1: a recurring decimal 0.4545… = 45/100 + 45/10000 + …, the heights of a bouncing ball, the areas of shapes that shrink by the same factor each time. Its sum is a/(1 − r).
Write the first term a and the ratio r of the repeating part, check |r| < 1, use a/(1 − r), and then add any part that is not repeated (the whole number, or the first drop of the ball).
math: Write the recurring decimal 2.626262…
The recurring part is 31/50 + 31/50 × 1/100 + …: a GP with r = 1/100
Add the whole-number part 2: 260/99

chapter.title: Does a geometric series converge, and to what?
text: A geometric series a + ar + ar² + … converges (has a sum to infinity) exactly when |r| < 1; then the terms shrink to 0 and S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the series diverges.
Find r = (second term) ÷ (first term). If |r| < 1 work out a/(1 − r); otherwise say it diverges — never use the formula without this check.
math: Consider the geometric series −9 + 6 − 4 + ⋯. Which statement is true?
r = −2/3: |r| < 1, so the series converges
So: The series converges, and its sum to infinity is −27/5

screens.title: The method
text: Find r by dividing the second term by the first, then work out a r^(n − 1), keeping track of the sign.
math: Find the 9th term of the geometric progression −3, 9, −27, …

screens.title: Keep multiplying
text: Write the terms out, multiplying by r each time, until you reach the term asked for.
Count the multiplications: one fewer than the term's position.
math: Find the 5th term of the geometric progression 9, −27, 81, …

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the 8th term of the geometric progression −3, 9, −27, …” A common wrong answer is 81.
The common difference was used as in an AP; each term here is −3 times the one before.
math: Not 81, but 6561

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use integer exponent laws. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find r by dividing the second term by the first, then work out a r^(n − 1), keeping track of the sign.

modules.title: The sum to infinity of an arithmetico-geometric series

chapter.title: The sum to infinity of an arithmetico-geometric series
text: In an AGP the coefficients form an AP and the powers of r a GP. Subtracting rS from S lines up equal powers of r, and the differences of the AP are all d, leaving a GP.
math: Find the sum to infinity of the arithmetico-geometric series 4 + 7(1/4) + 10(1/4)² + 13(1/4)³ + ⋯
Subtract r times the series from itself: S(1 − r) = 4 + 3r + 3r² + ⋯
The geometric part sums to 3/4/(1 − 1/4), so S(1 − r) = 5
Divide by 1 − r = 3/4: S = 20/3
chapter.tip: Only the geometric part was summed, as if every coefficient were the first one; the coefficients grow by d each time.

chapter.title: The harmonic mean of two numbers
text: Numbers are in harmonic progression when their reciprocals are in AP. The harmonic mean H of a and b is the middle one: 1/H is the average of 1/a and 1/b, so H = 2ab/(a + b).
Add the reciprocals, halve, and turn the result upside down — or use 2ab/(a + b) directly.
math: Find the harmonic mean of 1 and 16.

screens.title: The method
text: Write S and rS one place apart, subtract to get S(1 − r) = a + dr + dr² + ⋯ = a + dr/(1 − r), then divide by 1 − r.
math: Find the sum to infinity of the arithmetico-geometric series 7 + 12(3/4) + 17(3/4)² + 22(3/4)³ + ⋯
Subtract r times the series from itself: S(1 − r) = 7 + 5r + 5r² + ⋯
The geometric part sums to 15/4/(1 − 3/4), so S(1 − r) = 22
Divide by 1 − r = 1/4: S = 88

screens.title: Use the formula
text: Check it by adding the first few terms: the totals approach your answer.
math: Find the sum to infinity of the arithmetico-geometric series 6 + 12(2/3) + 18(2/3)² + 24(2/3)³ + ⋯
Subtract r times the series from itself: S(1 − r) = 6 + 6r + 6r² + ⋯
The geometric part sums to 4/(1 − 2/3), so S(1 − r) = 18
Divide by 1 − r = 1/3: S = 54

text: A question: “Find the sum to infinity of the arithmetico-geometric series 4 + 9(2/5) + 14(2/5)² + 19(2/5)³ + ⋯” A common wrong answer is 20/3.
Only the geometric part was summed, as if every coefficient were the first one; the coefficients grow by d each time.

text: Each step builds on another skill: Use geometric sequences and series. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write S and rS one place apart, subtract to get S(1 − r) = a + dr + dr² + ⋯ = a + dr/(1 − r), then divide by 1 − r.

modules.title: Using the laws of logarithms: log N in terms of log 2 and log 3

chapter.title: Using the laws of logarithms: log N in terms of log 2 and log 3
text: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y and log xⁿ = n log x. With log 10 = 1, log 5 = log(10/2) = 1 − log 2.
math: Given log 2 = a and log 3 = b (logarithms to base 10), express log 6 in terms of a and b.
Write 6 with powers of 2, 3 and 5: 2¹ × 3¹ × 5⁰
log(xy) = log x + log y and log xⁿ = n log x give a + b

chapter.title: Evaluating a logarithm by writing both numbers as powers of one base
text: log_B X = y means Bʸ = X. If B = cⁱ and X = cʲ, then (cⁱ)ʸ = cʲ, so iy = j and y = j/i.
Write the base and the number as powers of the same prime, then divide the power of the number by the power of the base.
math: Evaluate log₁₂₅ 3125.
Write both as powers of 5: 125 = 5³, 3125 = 5⁵
(c^3)^y = c^5 when 3y = 5, so the logarithm is 5/3

chapter.title: Solving log x + log(x ± c) = k
text: log x + log y = log(xy), and log_B N = k means N = Bᵏ. A logarithm is only defined for positive numbers, so every root must be checked.
Combine the logs into one, rewrite as x(x ± c) = Bᵏ, solve the quadratic, and keep only roots that make both x and x ± c positive.
math: Solve log₇ x + log₇(x − 6) = 1. Give every solution, separated by commas.
log x + log y = log(xy), and log_B(…) = 1 means … = 7¹: x(x − 6) = 7
Solve the quadratic: x = 7 or x = −1
Only x = 7 keeps both logarithms defined

chapter.title: Solving simple exponential equations by writing powers of one base
text: If aᵐ = aⁿ with a > 0, a ≠ 1, then m = n. So an exponential equation whose two sides are powers of the same number becomes an ordinary equation in the powers.
Write each base as a power of one prime (9 = 3², 27 = 3³), use (cⁱ)ᵗ = c^(it) on the whole exponent, equate the exponents and solve.
math: Solve 4^(x + 1) = 2^x.
Write both sides as powers of 2 and equate the powers: 2(x + 1) = 1x

chapter.title: Change of base: products and sums of logarithms
text: Change of base: log_a x = log x / log a (any base for both). So log_a b × log_b c = log_a c, and 1/log_a x = log_x a.
Rewrite each logarithm as a quotient of logarithms to one base, cancel what is common, then evaluate using powers of the same prime.
math: Using the change of base rule, evaluate log₅ 3 × log₃ 25.
Change of base: log 3/log 5 × log 25/log 3 = log 25/log 5
So the value is 2

screens.title: The method
text: Write the number as a product of powers of 2, 3 and 5 (a decimal is a whole number over a power of 10), take logs term by term, and replace log 5 by 1 − a.
math: Given log 2 = a and log 3 = b (logarithms to base 10), express log 259.2 in terms of a and b.
Write 259.2 with powers of 2, 3 and 5: 2⁴ × 3⁴ × 5⁻¹
log(xy) = log x + log y and log xⁿ = n log x give 5a + 4b − 1

screens.title: Check with a calculator
text: Put these into your answer: it should match log of the number to four decimal places.
math: Given log 2 = a and log 3 = b (logarithms to base 10), express log 21600 in terms of a and b.
Write 21600 with powers of 2, 3 and 5: 2⁵ × 3³ × 5²
log(xy) = log x + log y and log xⁿ = n log x give 3a + 3b + 2

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Given log 2 = a and log 3 = b (logarithms to base 10), express log 51.84 in terms of a and b.” A common wrong answer is 2a + 2b.
log 5 was taken as log 2 + log 3, because 2 + 3 = 5; logs turn products into sums, and 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so log 5 = 1 − a.
math: Not 2a + 2b, but 6a + 4b − 2

text: Each step builds on another skill: Use integer exponent laws. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write the number as a product of powers of 2, 3 and 5 (a decimal is a whole number over a power of 10), take logs term by term, and replace log 5 by 1 − a.

modules.title: Solving a quadratic with negative discriminant over ℂ

chapter.title: Solving a quadratic with negative discriminant over ℂ
text: The quadratic formula works over ℂ: when b² − 4ac < 0, √(b² − 4ac) = i√(4ac − b²), so the roots are −b/(2a) ± i√(4ac − b²)/(2a), a conjugate pair.
math: Solve x² + 3x + 10 = 0 over the complex numbers. The roots are p + qi and p − qi with q > 0; write the pair (p, q).
b² − 4ac = −31 < 0: the roots are not real
chapter.tip: √(31) was not divided by 2a = 2; the whole of −b ± √(b² − 4ac) is divided by 2a.

chapter.title: A real quadratic from one complex root
text: A polynomial with real coefficients has its non-real roots in conjugate pairs: if a + bi is a root, so is a − bi. Their sum is 2a and their product is a² + b².
Write the quadratic as k(x² − (sum)x + product) and read off p and q.
math: The number −1 + 5i is a root of x² + px + q = 0, where p and q are real. Find (p, q).
Real coefficients: the conjugate −1 − 5i is also a root
Sum of roots = −2
Product of roots = a² + b² = 26
(x² − (sum)x + product), so (p, q) = (2, 26)

screens.title: The method
text: Find D = b² − 4ac, write √D = i√(−D) and simplify the surd, then divide both −b and √(−D) by 2a.
math: Solve x² + 3x + 11 = 0 over the complex numbers. The roots are p + qi and p − qi with q > 0; write the pair (p, q).

chapter.title: Counting the elements of Cartesian products
text: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Each of the n(A) first entries goes with each of the n(B) second entries, so n(A × B) = n(A)·n(B).

Multiply: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30

chapter.title: Reading the sets from a Cartesian product
text: In A × B every pair has its first entry from A and its second entry from B, and every combination appears.

math: A × B = {(−3, −3), (−3, 0), (−3, 3), (−1, −3), (−1, 0), (−1, 3)}. Find the set B. Write its elements separated by commas.

The last point of the region it touches gives the maximum.
math: Maximise Z = 7x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 9, 4x + 5y ≤ 40, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum value of Z?
The corner points of the feasible region are (0, 0), (9, 0), (5, 4), (0, 8)
Z at the corners: 0, 63, 43, 16; the greatest is 63

modules.title: Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices

chapter.title: Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices
text: Entry (i, j) of AB combines row i of A with column j of B: multiply matching entries and add. In general AB ≠ BA.
math: row 1 of A with each of the columns of B: [0, −17]
row 2 of A with each of the columns of B: [0, −1]
chapter.tip: Matching entries were multiplied; in a matrix product each entry is a row of A times a column of B, added up.

chapter.title: Solving a matrix equation kX ± A = B
text: Matrices are equal when every pair of matching entries is equal, so a matrix equation is solved like a number equation, entry by entry.
Move A to the other side (subtract it, or add it if it was subtracted), then divide every entry by k.
math: A = [[5, −3], [4, 2]] and B = [[−1, 0], [13, −7]]. Find the matrix X such that 3X + A = B, written as [[a, b], [c, d]].
Subtract A on both sides: the right side is [[−6, 3], [9, −9]]
Divide every entry by 3: X = [[−2, 1], [3, −3]]

chapter.title: A matrix product as a total bill
text: A row of quantities times a column of prices is a bill: each quantity is multiplied by its own price and the products are added. QP does this for every row at once.
Check the orders: (2 × 3)(3 × 1) gives 2 × 1. For each row of Q, multiply the three entries by the three prices and add.
math: Q = [[1, 2, 9], [3, 8, 1]] (order 2 × 3) and P = [[50], [45], [60]] (order 3 × 1). Find QP, written as a column [[a], [b]].
Row (1,2,9) times column (50,45,60): 680
Row (3,8,1) times column (50,45,60): 570

chapter.title: Constructing a matrix from a rule aᵢⱼ (and its transpose)
text: A = [aᵢⱼ] of order m × n has m rows and n columns; aᵢⱼ is the entry in row i and column j. The transpose Aᵀ has the rows of A as its columns, so it has order n × m.
Draw an empty m × n grid. For each cell put in its row number i and column number j and work out the rule. For Aᵀ, write the first row of A as the first column, and so on.
math: Construct the 1 × 3 matrix A = [aᵢⱼ] whose elements are given by aᵢⱼ = ij. Write A as [[…], […]], row by row.
Put i = row number and j = column number into aᵢⱼ = ij: A = [[1, 2, 3]]

chapter.title: The order and the type of a matrix
text: The order of a matrix is rows × columns. A row matrix has one row, a column matrix one column, a square matrix as many rows as columns. A diagonal matrix is square with zeros off the main diagonal; a scalar matrix is diagonal with equal diagonal entries; the identity is scalar with 1s; a zero matrix has every entry 0.
Count the rows, then the columns. Then check, from the most general to the most special: square? zeros off the diagonal? equal diagonal entries? are they 1? (or are all entries 0?)
math: A = [[1], [−5]]. What is the order of A?
A has 2 rows and 1 column: order 2 × 1
So the answer is order 2 × 1

chapter.title: Equality of matrices
text: Two matrices are equal when they have the same order and every pair of corresponding entries is equal.
Set each entry on the left equal to the entry in the same position on the right, then solve the equations you get.
math: If [[x + 3, 2y], [z − 4, 7]] = [[3, −6], [−7, 7]], find x, y and z. Write the answer as (x, y, z).
Equal matrices have equal corresponding entries: three equations
Solving: (0, −3, −3)

chapter.title: Modelling a situation with a matrix product
text: When each of several producers makes several items, and each item needs fixed amounts of resources, the totals are a matrix product: (production matrix) × (needs per item matrix). The inner orders must match: (2 × 3)(3 × 2).

Write one row per producer and one column per item for the production; one row per item and one column per resource for the needs. Multiply: each entry is a row of quantities times a column of needs, added up.
math: Two school canteens in Coimbatore make idlis, dosas and vadas. On a day canteen P makes 1 dozen idlis, 1 dozen dosas and 3 dozen vadas, and canteen Q makes 2, 1 and 2 dozen. One dozen idlis needs 1 cup of batter and 2 spoons of oil, a dozen dosas 3 cups and 3 spoons, and a dozen vadas 5 cups and 4 spoons. Using a matrix product of the 2 × 3 production matrix and the 3 × 2 needs matrix, find for each canteen the total batter and the total oil. Write the product as [[a, b], [c, d]] (canteen P first; batter, then oil).
Multiply rows × columns: [[19, 17], [15, 15]]

chapter.title: Rotating and reflecting points with a 2 × 2 matrix
text: Multiplying a column [[x], [y]] by a 2 × 2 matrix moves the point (x, y); the matrix [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]] turns the plane through θ anticlockwise about the origin. Rotation and reflection matrices are orthogonal: TTᵀ = I.
Work out T[[x], [y]]: first entry = (row 1 of T)·(x, y), second entry = (row 2 of T)·(x, y).
math: The matrix T = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] represents a rotation through 270° anticlockwise about the origin. Find the image of the point (−2, −4) by working out T[[−2], [−4]]. Write it as (x, y).

chapter.title: The inverse of an orthogonal matrix
text: A square matrix is orthogonal when AAᵀ = AᵀA = I. Then A⁻¹ = Aᵀ — no determinant or adjoint is needed. Rotations and reflections of the plane have orthogonal matrices.
Check (or use, if given) AAᵀ = I, then write A⁻¹ = Aᵀ by turning the rows of A into columns.
math: A = [[3/5, −4/5], [−4/5, −3/5]] is an orthogonal matrix (AAᵀ = I). Find A⁻¹, written as a matrix (fractions are fine as entries).
For an orthogonal matrix AAᵀ = I, so A⁻¹ = Aᵀ

chapter.title: Encoding and decoding a message with a matrix
text: A message can be hidden by multiplying columns of letter numbers by an invertible matrix A: C = AM. The receiver, who knows A, recovers M = A⁻¹C. A matrix with determinant ±1 has an inverse with whole-number entries.
To encode, multiply A by the column of letter numbers. To decode, find A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A and multiply it by the coded column; then turn the numbers back into letters.
math: In a matrix code, each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet (A = 1, B = 2, …, Z = 26), a pair of letters is written as a column M = [[m₁], [m₂]], and the coded column is C = AM with A = [[3, 2], [4, 3]]. A coded column [[13], [19]] is received. Decode it using A⁻¹: find (m₁, m₂).
A⁻¹[[13], [19]] = (1, 5), the letters AE

screens.title: The method
text: For each of the four entries take a row of A and a column of B, multiply pairwise and add; keep the signs.
math: row 1 of A with each of the columns of B: [6, −3]
row 2 of A with each of the columns of B: [−1, 8]

screens.title: Column by column
text: Column j of AB is A times column j of B.
So find A[e, g] and A[f, h] (as column vectors) and stand them side by side.
math: row 1 of A with each of the columns of B: [3, 6]
row 2 of A with each of the columns of B: [1, 8]

Matching entries were multiplied; in a matrix product each entry is a row of A times a column of B, added up.

modules.title: Solving three equations by X = A⁻¹B

chapter.title: Solving three equations by X = A⁻¹B
text: A system AX = B with |A| ≠ 0 has exactly one solution, X = A⁻¹B, and A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
math: Solve by the matrix method (X = A⁻¹B): 2y + 2z = 6; x + y + z = 5; −x + 2y + 3z = 6. Write the solution as (x, y, z).
|A| = −2 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)
adj A = (matrix of cofactors)ᵀ = [[1, −2, 0], [−4, 2, 2], [3, −2, −2]]
X = (1/|A|) adj A · B: adj A · B = (−4, −2, −4), divided by −2, gives (2, 1, 2)
chapter.tip: The matrix of cofactors was used instead of its transpose; adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix.

chapter.title: Solving two equations with an inverse matrix
text: If |A| ≠ 0 then A has an inverse and AX = B gives X = A⁻¹B. For a 2 × 2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/|A|)[[d, −b], [−c, a]].
Find |A| = ad − bc, write the adjoint (swap a and d, negate b and c), multiply it by B and divide by |A|.
math: Use the inverse of A = [[1, 2], [3, 2]] to solve AX = B, where X = [[x], [y]] and B = [[21], [27]]. Write the solution as (x, y).

chapter.title: Word problems with three unknowns, solved by the inverse, Cramer's rule or Gaussian elimination
text: Each fact in the story gives one linear equation in the three unknowns; together they form AX = B. With |A| ≠ 0 there is exactly one solution, found by X = A⁻¹B, by Cramer's rule (x = Δ₁/Δ, …) or by Gaussian elimination (row-reduce [A | B] and back-substitute).
Name the unknowns (x, y, z), write one equation per fact, write A and B, then use the method asked for. Check the answer in every fact of the story.
math: At a stationery shop in Erode, Anu buys 2 notebooks and 3 erasers for ₹29; Ravi buys 2 notebooks and 4 erasers for ₹32; Meena buys 2 notebooks, 1 pen and 1 eraser for ₹28. Form the equations and solve them by Cramer's rule to find the price of one notebook, one pen and one eraser, in rupees. Write the answer as (x, y, z).
|A| = −2 ≠ 0, so there is exactly one solution

screens.title: The method
text: Find |A|; find the nine cofactors and transpose them to get adj A; multiply adj A by B and divide by |A|.
math: Solve by the matrix method (X = A⁻¹B): x + 3y − z = −1; −2x − 2y − z = 8; x + 3y + 2z = −7. Write the solution as (x, y, z).
|A| = 12 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)
adj A = (matrix of cofactors)ᵀ = [[−1, −9, −5], [3, 3, 3], [−4, 0, 4]]
X = (1/|A|) adj A · B: adj A · B = (−36, 0, −24), divided by 12, gives (−3, 0, −2)

screens.title: Cramer's rule
text: x = |A₁|/|A|, y = |A₂|/|A|, z = |A₃|/|A|, where Aᵢ is A with column i replaced by B.
Check by substituting the values back into each equation.
math: Solve by the matrix method (X = A⁻¹B): −x − 2y + 3z = 2; −x + y = −1; −2x − y + z = 5. Write the solution as (x, y, z).
|A| = 6 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)
adj A = (matrix of cofactors)ᵀ = [[1, −1, −3], [1, 5, −3], [3, 3, −3]]
X = (1/|A|) adj A · B: adj A · B = (−12, −18, −12), divided by 6, gives (−2, −3, −2)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve by the matrix method (X = A⁻¹B): −2x + 2z = 0; 2y + z = −4; x + y + z = −5. Write the solution as (x, y, z).” A common wrong answer is (−1, −1, −2).
The matrix of cofactors was used instead of its transpose; adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Evaluate and apply determinants; Find minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse of a square matrix (up to 3x3). If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find |A|; find the nine cofactors and transpose them to get adj A; multiply adj A by B and divide by |A|.

modules.title: A cubic whose roots are in progression

chapter.title: A cubic whose roots are in progression
text: Roots in AP can be written a − d, a, a + d: their sum is 3a. Roots in GP can be written a/r, a, ar: their product is a³. Vieta then gives the middle root.
math: The roots of 2x³ − 12x² + 22x − 12 = 0 are in arithmetic progression. Solve the equation. Write the roots separated by commas.
The middle root is 12 ÷ 6 = 2
Dividing by (x − 2) leaves 2x² − 8x + 6
The roots are 1, 2, 3

chapter.title: Solving a cubic with the rational root theorem
text: If p/q (in lowest terms) is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.
List the possible p/q, test them (whole numbers first), divide by the factor you find and solve the quadratic that is left.
math: Solve 3x³ − 16x² + 25x − 12 = 0. (All its roots are rational: try ± (a factor of the constant term)/(a factor of the leading coefficient).) Write the roots separated by commas.
Possible rational roots: ±(factors of 12)/(factors of 3)
p(1) = 0, so x − (1) is a factor
Dividing leaves 3x² − 13x + 12
The roots are 1, 4/3, 3

chapter.title: A cubic equation from a volume
text: x(x + a)(x + b) = V expands to a cubic with one sign change, so it has exactly one positive root; a whole-number root divides the constant term V.
Estimate: x is a little less than ∛V. Test the divisors of V near that estimate until one gives V.
math: The equation x³ + 11x² + 24x − 8500 = 0 has exactly one positive root, and it is a whole number. Find it.
The signs + + + − change once, so there is exactly one positive root (Descartes)
A whole-number root divides 8500
x = 17 makes the polynomial 0

chapter.title: Solving a reciprocal equation
text: A reciprocal equation is unchanged when x is replaced by 1/x: its coefficients read the same forwards and backwards (or with signs changed). So its roots come in pairs t, 1/t, and dividing by x² and putting y = x + 1/x halves the degree.
For an odd degree, first take out the factor x + 1 (or x − 1). Divide by x², group (x² + 1/x²) and (x + 1/x), use x² + 1/x² = y² − 2, solve the quadratic in y, then solve x + 1/x = y for each y.
math: 8x⁴ − 54x³ + 101x² − 54x + 8 = 0 is a reciprocal equation. Solve it by dividing by x² and putting y = x + 1/x. Give every root, separated by commas.
Dividing by x² and putting y = x + 1/x gives a quadratic in y: y = 5/2 or y = 17/4
Solving x + 1/x = y for each y: x = 1/3, 1/2, 2, 4

chapter.title: Equations reducible to quadratics: √x and exponential substitutions
text: Some equations that are not polynomials become quadratics after a substitution: x − 5√x + 6 = 0 is y² − 5y + 6 = 0 with y = √x, and 4^x − 6·2^x + 8 = 0 is y² − 6y + 8 = 0 with y = 2^x.
Spot the substitution, solve the quadratic in y, then go back to x — and reject any value of y the substitution cannot take (√x ≥ 0, 2^x > 0). Check each x in the original equation.
math: Solve x − 7√x + 10 = 0 for real x (put y = √x). Give every solution, separated by commas.
With y = √x the equation becomes a quadratic: y = 2 or y = 5
Back to x: 4, 25

chapter.title: A volume condition giving a cubic equation
text: Writing the volume in terms of one unknown dimension gives a cubic equation. Only a positive root makes sense, and a whole-number root must divide the constant term.
Write V = (length)(breadth)(height) in x, expand to a cubic = 0, then test whole numbers near ∛V (factors of the constant term) until one fits; check every dimension is positive.
math: A cardboard carton in the shape of a cuboid has a square base of side x cm and a height of (x − 3) cm. Its volume is 700 cm³. Form a cubic equation in x and solve it to find x, in cm.
Volume = 700 gives x³ − 3x² − 700 = 0
The coefficients change sign once, so there is exactly one positive root (Descartes' rule)
x = 10 makes the cubic 0 (it divides the constant term)

screens.title: The method
text: For an AP, a = (−b/leading coefficient)/3; for a GP, a³ = −(constant)/(leading coefficient). Check a is a root, divide by (x − a) and solve the quadratic.
math: The roots of 2x³ − 2x = 0 are in arithmetic progression. Solve the equation. Write the roots separated by commas.
The middle root is 0 ÷ 6 = 0
Dividing by (x − 0) leaves 2x² − 2
The roots are −1, 0, 1

screens.title: Synthetic division
text: Once the middle root a is known, divide the coefficients by a in a synthetic-division table.
The bottom row gives the quadratic; factorise it for the other two roots.
math: The roots of 2x³ + 14x² − 42x − 54 = 0 are in geometric progression. Solve the equation. Write the roots separated by commas.
The middle root is 54 ÷ 2 = −1
Dividing by (x + 1) leaves 2x² + 12x − 54
The roots are −9, −1, 3

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Relate roots and coefficients of polynomial equations; Apply remainder and factor theorems. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: For an AP, a = (−b/leading coefficient)/3; for a GP, a³ = −(constant)/(leading coefficient). Check a is a root, divide by (x − a) and solve the quadratic.
