modules.title: Finding the other roots from a surd root

chapter.title: Finding the other roots from a surd root
text: If a polynomial has rational coefficients and u + √w is a root (√w irrational), then its conjugate u − √w is a root too.
math: 2 + √5 is a root of x³ + x² − 21x − 5 = 0. Find the other two roots. Write them separated by commas.
The coefficients are rational, so the conjugate 2 − √5 is also a root
Dividing the cubic by x² − 4x − 1 leaves x − (−5), so the third root is −5
chapter.tip: Both parts of the root changed sign; the conjugate of 2 + √5 changes only the sign of the surd: 2 − √5.

chapter.title: Descartes' rule of signs
text: The number of positive roots of p(x) = 0 is at most the number of sign changes in its coefficients (and differs from it by an even number). For negative roots, count the changes in p(−x).
Write the signs of the non-zero coefficients in order, skipping zeros, and count the changes. For p(−x), first change the sign of each odd-power coefficient.
math: Use Descartes' rule of signs to find the greatest possible number of positive real roots of 5x⁵ − 8x² + x + 2 = 0.
Signs: + − + +, so 2 changes

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply (x − (u + √w))(x − (u − √w)) = x² − 2ux + (u² − w), divide the cubic by this quadratic, and read the third root from the linear factor left over.
math: −1 + √5 is a root of x³ − 2x² − 12x + 16 = 0. Find the other two roots. Write them separated by commas.
The coefficients are rational, so the conjugate −1 − √5 is also a root
Dividing the cubic by x² + 2x − 4 leaves x − (4), so the third root is 4

strategies.title: Use the sum of the roots

screens.title: Use the sum of the roots
text: The three roots add up to −(coefficient of x²).
The two conjugate roots add up to 2u, so the third root is −(coefficient of x²) − 2u.
math: −2 + √7 is a root of x³ − x² − 23x + 15 = 0. Find the other two roots. Write them separated by commas.
The coefficients are rational, so the conjugate −2 − √7 is also a root
Dividing the cubic by x² + 4x − 3 leaves x − (5), so the third root is 5

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “−1 + √5 is a root of x³ − x² − 10x + 12 = 0. Find the other two roots. Write them separated by commas.” A common wrong answer is 1 − √5, 3.
Both parts of the root changed sign; the conjugate of −1 + √5 changes only the sign of the surd: −1 − √5.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use algebraic identities; Apply remainder and factor theorems. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Multiply (x − (u + √w))(x − (u − √w)) = x² − 2ux + (u² − w), divide the cubic by this quadratic, and read the third root from the linear factor left over.

modules.title: Symmetric functions of the roots of a cubic

chapter.title: Symmetric functions of the roots of a cubic
text: For ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 with roots α, β, γ: α + β + γ = −b/a, αβ + βγ + γα = c/a and αβγ = −d/a.
math: α, β and γ are the roots of x³ + x² + 5x + 6 = 0. Find 1/α + 1/β + 1/γ.
Σα = −1, Σαβ = 5, αβγ = −6
Write it with these sums: Σαβ/αβγ
Substitute: −5/6
chapter.tip: 1/(α + β + γ) was found; the sum of reciprocals is (αβ + βγ + γα)/αβγ.

chapter.title: Forming a quadratic with transformed roots
text: A quadratic with leading coefficient 1 and zeros r₁, r₂ is x² − (r₁ + r₂)x + r₁r₂. For x² + px + q, α + β = −p and αβ = q.
Write the new sum and product in terms of α + β and αβ (e.g. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ), substitute, and write x² − (sum)x + (product).
math: α and β are the roots of x² − 5x + 3 = 0. Find the quadratic expression x² + bx + c (leading coefficient 1) whose zeros are −2α and −2β.
α + β = 5, αβ = 3
New sum of zeros: −10
New product of zeros: 12
x² − (sum)x + (product) = x² + 10x + 12

chapter.title: Roots and coefficients: the measurements of a box
text: If α, β, γ are the roots of x³ − px² + qx − r = 0 then α + β + γ = p, αβ + βγ + γα = q and αβγ = r. For a box with edges α, β, γ these are a quarter of the edge length, half the surface area, and the volume.
Read p, q and r from the equation (watch the signs), then write the quantity asked for in terms of them: surface area 2q, edges 4p, volume r, diagonal² = p² − 2q.
math: The length, breadth and height of a cuboid-shaped box, in cm, are the three roots of x³ − 16x² + 80x − 128 = 0. Without solving the equation, use the relations between roots and coefficients to find the total surface area of the box, in cm².
For x³ − px² + qx − r = 0: α + β + γ = 16, αβ + βγ + γα = 80, αβγ = 128
So the value asked for is 160

screens.title: The method
text: Rewrite the expression using only these three sums (e.g. α² + β² + γ² = (Σα)² − 2Σαβ, 1/α + 1/β + 1/γ = Σαβ/αβγ), then substitute.
math: α, β and γ are the roots of x³ + 3x² − 4x + 1 = 0. Find α² + β² + γ².
Σα = −3, Σαβ = −4, αβγ = −1
Write it with these sums: (Σα)² − 2Σαβ
Substitute: 17

screens.title: The signs alternate
text: Divide by a: x³ − (Σα)x² + (Σαβ)x − αβγ.
So the signs go −, +, − as you move along the coefficients.
math: α, β and γ are the roots of 3x³ + 3x² − 2x + 1 = 0. Find α² + β² + γ².
Write it with these sums: (Σα)² − 2Σαβ
Substitute: 7/3

text: A question: “α, β and γ are the roots of 3x³ − 6x² + 6x + 5 = 0. Find 1/α + 1/β + 1/γ.” A common wrong answer is 1/2.
1/(α + β + γ) was found; the sum of reciprocals is (αβ + βγ + γα)/αβγ.
math: Not 1/2, but −6/5

modules.title: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix

chapter.title: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
text: A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A, and it exists only when |A| ≠ 0. For [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
math: |A| = ad − bc = 6 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)
Divide every entry by 6: [[0, −1], [1/6, 2/3]]
chapter.tip: The adjoint was given; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|, so every entry must be divided by 6.

chapter.title: The adjoint of a 3 × 3 matrix
text: adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, and A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I, so A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| when |A| ≠ 0.
For each entry find its minor (the 2 × 2 determinant left when its row and column are deleted), attach the sign (−1)^(i + j), then transpose the whole matrix.
math: Minors (delete the row and column of each entry): [[−8, −2, 6], [3, −3, 9], [2, 8, 6]]

screens.title: The method
text: Find |A| = ad − bc; swap a and d, change the signs of b and c; divide every entry by |A|.
math: |A| = ad − bc = 15 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)
Divide every entry by 15: [[0, 1/5], [−1/3, 4/15]]

screens.title: Row-reduce [A | I]
text: Write A and I side by side and use row operations to turn A into I.
The same operations turn I into A⁻¹; check that AA⁻¹ = I.
math: |A| = ad − bc = −6 (not 0, so A⁻¹ exists)

chapter.title: The rank of a 3 × 4 matrix
text: The rank is the number of non-zero rows in an echelon form: the number of rows that are not combinations of the others.

Count the non-zero rows: rank = 1

chapter.title: The inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix by the Gauss–Jordan method
text: Each elementary row operation is multiplication on the left by an invertible matrix. If the operations turn A into I, their product is A⁻¹ — so doing the same operations to I produces A⁻¹.

Write [A | I]. Make the first column (1, 0, 0) using row swaps and Rᵢ → Rᵢ + kRⱼ (and Rᵢ → cRᵢ), then the second column, then the third, always on whole rows. Read A⁻¹ from the right half and check AA⁻¹ = I.

Use Rᵢ ↔ Rⱼ, Rᵢ → Rᵢ + kRⱼ until the left half is I: [I | A⁻¹]

Count the non-zero rows: rank = 1

modules.title: Deciding the number of solutions of a 3 × 3 system by ranks

chapter.title: Deciding the number of solutions of a 3 × 3 system by ranks
text: AX = B is consistent exactly when ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]). If that common rank equals the number of unknowns there is one solution; if it is smaller there are infinitely many.
math: Use the rank method to decide how many solutions this system has: x + y + z = 2, 3x + y + 2z = 7, −4x − z = −9.
Row-reduce A: it has 3 non-zero rows, so ρ(A) = 3
Row-reduce [A | B]: ρ([A | B]) = 3
ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) = 3 = number of unknowns: exactly one solution
chapter.tip: Equal ranks were read as 'infinitely many solutions'. Equal ranks mean the system is consistent; the solution is unique when that rank equals the number of unknowns (3).

chapter.title: Finding the parameter values that make a system singular or consistent
text: A unique solution needs |A| ≠ 0. When |A| = 0 the third row is a combination of the other two; the system is consistent (infinitely many solutions) only if the right sides follow the same combination.
For λ: expand |A| (it is linear in λ) and solve |A| = 0. For μ: find m, k with R₃ = mR₁ + kR₂ from the x and y columns, then μ = m b₁ + k b₂.

Expanding, |A| = −4(λ + 3)
|A| = 0 when λ = −3: then there is no unique solution

text: When ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) = 2 for three unknowns, one equation is a combination of the others and one unknown is free; the solutions form a line, described by one parameter.

By row reduction, ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) = 2 < 3: infinitely many solutions
Keep two independent equations, put z = t
Solve for x and y in terms of t: (2, −6, −1, 4)

modules.title: The identity element and inverses for a binary operation

chapter.title: The identity element and inverses for a binary operation
text: The identity e leaves every element unchanged: a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a. An inverse of a is an element b with a ∗ b = b ∗ a = e. Both depend on the rule, not on ordinary + or ×.
math: On ℤ, the binary operation ∗ is defined by a ∗ b = a + b − 6. Find the inverse of −4.
Solve a ∗ e = a for every a: e = 6
Solve −4 ∗ b = 6: b = 16
chapter.tip: −(−4) (the inverse for ordinary addition) was given; the inverse b must satisfy −4 ∗ b = e for this operation's identity e.

chapter.title: Is a binary operation commutative, associative, both or neither?
text: Commutative: a ∗ b = b ∗ a for all a, b. Associative: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c. Either can hold without the other.
Swap a and b in the rule and compare. Then work out (a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) in full and compare. One counter-example (with actual numbers) is enough to show a property fails.
math: On ℝ, a binary operation ∗ is defined by a ∗ b = (a + b)/3. Which is true?
a ∗ b and b ∗ a are equal
(a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) are not equal
So ∗ is commutative but not associative

chapter.title: Binary operations modulo n, by a table and on matrices
text: ∗ is a binary operation on S when a ∗ b is in S for every a, b in S (closure). It is commutative when a ∗ b = b ∗ a for all a, b, and associative when (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c. For a finite set the table shows everything: commutative means the table is symmetric about its leading diagonal.

For closure, look for a pair whose answer falls outside S. For commutativity, swap a and b (or compare the table with its mirror image). For associativity, work out both groupings — with letters for a rule, with all triples (or a counter-example) for a table; matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative.
math: Let S = {1, 2, 3} and a ∗ b = (ab) mod 4, the remainder on dividing ab by 4. Is ∗ a binary operation on S?
2 × 2 = 4, whose remainder is 0, and 0 is not in S
So the true statement is option B

screens.title: The method
text: Write a ∗ e = a with the rule and solve for e (it must not depend on a). Then write a ∗ b = e with the given a and solve for b.
math: On ℚ − {0}, the binary operation ∗ is defined by a ∗ b = ab/8. Find the inverse of 5.
Solve a ∗ e = a for every a: e = 8
Solve 5 ∗ b = 8: b = 64/5

screens.title: Guess and check
text: Try a candidate e with two or three different values of a: if a ∗ e = a every time, e is the identity.
For the inverse, work out a ∗ b with your b: you must get e.
math: On ℤ, the binary operation ∗ is defined by a ∗ b = a + b − 9. Find the inverse of −5.
Solve a ∗ e = a for every a: e = 9
Solve −5 ∗ b = 9: b = 23

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “On ℚ − {1/3}, the binary operation ∗ is defined by a ∗ b = a + b − 3ab. Find the inverse of 4.” A common wrong answer is −4.
−4 (the inverse for ordinary addition) was given; the inverse b must satisfy 4 ∗ b = e for this operation's identity e.
math: Not −4, but 4/11

modules.title: Classifying a function as one-one, onto or bijective

chapter.title: Classifying a function as one-one, onto or bijective
text: One-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is an output. Both depend on the domain and codomain, not only on the formula.
math: f: ℝ → ℝ is given by f(x) = −x² − 1. Which is true?
If f(x₁) = f(x₂), then not always x₁ = x₂
f(x) = y is not solvable for some y in the codomain
So f is neither one-one nor onto
chapter.tip: Only the values y ≥ −1 were thought of; the codomain ℝ also contains values that x² never reaches.

screens.title: The method
text: For one-one, set f(x₁) = f(x₂) and see whether x₁ = x₂ follows. For onto, take any y in the codomain, solve f(x) = y, and check the solution lies in the domain.
math: f: ℝ → [−2, ∞) is given by f(x) = 2x² − 2. Which is true?
If f(x₁) = f(x₂), then not always x₁ = x₂
f(x) = y is solvable for every y in the codomain
So f is onto but not one-one

screens.title: Horizontal lines
text: Draw horizontal lines y = c for c in the codomain.
One-one: no line meets the graph twice. Onto: every such line meets it at least once.
math: f: ℝ → ℝ is given by f(x) = −x² − 3. Which is true?
If f(x₁) = f(x₂), then not always x₁ = x₂
f(x) = y is not solvable for some y in the codomain
So f is neither one-one nor onto

modules.title: Testing a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity

chapter.title: Testing a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
text: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a in A. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
math: On A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)}. Which statement about R is true?
Is every (a, a) in R? no
Does each (a, b) have its reverse (b, a)? yes
Does each chain (a, b), (b, c) have (a, c)? no
chapter.tip: Reflexive needs (a, a) for EVERY a in A; one missing pair is enough to fail.

chapter.title: The fewest pairs that make a relation an equivalence relation
text: The smallest equivalence relation containing R splits A into classes of elements linked by R; within a class every element is related to every element.
Join elements that appear together in a pair of R into classes; a class of n elements needs n² pairs; add up, then subtract the pairs R already has.
math: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, R = {(1, 3), (3, 1), (4, 3)}. What is the least number of ordered pairs that must be added to R to make it an equivalence relation?
R links the elements into classes of sizes 3 + 1
An equivalence relation with these classes has 10 pairs (a class of size n gives n² pairs)
Pairs to add: 10 − 3 = 7

screens.title: The method
text: Check the three properties one by one: list the (a, a) pairs; pair each element with its reverse; and for each pair (a, b) look for pairs starting with b.
math: On A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)}. Which statement about R is true?
Is every (a, a) in R? no
Does each (a, b) have its reverse (b, a)? no
Does each chain (a, b), (b, c) have (a, c)? no

Reflexive: 1s on the diagonal. Symmetric: the table equals its mirror image. Transitive: wherever row a has a 1 in column b, row a must contain every 1 of row b.
math: On A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 1), (1, 2), (3, 1)}. Which statement about R is true?
Is every (a, a) in R? no
Does each (a, b) have its reverse (b, a)? no
Does each chain (a, b), (b, c) have (a, c)? no

chapter.title: The derivative from first principles

modules.title: Intervals where a cubic is increasing or decreasing

chapter.title: Intervals where a cubic is increasing or decreasing
text: f is strictly increasing where f′(x) > 0 and strictly decreasing where f′(x) < 0; the sign of f′ can only change at its roots.

chapter.title: The local maximum or minimum value of a cubic
text: At a local maximum f′ changes from + to − (f″ < 0 there); at a local minimum from − to + (f″ > 0).

chapter.title: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
text: A continuous function on a closed interval has an absolute maximum and minimum, and they occur either at a turning point inside or at an end point.

The least of these is −45

chapter.title: Rates of change of related quantities
text: If a quantity Q depends on x and x changes with time, then dQ/dt = (dQ/dx) × (dx/dt): the rates are linked by the chain rule.

Substitute the values: 104

chapter.title: Classifying a critical point by the second-derivative test
text: At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0): if f″(c) < 0 the graph bends downward there, so c is a local maximum; if f″(c) > 0 it bends upward, a local minimum; if f″(c) = 0 the test gives no conclusion.

dy/dx at x = 1 is −7

modules.title: Choosing k to make a function continuous

chapter.title: Choosing k to make a function continuous
text: f is continuous at a when lim (x → a) f(x) exists and equals f(a): the left limit, the right limit and the value all agree.
math: f(x) = kx + 3 for x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 2x² + 3 for x > 1. Find the value of k for which f is continuous at x = 1.
The limit of the other piece at the point is 2
Continuity needs f(a) = that limit, so k = 2
chapter.tip: 3 was moved across without changing its sign: k + 3 = 5 was written as k = 5 + 3. Moving a number to the other side changes its sign: k = 5 − 3.

chapter.title: Is a piecewise function continuous on ℝ or on an interval?
text: A function is continuous on a set when it is continuous at every point of it. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, so a piecewise function can only fail where its formula changes, and there it fails exactly when the two pieces do not meet.

List the points where the formula changes that lie in the set. At each one, work out the value of the left piece and of the right piece there (and f at the point). Equal values: continuous there; different: a discontinuity.
math: f(x) = −x + 4 for x < 2; x² − 2x for 2 ≤ x < 3; and −2x + 9 for x ≥ 3. Which statement about the continuity of f on ℝ is true?
A polynomial is continuous everywhere, so each piece is a polynomial, so f is continuous away from x = a and x = b
Compare the two pieces at each break point (right-hand value minus left-hand value): jumps 2 at x = 2, 0 at x = 3
So the true statement is option C

screens.title: The method
text: Find the limit of the formula near a (substitute for a polynomial; use sin θ/θ → 1, 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), rationalising or factorising otherwise), then set f(a) equal to it.
math: f(x) = kx + 3 for x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 2x² for x > 1. Find the value of k for which f is continuous at x = 1.
The limit of the other piece at the point is −1
Continuity needs f(a) = that limit, so k = −1

screens.title: Left value, right value
text: For a function in two pieces, work out each piece at x = a.
Continuity means the two values are equal: that is an equation for k.
math: f(x) = sin(4x)/x for x ≠ 0, and f(0) = k. Find the value of k for which f is continuous at x = 0.
The limit of the other piece at the point is 4
Continuity needs f(a) = that limit, so k = 4

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “f(x) = sin(x)/(3x) for x ≠ 0, and f(0) = k. Find the value of k for which f is continuous at x = 0.” A common wrong answer is 3.
The ratio was turned over, giving 3: the number in the sine goes on top, since sin(x)/(3x) = (1/3) × sin(x)/x, which tends to 1/3.
math: Not 3, but 1/3

modules.title: Definite integrals over [−a, a] using odd and even functions

chapter.title: Definite integrals over [−a, a] using odd and even functions
text: If f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0: the areas on the two sides cancel. If f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
math: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ (x e^(x²) + 2x² + 4) dx.
x e^(x²) is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), so its integral over [−a, a] is 0
The even part gives 2∫₀¹ (2x² + 4) dx
chapter.tip: Every term was taken to vanish over a symmetric interval; only the odd part does. The even part kx² + m gives twice its integral from 0 to a.

chapter.title: Definite integrals with the property ∫ f(x) dx = ∫ f(a + b − x) dx
text: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx: replacing x by a + b − x runs over the same interval backwards. For g(x)/(g(x) + g(a + b − x)), the two forms add up to 1.
Call the integral I, write it again with x replaced by a + b − x, add the two: 2I = ∫ₐᵇ 1 dx = b − a, so I = (b − a)/2.
math: Evaluate ∫₄¹⁴ x³/(x³ + (18 − x)³) dx.
Replace x by 18 − x: I = ∫ g(a + b − x)/(g(a + b − x) + g(x)) dx
Add the two forms: 2I = ∫ 1 dx = 14 − 4 = 10
So I = 5

chapter.title: Splitting the interval: |x − c| and the greatest integer function
text: ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫ᶜᵇ f for any c in between. Split where the formula changes: at x = c for |x − c|, at each integer for [x].
Find where the integrand changes its formula, split the interval there, write each piece without | | or [ ], integrate each piece and add.
math: Evaluate ∫₋₂⁴ |x − 1| dx.
Split: ∫₋₂¹ (1 − x) dx + ∫₁⁴ (x − 1) dx
Add the pieces: 9

screens.title: The method
text: Split the integrand into its odd part and its even part, drop the odd part, and integrate the even part from 0 to a and double it.
math: Evaluate ∫₋₃³ (x³ cos x + 2) dx.
x³ cos x is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), so its integral over [−a, a] is 0
The even part gives 2∫₀³ (2) dx

screens.title: Substitute x = −t
text: Write ∫₋ₐᵃ f = ∫₋ₐ⁰ f + ∫₀ᵃ f and put x = −t in the first integral.
It becomes ∫₀ᵃ f(−t) dt, which is −∫₀ᵃ f for an odd f and +∫₀ᵃ f for an even f.
math: Evaluate ∫₋₃³ (x³ cos x + 4) dx.
x³ cos x is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), so its integral over [−a, a] is 0
The even part gives 2∫₀³ (4) dx

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Evaluate ∫₋₃³ (x³ cos x + 3) dx.” A common wrong answer is 0.
Every term was taken to vanish over a symmetric interval; only the odd part does. The even part kx² + m gives twice its integral from 0 to a.
math: Not 0, but 18

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Evaluate definite integrals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Split the integrand into its odd part and its even part, drop the odd part, and integrate the even part from 0 to a and double it.

modules.title: Choosing a and b to make a piecewise function differentiable

chapter.title: Choosing a and b to make a piecewise function differentiable
text: Differentiable at c means the left and right derivatives at c are equal; this also needs f to be continuous at c (the pieces must meet).
math: f(x) = x² + ax + b for x < 1, and f(x) = −3x + 4 for x ≥ 1. Find a and b so that f is differentiable at x = 1. Write the answer as (a, b).
Equal one-sided derivatives: 2(1) + a = −3, so a = −5
Equal values at x = 1 (continuity): b = 5
chapter.tip: The slopes were matched as a = −3, forgetting the 2x from x²: the left derivative at x = 1 is 2(1) + a.

screens.title: The method
text: Match the slopes of the two pieces at x = c to find a; then match their values at x = c to find b.

Equal one-sided derivatives: 2(−1) + a = −5, so a = −3
Equal values at x = −1 (continuity): b = −1

screens.title: One tangent line
text: The line px + q must be the tangent to the parabola at x = c.
So the parabola must pass through (c, pc + q) with slope p there.
math: f(x) = x² + ax + b for x < −1, and f(x) = −5x − 3 for x ≥ −1. Find a and b so that f is differentiable at x = −1. Write the answer as (a, b).
Equal one-sided derivatives: 2(−1) + a = −5, so a = −3
Equal values at x = −1 (continuity): b = −2

The slopes were matched as a = −3, forgetting the 2x from x²: the left derivative at x = 1 is 2(1) + a.

modules.title: Separating the variables in an initial value problem

chapter.title: Separating the variables in an initial value problem
text: When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, the variables can be separated: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, and each side integrated.
math: Solve the differential equation dy/dx = −4xy, given that y = 1 when x = 0. Write y in terms of x.
Separate the variables: dy/y = −4x dx
Integrate both sides: log y = −2x² + C
Use y = 1 at the starting point to find the constant: y = e^(−2x²)
chapter.tip: The y on the right was ignored and only (px + q) was integrated; divide by y first: dy/y = (px + q) dx.

chapter.title: The order and degree of a differential equation
text: The order is that of the highest derivative in the equation; the degree (defined when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives) is the power of that highest derivative.
Find the derivative with the most dashes (the largest k in dᵏy/dxᵏ): that k is the order. Its power is the degree; powers of lower derivatives do not matter.
math: Find the order and the degree of the differential equation (dy/dx)² − y⁶ = eˣ. Write the answer as (order, degree).
The highest derivative is dy/dx: order 1
It appears to the power 2: degree 2

chapter.title: A linear differential equation with an integrating factor
text: For dy/dx + Py = Q, multiplying by the integrating factor e^(∫P dx) turns the left side into the derivative of y × IF.
Find IF = e^(∫P dx) (here xᵏ), write y × IF = ∫ Q × IF dx + C, divide by IF, and use the initial condition for C.
math: Solve dy/dx + 2y/x = 5x², x > 0, given that y = 2 when x = 1. Write y in terms of x.
Integrating factor: e^(∫2/x dx) = x²
Multiply through and integrate: y·x² = x⁵ + C
Use y(1) = 2: y = x³ + 1/x²

chapter.title: Ordinary or partial, linear or non-linear: classifying a differential equation
text: An ordinary differential equation has one independent variable (derivatives d/dx); a partial one has several (∂/∂x, ∂/∂y). It is linear when the unknown and its derivatives appear only to the first power, are not multiplied together and are not inside functions such as sin or e^( ).

First look at the derivative signs: d means ordinary, ∂ means partial. Then check every term containing the unknown: a square, a product of the unknown with a derivative, or a function of the unknown makes it non-linear; coefficients that depend only on x do not.
math: Is the differential equation x ∂u/∂x + y ∂u/∂y = 4u (u is the unknown function) ordinary or partial?
partial derivatives ∂: partial
So the answer is option B

chapter.title: dy/dx = f(ax + y + c) by a substitution that separates the variables
text: When dy/dx is a function of one combination v = ax + y + c, that combination is the natural new unknown: dv/dx = a + dy/dx depends on v alone, so the variables separate.

Put v = mx + y + c, so dy/dx = dv/dx − m. Rewrite the equation as dv/dx = g(v), separate and integrate (here ∫ dv/(v² + k²) = (1/k) tan⁻¹(v/k)), use the starting value, and finally write y = v − mx − c.
math: Solve dy/dx = (−3x + y − 2)² + 7, given that y = 2 when x = 0, by a substitution that makes the variables separable. Write y in terms of x.
Put v = −3x + y − 2: dv/dx = −3 + dy/dx = v² + 4
Separate: dv/(v² + 4) = dx, so (1/2) tan⁻¹(v/2) = x + C
Use the starting value and go back to y: y = 2tan(2x) + 3x + 2

screens.title: The method
text: Divide by y, integrate both sides (log y on the left, the natural logarithm), add one constant, exponentiate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.
math: Solve the differential equation dy/dx = (−3x − 1)y, given that y = 1 when x = 0. Write y in terms of x.
Separate the variables: dy/y = (−3x − 1) dx
Integrate both sides: log y = −3x²/2 − x + C
Use y = 1 at the starting point to find the constant: y = e^(−3x²/2 − x)

screens.title: Check by differentiating
text: Differentiate your y and see whether you get the right side of the equation.
Then put in the starting x and check you get the starting y.
math: Solve the differential equation dy/dx = (−2x + 1)y, given that y = 1 when x = 0. Write y in terms of x.
Separate the variables: dy/y = (−2x + 1) dx
Integrate both sides: log y = −x² + x + C
Use y = 1 at the starting point to find the constant: y = e^(−x² + x)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Solve the differential equation dy/dx = (−3x − 1)y, given that y = 2 when x = 0. Write y in terms of x.” A common wrong answer is −3x²/2 − x + 2.
The y on the right was ignored and only (px + q) was integrated; divide by y first: dy/y = (px + q) dx.
math: Not −3x²/2 − x + 2, but 2e^(−3x²/2 − x)

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Find antiderivatives. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Divide by y, integrate both sides (log y on the left, the natural logarithm), add one constant, exponentiate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.

modules.title: A homogeneous differential equation with y = vx

chapter.title: A homogeneous differential equation with y = vx
text: In a homogeneous equation dy/dx depends only on y/x. Putting y = vx (so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx) turns it into a separable equation in v and x.
math: Solve the homogeneous differential equation dy/dx = (4y + 4x)/x, x > 0, given that y = 0 when x = 1. Write y in terms of x.
Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx: v + x dv/dx = …, so x dv/dx = 3v + 4
Separate and integrate x dv/dx = 3v + 4
chapter.tip: With y = vx, dy/dx was taken as dv/dx; by the product rule dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.

screens.title: The method
text: Substitute y = vx and dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, simplify to x dv/dx = g(v), separate and integrate, put v = y/x back, and use the initial condition.
math: Solve the homogeneous differential equation dy/dx = (3x² + y²)/(xy), x > 0, given that y = 3 when x = 1. Write y in terms of x.
Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx: v + x dv/dx = …, so x dv/dx = 3/v
Separate and integrate x dv/dx = 3/v
Use y(1) = 3: y = x√(6log x + 9)

screens.title: Check your answer
text: Differentiate your y and work out the right side of the equation with it.
They must agree, and your y must equal the given value at x = 1.
math: Solve the homogeneous differential equation dy/dx = (4y + 4x)/x, x > 0, given that y = 2 when x = 1. Write y in terms of x.
Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx: v + x dv/dx = …, so x dv/dx = 3v + 4
Separate and integrate x dv/dx = 3v + 4

∫ v dv = v²/2; the factor 2 was lost when solving for v².

chapter.title: Second-order derivatives
text: The second derivative d²y/dx² is the derivative of dy/dx: how fast the slope itself is changing.
math: If y = 3xe^(−x), find d²y/dx².
Differentiate again: d²y/dx² = 3e^(−x)(x − 2)

chapter.title: The differential equation satisfied by a family of functions
text: y = eʳˣ satisfies y″ + py′ + qy = 0 exactly when r² + pr + q = 0. A family with two arbitrary constants comes from the two roots of that quadratic.
Read off the roots r₁, r₂ from the exponents (a repeated root for (A + Bx)eᵐˣ, a ± ib for eᵃˣ(A cos bx + B sin bx)); then p = −(r₁ + r₂) and q = r₁r₂.

Find dy/dx and d²y/dx²
Eliminate A and B (or use the roots of r² + pr + q = 0): (p, q) = (10, 25)

text: Differentiate once (product and chain rules), simplify, then differentiate the result again; collect like terms at the end.

math: If y = 4xe^(2x), find d²y/dx².

modules.title: Domain and range of the principal value branches of the inverse trigonometric functions

chapter.title: Domain and range of the principal value branches of the inverse trigonometric functions
text: No trigonometric function is one-one on its whole domain, so to invert it we keep one piece on which it is one-one and takes every value once: the principal value branch. sin⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ give angles in [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ and sec⁻¹ in [0, π], tan⁻¹ in (−π/2, π/2), cot⁻¹ in (0, π); sec⁻¹ leaves out π/2 and cosec⁻¹ leaves out 0.
math: What is the domain of sin⁻¹ (the set of real numbers x for which sin⁻¹(x) is defined)?
For sin⁻¹: domain [−1, 1]
So the answer is option B
chapter.tip: The principal range of sin⁻¹ was given instead of its domain: the domain is the set of numbers x that sin⁻¹ accepts.

chapter.title: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions
text: Each inverse function returns one angle from its principal range: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹ in [0, π]. That is why it has a single value.
Find the standard angle whose ratio is the argument, then make sure it lies in the principal range: for a negative argument use −θ (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) or π − θ (cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cot⁻¹).
math: Find the value of cos⁻¹(1/2) using principal values. Write the answer in terms of π (you may type pi).
Add the principal values: π/3

chapter.title: sin⁻¹(sin θ), cos⁻¹(cos θ) and tan⁻¹(tan θ)
text: sin⁻¹(sin θ) is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with the same sine as θ; it equals θ only when θ is already in that range (similarly [0, π] for cos⁻¹ and (−π/2, π/2) for tan⁻¹).
Find an angle in the principal range with the same ratio: use sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(2π − θ) = cos θ, tan(θ − π) = tan θ, and add or remove whole turns.
math: Find the value of tan⁻¹(tan(2π/3)). Write the answer in terms of π (you may type pi).
2π/3 has the same ratio as −π/3 (a whole number of turns removed)
The angle in (−π/2, π/2) with the same ratio is −π/3

chapter.title: Domain and range of the inverse trigonometric functions
text: Each inverse function undoes its function on one branch: sin⁻¹ has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹ [−1, 1] and [0, π]; tan⁻¹ ℝ and (−π/2, π/2); cot⁻¹ ℝ and (0, π); sec⁻¹ (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) and [0, π] without π/2; cosec⁻¹ (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) and [−π/2, π/2] without 0.
For f⁻¹(x/k), x/k must lie in the basic domain, so multiply its end points by k. For a·f⁻¹(x), multiply the range's end points by a.
math: What is the domain of y = 4 sin⁻¹(x/2)?
For sin⁻¹: [−2, 2]
So the answer is C

chapter.title: Equations and sum formulae with inverse tangents
text: tan⁻¹ u ± tan⁻¹ v = tan⁻¹((u ± v)/(1 ∓ uv)) (for the sum, when uv < 1) comes from tan(A ± B). Taking tan of both sides turns an equation in inverse tangents into an ordinary equation.

Combine the inverse tangents with the formula, take tan of both sides (tan(π/4) = 1), solve, and check each answer in the original equation (reject values that make the left side negative or break the condition).
math: Find x if tan⁻¹(1/9) − tan⁻¹(1/8) = tan⁻¹ x.
Use tan⁻¹ u − tan⁻¹ v = tan⁻¹((u − v)/(1 + uv))

screens.title: The method
text: For the range, recall the branch and remove the angles where the function itself is not defined (π/2 for sec, 0 for cosec, the end points for tan and cot). For the domain, ask which values the function takes on the branch: [−1, 1] for sin and cos, every real number for tan and cot, x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 1 for sec and cosec.
math: Which one of these angles is a possible principal value of cos⁻¹(x), for some real number x?
For cos⁻¹: principal values lie in [0, π]
So the answer is option C

screens.title: Reflect the graph
text: Draw y = sec x for 0 ≤ x ≤ π: it is not defined at π/2 and its values are ≤ −1 or ≥ 1.
Reflecting that piece in the line y = x gives y = sec⁻¹ x: its domain is the old set of values and its range is the old piece of x-axis.
math: Which one of these angles is a possible principal value of tan⁻¹(x), for some real number x?
For tan⁻¹: principal values lie in (−π/2, π/2)
So the answer is option B

screens.title: A common wrong answer

chapter.title: Implicit differentiation of a second-degree curve
text: y is a function of x, so every y term picks up a factor dy/dx by the chain rule: d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx, and d/dx(xy) = y + x dy/dx.

text: If every term of f has degree n, scaling (x, y) by t scales f by tⁿ; differentiating that at t = 1 gives x f_x + y f_y = n f.
Check the degree of each term, work out f at the point, and multiply by the degree. (Working out both partial derivatives directly gives the same number.)
math: f(x, y) = 2x² + xy − y² is a homogeneous function. Find the value of x ∂f/∂x + y ∂f/∂y at (2, 1).
Every term has degree 2
By Euler's theorem, x f_x + y f_y = 2 × 9 = 18

chapter.title: The chain rule for w = f(x, y) with x and y depending on t
text: When w depends on x and y, and both depend on t, a small change in t moves both: dw/dt = (∂w/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂w/∂y)(dy/dt).
Find x and y at the given t, the partial derivatives ∂w/∂x and ∂w/∂y there, and dx/dt and dy/dt; multiply in pairs and add.
math: w = −x² − 3xy, where x = −3t + 2 and y = t² + 1. Use the chain rule to find dw/dt when t = 1.

screens.title: The method
text: Go term by term: a term without the variable gives 0; in a term with the variable, keep the other letters as a constant factor and use the power rule.
math: For f(x, y) = 3x²y³ − 2x⁴ + y⁴, find ∂f/∂x.
Treat y as a constant
Differentiate each term with respect to x: 6xy³ − 8x³

strategies.title: Put a number in for the other letter

screens.title: Put a number in for the other letter
text: For ∂f/∂x, imagine y = 2: the function becomes an ordinary function of x.
Differentiate it, then put y back where the 2 was.
math: For f(x, y) = 3xy³ + 2x³ + 3y³, find ∂f/∂x.
Treat y as a constant
Differentiate each term with respect to x: 3y³ + 6x²

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “For f(x, y) = 3xy² + 2x⁴ + 2y⁴, find ∂f/∂x.” A common wrong answer is 3y² + 8x³ + 8y³.
The term 2y⁴ was differentiated too; for ∂f/∂x, y is held constant, so that term gives 0.
math: Not 3y² + 8x³ + 8y³, but 3y² + 8x³

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Apply differentiation rules. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Go term by term: a term without the variable gives 0; in a term with the variable, keep the other letters as a constant factor and use the power rule.

modules.title: Integrating by partial fractions (two linear factors)

chapter.title: Integrating by partial fractions (two linear factors)
text: A fraction over (x − a)(x − b) is a sum A/(x − a) + B/(x − b), and each of those integrates to a logarithm.
math: Find ∫ (−2x + 7)/(x² − 5x + 6) dx.
Factorise the denominator: (x − 2)(x − 3)
Split into partial fractions: −3/(x − 2) + 1/(x − 3)
Integrate each part: ∫ dx/(x − a) = ln|x − a|, so the answer is −3ln|x − 2| + ln|x − 3| + C
chapter.tip: The answer ln|x² − 5x + 6| was used; that is only right when the top is exactly the derivative of the bottom. Split into partial fractions first.

screens.title: The method
text: Factorise the denominator; find A by covering (x − a) and putting x = a in what is left, and B likewise; integrate to A ln|x − a| + B ln|x − b| + C.
math: Find ∫ (−6x + 9)/(x² − 3x) dx.
Factorise the denominator: (x)(x − 3)
Split into partial fractions: −3/(x) + −3/(x − 3)
Integrate each part: ∫ dx/(x − a) = ln|x − a|, so the answer is −3ln|x| − 3ln|x − 3| + C

screens.title: Compare coefficients
text: Write px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a).
Match the x terms and the constant terms to get two equations for A and B.
math: Find ∫ (−x + 5)/(x² − 5x + 6) dx.
Factorise the denominator: (x − 2)(x − 3)
Split into partial fractions: −3/(x − 2) + 2/(x − 3)
Integrate each part: ∫ dx/(x − a) = ln|x − a|, so the answer is −3ln|x − 2| + 2ln|x − 3| + C

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find ∫ (−4x + 7)/(x² − x − 6) dx.” A common wrong answer is ln|x² − x − 6| + C.
The answer ln|x² − x − 6| was used; that is only right when the top is exactly the derivative of the bottom. Split into partial fractions first.
math: Not ln|x² − x − 6| + C, but −3ln|x + 2| − ln|x − 3| + C

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve quadratic equations; Find antiderivatives. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Factorise the denominator; find A by covering (x − a) and putting x = a in what is left, and B likewise; integrate to A ln|x − a| + B ln|x − b| + C.

modules.title: ∫ sinᵐx cosⁿx over [0, π/2] or [0, π] by reduction formulae

chapter.title: ∫ sinᵐx cosⁿx over [0, π/2] or [0, π] by reduction formulae
text: Integrating by parts once gives a formula that lowers a power by 2: ∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿx dx = ((n − 1)/n) ∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿ⁻²x dx, ending at π/2 (power 0) or 1 (power 1).
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin²x cos³x dx.
Lower the powers two at a time, Iₘ,ₙ = (m − 1)/(m + n) Iₘ₋₂,ₙ (and the same for n): over [0, π/2] the value is 2/15
chapter.tip: A factor π/2 was put in; it appears only when both powers are even, and here the reduction ends at ∫ sin x dx or ∫ cos x dx, which is 1.

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the fractions (n − 1)/n, (n − 3)/(n − 2), … down to 1/2 or 2/3; include π/2 only when every power is even. For sinᵐ cosⁿ, the denominators are m + n, m + n − 2, ….
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π of sin⁸x cos⁸x dx.
Lower the powers two at a time, Iₘ,ₙ = (m − 1)/(m + n) Iₘ₋₂,ₙ (and the same for n): over [0, π/2] the value is 35π/65536
Over [0, π] it is twice that: 35π/32768

screens.title: The double-factorial pattern
text: Write (m − 1)(m − 3)… × (n − 1)(n − 3)… over (m + n)(m + n − 2)…, each down to 1 or 2.
Multiply by π/2 when m and n are both even.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π of cos⁸x dx.
Lower the powers two at a time, Iₘ,ₙ = (m − 1)/(m + n) Iₘ₋₂,ₙ (and the same for n): over [0, π/2] the value is 35π/256
Over [0, π] it is twice that: 35π/128

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin⁸x cos⁸x dx.” A common wrong answer is 35/32768.
When both powers are even, the reduction ends at ∫ 1 dx over [0, π/2], which is π/2; that factor was left out.

modules.title: A coefficient in a Maclaurin series

chapter.title: A coefficient in a Maclaurin series
text: A Maclaurin series writes f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) xⁿ/n!; for standard functions the pattern is known, and replacing x by ax multiplies the xⁿ term by aⁿ.
math: Find the coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin series of e^(x).
The general term of the standard series is xⁿ/n!
Put u = x and pick out the x³ term: its coefficient is 1/6
chapter.tip: The 3! in the denominator was left out: eᵘ = Σ uⁿ/n!.

chapter.title: A coefficient in the Taylor series about a point a
text: Near x = a, f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)²/2! + …: the coefficient of (x − a)ᵏ is f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)/k!. For a polynomial the series is just the polynomial rewritten in powers of (x − a).
Differentiate k times, put x = a, and divide by k!. (For a polynomial you can instead put x = a + t, expand, and read off the coefficient of tᵏ.)
math: Find the coefficient of (x − 3)³ in the Taylor series of f(x) = x⁵ about x = 3.
f⁽ᵏ⁾(a) = 540 for k = 3
Divide by 6: the coefficient is 90

screens.title: The method
text: Write the standard series in u, put u = ax, and read off the xᵏ term: a power of a, the right sign, and the right denominator (k! for eˣ, sin, cos; k for ln; none for 1/(1 − u)).
math: Find the coefficient of x² in the Maclaurin series of e^(x).
The general term of the standard series is xⁿ/n!
Put u = x and pick out the x² term: its coefficient is 1/2

screens.title: From the derivatives
text: Differentiate f k times and put x = 0.
Divide by k!: that is the coefficient of xᵏ.
math: Find the coefficient of x⁶ in the Maclaurin series of cos(3x).
The general term of the standard series is (−1)ʳ x²ʳ/(2r)!
Put u = 3x and pick out the x⁶ term: its coefficient is −81/80

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the coefficient of x⁶ in the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + 2x).” A common wrong answer is −4/45.
The term was divided by 6! (as in the series for eˣ) instead of by 6.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use binomial, exponential and logarithmic series. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Write the standard series in u, put u = ax, and read off the xᵏ term: a power of a, the right sign, and the right denominator (k! for eˣ, sin, cos; k for ln; none for 1/(1 − u)).

modules.title: Volume of a solid of revolution

chapter.title: Volume of a solid of revolution
text: Cut the solid into thin discs perpendicular to the axis: a disc of radius r and thickness dx has volume πr² dx, so the volume is π∫ r² dx.
math: The region bounded by y = √(5x), the x-axis and the line x = 6 is rotated through 360° about the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed, in cubic units, in terms of π.
Square the radius of a slice: y² = 5x
V = π∫ from 0 to 6 of 5x dx = 90π
chapter.tip: The radius was integrated instead of its square; a disc's area is πy², so V = π∫y² dx.

screens.title: The method
text: Write the radius of a slice in terms of the variable along the axis (y for the x-axis, x for the y-axis), square it, integrate over the range and keep π.
math: The region bounded by y = √(5x), the x-axis and the line x = 4 is rotated through 360° about the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed, in cubic units, in terms of π.
Square the radius of a slice: y² = 5x
V = π∫ from 0 to 4 of 5x dx = 40π

screens.title: Cylindrical shells
text: For a rotation about the y-axis, slice the region into thin vertical strips at distance x.
Each strip sweeps a shell of volume 2πx × (height) × dx; add them up: V = 2π∫ x × height dx.
math: The region bounded by y = √(4x), the x-axis and the line x = 3 is rotated through 360° about the x-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed, in cubic units, in terms of π.
Square the radius of a slice: y² = 4x
V = π∫ from 0 to 3 of 4x dx = 18π

The radius was integrated instead of its square; a disc's area is πy², so V = π∫y² dx.
math: Not 50π/3, but 125π/2

modules.title: Improper integrals and the gamma integral

chapter.title: Improper integrals and the gamma integral
text: An integral to ∞ means the limit of the integral to b as b → ∞; when the integrand dies away fast enough, that limit is a finite number. The gamma integral Γ(n + 1) = ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−x) dx = n! packages repeated integration by parts.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x³ dx.
Use the antiderivative, then the limit as the upper end → ∞
The integral converges to 1/2
chapter.tip: The antiderivative was evaluated as (value at the bottom) − (value at the top limit); it is top − bottom, and the top value tends to 0.

screens.title: The method
text: Find the antiderivative (or use Γ(n + 1)/aⁿ⁺¹ for ∫ xⁿe^(−ax)), evaluate from the lower end to b, and let b → ∞.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x⁵ e^(−x) dx.
Use the gamma integral ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−ax) dx = n!/aⁿ⁺¹
The integral converges to 120

strategies.title: Integration by parts, step by step

screens.title: Integration by parts, step by step
text: For ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−ax) dx, integrate by parts once: it becomes (n/a) × ∫₀^∞ xⁿ⁻¹e^(−ax) dx.
Repeat down to ∫₀^∞ e^(−ax) dx = 1/a.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4x) sin x dx.
Use integration by parts twice (or the standard result)
The integral converges to 1/17

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x⁵ e^(−3x) dx.” A common wrong answer is 40/81.
The power of 3 was taken as 5; the gamma integral gives n!/aⁿ⁺¹, so it is 3⁶.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Integrate by substitution and parts; Evaluate elementary limits. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

modules.title: Centre and radius of a circle from its general equation

chapter.title: Centre and radius of a circle from its general equation
text: Completing the square turns x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 into (x + g)² + (y + f)² = g² + f² − c: a circle with centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle x² + y² − 10x + 10y + 45 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −5, f = 5, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (5, −5)
chapter.tip: The centre was read with the wrong signs: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f).

chapter.title: The focus of a parabola
text: y² = 4ax is the set of points as far from the focus (a, 0) as from the directrix x = −a; shifting the vertex to (h, k) shifts the focus by the same amount.
Read the vertex (h, k); set the coefficient of the linear bracket equal to 4a; move a from the vertex along the axis (the direction of the unsquared variable, the sign of a giving the way).
math: Find the coordinates of the focus of the parabola x² = −16y.
The vertex is (0, 0)
Move a units from the vertex along the axis: the focus is (0, −4)

chapter.title: Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola
text: Eccentricity e = c/a compares the distance from the centre to a focus with the semi-axis on which the foci lie; for an ellipse c² = a² − b² (e < 1), for a hyperbola c² = a² + b² (e > 1).
Write the equation in standard form, decide which axis is the major (or transverse) one, find c² by the right rule, and divide c by that semi-axis.
math: Find the eccentricity of the hyperbola x²/36 − y²/9 = 1.

chapter.title: Areas bounded by a parabola or an ellipse
text: An area between curves is ∫ (top − bottom) dx between the points where they meet; symmetry lets you find one part and multiply.
Sketch the region, find where the curves meet, write the vertical gap (top minus bottom), integrate between the meeting points, and use symmetry (×2 for a parabola about its axis, ×4 for an ellipse).
math: Find the area of the part of the ellipse region that lies in the first quadrant, for the ellipse x²/25 + y² = 1.
Area = ∫ from 0 to 5 of √(1 − x²/25) dx
Integrate and substitute the limits: 5π/4

chapter.title: Which conic does an equation represent?
text: For A x² + C y² + D x + E y + F = 0 (no xy term), the squared terms decide the shape: one squared variable gives a parabola, equal coefficients a circle, same signs an ellipse, opposite signs a hyperbola.
Look only at the x² and y² coefficients first; then, if you want to be sure, complete the squares to see the standard form.
math: Which curve does the equation x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 11 = 0 represent?
Look at the x² and y² coefficients (1 and 1): equal coefficients
So the curve is a circle

chapter.title: Conic sections as sections of a double cone
text: Let α be the semi-vertical angle and β the angle between the cutting plane and the axis. Not through the vertex: β = 90° gives a circle, α < β < 90° an ellipse, β = α a parabola, β < α a hyperbola (both nappes are cut). Through the vertex: β > α gives a point, β = α a single line, β < α a pair of intersecting lines.
Compare β with α (and with 90°), then ask whether the plane passes through the vertex; that decides between the curve and its degenerate case.
math: A right circular double cone has a semi-vertical angle of 35° (the angle between its axis and its slant side). A plane makes an angle of 35° with the axis of the cone and does not pass through the vertex. What is the section (the curve in which the plane cuts the cone)?
Compare the plane's angle with the axis, β = 35°, with the semi-vertical angle α = 35°: β = α
The plane is not through the vertex
So the section is option B

chapter.title: The equation of a circle from given conditions
text: A circle is all the points at distance r from its centre (h, k): (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Expanded, it is x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 with g = −h, f = −k, c = h² + k² − r².
Use the data to find the centre and r² (a midpoint for a diameter; a distance for a point on the circle; equal distances from three points), then expand (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² and collect terms.
math: Find the equation of the circle with centre (−1, −3) that passes through the point (−1, −5). Write its equation in the form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 and type the left-hand side.
Use r² = (distance from the centre to the point)²: the centre is (−1, −3)
r² = 4
Expand (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²: x² + y² + 2x + 6y + 6 = 0

chapter.title: Is a point inside, on or outside a circle?
text: For S(x, y) = x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c, S(x₁, y₁) = (distance from the centre)² − r². So the point is inside when S(x₁, y₁) < 0, on the circle when it is 0, and outside when it is positive.
Substitute the point into the left-hand side of the equation (with x² and y² having coefficient 1) and look at the sign of the result.
math: Where does the point (1, −2) lie relative to the circle x² + y² + 4x + 6y + 9 = 0?
Put (1, −2) into the left-hand side: 6
Positive, so the answer is option B

chapter.title: Latus rectum, directrix, foci and axes of a parabola, ellipse or hyperbola
text: For y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, axis y = 0, latus rectum 4a. For x²/a² ± y²/b² = 1 (foci on the x-axis): c² = a² ∓ b², foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0), e = c/a, directrices x = ±a/e, latus rectum 2b²/a, axes 2a and 2b.
Bring the equation to standard form, read a and b (a goes with the axis carrying the foci), find c by the right rule, and use the formula for the part asked.
math: For the hyperbola y²/16 − x²/9 = 1, find the length of its transverse axis.
From y²/16 − x²/9 = 1: a = 4, b = 3
c² = a² + b², so c = 5
So the answer is 8

chapter.title: The equation of an ellipse or a hyperbola from given data
text: An ellipse with foci (±c, 0) and vertices (±a, 0) has b² = a² − c²; a hyperbola has b² = c² − a². With e = c/a, a point on the curve, or the latus rectum 2b²/a, the same three numbers a, b, c are linked.

Find a and c from the data (c from the foci; a from the vertices, from e = c/a, from the focal-distance sum or difference at the given point, or from 2b²/a), then b² by the right rule, and put a² and b² under the right squares.
math: A hyperbola has foci (±13, 0) and vertices (±5, 0). Its equation is x²/A − y²/B = 1. Find A and B, typed as (A, B).
From the data, a = 5

chapter.title: The equation of a parabola from its focus, directrix, a point or its latus rectum
text: A parabola with vertex at the origin and axis along the x-axis is y² = 4ax: its focus is (a, 0), its directrix x = −a and its latus rectum has length 4|a|. Along the y-axis it is x² = 4ay.
Find a from the data (the focus, minus the directrix, the latus rectum ÷ 4 with the right sign, or by putting the point into y² = 4ax), then k = 4a.
math: A parabola has its vertex at the origin, its axis along the y-axis, and passes through the point (−1, 6). Its equation is x² = ky. Find k.
From the data, a = 1/24

chapter.title: Conics in real life: arches, reflectors, cables and orbits
text: Parabolic arches and hanging bridge cables follow y = (constant) × x² from their lowest or highest point; a reflector sends light from its focus out parallel to its axis; arches can be half-ellipses; planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus.

Put the origin at the vertex or centre, write the standard equation, find its constant from one known point (an end of the span, the rim of the dish, the top of a tower), then substitute the point you need.
math: A comet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. The major axis of the orbit is 68 million km long and the eccentricity is 0.7. Find the comet's greatest distance from the Sun, in million km.
Model: nearest a(1 − e), farthest a(1 + e)
So the answer is 289/5

chapter.title: Which conic does a general second-degree equation with an xy term represent?
text: For Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (not degenerate), turning the axes removes the xy term without changing B² − 4AC. So B² − 4AC < 0 gives an ellipse, = 0 a parabola, > 0 a hyperbola.
Read A (the x² coefficient), B (the xy coefficient) and C (the y² coefficient), work out B² − 4AC and read off its sign.
math: Which curve does the equation 3x² − 2xy + 2y² − 2y − 12 = 0 represent?
Negative: an ellipse (option C)

screens.title: The method
text: Make the x² and y² coefficients 1 by dividing; halve the x and y coefficients to get g and f; the centre is (−g, −f); r = √(g² + f² − c).
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle 3x² + 3y² − 18x − 6y − 42 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Divide by 3: x² + y² − 6x − 2y − 14 = 0
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −3, f = −1, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (3, 1)

screens.title: Complete the square directly
text: Group the x terms and the y terms: (x² − 4x) + (y² + 6y) = −c.
Add the squares of half the coefficients to both sides: (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 4 + 9 − c.
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle 2x² + 2y² − 12x + 8y + 24 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Divide by 2: x² + y² − 6x + 4y + 12 = 0
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −3, f = 2, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (3, −2)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the centre and the radius of the circle 3x² + 3y² − 30x − 18y + 75 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.” A common wrong answer is (−5, −3, 3).
The centre was read with the wrong signs: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f).

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Simplify radicals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Make the x² and y² coefficients 1 by dividing; halve the x and y coefficients to get g and f; the centre is (−g, −f); r = √(g² + f² − c).

modules.title: The locus of a point whose distances from two points are in a fixed ratio

chapter.title: The locus of a point whose distances from two points are in a fixed ratio
text: A locus is the set of all points that obey a condition. Writing each distance with the distance formula turns the condition into an equation in x and y.
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(2, 3) is always 2 times its distance from B(3, 1). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 2·PB to remove the roots: (x − 2)² + (y − 3)² = 4[(x − 3)² + (y − 1)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 3x² + 3y² − 20x − 2y + 27 = 0
Divide by 3 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² − (20/3)x − (2/3)y + 9 = 0
chapter.tip: The ratio was applied the other way round (PB = 2·PA). Here P is 2 times as far from A as from B.

chapter.title: The locus of a point equidistant from a point and a line
text: Every point of the locus is as far from the point as from the line, so the two distances can be set equal. The curve is a parabola with S as its focus and the line as its directrix.
For P(x, y), the distance to S comes from the distance formula and the distance to the line x = h is |x − h|. Square both, set them equal, expand, and make x the subject.
math: A point P moves so that it is always the same distance from the point S(−3, 0) as from the line x = 3. Find the equation of the locus of P in the form x = (an expression in y), and type the expression in y.
PS² = (distance to the line)²: (x + 3)² + y² = (x − 3)²
Expand; the x² terms cancel: −12x = y²
Divide by −12: x = −(1/12)y²

screens.title: The method
text: Let P be (x, y). Write PA and PB with the distance formula, square both sides to remove the roots, expand, collect all terms on one side and divide by the coefficient of x².
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(−4, −5) is always 2 times its distance from B(−3, −2). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 2·PB to remove the roots: (x + 4)² + (y + 5)² = 4[(x + 3)² + (y + 2)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 3x² + 3y² + 16x + 6y + 11 = 0
Divide by 3 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² + (16/3)x + 2y + 11/3 = 0

strategies.title: Check with a point you know is on the locus

screens.title: Check with a point you know is on the locus
text: The point that divides AB internally in the ratio k : 1 is k times as far from A as from B, so it lies on the locus.
Substitute it into your equation: the left-hand side must be 0. If it is not, look for a squaring or sign slip.
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(−4, 1) is always 3 times its distance from B(−2, −3). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 3·PB to remove the roots: (x + 4)² + (y − 1)² = 9[(x + 2)² + (y + 3)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 8x² + 8y² + 28x + 56y + 100 = 0
Divide by 8 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² + (7/2)x + 7y + 25/2 = 0

text: A question: “A point P moves so that its distance from A(−3, −4) is always 3 times its distance from B(2, −2). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.” A common wrong answer is x² + y² + (29/4)x + (17/2)y + 217/8.
The ratio was applied the other way round (PB = 3·PA). Here P is 3 times as far from A as from B.

text: Each step builds on another skill: Use coordinate distance and section formulas. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Let P be (x, y). Write PA and PB with the distance formula, square both sides to remove the roots, expand, collect all terms on one side and divide by the coefficient of x².

modules.title: The slopes of a pair of lines through the origin

chapter.title: The slopes of a pair of lines through the origin
text: A homogeneous equation ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 factorises into two linear factors through the origin; putting y = mx turns it into a quadratic whose roots are the slopes.
math: The equation 30x² + 11xy + y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: m² + 11m + 30 = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots −11, product 30): the slopes are −6 and −5

chapter.title: The angle between a pair of lines through the origin
text: For ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 the slopes satisfy m₁ + m₂ = −2h/b and m₁m₂ = a/b, so tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| becomes |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.
Read a, h (half the xy coefficient) and b, work out h² − ab, and use tan θ = |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.
math: Find tan θ, where θ is the acute angle between the pair of lines 3x² − 4xy + y² = 0.
Compare with ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0: a = 3, h = −2, b = 1
h² − ab = 1

chapter.title: The angle bisectors of a pair of lines through the origin
text: The two angle bisectors of the lines ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are the lines whose points are equally far from both; together they are (x² − y²)/(a − b) = xy/h, that is h(x² − y²) − (a − b)xy = 0.
Read a (the x² coefficient), 2h (the xy coefficient) and b (the y² coefficient), write h(x² − y²) = (a − b)xy and divide by h to get x² + kxy − y² = 0.
math: The equation xy + y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Their angle bisectors together have an equation of the form x² + kxy − y² = 0. Find k.
The bisectors of ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are (x² − y²)/(a − b) = xy/h with a = 0, h = 1/2, b = 1
So the bisectors are x² + 2xy − y² = 0

screens.title: The method
text: Substitute y = mx, divide by x², and solve bm² + 2hm + a = 0. Check: the sum of the slopes is −2h/b and the product is a/b.
math: The equation −20x² + 11xy + 3y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: 3m² + 11m − 20 = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots −11/3, product −20/3): the slopes are −5 and 4/3

screens.title: Factorise directly
text: Treat the equation as a quadratic in y and factorise it into (q₁y − p₁x)(q₂y − p₂x).
Each factor set to zero is one line; read off its slope p/q.
math: The equation −5xy + 2y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: 2m² − 5m = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots 5/2, product 0): the slopes are 0 and 5/2

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve quadratic equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Substitute y = mx, divide by x², and solve bm² + 2hm + a = 0. Check: the sum of the slopes is −2h/b and the product is a/b.

modules.title: The equation of a line through two points

chapter.title: The equation of a line through two points
text: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the slope from the two given points fixes its direction, and either point fixes its position.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(−1, −5) and B(4, 5). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = 10/5 = 2
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = −3
So y = 2x − 3
chapter.tip: The slope was found as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run, (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

chapter.title: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line
text: The shortest way from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. Its length is |ax₀ + by₀ + c| divided by √(a² + b²), the length of the normal vector (a, b).
Substitute the point into ax + by + c, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b²). Simplify the surd.
math: Find the perpendicular distance from the point (0, 0) to the line 3x + 5y + 4 = 0.
Put the point into ax + by + c: 4
Distance = |ax₀ + by₀ + c|/√(a² + b²) = 2√34/17

chapter.title: The distance between two parallel lines
text: Parallel lines can be written with the same x and y coefficients; then they differ only in the constant, and the gap between them is |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).
Divide one equation so the x and y coefficients match the other, then use |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).
math: Find the distance between the parallel lines y + 5 = 0 and y + 11 = 0.
The x and y coefficients already match: y + 11 = 0
Distance = |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²) = 6/√1 = 6

chapter.title: The angle between two lines in general form
text: The angle between two lines is the difference of their inclinations, so tan θ = (m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂) from the subtraction formula for tan; the absolute value gives the acute angle.
Find each slope as −a/b, then work out |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
math: Find tan θ, where θ is the acute angle between the lines 5x + 4y − 4 = 0 and −x + y + 4 = 0.
The slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b: the slopes are −5/4 and 1

chapter.title: Parallel, perpendicular or neither
text: The slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
Find both slopes (or test a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0 for parallel and a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0 for perpendicular, which also works for vertical lines).
math: Are the lines 6x − y + 3 = 0 and 6x − y − 3 = 0 parallel, perpendicular, or neither?
a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0 (0 means parallel)
a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 37 (0 means perpendicular)
So the lines are parallel

chapter.title: Slope from the inclination, and the inclination from the slope
text: The inclination θ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x-axis (0° ≤ θ < 180°); its slope is m = tan θ. Upward lines have acute θ and positive slope; downward lines have obtuse θ and negative slope.

Slope from the angle: m = tan θ (exact values for 30°, 45°, 60° and their supplements). Angle from the slope: find the acute angle with tan = |m|, and use 180° minus it when m is negative. Then y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
math: A straight line has slope √3/3. Find its inclination θ in degrees (0° ≤ θ < 180°).
tan θ = √3/3 with 0° ≤ θ < 180° gives θ = 30°

chapter.title: Collinear points by equal slopes
text: Three points lie on one straight line exactly when the slope from the first to the second equals the slope from the first to the third (or from the second to the third).
Work out the slope of AB, write the slope of AC with k in it, set them equal and solve for k.
math: The points A(3, 2), B(5, 0) and C(0, k) are collinear. Using slopes, find k.
Slope of AB = −2/2 = −1
Collinear points give equal slopes: slope AC = slope AB, so k = 5

chapter.title: Equations of lines in point–slope, intercept and normal form, and lines parallel to the axes
text: A line is fixed by a point and a slope (y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)), by its intercepts (x/a + y/b = 1), or by the length p and direction ω of the perpendicular from the origin (x cos ω + y sin ω = p). Lines parallel to the axes are simply x = k or y = k.
Pick the form that matches the data, put the numbers in, and rearrange to y = mx + c (or read off k for a line parallel to an axis).
math: The segment of a line between the coordinate axes is bisected at the point (3, 2). Find the equation of the line. Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
Use x/a + y/b = 1 with a, b twice the coordinates
So the answer is −(2/3)x + 4

chapter.title: The parametric form of a line: the point at a given distance
text: Every point of the line through (x₁, y₁) with inclination θ can be written as x = x₁ + r cos θ, y = y₁ + r sin θ, where r is the signed distance from (x₁, y₁) along the line.
Write cos θ and sin θ, put them into the parametric equations, then substitute the given r (negative r goes the other way).
math: A line passes through A(−4, −2) and makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, where cos θ = −3/5 and sin θ = 4/5. Write its parametric equations x = x₁ + r cos θ, y = y₁ + r sin θ (r is the signed distance from A) and find the point with r = −5. Type it as (x, y).
Parametric form: x = −4 + r(−3/5), y = −2 + r(4/5)

chapter.title: From the general form Ax + By + C = 0: slope, intercepts, normal form, parallel and perpendicular lines
text: Ax + By + C = 0 can be rewritten as y = −(A/B)x − C/B (slope and y-intercept), as x/(−C/A) + y/(−C/B) = 1 (intercepts), or, dividing by ∓√(A² + B²), as x cos ω + y sin ω = p with p > 0. Parallel lines share A : B; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.

Make y the subject to read the slope and y-intercept; move C across and divide to get the intercept form; divide by √(A² + B²), with the sign chosen to make the right-hand side positive, for the normal form.
math: Write the line 3x − y − 5 = 0 in intercept form x/a + y/b = 1. What is its x-intercept a?
Rearrange: y = 3x − 5
So the answer is 5/3

chapter.title: Are two points on the same side of a line?
text: A line ax + by + c = 0 splits the plane into two half-planes: on one side ax + by + c is positive, on the other negative, and on the line it is zero.
Put each point into ax + by + c. Same signs: the same side. Opposite signs: opposite sides. Zero: the point is on the line.
math: Where do the points P(−3, −2) and Q(−4, 3) lie relative to the line 2x − 2y − 1 = 0?
Put P and Q into the left-hand side: −3 and −15
Same signs: the same side (option B)

chapter.title: A line through the point of intersection of two given lines
text: For any λ, L₁ + λL₂ = 0 is a straight line through the point where L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0 meet. One more condition (a point, or a slope) picks out the value of λ.
Either solve L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0 for the point of intersection and use the condition, or write L₁ + λL₂ = 0, apply the condition to find λ, and simplify.
math: Find the equation of the line through the point of intersection of x + y + 4 = 0 and 3x − 2y − 3 = 0 that passes through (3, −1). (You may use the family L₁ + λL₂ = 0.) Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
L₁ + λL₂ = 0 passes through the intersection for every λ
Use the condition: the condition fixes λ; the line passes through (−1, −3)

screens.title: The method
text: Find m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and rearrange to y = mx + c.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(1, 5) and B(3, 4). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = −1/2 = −1/2
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = 11/2

screens.title: Two-point form
text: Write (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
Cross-multiply and make y the subject.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(−1, −2) and B(2, 6). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = 8/3 = 8/3
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = 2/3

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the equation of the straight line through A(−2, 5) and B(−1, −5). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).” A common wrong answer is −(1/10)x + 24/5.
The slope was found as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run, (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

modules.title: The tangent or normal to a circle or parabola at a point

chapter.title: The tangent or normal to a circle or parabola at a point
text: The tangent at a point has the slope of the curve there (from implicit differentiation or the standard formulas); the normal is perpendicular to it.
math: Find the equation of the normal to the circle x² + y² = 10 at the point (3, −1). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve x² + y² = 10 at the point (the tangent's slope) is 3
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its slope is −1/3
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −(1/3)x
chapter.tip: The tangent was given; the normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the point, so its slope is −1/(tangent slope).

chapter.title: The condition for y = mx + c to be a tangent
text: A line is a tangent when it meets the conic in exactly one point: substituting y = mx + c gives a quadratic in x whose discriminant is 0.
Use the standard conditions: parabola y² = 4ax: c = a/m; circle x² + y² = r²: c² = r²(1 + m²); ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² + b²; hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² − b².
math: Find the positive value of c for which the line y = x + c is a tangent to the ellipse x² + y²/16 = 1.
For this conic, y = mx + c is a tangent when c² = a²m² + b²
Substitute m and the constants: 17
So c = √17

chapter.title: Tangents and normals to an ellipse or a hyperbola, with points in parametric form
text: The tangent to x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 at (x₁, y₁) is xx₁/a² + yy₁/b² = 1; for the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 it is xx₁/a² − yy₁/b² = 1. The normal is the perpendicular line through the same point. In parametric form the points are (a cos θ, b sin θ) and (a sec θ, b tan θ).

Find the point (from θ if it is given in parametric form), write the tangent by the rule (or find dy/dx by implicit differentiation), and rearrange to y = mx + c; for the normal use slope −1/m through the point.
math: Find the equation of the tangent to the ellipse x²/9 + y²/16 = 1 at the point (12/5, 12/5). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The point is (12/5, 12/5)
Differentiating (or from xx₁/a² ± yy₁/b² = 1), the tangent's slope is −16/9

screens.title: The method
text: Circle x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): tangent xx₁ + yy₁ = r². Parabola y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): tangent ty = x + at², normal y = −tx + 2at + at³. Rearrange to y = mx + c.
math: Find the equation of the tangent to the parabola y² = 8x at the point (18, −12). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve y² = 8x at the point (the tangent's slope) is −1/3
The tangent has slope −1/3
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −(1/3)x − 6

screens.title: Differentiate implicitly
text: Differentiate the curve's equation with respect to x and solve for dy/dx at the point.
That is the tangent slope; the normal slope is −1 divided by it. Then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
math: Find the equation of the normal to the parabola y² = 20x at the point (5, 10). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve y² = 20x at the point (the tangent's slope) is 1
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its slope is −1
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −x + 15

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the equation of the tangent to the parabola y² = 16x at the point (36, −24). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.” A common wrong answer is 3x − 132.
The normal (the line along the radius or perpendicular to the curve) was given; the tangent touches the curve, perpendicular to the normal.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use straight-line equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Circle x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): tangent xx₁ + yy₁ = r². Parabola y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): tangent ty = x + at², normal y = −tx + 2at + at³. Rearrange to y = mx + c.
