modules.title: The distance between two points in space

chapter.title: The distance between two points in space
text: In space, Pythagoras is used twice: across the floor (x and y) and then up (z), giving √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).
math: Find the distance between the points P(4, −2, 0) and Q(1, −5, −3).
Differences of the coordinates: (−3, −3, −3)
Sum of their squares: (−3)² + (−3)² + (−3)² = 27
Distance = √27 = 3√3
chapter.tip: The differences were added; in space the straight distance is √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).

chapter.title: The point dividing a segment in space in a ratio
text: The point that divides AB in the ratio m : n is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, the same in every coordinate.
P = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n)). For the midpoint, m = n = 1.
math: Find the coordinates of the point that divides the segment from A(−5, −1, 3) to B(−4, 3, −2) internally in the ratio 1 : 3. Type it as (x, y, z).
Weight B by 1 and A by 3: (1·B + 3·A)

chapter.title: Where a point lies in space: octant, plane or axis
text: The three coordinate planes (xy, yz, zx) divide space into eight octants. A zero coordinate puts a point on a coordinate plane; two zeros put it on an axis.

Count the zero coordinates. None: use the signs of x, y and z to name the octant. One zero (say z = 0): the point is in the plane of the other two axes (the xy-plane). Two zeros: the point is on the remaining axis.
math: Where does the point (0, 1, −5) lie?
Signs of (x, y, z): 0, +, −
So the point lies in the yz-plane

chapter.title: Collinear points and the kind of triangle in space, by the distance formula
text: The distance formula in space, √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²), gives the three side lengths. Their sizes decide the figure: collinear when two add to the third, right-angled when Pythagoras holds, isosceles when two are equal.
Work out AB², BC² and AC². Test, in order: do the two shorter lengths add up to the longest (collinear)? Do the two smaller squares add up to the largest (right-angled)? Are two equal (isosceles)?
math: The points A(1, 2, 2), B(2, 1, 0) and C(0, 3, 4) are given in space. Use the distance formula to decide which statement is true.
AB² = 6, BC² = 24, AC² = 6
The two shorter distances add up to the longest, so the points are collinear

chapter.title: The centroid of a triangle in space
text: As in the plane, the centroid of a triangle in space is the average of its vertices: G = ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3, (z₁ + z₂ + z₃)/3).
Add the three x-coordinates and divide by 3; do the same for y and for z.
math: Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices A(−2, 0, −3), B(−1, −4, 3) and C(6, −5, 0). Give it as (x, y, z).
Add the coordinates: (3, −9, 0)
Divide each by 3: (1, −3, 0)

chapter.title: The point dividing a segment in space externally
text: P divides AB externally in m : n when P is on line AB but outside the segment, with PA : PB = m : n. Replacing n by −n in the section formula gives P = (mB − nA)/(m − n).
For each coordinate work out (m × B − n × A) and divide by m − n.
math: Find the point that divides the segment joining A(−2, −4, 2) and B(−4, −2, 1) externally in the ratio 2 : 3. Give it as (x, y, z).
P = (mB − nA)/(m − n) with m = 2, n = 3: each coordinate is (2 × B − 3 × A)/-1

screens.title: The method
text: Subtract the coordinates, square each difference, add, and take the square root. Simplify the surd.
math: Find the distance between the points P(−3, 3, 5) and Q(−1, 1, −2).
Differences of the coordinates: (2, −2, −7)
Sum of their squares: 2² + (−2)² + (−7)² = 57
Distance = √57 = √57

screens.title: The diagonal of a box
text: Think of a cuboid with edges |Δx|, |Δy| and |Δz|.
The distance between the points is the space diagonal of that box.
math: Find the distance between the points P(−2, −3, −2) and Q(4, 4, 1).
Differences of the coordinates: (6, 7, 3)
Sum of their squares: 6² + 7² + 3² = 94
Distance = √94 = √94

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the distance between the points P(1, 4, −3) and Q(−1, −4, 4).” A common wrong answer is 17.
The differences were added; in space the straight distance is √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).
math: Not 17, but 3√13

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Simplify radicals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Subtract the coordinates, square each difference, add, and take the square root. Simplify the surd.

modules.title: Direction cosines of the line through two points

chapter.title: Direction cosines of the line through two points
text: Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the axes; they are the components of a unit vector along the line, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
math: Find the direction cosines of the line through A(−3, 1, −2) and B(4, −1, −2), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).
Direction ratios: B − A = (7, −2, 0)
Length |AB| = √53
Divide each ratio by the length: (7√53/53, −2√53/53, 0)
chapter.tip: These are direction ratios; direction cosines are the ratios divided by the length √53, so that l² + m² + n² = 1.

chapter.title: Parallel, intersecting or skew lines
text: In space two lines are parallel (directions are multiples), intersecting (they share a point), or skew (neither: not parallel and never meet).

If the directions are multiples, the lines are parallel. Otherwise set the general points equal, solve two of the coordinate equations for λ and μ, and test the third: it holds for intersecting lines and fails for skew lines.
math: Are the lines r⃗ = (−î + 2ĵ − 2k̂) + λ(î + ĵ + k̂) and r⃗ = (î + 3ĵ + k̂) + μ(−2î − 2ĵ − 2k̂) parallel, intersecting, or skew?
u × v = (0, 0, 0) (zero means the directions are parallel)
(B − A)·(u × v) = 0 (zero means the lines lie in one plane and meet)
So the lines are parallel

chapter.title: The angle between two lines in space
text: The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors; the dot product gives its cosine, and |u·v| gives the acute angle. cos θ = 0 means the lines are perpendicular.
Take the direction vectors u and v (the vectors multiplied by λ and μ), and work out cos θ = |u·v|/(|u||v|).
math: Find cos θ, where θ is the acute angle between the lines r⃗ = (−2î + ĵ − 2k̂) + λ(−2ĵ + k̂) and r⃗ = (2ĵ) + μ(î + 3ĵ + 2k̂).
Dot product of the direction vectors: u·v = −4

chapter.title: The foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line in space
text: The shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to the line, so the foot Q is the point of the line with PQ·d = 0.
Write a general point Q = a + λd of the line, form PQ = Q − P, solve PQ·d = 0 for λ, and substitute back.
math: Find the foot of the perpendicular from the point P(−4, −1, 3) to the line r⃗ = (−3î − 2ĵ) + λ(−î − ĵ + k̂). Type it as (x, y, z).
A general point of the line: Q = (−3 + −λ, −2 + −λ, 0 + λ)
PQ is perpendicular to the direction d: (Q − P)·d = 0 gives 3λ = 3, so λ = 1
Put λ = 1 into the general point: (−4, −3, 1)

chapter.title: Vector and Cartesian equations of a line in space
text: A line through the point A with direction b⃗ is r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗ (vector form), or (x − a₁)/b₁ = (y − a₂)/b₂ = (z − a₃)/b₃ (Cartesian form). The denominators are direction ratios and the numerators show the point.

To convert Cartesian to vector form, first make the coefficients of x, y and z equal to +1 in the numerators (divide top and bottom), then read the point from the numerators and the direction from the denominators. Through two points, use b⃗ − a⃗ as the direction.
math: Find the equation of the line through A(2, −2, −1) parallel to the line (2x − 1)/2 = (y + 1)/2 = (2 − z)/1. Write it as r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗, where a⃗ is the position vector of A and b⃗ = (b₁, b₂, b₃) are the denominators of the given line once it is written as (x − x₀)/b₁ = (y − y₀)/b₂ = (z − z₀)/b₃. Type (a₁, a₂, a₃, b₁, b₂, b₃).
Standard form: the same direction as the given line, through A

chapter.title: The point of intersection of two lines in space
text: Two lines in space meet when some point is on both: a⃗ + λu⃗ = b⃗ + μv⃗ for one pair λ, μ. That is three equations in two unknowns; they intersect when the third equation agrees with the λ, μ found from two of them.
Write the x, y and z equations, solve two of them for λ and μ, check the third, and substitute λ into the first line (or μ into the second).
math: Show that the lines r⃗ = (−4î − ĵ + 2k̂) + λ(3î + ĵ − 2k̂) and r⃗ = (−5î − 4ĵ + 2k̂) + μ(2î + 2ĵ − k̂) intersect, and find their point of intersection. Type it as (x, y, z).
Set a⃗ + λu⃗ = b⃗ + μv⃗ componentwise
Solve two of the equations: λ = 1, μ = 2 (the third equation checks)
Substitute: the point is (−1, 0, 0)

screens.title: The method
text: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), and divide each ratio by it.
math: Find the direction cosines of the line through A(2, 3, −1) and B(1, 1, 2), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).
Direction ratios: B − A = (−1, −2, 3)
Length |AB| = √14
Divide each ratio by the length: (−√14/14, −√14/7, 3√14/14)

screens.title: Make a unit vector
text: Write AB as a vector a î + b ĵ + c k̂.
Divide by its magnitude: the components of the unit vector are l, m and n.
math: Find the direction cosines of the line through A(0, 2, −4) and B(−4, 4, 2), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).
Direction ratios: B − A = (−4, 2, 6)
Length |AB| = 2√14
Divide each ratio by the length: (−√14/7, √14/14, 3√14/14)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the direction cosines of the line through A(−2, 4, 2) and B(−3, 1, −3), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).” A common wrong answer is (−1, −3, −5).
These are direction ratios; direction cosines are the ratios divided by the length √35, so that l² + m² + n² = 1.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Locate points in three dimensions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), and divide each ratio by it.

modules.title: The shortest distance between skew lines

chapter.title: The shortest distance between skew lines
text: The shortest segment joining two skew lines is perpendicular to both, so it runs along u × v. Its length is the projection of any joining vector B − A onto u × v.
math: Find the shortest distance between the lines r⃗ = (2î − ĵ) + λ(î − ĵ + k̂) and r⃗ = (2î − ĵ − k̂) + μ(−2î − ĵ − k̂).
The common perpendicular is u × v = (2, −1, −3)
The vector joining the given points: B − A = (0, 0, −1)
Shortest distance = |(B − A)·(u × v)|/|u × v| = 3/√14 = 3√14/14
chapter.tip: The distance between the two points written in the equations was found; the shortest distance is measured along the common perpendicular u × v.

chapter.title: The distance between parallel lines in space
text: For parallel lines the perpendicular gap is the height of the parallelogram formed by B − A and the direction u: area |(B − A) × u| divided by the base |u|.
Find B − A, compute (B − A) × u, and divide its length by |u|.
math: The lines r⃗ = (−2î − 2ĵ + 2k̂) + λ(î − 2k̂) and r⃗ = (−2î − 5ĵ + 5k̂) + μ(−î + 2k̂) are parallel. Find the distance between them.

screens.title: The method
text: Work out u × v, then d = |(B − A)·(u × v)| / |u × v|.
math: Find the shortest distance between the lines r⃗ = (î − 2k̂) + λ(−2î + 2k̂) and r⃗ = (4î − 2ĵ − 5k̂) + μ(2î + 2ĵ).
The common perpendicular is u × v = (−4, 4, −4)
The vector joining the given points: B − A = (3, −2, −3)
Shortest distance = |(B − A)·(u × v)|/|u × v| = 8/√48 = 2√3/3

screens.title: Minimise the distance
text: Write general points P = A + λu and Q = B + μv.
Make PQ perpendicular to both u and v (two equations), solve for λ and μ, and find |PQ|.
math: Find the shortest distance between the lines r⃗ = λ(−2î − 2k̂) and r⃗ = (−î − 3ĵ + k̂) + μ(2î + ĵ).
The common perpendicular is u × v = (2, −4, −2)
The vector joining the given points: B − A = (−1, −3, 1)
Shortest distance = |(B − A)·(u × v)|/|u × v| = 8/√24 = 2√6/3

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the shortest distance between the lines r⃗ = (−î − ĵ − k̂) + λ(−2î + 2ĵ − 2k̂) and r⃗ = (2î + ĵ + 2k̂) + μ(−2î − k̂).” A common wrong answer is √22.
The distance between the two points written in the equations was found; the shortest distance is measured along the common perpendicular u × v.
math: Not √22, but 5√6/6

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use dot and cross products; Represent lines in space. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Work out u × v, then d = |(B − A)·(u × v)| / |u × v|.

modules.title: The distance from a point to a plane

chapter.title: The distance from a point to a plane
text: The shortest distance from a point to a plane is along the normal (a, b, c); dividing ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d by |n| measures it in units of length.
math: Find the distance of the point (0, −3, 2) from the plane 2x + 2y − z + 1 = 0.
Put the point into ax + by + cz + d: −7
Distance = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d|/√(a² + b² + c²) = 7/3
chapter.tip: The value of ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d was negative and its sign was kept; a distance is never negative.

chapter.title: The point where a line meets a plane
text: Every point of the line is a + λu for some λ; the meeting point is the one whose coordinates also satisfy the plane's equation.
Substitute x, y, z of the general point into the plane, solve the linear equation for λ, and put λ back into the line.
math: Find the point where the line r⃗ = (2ĵ + k̂) + λ(−ĵ + 2k̂) meets the plane 3x + z = 3. Type it as (x, y, z).
Put the general point a + λu into the plane: 1 + 2λ = 3
Solve: λ = 1
The meeting point is a + 1u = (0, 1, 3)

chapter.title: The image of a point in a plane
text: The image Q of P in a plane is on the normal line through P, the same distance on the other side: the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of PQ.
Write the line P + λn, find λ where it meets the plane (the foot), then double that λ to reach the image.
math: Find the image (reflection) of the point P(−4, 3, 3) in the plane 2x + y − z = −14. Type it as (x, y, z).
The line through P along the normal: P + λ((2, 1, −1))
It meets the plane at λ = −1: the foot is (−6, 2, 4)
The foot is the midpoint of P and its image, so the image is (−8, 1, 5)

chapter.title: The equation of a plane from three points, a point and a normal, its intercepts, a line and a point, or its normal form
text: A plane is fixed by a point A on it and a normal vector n⃗: n⃗ · (r⃗ − a⃗) = 0. Three points give the normal as (B − A) × (C − A); intercepts give x/a + y/b + z/c = 1; the normal form r⃗ · n̂ = p uses the unit normal and the distance p from the origin.
Find a normal vector and a point from the data, write n⃗ · r⃗ = n⃗ · a⃗, clear fractions and remove any common factor.
math: A plane is at a distance of 1 unit from the origin, and the perpendicular from the origin to it is along the vector 2î − ĵ + 2k̂. Using the normal form r⃗ · n̂ = p, find its equation. Write it as ax + by + cz = d with whole numbers having no common factor and the first non-zero one of a, b, c positive. Type (a, b, c, d).
Find the normal: r⃗ · n̂ = p with n̂ = n⃗/|n⃗|

chapter.title: The angle between two planes, or between a line and a plane
text: The angle between two planes is the angle between their normals: cos θ = |n⃗₁ · n⃗₂|/(|n⃗₁||n⃗₂|). A line with direction b⃗ makes an angle φ with a plane of normal n⃗ where sin φ = |b⃗ · n⃗|/(|b⃗||n⃗|), because the line makes 90° − φ with the normal.
Read the normal vectors (the coefficients of x, y, z) and the line's direction, work out the dot product and the two lengths, and divide; simplify the surd.
math: Find cos θ, where θ (0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°) is the angle between the planes 2x − y + z = −6 and x − z = 8.
Use the normals 2î − ĵ + k̂ and î − k̂
|dot product| = 1
Divide by √6 × √2: √3/6

screens.title: The method
text: Substitute the point into ax + by + cz + d, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b² + c²).
math: Find the distance of the point (4, 4, 4) from the plane x − 4y − 4z + 6 = 0.
Put the point into ax + by + cz + d: −22
Distance = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d|/√(a² + b² + c²) = 2√33/3

screens.title: Walk along the normal
text: The line through the point along (a, b, c) meets the plane at the foot of the perpendicular.
Find that point, then use the distance formula.
math: Find the distance of the point (1, 4, 0) from the plane x + 2y + 2z − 5 = 0.
Put the point into ax + by + cz + d: 4
Distance = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d|/√(a² + b² + c²) = 4/3

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the distance of the point (−1, −4, 1) from the plane x − y + 4z + 5 = 0.” A common wrong answer is 2/3.
The denominator is √(a² + b² + c²) = √18, not 18.
math: Not 2/3, but 2√2

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Locate points in three dimensions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Substitute the point into ax + by + cz + d, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b² + c²).

modules.title: Multiplying and dividing complex numbers

chapter.title: Multiplying and dividing complex numbers
text: Complex numbers multiply like brackets in algebra, with i² = −1. Dividing uses the conjugate: (c + di)(c − di) = c² + d² is real.
math: Write (3 + 2i)(−5 + 6i) in the form x + iy. Type the answer as the pair (x, y).
Multiply every part by every part: −15 + 8i + 12i²
Use i² = −1 and collect: (−27, 8)
chapter.tip: Only the real parts and the imaginary parts were multiplied together; every part of one bracket multiplies every part of the other.

chapter.title: The modulus of a product or quotient of complex numbers
text: The modulus is the distance from the origin in the Argand plane. Moduli multiply and divide: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|.
Find |z₁| = √(a² + b²) and |z₂| = √(c² + d²), then multiply or divide them and simplify the surd.
math: Find |z|, where z = (−4 − 2i)(2).
The moduli: |z₁| = 2√5, |z₂| = 2
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| = 4√5

chapter.title: Powers of i
text: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and then the pattern repeats, so only the remainder of the power on division by 4 matters.
Divide the power by 4 and keep the remainder r (from 0 to 3, also for negative powers); then iⁿ = iʳ.
math: Simplify i⁸⁷.
87 = 4 × 21 + 3: the remainder is 3
The powers repeat every 4, so i³ = −i

chapter.title: The square root of a complex number
text: If (x + iy)² = a + bi, then x² − y² = a and 2xy = b; also x² + y² = |a + bi|. Adding and subtracting gives x² and y².
Find |a + bi|. Then x² = (|z| + a)/2 and y² = (|z| − a)/2; choose x > 0 and give y the sign that makes 2xy = b.
math: Find the square root of 9 + 40i that has a positive real part. Type it as (x, y) for x + iy.
x² = (|z| + real part)/2 = (41 + 9)/2, so x = 5
y = (imaginary part)/(2x) = 40/10 = 4

chapter.title: Adding and subtracting complex numbers, and the multiplicative inverse
text: Complex numbers add and subtract part by part: real with real, imaginary with imaginary. The inverse 1/z uses the conjugate: z z̄ = a² + b² is a real number.

For a sum or difference, combine the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. For 1/(a + bi), multiply the top and the bottom by a − bi to get (a − bi)/(a² + b²), then split into real and imaginary parts.
math: Write (1 + 4i) + (3 − 3i) in the form x + iy. Type the answer as the pair (x, y).
Real parts: 1 and 3 give 4
Imaginary parts: 4 and −3 give 1

chapter.title: Conjugates of complex numbers and their properties
text: The conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi: its reflection in the real axis. Conjugation respects arithmetic: conj(z₁ ± z₂) = z̄₁ ± z̄₂, conj(z₁z₂) = z̄₁z̄₂, conj(z₁/z₂) = z̄₁/z̄₂, and z z̄ = |z|² = a² + b².
Either work out the product or quotient first and then change the sign of its imaginary part, or conjugate each number first and then combine them; both give the same answer.
math: Find z̄₁ z₂, where z₁ = −1 − i and z₂ = 3 + 3i, in the form x + iy. Type it as the pair (x, y).
The conjugate of −1 − i is −1 + i
Work it out: (−6, 0)

screens.title: The method
text: Product: expand, replace i² by −1, collect real and imaginary parts. Quotient: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, then divide each part by c² + d².
math: Write (−3 − 5i)(−2 − 2i) in the form x + iy. Type the answer as the pair (x, y).
Multiply every part by every part: 6 + 16i + 10i²
Use i² = −1 and collect: (−4, 16)

strategies.title: Turn and stretch in the Argand plane

screens.title: Turn and stretch in the Argand plane
text: Multiplying by c + di stretches by |c + di| and turns by its argument.
Dividing undoes that: shrink by |c + di| and turn back.
math: Write (1 − 4i) ÷ (5 − 5i) in the form x + iy. Type the answer as the pair (x, y).
Multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate 5 + 5i: (25 − 15i)/50
Split into real and imaginary parts: (1/2, −3/10)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write (−4 − 5i) ÷ (3i) in the form x + iy. Type the answer as the pair (x, y).” A common wrong answer is (5/3, −4/3).
(c + di)(c − di) = c² + d² = 9; it was worked out as c² − d².

modules.title: The principal argument of a complex number

chapter.title: The principal argument of a complex number
text: The argument is the angle from the positive real axis to the point z in the Argand plane; the principal argument is the one in (−π, π].
math: Find the principal argument θ (−π < θ ≤ π) of z = −8. Write θ in radians, in terms of π (you may type pi).
The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| is 0
Use the quadrant (signs of the parts): θ = π
chapter.tip: The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| was given; z is not in the first quadrant, so the argument is found from α using the signs of x and y.

chapter.title: Multiplying and dividing in polar form
text: In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments; dividing divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.
Multiply (or divide) r₁ and r₂, add (or subtract) the arguments, and bring the result into (−π, π] by adding or subtracting 2π.
math: z₁ = 4(cos (−5π/6) + i sin (−5π/6)) and z₂ = 4(cos (−π/2) + i sin (−π/2)). Find the principal argument θ (−π < θ ≤ π) of z₁/z₂. Write θ in radians, in terms of π (you may type pi).
(The modulus is r₁/r₂ = 1; it does not change the argument.)
Subtract the arguments: −π/3
The principal argument (add or subtract 2π if needed): −π/3

text: Find the acute angle α with tan α = |y/x|. Then use the quadrant: first α, second π − α, third −(π − α), fourth −α.
math: Find the principal argument θ (−π < θ ≤ π) of z = 3 + 3i. Write θ in radians, in terms of π (you may type pi).
The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| is π/4
Use the quadrant (signs of the parts): θ = π/4

screens.title: Sketch the point
text: Plot z in the Argand plane and mark the angle from the positive real axis.
Anticlockwise angles are positive, clockwise ones negative; choose the one between −π and π.
math: Find the principal argument θ (−π < θ ≤ π) of z = 1 + i. Write θ in radians, in terms of π (you may type pi).
The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| is π/4
Use the quadrant (signs of the parts): θ = π/4

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the principal argument θ (−π < θ ≤ π) of z = −9. Write θ in radians, in terms of π (you may type pi).” A common wrong answer is 0.
The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| was given; z is not in the first quadrant, so the argument is found from α using the signs of x and y.
math: Not 0, but π

modules.title: The circle described by a condition on |z|

chapter.title: The circle described by a condition on |z|
text: |z − w| is the distance from z to w in the Argand plane, so |z − w| = r is a circle with centre w and radius r. A ratio of distances (not 1) is also a circle.
math: In the Argand plane, the points z with |3z − (5 + 5i)| = 4 form a circle. Find its centre x₀ + iy₀ and its radius r. Type them as (x₀, y₀, r).
|z − w| = r is the circle with centre w and radius r: (5/3, 5/3, 4/3)
chapter.tip: |z − w| = r has centre w (not −w): read the centre with the sign it has after the minus.

screens.title: The method
text: Write the condition with |z − w| alone: divide out a factor of z first. For |z − z₁| = k|z − z₂|, put z = x + iy, square, expand, and complete the squares.
math: In the Argand plane, the points z with |z − (2 + 4i)| = 2|z − (−3 − i)| form a circle. Find its centre x₀ + iy₀ and its radius r. Type them as (x₀, y₀, r).
Write z = x + iy and square: |z − z₁|² = 4|z − z₂|²
Expand and divide by 3: x² + y² + (28/3)x + (16/3)y + 20/3 = 0
Complete the squares to read the centre and radius: (−14/3, −8/3, 10√2/3)

screens.title: Read it as a distance
text: |kz − w| = r means k·|z − w/k| = r.
So z is always r/k away from w/k: that is a circle.
math: In the Argand plane, the points z with |z − (−4 + 3i)| = 2|z − (2 − 4i)| form a circle. Find its centre x₀ + iy₀ and its radius r. Type them as (x₀, y₀, r).
Write z = x + iy and square: |z − z₁|² = 4|z − z₂|²
Expand and divide by 3: x² + y² − 8x + (38/3)y + 55/3 = 0
Complete the squares to read the centre and radius: (4, −19/3, 2√85/3)

modules.title: Powers of a complex number by de Moivre's theorem

chapter.title: Powers of a complex number by de Moivre's theorem
text: In polar form, raising to a power raises the modulus to that power and multiplies the argument: (r(cos θ + i sin θ))ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
math: Use de Moivre's theorem to write (1 + √3 i)⁶ in the form x + iy. Type the answer as (x, y).
In polar form the base is 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3)
De Moivre: raise the modulus to the power 6 and multiply the argument by 6: 64(cos 2π + i sin 2π)
Evaluate cos and sin of 2π: (64, 0)
chapter.tip: Each part was raised to the power separately; (x + iy)ⁿ is not xⁿ + iⁿyⁿ. Use the polar form.

chapter.title: The nth roots of a complex number
text: zⁿ = w has n roots, all with modulus |w|^(1/n), spaced evenly round a circle: their arguments differ by 2π/n.
Write w = R(cos φ + i sin φ). The roots have arguments (φ + 2mπ)/n for m = 0, 1, …, n − 1; bring each into [0, 2π).
math: Solve z³ = −8. Every solution has modulus 2. Give the arguments θ of all the solutions, with 0 ≤ θ < 2π, as the numbers k with θ = kπ, separated by commas (for example 1/4, 5/4).

modules.title: The addition rule for two events

chapter.title: The addition rule for two events
text: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap A ∩ B twice, so it is taken away once: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). 'Neither' is the complement of A ∪ B.
math: For two events A and B, P(A) = 18/19, P(B) = 14/19 and P(A ∩ B) = 13/19. Find P(A ∪ B).
chapter.tip: P(A) + P(B) counts the outcomes in both events twice; subtract P(A ∩ B) once.

chapter.title: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Exhaustive events cover the whole sample space (A ∪ B = S).
Find A ∩ B: empty means mutually exclusive. Find A ∪ B: the whole sample space means exhaustive. Each property is checked separately.
math: A spinner with 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8 is spun once. Let A = {2, 7} and B = {5, 6}. Which describes the events A and B?
A ∩ B = ∅
So A and B are mutually exclusive, but not exhaustive

chapter.title: Events as sets of outcomes: not A, A and B, A or B
text: An event is a subset of the sample space S. 'A or B' is the union A ∪ B, 'A and B' the intersection A ∩ B, and 'not A' the complement A′ = S − A.
List the outcomes of A and of B from S. Then: for A ∪ B take every outcome in either list; for A ∩ B only those in both; for A′ those of S not in A; for A ∩ B′ those of A not in B.
math: A ball is drawn from a bag of twelve balls numbered 1 to 12, so the sample space is S = {1, 2, …, 12}. Let A be the event "the number is greater than 6" and B the event "the number is less than 5". Write the event A ∪ B (A or B) as a set of outcomes (list the numbers, separated by commas).

chapter.title: The addition theorem for three events
text: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) − P(A ∩ B) − P(B ∩ C) − P(A ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C): add the singles, take away the double counting of the pairs, and add back the triple overlap, which was taken away once too often.

Add the three probabilities, subtract the three pairwise ones, add the triple one. For 'none of them', take the result away from 1. For 'exactly one', subtract the pairs twice and add the triple three times.
math: Subtract P(A ∩ B) + P(B ∩ C) + P(A ∩ C) = 14/27
Add back P(A ∩ B ∩ C): P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = 7/9

screens.title: The method
text: Write the addition rule, put in the values you know, and solve for the one you need; for 'neither' use 1 − P(A ∪ B), and for 'A but not B' use P(A) − P(A ∩ B).
math: For two events A and B, P(A) = 1/10, P(B) = 13/20 and P(A ∩ B) = 0. Find P(A ∩ B′), the probability that A happens but B does not.

screens.title: Fill a Venn diagram
text: Put P(A ∩ B) in the overlap first.
Then A only = P(A) − overlap, B only = P(B) − overlap, and outside = 1 − (all three regions).
math: For two events A and B, P(A) = 13/29, P(B) = 19/29 and P(A ∩ B) = 11/29. Find P(A ∩ B′), the probability that A happens but B does not.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “For two events A and B, P(A) = 3/7, P(B) = 1/2 and P(A ∩ B) = 2/7. Find P(A′ ∩ B′), the probability that neither A nor B happens.” A common wrong answer is 1/14.
1 − P(A) − P(B) removes the overlap twice; add P(A ∩ B) back.
math: Not 1/14, but 5/14

modules.title: Bayes' theorem: which source produced it

chapter.title: Bayes' theorem: which source produced it
text: Bayes' theorem reverses a condition: P(source | result) = P(source and result) / P(result), where P(result) adds up over all the sources (total probability).
math: A factory has 3 machines. Machine A makes 30%, Machine B makes 20% and Machine C makes 50% of the bolts. 8% of A's, 8% of B's and 2% of C's bolts are defective. A bolt is picked at random and is found to be defective. Find the probability that it was made by machine C.
P(machine and defective) = 50% × 2% = 0.01
Total probability of a defective bolt = 0.05
Bayes: divide the machine's share of defectives by the total: 10/50
chapter.tip: The defect rates were compared without the machines' shares; a machine that makes more bolts also makes more of the defective ones. Multiply each rate by the share first.

chapter.title: Bayes' theorem: which bag the ball came from
text: Bayes' theorem turns the question round: P(Bag I | red) = P(Bag I and red) / P(red), and P(red) adds up the red branches of both bags (total probability).
Draw a tree: first the bag (with the die's probabilities), then the colour. Multiply along each red branch; divide the Bag I red branch by the sum of both red branches.
math: A die is thrown. If it shows a 1, 2 or 3, a ball is drawn from Bag I, which has 6 red and 1 black balls; otherwise a ball is drawn from Bag II, which has 6 red and 5 black balls. The ball drawn is red. Find the probability that it was drawn from Bag I.
Bag I and red: 1/2 × 6/7
Bag II and red: 1/2 × 6/11
Add the two branches: P(red), the total probability
Bayes: P(Bag I | red) = P(Bag I and red) ÷ P(red)

screens.title: The method
text: For each source multiply its share by its rate; add these for the total probability; divide the chosen source's product by the total.
math: A factory has 3 machines. Machine A makes 20%, Machine B makes 10% and Machine C makes 70% of the bolts. 7% of A's, 2% of B's and 1% of C's bolts are defective. A bolt is picked at random and is found to be defective. Find the probability that it was made by machine B.
P(machine and defective) = 10% × 2% = 0.002
Total probability of a defective bolt = 0.023
Bayes: divide the machine's share of defectives by the total: 2/23

screens.title: Count 10 000 items
text: Imagine 10 000 items: split them by share, then count the faulty ones from each source.
The answer is the faulty ones from the chosen source divided by all the faulty ones.
math: A factory has 3 machines. Machine A makes 40%, Machine B makes 50% and Machine C makes 10% of the bolts. 5% of A's, 6% of B's and 4% of C's bolts are defective. A bolt is picked at random and is found to be defective. Find the probability that it was made by machine B.
P(machine and defective) = 50% × 6% = 0.03
Total probability of a defective bolt = 0.054
Bayes: divide the machine's share of defectives by the total: 30/54

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A factory has 3 machines. Machine A makes 50%, Machine B makes 30% and Machine C makes 20% of the bolts. 3% of A's, 2% of B's and 1% of C's bolts are defective. A bolt is picked at random and is found to be defective. Find the probability that it was made by machine C.” A common wrong answer is 1/6.
The defect rates were compared without the machines' shares; a machine that makes more bolts also makes more of the defective ones. Multiply each rate by the share first.
math: Not 1/6, but 2/23

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Calculate conditional probabilities. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: For each source multiply its share by its rate; add these for the total probability; divide the chosen source's product by the total.

modules.title: Binomial probabilities

chapter.title: Binomial probabilities
text: In n independent trials with success probability p, any one order of r successes has probability pʳqⁿ⁻ʳ, and there are nCr such orders.
math: X has a binomial distribution with n = 3 and p = 4/7. Find P(X ≤ 1).
For a binomial distribution: P(X = k) = 3Cₖ (4/7)ᵏ (3/7)^(3 − k)
Add P(X = k) for k = 0, 1
That sum is the answer
chapter.tip: 'At most 1' includes every value from 0 up to 1, not only X = 1.

chapter.title: Mean and variance of a binomial distribution
text: A binomial count is a sum of n independent 0–1 trials, each with mean p and variance pq, so the mean is np and the variance is npq.
Mean = np, variance = npq with q = 1 − p. Going back: q = variance ÷ mean, p = 1 − q, n = mean ÷ p.
math: X has a binomial distribution with n = 7 and p = 1/4. Find the mean and the variance of X. Type them as (mean, variance).

chapter.title: One-point, two-point and Bernoulli distributions
text: A one-point distribution always gives the same value (variance 0). A two-point distribution gives u with probability p and v with probability 1 − p; with u = 1 and v = 0 it is the Bernoulli distribution, with mean p and variance p(1 − p).
Make the table of values and probabilities. Mean: Σ x P(x). Variance: Σ x² P(x) minus the square of the mean (for two points this simplifies to (u − v)² p(1 − p)).
math: A seed germinates with probability 4/9. Let X = 1 if it germinates and X = 0 if it does not (a Bernoulli random variable). Find the mean of X.
E(X) = p
So the answer is 4/9

screens.title: The method
text: Use P(X = k) = nCk pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ with q = 1 − p. For 'at least' or 'at most', add the values needed, or use 1 minus the complement when that is shorter.
math: X has a binomial distribution with n = 3 and p = 5/9. Find P(X = 3).
For a binomial distribution: P(X = k) = 3Cₖ (5/9)ᵏ (4/9)^(3 − k)
Add P(X = k) for k = 3
That sum is the answer

screens.title: Count the paths of a tree
text: Each trial branches into success (p) and failure (q).
Every path with r successes has the same probability; count the paths with nCr.

For a binomial distribution: P(X = k) = 4Cₖ (2/5)ᵏ (3/5)^(4 − k)
Add P(X = k) for k = 0, 1
Use the complement: subtract that sum from 1

modules.title: Probability from a density function

chapter.title: Probability from a density function
text: For a continuous random variable, probability is AREA under the density curve: P(b ≤ X ≤ c) is the integral of f(x) from b to c, and the whole area is 1.
math: A continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = x²/72 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 6, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Find P(X ≤ 1).
Integrate the density from 0: F(x) = x³/216
chapter.tip: The density value f(1) was taken as the probability; for a continuous variable the probability is the AREA under f, found by integrating.

chapter.title: The constant that makes a density function
text: A density never gives negative values and the total area under it is exactly 1 (X must take some value).
Integrate k xⁿ over the interval where f is not zero, set the result equal to 1 and solve for k.
math: The function f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 9, and f(x) = 0 otherwise, is a probability density function. Find the value of k.
The total area is k(9³ − 0³)/3 = 729k/3
Set it equal to 1: k = 3/729 = 1/243

chapter.title: From a density to the distribution function, and back
text: For a continuous random variable, F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ f(t) dt from the left end up to x, and f(x) = F′(x) wherever F is differentiable: integrating and differentiating go back and forth.
From f to F: integrate f from the start of the interval to x (check that F at the right end is 1). From F to f: differentiate F.
math: A continuous random variable X has density f(x) = 1/6 for 2 ≤ x ≤ 8 (and 0 otherwise). Find its distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) for 2 ≤ x ≤ 8.
F(x) = ∫ 1/6 dt from the left end to x = (x − 2)/6

chapter.title: Mean and variance of a continuous random variable; properties of expectation
text: For a density f, E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx and Var(X) = ∫ x² f(x) dx − [E(X)]². For any random variable, E(cX + d) = cE(X) + d and Var(cX + d) = c²Var(X): shifting moves the mean but not the spread, scaling by c scales the spread by c².
Integrate x f(x) (and x² f(x)) over the interval; for a linear change of X use the two properties.
math: A random variable X has mean E(X) = 4. Find E(−3X + 5).
Use E(cX + d) = cE(X) + d

screens.title: The method
text: Integrate the density from the lower limit to the upper limit (or find F(x) = P(X ≤ x) first), then subtract: F(c) − F(b).
math: A continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = x²/72 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 6, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Find P(X ≤ 3).
Integrate the density from 0: F(x) = x³/216

screens.title: Find the distribution function first
text: F(x) = ∫ f(t) dt from 0 to x. For f(x) = (n + 1)xⁿ/aⁿ⁺¹ this gives F(x) = (x/a)ⁿ⁺¹.
Check F(a) = 1, then P(b ≤ X ≤ c) = F(c) − F(b).
math: A continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 4x³/625 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Find P(3 ≤ X ≤ 4).
Integrate the density from 0: F(x) = x⁴/625

screens.title: See it as an area (when f is a straight line)
text: When f(x) = 2x/a², the graph from 0 to a is a triangle of base a and height 2/a: area 1.
P(X ≤ c) is the smaller triangle with base c and height 2c/a², whose area is c²/a².

Integrate the density from 0: F(x) = x³/27

modules.title: Probabilities of independent events

chapter.title: Probabilities of independent events
text: A and B are independent when knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
math: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.9 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A ∪ B).
Combine: P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 47/50
chapter.tip: 'At least one' was worked out as 'both'.

chapter.title: Independent or mutually exclusive?
text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Independent events have P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Two events that both can happen cannot be both.
Count n(A), n(B) and n(A ∩ B). If n(A ∩ B) = 0 they are mutually exclusive. Otherwise compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).
math: A number is chosen at random from 1, 2, 3, …, 18. Let A be the event "the number is a multiple of 5" and B the event "the number is at most 9". Which statement is true?
Compare N × n(A ∩ B) = 18 with n(A) × n(B) = 27: A and B are neither independent nor mutually exclusive

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply for 'both'. Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) for 'at least one', complements (1 − P) for 'not', and add the two separate ways for 'exactly one'.
math: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.9 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A ∩ B).
Combine: P(A ∩ B) = 9/25

screens.title: A 10 by 10 grid
text: Shade 10 × P(A) rows for A and 10 × P(B) columns for B in a 10 by 10 grid of equally likely squares.
Both is the overlap of rows and columns; count the squares you need and divide by 100.
math: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.6. Find the probability that exactly one of A and B happens.
Combine: P(A) + P(B) − 2P(A ∩ B) = 1/2

chapter.title: The law of total probability (two bags)
text: When the outcome can come about in separate ways (a partition: Bag I or Bag II), its probability is the sum over the ways of P(way) × P(outcome | way).

P(Bag II) × P(red | Bag II) = 1/3 × 2/3 = 2/9

modules.title: A statement and its converse

chapter.title: A statement and its converse
text: The converse of 'if P then Q' is 'if Q then P'. A statement can be true while its converse is false, so each needs its own check.
math: For whole numbers n, consider the statement: "If n is a multiple of 5, then n is a multiple of 11." Which is correct about this statement and its converse?
The converse swaps the parts: "If n is a multiple of 11, then n is a multiple of 5."
The statement is false; the converse is false
chapter.tip: One example where both parts are true was taken as proof; a general statement needs every case, and one counterexample shows it is false.

chapter.title: A counterexample to a 'prime for every n' claim
text: A claim about EVERY n is false as soon as one n fails; that n is a counterexample. Checking many n that work never proves the claim.
Work out the value for n = 1, 2, 3, … in order and test each for a factor (try primes up to its square root). The first value with a factor gives the answer.
math: Karthik claims: "n² − 5n + 197 is a prime number for every positive whole number n." Find the smallest positive whole number n for which n² − 5n + 197 is NOT prime; it shows the claim is false.
For n = 1 to 5 the values are all prime
At n = 6 the value is 203 = 7 × 29, not prime

screens.title: The method
text: Try to find a counterexample: a case where the 'if' part is true and the 'then' part is false. If none can exist, the statement is true; one counterexample makes it false.
math: For whole numbers n, consider the statement: "If n is a multiple of 19, then n² is a multiple of 19." Which is correct about this statement and its converse?
The converse swaps the parts: "If n² is a multiple of 19, then n is a multiple of 19."
The statement is true; the converse is true

screens.title: Think in factors
text: Every multiple of a is a multiple of b exactly when b divides a (6 → 3 works, 3 → 6 does not: 9).

chapter.title: Variance of a frequency distribution
text: Variance is the mean of the squared distances from the mean; squaring stops positive and negative deviations from cancelling.

chapter.title: The period of a trigonometric function
text: sin, cos, sec and cosec repeat every 2π; tan and cot every π. Replacing x by kx makes the graph repeat k times as fast; the number in front and the shift inside do not change the period.
Take the basic period (2π or π) and divide it by k.

sin x repeats every 2π

text: On the unit circle, the real number t is an arc length; the point it reaches is (cos t, sin t). This defines sin and cos for every real number, and the quadrant of the point gives their signs.

a/sin A = b/sin B, so b = 10 sin 120°/sin 45°

The sides were taken in the same ratio as the angles; sides are in the ratio of the SINES of the opposite angles.
math: Not 99/2, but 11√2

modules.title: Linear combinations of vectors in components

chapter.title: Linear combinations of vectors in components
text: Vectors in î, ĵ, k̂ form are added and scaled component by component, because î, ĵ and k̂ point in independent directions.
math: If a = −î − 4ĵ − 4k̂ and b = 3î − 4ĵ + 4k̂, find 3a − 3b. Write it as components (x, y, z).
Add (−9, 12, −12) component by component: (−12, 0, −24)
chapter.tip: The number in front of a vector was multiplied into its first component only; it multiplies every component.

chapter.title: Magnitude of the vector joining two points
text: The vector AB is OB − OA; its length is √(x² + y² + z²), Pythagoras used twice.
Subtract A's components from B's, square the three differences, add, and take the square root (simplify the surd).
math: Points A and B have position vectors −6î − k̂ and 3î + 3ĵ + 4k̂. Find the magnitude |AB| of the vector AB. Give the exact value.
x² + y² + z² = 115

chapter.title: The section formula with position vectors
text: R divides PQ in m : n internally when PR : RQ = m : n with R between P and Q; then r = (mq + np)/(m + n). Externally, R is outside the segment and r = (mq − np)/(m − n).
Choose the formula, multiply q by m and p by n, add (or subtract), and divide each component by m + n (or m − n).
math: Points P and Q have position vectors 5î + 5ĵ − 4k̂ and −3î − 5ĵ + k̂. Find the position vector of the point R that divides PQ internally in the ratio 4 : 1. Write its components as (x, y, z).
Component by component: r = (−7/5, −3, 0)

chapter.title: Scalars, vectors and kinds of vectors
text: A scalar has only a size (mass, time, speed, work); a vector has a size and a direction (displacement, velocity, force). Equal vectors have the same length and direction; −a has the same length and the opposite direction; collinear vectors lie along parallel lines (b = λa); a unit vector has length 1; the zero vector has length 0; co-initial vectors start at the same point.
Ask whether a direction is needed. For two vectors in components compare them: b = a (equal), b = −a (negative), b = λa (collinear), otherwise not collinear. For one vector find its length.
math: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
So the answer is A: mass

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply every component of a by p and every component of b by q, then add the matching components.
math: If a = −2î + ĵ and b = −5î + ĵ − 5k̂, find −3a − b. Write it as components (x, y, z).
Add (5, −1, 5) component by component: (11, −4, 5)

screens.title: Write them as columns
text: Write each vector as a column of three numbers.
Scale each column, then add across each row.
math: If a = −î + 4ĵ − 3k̂ and b = −4î − 2ĵ + 4k̂, find −3a − 3b. Write it as components (x, y, z).
Add (12, 6, −12) component by component: (15, −6, −3)

modules.title: Direction cosines of a vector joining two points

chapter.title: Direction cosines of a vector joining two points
text: The direction cosines (l, m, n) of a vector are the cosines of the angles it makes with the x-, y- and z-axes; they are the components of the unit vector, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
math: A and B are the points (3, −3, 2) and (−1, −1, 6). Find the direction cosines of the vector AB. Write them as (l, m, n); square roots may stay in the answer.
Direction ratios: B − A = (−4, 2, 4)
Divide each by 6: (−2/3, 1/3, 2/3)
chapter.tip: The direction ratios (the components of AB) were given; direction cosines are the components divided by the length |AB|.

Direction ratios: B − A = (4, −3, 5)

screens.title: Think of the angles
text: The angle α with the x-axis has cos α = (x-component)/(length), as in a right triangle.
Do the same for the y- and z-axes.
math: A and B are the points (−2, −2, 3) and (−7, −8, −3). Find the direction cosines of the vector AB. Write them as (l, m, n); square roots may stay in the answer.
Direction ratios: B − A = (−5, −6, −6)

modules.title: The angle between two vectors (cos θ)

chapter.title: The angle between two vectors (cos θ)
text: a · b = |a| |b| cos θ, and a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃; together they give the angle. a · b = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
math: Find cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors a = 4î + 2ĵ and b = −2î + 4ĵ − 3k̂. Give the exact value.
a · b = 0

chapter.title: Projection of one vector on another
text: The projection of a on b is the length of a's shadow on the line of b: |a| cos θ = a · b/|b|. It is negative when the angle is obtuse.
Find a · b and |b|, divide, and rationalise.
math: Find the projection of the vector a = 4î + ĵ + k̂ on the vector b = 4î − 3ĵ − 3k̂. Give the exact value.

chapter.title: The cross product in components
text: a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b (right-hand rule), with length |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram on a and b.
Expand the determinant with rows (î ĵ k̂), (a₁ a₂ a₃), (b₁ b₂ b₃): î(a₂b₃ − a₃b₂) − ĵ(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁) + k̂(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
math: Find a × b for a = −4î + 2ĵ + 3k̂ and b = î + ĵ − 4k̂. Write it as components (x, y, z).
î: a₂b₃ − a₃b₂ = −11
ĵ: −(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁) = −13
k̂: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = −6

chapter.title: Area of a triangle by the cross product
text: |AB × AC| = |AB||AC| sin A is the area of the parallelogram on AB and AC; the triangle is half of it.
Find AB and AC, their cross product, its length, and halve it.
math: Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(−1, 4, 0), B(2, −1, 3) and C(3, 3, −4). Give the exact value.

chapter.title: Area of a parallelogram by the cross product
text: |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ is the base times the height of the parallelogram on a and b. If d₁ and d₂ are the diagonals, the sides are (d₁ ± d₂)/2, and the area is ½|d₁ × d₂|.
Find the cross product with the determinant, then its length; halve it when the vectors given are the diagonals.
math: Find the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are given by the vectors a = −î + ĵ + 2k̂ and b = −î − 3ĵ − 4k̂. Give the exact value.
The cross product is (2, −6, 4)

chapter.title: The torque of a force about a point
text: The torque (moment) of a force F acting at P about a point A is τ = r × F with r = AP = P − A: a vector perpendicular to r and F whose length |r||F| sin θ measures the turning effect.
Find the arm r = P − A, then the cross product r × F with the determinant.
math: A force F = −2î + ĵ + 3k̂ (in newtons) acts at the point P(0, 1, 2). Find the torque (moment) of F about the point A(0, 1, −2), as components (x, y, z). Coordinates are in metres.
The arm is r = P − A = (0, 0, 4)

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply matching components and add (a · b), find |a| and |b|, then cos θ = a · b/(|a| |b|); rationalise.
math: Find cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors a = −4î − 3ĵ − 4k̂ and b = î − 2ĵ + k̂. Give the exact value.

screens.title: Use the cosine rule
text: a, b and a − b form a triangle with sides |a|, |b| and |a − b|.
cos θ = (|a|² + |b|² − |a − b|²)/(2|a||b|), the same as the dot-product formula.
math: Find cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors a = 4î − 4ĵ − 4k̂ and b = 2î − ĵ + 4k̂. Give the exact value.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors a = −3î + 3ĵ + 3k̂ and b = 2k̂. Give the exact value.” A common wrong answer is 6.
Only a · b was found; cos θ = a · b / (|a| |b|), so divide by both lengths.
math: Not 6, but √3/3

text: Each step builds on another skill: Operate on vectors. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Multiply matching components and add (a · b), find |a| and |b|, then cos θ = a · b/(|a| |b|); rationalise.

chapter.title: The scalar triple product
text: [a b c] = a · (b × c) is the determinant with rows a, b, c; its size is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c, and it is 0 exactly when they are coplanar.

The 2 × 2 minors of b and c: (−4, −3, 2)
Expand along a = (1, 2, −3) with signs +, −, +: −4
chapter.tip: Two of the vectors were swapped ([b a c]); swapping two rows changes the sign of the triple product.

chapter.title: Coplanar vectors: find λ
text: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when the parallelepiped they make is flat: [a b c] = 0.
Write the determinant with rows a, b, c (λ in it), expand to get an expression in λ, set it equal to 0 and solve.

Set it to 0: λ = 3

text: a × (b × c) is perpendicular to b × c, so it lies in the plane of b and c: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.
Work out the two dot products a · c and a · b, then form (a · c)b − (a · b)c component by component.

Work out the determinant with rows a, b, c, take its absolute value, and divide by 6 for a tetrahedron.

The 2 × 2 minors of b and c: (−1, 1, 0)

The 2 × 2 minors of b and c: (−6, −4, −1)
Expand along a = (0, −1, −2) with signs +, −, +: −2

modules.title: The centres of a triangle and the lines that meet there

chapter.title: The centres of a triangle and the lines that meet there
text: A triangle has four kinds of special lines, three of each kind, and the three of a kind always meet at one point: medians at the centroid, altitudes at the orthocentre, perpendicular bisectors of the sides at the circumcentre, and angle bisectors at the incentre.
math: In △ABC, D is the midpoint of BC and AD = 24 cm. One of the four centres of the triangle is the point P on AD with AP = 16 cm and PD = 8 cm. Which centre is P?
This describes the centroid.
chapter.tip: A point well inside the triangle was taken to be the incentre. The incentre lies on the angle bisectors; a point on the line from a corner to a midpoint, two thirds of the way along, is the centroid.

chapter.title: The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1
text: The three medians of a triangle meet at the centroid G, and G cuts each median into two parts in the ratio 2 : 1, the longer part next to the corner. So AG is 2/3 of AD and GD is 1/3 of AD.
Split the median into 3 equal parts. AG is 2 parts, GD is 1 part, AD is all 3. Find one part from the length you know, then multiply.
math: In △ABC, AD is a median (D is the midpoint of BC) and G is the centroid. If AD = 15 cm, find AG, in cm.
One part: AD = 15 cm makes 3 parts, so one part is 5 cm
2 parts of 5 cm: 10 cm

chapter.title: The angle between two angle bisectors at the incentre
text: IB and IC cut ∠B and ∠C in half, so in △BIC the angles at B and C add up to half of (∠B + ∠C) = half of (180° − ∠A). What is left of 180° is ∠BIC = 90° + ∠A/2.
Find ∠B + ∠C (180° − ∠A if only ∠A is given), halve it, and take the result from 180°. Going backwards: ∠A = 2 × (∠BIC − 90°).
math: In △ABC, ∠A = 84°. The bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at the incentre I. Find ∠BIC, in degrees.
IB and IC halve ∠B and ∠C, so the two base angles of △BIC add up to 96° ÷ 2 = 48°

screens.title: The method
text: Ask what each line does. Corner to midpoint of the opposite side: median (centroid, the balance point). Corner, at right angles to the opposite side: altitude (orthocentre). Through a midpoint at right angles: perpendicular bisector (circumcentre, equally far from the corners). Halving an angle: angle bisector (incentre, equally far from the sides).
math: In △LMN, D is the midpoint of MN and LD = 27 cm. One of the four centres of the triangle is the point P on LD with LP = 18 cm and PD = 9 cm. Which centre is P?
This describes the centroid.

screens.title: Fold a paper triangle
text: Fold one corner onto another: the crease is the perpendicular bisector of that side, and every point on it is equally far from the two corners. The three such creases meet at the circumcentre.
Fold one side onto the next so the crease runs through their corner: that crease halves the angle. The three such creases meet at the incentre, equally far from the sides.
math: P is the orthocentre of △UVW. Which three lines of the triangle all pass through P?
This describes the three altitudes.

screens.title: Two circles, two centres
text: The circle through the three corners is the circumcircle; its centre is the circumcentre (circum = around).
The circle inside touching the three sides is the incircle; its centre is the incentre (in = inside).
math: P is the orthocentre of △XYZ. Which three lines of the triangle all pass through P?
This describes the three altitudes.

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “In △KLN, D is the midpoint of LN and KD = 9 cm. One of the four centres of the triangle is the point P on KD with KP = 6 cm and PD = 3 cm. Which centre is P?” A common wrong answer is 0.
A point well inside the triangle was taken to be the incentre. The incentre lies on the angle bisectors; a point on the line from a corner to a midpoint, two thirds of the way along, is the centroid.
math: Not 0, but D
